topics.title: What pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is
topics.orientation: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, usually shortened to PDAC, is the disease most people mean when they say 'pancreatic cancer'. This entry explains which cells it comes from, what changes turn them into a cancer, and why its behavior follows from its biology and its position in the body.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: The pancreas is a gland lying behind the stomach with two jobs. Its exocrine tissue, more than nine-tenths of the organ, makes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate and delivers them through a branching duct system into the duodenum. Its endocrine islets release insulin and glucagon into the blood. PDAC arises from the exocrine compartment, in cells that look like the lining of those ducts, not from the islets.
section1.full: The exocrine pancreas produces roughly 2.5 liters of juice a day [[SEC-ANAT-03]]. Acinar cells, arranged in grape-like clusters, release enzymes such as lipase, amylase and trypsinogen when the hormone cholecystokinin signals that food has arrived; the cells lining the ducts add bicarbonate through CFTR channels (the same chloride channel that is faulty in cystic fibrosis) under the control of secretin, which neutralizes stomach acid so the enzymes can work [[ANAT-009]]. The head of the gland is cradled by the duodenum, crossed by the lower bile duct, and lies against the superior mesenteric vein, the portal vein and the superior mesenteric artery, with lymph node stations and the autonomic nerve plexus converging on the same plane; in about 16% of people the right hepatic artery takes a variant course through this space [[ANAT-007]]. This geography shapes the cancer. A tumor in the head blocks the bile duct early and causes jaundice, which is why head tumors tend to be found sooner; tumors in the body and tail grow silently and were already metastatic at diagnosis in 69% and 84% of cases in a Dutch national registry, against 42% for head tumors [[ANAT-003]]. Islets are about twice as dense in the tail as in the head, which is one reason the glucose effects of the disease are not simply a matter of lost tissue [[ANAT-005]].

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: PDAC is a cancer of duct-like cells that almost always carries a mutation in the gene KRAS, which locks a growth switch in the on position. It usually starts from microscopic precursor lesions called PanINs, grows inside a dense scar-like stroma, invades nerves and vessels early, and spreads most often to the liver and the lining of the abdomen. These traits, more than its location, explain why it is hard to detect and to treat.
section2.full: The cancer is called 'ductal' because its cells resemble duct lining under the microscope, although in mice most precursor lesions begin in acinar cells that have reprogrammed into a duct-like state [[ORIG-012]]. A KRAS mutation is the first and most consistent change, present in more than 90% of even the lowest-grade precursor lesions [[ORIG-002]] and in 87-92% of invasive tumors [[GENE-002]][[GENE-024]]. Progression to invasion is marked less by new point mutations than by physical loss of the chromosome regions carrying the tumor-suppressor genes CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4 [[ORIG-023]], and in most invasive tumors the genome has been reshaped by catastrophic errors of cell division, with chromosome shattering in 65% and whole-genome doubling in 45% of 107 sequenced cancers [[GENE-003]]. The result is a tumor of only a few centimeters whose cells have already grown along nerves in about 80% of resected cases [[ANAT-013]] and, by genetic reconstruction of autopsy cases, have usually seeded distant sites before diagnosis [[SURG-002]]. That early dissemination, rather than the size of the lump in the pancreas, is what drives the treatment decisions described throughout this atlas.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The genomic studies behind this entry describe what a typical PDAC carries: about 63 alterations per tumor clustering into roughly 12 core pathways, each disrupted in 67-100% of cancers, though the exact gene hit differs from tumor to tumor [[GENE-001]]. Two findings alter the familiar picture of a slow, stepwise disease. Precursor lesions are extremely common in ordinary adult pancreases, on the order of hundreds per organ, and nearly all carry KRAS mutations, so the overwhelming majority never progress [[ORIG-001]]. And the final steps to invasion often happen in bursts rather than one mutation at a time [[GENE-003]]. Together they mean a KRAS mutation is necessary but far from sufficient, and that what limits progression remains an open question.
research_notes.how_studied: Whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing of microdissected tumors identifies which genes are mutated, deleted or amplified; copy-number methods are essential because CDKN2A and SMAD4 are usually lost by deletion rather than by a spelling change, which mutation-only panels under-report [[GENE-002]][[GENE-024]]. Three-dimensional mapping of resected pancreases counts precursor lesions per cubic centimeter [[ORIG-001]]. Lineage tracing in genetically engineered mice tags acinar or duct cells with a fluorescent marker and follows which population gives rise to lesions [[ORIG-012]]. National cancer registries link tumor location to stage at diagnosis [[ANAT-003]]. Each method answers a different question, which is why cell-of-origin claims come from mice while frequency claims come from human tissue.

mechanism_notes.text: Why only a tiny minority of the hundreds of KRAS-mutant precursor lesions in a normal pancreas ever progress is unexplained by the mutation itself. One hypothesis is that focal inflammation releases the senescence brake, the built-in halt on cell division, on a KRAS-mutant lesion, and continued division in a lesion that has lost checkpoint restraint is what allows the chromosomal losses at CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4 to accumulate and be selected [[INF-ORIG-01]][[ORIG-001]][[ORIG-023]]. The competing view is that progression is cell-intrinsic and random, with the inflammatory hotspot a consequence rather than a cause.

glossary.definition: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the common form of pancreatic cancer, arising from duct-like cells of the exocrine pancreas.
The part of the pancreas that makes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate and sends them into the intestine through ducts.
A gene whose protein relays growth signals; a mutation that locks it on is the first step in nearly every pancreatic cancer.
Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia, a microscopic precursor lesion in a small duct that can, rarely, progress to cancer.
The dense, scar-like supporting tissue of fibroblasts, matrix and immune cells that surrounds pancreatic cancer cells.

related.statement: PDAC arises in the exocrine tissue that makes up most of the pancreas.
A KRAS mutation is the initiating genetic change in nearly every PDAC.
Microscopic PanIN lesions are the precursors from which most PDAC develops.
Most PDACs arise in the head of the pancreas, where they block the bile duct early and are found sooner than body or tail tumors.
A PDAC tumor contains a dense scar-like stroma that often outweighs the cancer cells themselves.
PDAC is the most common and most aggressive of several distinct pancreatic tumor types.

faq.q: Is PDAC the same thing as pancreatic cancer?
faq.a: PDAC is the most common type and accounts for the large majority of cases, so most statistics labeled 'pancreatic cancer' describe it. Neuroendocrine, acinar and cyst-derived tumors of the pancreas are different diseases with different courses [[ANAT-008]][[ORIG-017]].

faq.q: Why is it usually found late?
faq.a: The pancreas sits deep behind the stomach, early tumors cause few specific symptoms, and tumors in the body and tail do not block the bile duct, so they rarely cause jaundice; in a national registry 69-84% of body and tail tumors were already metastatic at diagnosis against 42% of head tumors [[ANAT-003]].

topics.title: How PDAC differs from other pancreatic tumors
topics.orientation: 'Pancreatic cancer' is a label that covers several diseases starting in the same organ but behaving very differently. Knowing which one the pathology report names is the first step to understanding every number that follows.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: The pancreas contains several different cell types, and each can give rise to its own kind of tumor. Duct-lining cells are the source of ductal adenocarcinoma. Acinar cells, which make digestive enzymes, give rise to the rare acinar cell carcinoma. Islet cells, which make hormones, give rise to neuroendocrine tumors. Mucus-producing cysts can harbor precursor lesions. And the bile duct, ampulla and duodenum beside the pancreatic head produce cancers that are often grouped with it.
section1.full: Islet cells secrete insulin, glucagon and other hormones directly into the blood, and the tumors that arise from them keep that identity: pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PNETs) are rare, at about 2 cases per million people per year in older US registry data, and about nine in ten make no excess hormone and so cause no hormone symptoms [[ANAT-008]]. Acinar cells are the enzyme factories of the gland; acinar cell carcinoma is rarer still, tends to appear at a younger age, and in a population registry was resected far more often than ductal cancer and carried a median survival of 47 months, a different course from ductal adenocarcinoma in the same database [[ANAT-044]]. Cysts are a separate route: intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs) and mucinous cystic neoplasms are mucus-producing growths that can, over years, develop an invasive cancer within them, but most do not, and 53 small branch-duct IPMNs followed for a mean of 42 months produced no invasive cancer of their own [[ORIG-018]]. Finally, a 'periampullary' cancer is any tumor at the junction of the bile duct, pancreatic duct and duodenum; it may be pancreatic, biliary, ampullary or duodenal in origin, and the pathologist's call matters because these differ in behavior and treatment.

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Ductal adenocarcinoma accounts for the large majority of pancreatic cancers and is the most aggressive of the group, so most statistics labeled 'pancreatic cancer' describe it. The other tumors have their own staging, their own treatments and, usually, a far longer expected course. Reading a neuroendocrine or acinar survival figure as if it applied to PDAC, or the reverse, is one of the commonest sources of confusion.
section2.full: Neuroendocrine tumors illustrate the gap. In a US population registry the median survival after a neuroendocrine diagnosis was 28 months across all stages and 100 months for localized disease, even though 60% of patients had metastases when found; tumor grade and whether the tumor made hormones mattered more than size [[ANAT-008]]. Those tumors have their own drug treatments, none of which are used for ductal cancer. Within ductal cancer there are also variants. Adenosquamous carcinoma, in which part of the tumor takes on a squamous appearance, is more often poorly differentiated (its cells look less like normal tissue), larger and located in the body or tail, and in a 415-patient registry analysis its outcome after resection was worse than ordinary PDAC [[ANAT-023]]; body and tail tumors in general are enriched for the squamous molecular type, a gene-activity pattern linked to more aggressive behavior, which partly explains their poorer record [[ANAT-024]]. Invasive cancer that arises inside an IPMN is a true adenocarcinoma, yet stage for stage it carried a lower hazard of death than conventional PDAC (hazard ratio 0.58, a measure of the relative rate of death over follow-up), with a median survival after resection of 58 versus 18 months in one surgical series, and the precursor's epithelial subtype set the size of that advantage [[ORIG-017]]. When a report reads 'adenocarcinoma, pancreatobiliary type', it is describing conventional PDAC biology.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The registry studies here are descriptive: they show that tumor type is a stronger determinant of course than organ of origin. The neuroendocrine series relied on coded diagnoses without central pathology, so some tumors may have been misclassified [[ANAT-008]]. The acinar comparison is available to this atlas only as an abstract [[ANAT-044]]. The IPMN survival advantage survived adjustment for stage, which argues it reflects biology rather than earlier detection, though the series was single-institution and small in the rarer subtypes [[ORIG-017]]. The adenosquamous registry analysis lacked central pathology and reported only two-year survival [[ANAT-023]]. None of these are randomized comparisons; they describe what happened to groups of patients, not what any treatment caused.
research_notes.how_studied: Population cancer registries such as the US SEER program and national databases record histology codes, stage and survival for every reported case, which makes them the only practical way to study rare tumors such as neuroendocrine and acinar carcinoma [[ANAT-008]][[ANAT-044]]. Single-institution pathology series re-review resected specimens under the microscope to assign precursor subtype and invasive component, which registries cannot do [[ORIG-017]]. Molecular profiling by RNA sequencing assigns tumors to classical or squamous programs and links those programs to location and outcome [[ANAT-024]]. Registry breadth and pathology depth trade off against each other, so the strongest conclusions are those both approaches share.

glossary.definition: A tumor arising from hormone-producing islet-type cells of the pancreas, usually slower-growing than ductal adenocarcinoma.
A rare pancreatic cancer arising from the enzyme-making acinar cells, with a different course from ductal cancer.
Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm, a mucus-producing cystic growth in a pancreatic duct that can occasionally develop an invasive cancer.
Arising at the junction where the bile duct and pancreatic duct enter the duodenum; such cancers may be pancreatic, biliary, ampullary or duodenal.
A variant of ductal adenocarcinoma in which part of the tumor takes on a squamous, skin-like appearance under the microscope.

related.statement: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from islet-type hormone-producing cells, not from the duct cells that give rise to PDAC.
Acinar cell carcinoma arises from the enzyme-making acinar cells and follows a different course from PDAC.
An IPMN or mucinous cystic neoplasm can, over years, give rise to an invasive adenocarcinoma, though most never do.
Cancers of the ampulla and lower bile duct sit beside the pancreatic head and are grouped with PDAC as periampullary cancers.
Adenosquamous and body-tail tumors are enriched for the squamous molecular state that marks the more aggressive end of PDAC.
PDAC is the ductal adenocarcinoma that the other pancreatic tumor types are compared against.

faq.q: My report says neuroendocrine. Do the pancreatic cancer statistics apply to me?
faq.a: No. Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors are a different disease with their own staging and treatments, and in a US registry median survival was 28 months across all stages and 100 months for localized disease, far longer than the figures quoted for ductal cancer [[ANAT-008]].

faq.q: What does 'periampullary' mean on my scan report?
faq.a: It means the tumor sits where the bile duct and pancreatic duct meet the duodenum, and it could have started in any of those tissues. The pathologist's determination of origin matters because ampullary, bile-duct and duodenal cancers behave differently from PDAC.

faq.q: Does a pancreatic cyst mean I will get cancer?
faq.a: Most do not. Branch-duct IPMNs with small nodules followed for a mean of 42 months produced no IPMN-derived cancer, although about 2% of patients developed a separate cancer elsewhere in the gland, which is why cysts are kept under surveillance [[ORIG-018]].

topics.title: Stage, grade, resectability and fitness are different questions
topics.orientation: A pancreatic cancer is described by several independent measures. Stage says how far it has spread, grade says how abnormal the cells look, resectability says whether a surgeon can remove it with a clean margin, and fitness says whether a particular person can withstand the treatment. Each answers a different question, and they do not always line up.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: Stage is recorded with the TNM system: T for the size of the tumor, N for the number of lymph nodes containing cancer, M for distant metastasis, combined into stages I to IV. Grade describes how closely the cancer cells still resemble normal duct cells. Resectability is a surgical judgment from the scans about vessels and spread. Fitness, usually summarized as performance status, describes the patient rather than the tumor.
section1.full: In the current eighth edition of the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) system, T stage for pancreatic cancer is defined by size (up to 2 cm, 2 to 4 cm, over 4 cm), with involvement of the celiac, hepatic or superior mesenteric artery counted as T4 regardless of size, and N stage by the count of positive nodes (none, 1 to 3, 4 or more). When 1,525 resected patients from five centers were restaged, those nodal groups separated survival clearly, with five-year survival of 35.6%, 20.8% and 10.9% for N0, N1 and N2, whereas among node-negative patients tumor size made no difference [[DIAG-017]]. A separate validation arrived at closely similar cut points by statistical partitioning [[DIAG-003]]. Stage is therefore mostly a statement about nodes. Grade is assigned by the pathologist from the architecture and appearance of the cells; poorly differentiated tumors recur earlier [[SURG-007]]. Resectability is decided before any tissue is seen, from the relationship between tumor and the mesenteric vessels on a pancreas-protocol CT (computed tomography) scan, and the degree of contact predicts whether a vein must be removed but not whether the final margin will be clear [[DIAG-001]]. Performance status and comorbidity are scored separately, and an age-comorbidity burden was itself a predictor of early recurrence in a 957-patient series [[SURG-007]].

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: In pancreatic cancer these measures disagree often enough that each must be asked separately. A small tumor that encases the main vein beyond repair may be unresectable, while a larger tumor away from vessels may be removable. A fully resectable tumor in someone too frail for a Whipple operation will not be resected. And the stage assigned after surgery can differ from the stage estimated from scans.
section2.full: The clinical stage from imaging and the pathological stage from the removed specimen are different measurements, and the second is more complete: how thoroughly the pathologist samples the specimen changes the node count, the residual-tumor call and even whether a complete response is declared, particularly after chemotherapy [[SURG-005]]. Staging also explains only a minority of the variation in survival; the concordance statistic for the eighth edition is about 0.57 to 0.58, where 0.5 would be a coin toss [[DIAG-017]][[DIAG-003]]. That is because pancreatic cancer disseminates early and largely independently of the size of the primary, so a measure built on size and nodes captures only part of the biology [[SURG-009]]. Fitness enters because the treatments are demanding: the trial of adjuvant (post-surgery) FOLFIRINOX, a four-drug chemotherapy combination, that lengthened median survival to 53.5 months enrolled only patients under 80 who had recovered well from surgery, and most still needed dose reductions [[TX-003]]. One person's tumor might be stage IIB, grade 3 and borderline resectable, with a performance status of 1, and each of those four facts points the care team toward a different part of the plan.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The staging validations show that the eighth edition improved consistency between hospitals, eliminating a 13-month inter-institutional difference in median survival that the seventh edition's T3 category had produced [[DIAG-003]], but discrimination remains modest [[DIAG-017]]. Both studies were restricted to resected, mostly margin-negative patients at high-volume centers, so they describe the staging of operable disease rather than the whole population. The degree-of-contact study was restricted to head tumors and did not analyze arterial contact, which is the deciding factor in many borderline and locally advanced cases [[DIAG-001]]. None of these systems was built in the neoadjuvant era, and stage assigned after chemotherapy (ypTNM) is less well validated.
research_notes.how_studied: Staging systems are validated by applying the proposed categories to large cohorts with known outcomes and measuring how well they separate survival curves, summarized as a concordance statistic [[DIAG-017]]. Recursive partitioning searches for the size and node cut points that best split survival, which is how the 2 cm, 4 cm and four-node thresholds were chosen [[DIAG-003]]. Resectability criteria are tested by comparing the preoperative CT reading, re-reviewed blind, against what the surgeon found and what the pathologist saw in the vein wall [[DIAG-001]]. Pathology sampling effects are studied by comparing outcomes between specimens handled with standard and exhaustive protocols [[SURG-005]].

glossary.definition: The staging shorthand for tumor size (T), lymph node involvement (N) and distant metastasis (M).
A pathologist's score of how abnormal cancer cells look, from well differentiated (resembling normal cells) to poorly differentiated.
A simple scale of how well a person can carry out daily activities, used to judge fitness for treatment.
Judged from scans to be removable by surgery with a clear margin, based on vessel contact and absence of spread.
Stage assigned from the surgical specimen after preoperative treatment, which may differ from the stage estimated before it.

related.statement: Resectability categories are a separate axis from TNM stage and are decided from vessel contact on CT.
The number of cancer-containing lymph nodes is the component of stage that most strongly separates survival after resection.
The pathological stage, grade and margin status are read from the resected specimen described in the pathology report.
The degree of tumor-vessel contact on CT determines resectability, independently of the tumor's stage.
A resectable tumor of the pancreatic head is removed by a Whipple operation if the patient is fit enough to undergo it.

faq.q: My scan says stage II but the surgeon says it is not resectable. How can both be true?
faq.a: Stage counts size, nodes, arterial involvement and distant spread; resectability depends on whether the tumor can be separated from the mesenteric vessels with a clear margin. A stage II tumor that blocks the main vein beyond reconstruction is unresectable, while a larger tumor away from vessels may not be, because the degree of vessel contact predicts the need for vessel removal independently of stage [[DIAG-001]].

faq.q: Does a higher stage mean surgery is impossible?
faq.a: Not by itself. Stage III in the current system means either four or more positive nodes, which can only be counted from the resected specimen, or tumor involving a major artery; node-positive tumors are routinely removed, whereas arterial involvement is what makes a tumor locally advanced. Metastatic (stage IV) disease is the category in which surgery on the primary does not change the course [[DIAG-017]].

topics.title: Resectable, borderline resectable, locally advanced, metastatic
topics.orientation: Surgeons sort pancreatic cancers into four groups from the scans, based on whether the tumor touches the nearby blood vessels and whether it has spread. The words describe anatomy, not how malignant the cancer is.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: The pancreas is wrapped around the vessels that feed the intestine and liver: the superior mesenteric vein and portal vein run behind its neck, and the superior mesenteric artery, celiac axis and hepatic artery lie just beside the head and body. A tumor that grows into these vessels cannot be lifted away cleanly. Resectability categories are a shorthand for how much of a vessel's circumference the tumor touches on a CT (computed tomography) scan.
section1.full: On a pancreas-protocol CT scan the radiologist reports contact between tumor and each vessel as none, up to 180 degrees of the circumference, more than 180 degrees, or complete occlusion. 'Resectable' means no arterial contact and no more than limited contact with the vein. 'Borderline resectable' means contact that makes a clean margin uncertain: more than half the vein's circumference, or contact with an artery that a surgeon might still clear, sometimes by removing and reconstructing the vein. 'Locally advanced' means the tumor encases an artery or blocks the vein beyond reconstruction, so removal with a clear margin is not expected. 'Metastatic' means spread to the liver, peritoneum, lung or distant nodes, where surgery on the primary does not change the course. The degree of venous contact tracks the chance the vein wall is truly invaded: in 254 head resections, histologic invasion rose from 3% with no interface to 71-80% with more than 180 degrees of contact or occlusion [[DIAG-001]]. These definitions are set out in the US guideline framework for pancreatic adenocarcinoma [[SEC-SURG-11]]. The word 'borderline' refers to the border between removable and not removable, never to a border between benign and malignant. A borderline resectable PDAC is a fully malignant cancer; the term says only that the anatomy is uncertain.

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: The category chosen at diagnosis sets the first treatment step. Resectable tumors may go to surgery first or after a short course of chemotherapy; borderline tumors almost always receive chemotherapy first; locally advanced tumors receive chemotherapy with surgery considered only if the disease responds; metastatic disease is treated with drugs. The categories are revisited after treatment, and the scan-based label can lag behind what is actually removable.
section2.full: The categories matter because they predict margins and outcomes before treatment. In the resectable group, up-front surgery was 'futile', meaning the patient died or recurred within six months, in about 19% of 1,426 operations at high-volume centers, and CA 19-9 (carbohydrate antigen 19-9, a blood marker) adjusted for tumor size identified who was at highest risk [[SURG-008]]. In borderline disease, preoperative therapy raised the margin-negative resection rate from 40% to 72% in a randomized trial [[TX-004]]. In locally advanced disease, 20% of 415 patients reached resection after a median of five months of chemotherapy, and anatomic scoring of vessel involvement at presentation predicted who would [[SURG-019]][[SURG-020]]. After chemotherapy the labels become unreliable, because treated tumor and scar tissue look identical on CT: 28 of 40 tumors resected after FOLFIRINOX (a four-drug chemotherapy regimen) were still classified locally advanced or borderline on their post-treatment scans, yet 92% were removed with clear margins [[DIAG-004]]. For this reason surgical teams now explore patients whose disease has not progressed rather than rely on the restaging category alone [[SEC-DIAG-06]]. Whether a vein that is touched can be removed with a clear margin depends on planning the vein resection, not on the contact angle by itself [[DIAG-001]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The anatomic categories are a working consensus rather than a biological boundary. The tumor-vein interface study showed that contact predicts the need for vein resection with 89.5% positive predictive value above 180 degrees (meaning that when contact exceeded 180 degrees, the vein needed resection in 89.5% of cases), yet the margin-negative rate was the same across all contact grades once a vein resection was planned [[DIAG-001]]. That supports treating borderline disease as a surgical-planning category. The post-FOLFIRINOX series were small and single-center, and none quantified fibrosis against viable tumor at the interface, so the decoupling of scan appearance from resectability rests on surgical findings rather than on imaging science [[DIAG-004]][[DIAG-023]]. Conversion-to-surgery survival figures describe selected patients with favorable biology and should not be read as what chemotherapy achieves on average [[SURG-019]].
research_notes.how_studied: Resectability criteria are tested retrospectively by having a blinded reader re-grade preoperative CT scans and comparing the grades against operative findings, vein-wall histology and margin status [[DIAG-001]]. Post-treatment accuracy is tested by re-reviewing scans before and after chemotherapy with the same published criteria and recording how many 'unresectable' tumors were in fact removed [[DIAG-004]]. Cohort studies of locally advanced disease follow every patient in a multidisciplinary clinic and record who reached surgery, matching non-resected patients for treatment duration to limit immortal-time bias (the distortion that arises because patients who reach surgery had, by definition, already survived long enough to get there) [[SURG-019]]. Futility models are derived in one group of patients and validated in another [[SURG-008]].

mechanism_notes.text: After neoadjuvant therapy, persistent tumor-vessel contact on CT overwhelmingly turns out to be fibrosis rather than viable cancer. Viable tumor retains glucose uptake and restricted water diffusion whereas treated scar takes up little glucose and is less cellular, so a functional signal from PET or diffusion MRI at the residual contact may separate scar from tumor where anatomy cannot [[INF-DIAG-01]][[DIAG-008]][[DIAG-009]]. The caveat is that post-treatment inflammation also lights up on these scans, so functional imaging can over-call viable tumor just as anatomy over-calls contact.

glossary.definition: A tumor whose contact with nearby vessels makes a clean surgical margin uncertain; the word refers to removability, not to whether the cancer is malignant.
A tumor that encases an artery or blocks the main vein so that removal with a clear margin is not expected, without distant spread.
Tumor surrounding more than half the circumference of a blood vessel on a scan.
Tumor touching a blood vessel over half or less of its circumference on a scan.
Surgical removal in which no cancer cells are found at the cut edges of the specimen; it does not by itself mean cure.
An operation performed on a tumor originally judged unresectable after chemotherapy has brought it within reach.

related.statement: Contact with the superior mesenteric and portal veins is the main criterion separating resectable from borderline resectable disease.
Encasement of the superior mesenteric artery is what makes a tumor locally advanced rather than borderline.
Resectability categories are assigned from the degree of tumor-vessel contact reported on pancreas-protocol CT.
Borderline resectable and locally advanced categories are the settings in which chemotherapy before surgery is standard.
Restaging after chemotherapy often leaves a tumor in the same category even when it has become removable.
Borderline resectable tumors touching the vein are often removed with a planned vein resection and reconstruction.

faq.q: Does borderline resectable mean the cancer might be benign or borderline malignant?
faq.a: No. The term is purely anatomical: it describes a fully malignant cancer whose contact with nearby vessels makes a clean margin uncertain. 'Borderline' refers to the border between removable and not removable [[SEC-SURG-11]][[DIAG-001]].

faq.q: Can a locally advanced tumor become resectable?
faq.a: Sometimes. In a 415-patient series, 20% of locally advanced tumors were resected after a median of five months of chemotherapy, and those patients lived about twice as long as matched patients who were not resected, though they were also selected by favorable biology [[SURG-019]].

faq.q: The scan after chemotherapy still shows the tumor on the vessel. Does that mean surgery is off?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Scar tissue and treated tumor look the same on CT, and in one series 28 of 40 tumors resected after FOLFIRINOX, most with clear margins, still looked locally advanced or borderline on their post-treatment scans, which is why surgeons explore patients whose disease has not progressed [[DIAG-004]][[SEC-DIAG-06]].

topics.title: Why a treatment plan can change
topics.orientation: A plan made at diagnosis is a plan made with incomplete information. New findings from scans, blood tests, pathology and the way the body handles treatment are expected to revise it, and the tumor board exists to make those revisions deliberately.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: Pancreatic cancer care is planned by a multidisciplinary team: surgeons, medical oncologists, radiation oncologists, radiologists, pathologists and gastroenterologists meeting as a tumor board. Each contributes a different measurement, and the measurements arrive at different times. The plan is a best estimate from what is known that day, reviewed whenever a new measurement changes the picture. A changed plan usually means new information, not a mistake.
section1.full: Information accumulates in a fixed order. A CT (computed tomography) scan gives the first estimate of vessel contact and spread; an endoscopic ultrasound biopsy confirms the diagnosis and, in about nine of ten cases, yields enough DNA for full gene sequencing from the same needle pass [[DIAG-020]]. A CA 19-9 (carbohydrate antigen 19-9) level is drawn, but it can only be interpreted after a blocked bile duct has been drained, because obstruction inflates it reversibly [[DIAG-016]], and about one person in ten to twenty cannot make the marker at all [[DIAG-014]][[DIAG-015]]. Germline (inherited) and tumor sequencing, recommended in US guidelines for patients who are candidates for treatment, takes weeks and can reveal a BRCA mutation, mismatch-repair deficiency (a faulty DNA-repair system) or a gene fusion that opens a different drug [[SEC-DIAG-01]]. A staging laparoscopy, if performed, finds hidden spread in about 18% of patients whose scans looked localized [[DIAG-002]]. Then treatment itself generates data: restaging scans, marker trends, side effects and recovery. Hospital experience matters as well, since operative mortality after pancreatectomy is three to six times higher at very-low-volume than at very-high-volume hospitals [[SURG-003]], which is one reason a referral can change a plan.

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: In pancreatic cancer the plan changes more often than in most cancers because the disease is judged mainly from images that cannot see microscopic spread or distinguish scar from tumor. Chemotherapy before surgery is partly a test of the tumor's behavior; surgery may be called off if spread appears, or offered when a scan still looks unfavorable. A second opinion from a high-volume center can change the category itself.
section2.full: Consider a tumor labeled locally advanced at diagnosis. After months of FOLFIRINOX (a four-drug chemotherapy regimen) the scan may still show it touching the artery, because fibrosis and viable cancer have the same density on CT; a tumor board that reads the scan literally would withhold surgery, whereas one that explores non-progressing patients removed 40 of 47 such tumors with a 92% clear-margin rate [[DIAG-004]]. CT alone identified a resectable tumor after preoperative therapy only about two-thirds of the time, and adding PET (positron emission tomography) and CA 19-9 raised sensitivity (the share of truly resectable tumors correctly identified) to about 85% [[DIAG-009]]. The reverse also happens: a patient scheduled for surgery has a laparoscopy that finds peritoneal deposits, and the plan becomes systemic therapy [[DIAG-002]]. Pathology after surgery changes the next step again, since a high lymph-node ratio (the fraction of removed nodes containing cancer) [[SURG-007]] or a narrow margin clearance [[SEC-SURG-05]] raises recurrence risk and shapes adjuvant decisions. Even randomized evidence changes plans mid-stream: adding radiation to preoperative chemotherapy for borderline disease was expected to help and instead did not, so that arm of the trial was closed early [[TX-012]]. Each of these is a revision made because the picture sharpened, not because the first plan was wrong.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The studies here are about information quality rather than treatment effect. Restaging-accuracy data come from single-center retrospective series whose reference standard was partly non-pathologic [[DIAG-009]], and the post-FOLFIRINOX surgical series did not quantify fibrosis at the interface, so the decoupling of imaging from resectability is a clinical observation rather than a measured mechanism [[DIAG-004]]. The staging-laparoscopy yield of 18% comes from one center during a period when practice was evolving [[DIAG-002]]. The volume-mortality relationship is from US Medicare data in people over 65 with administrative coding [[SURG-003]]. Together they justify revisiting the plan at defined points; they do not say which revision is right for an individual.
research_notes.how_studied: Diagnostic-accuracy studies compare a test reading, such as CT resectability after chemotherapy, against a reference standard of surgical and pathological findings, reporting sensitivity and specificity [[DIAG-009]]. Yield studies count how often a procedure such as staging laparoscopy changes the stage [[DIAG-002]]. Marker-interpretation studies measure CA 19-9 before and after biliary drainage in benign and malignant obstruction to separate the obstruction effect from the tumor effect [[DIAG-016]]. Hospital-volume effects are studied in national administrative data, adjusting for patient factors [[SURG-003]]. Randomized trials with interim futility rules, such as the borderline-resectable radiation trial, show how evidence itself can close a treatment option while a trial is running [[TX-012]].

mechanism_notes.text: The commonest reason a surgical plan changes after chemotherapy is that anatomic imaging cannot tell treated scar from live tumor at the vessel interface. Because viable tumor keeps its glucose uptake and restricted diffusion while fibrosis does not, functional imaging may eventually let tumor boards make that call from the scan rather than at exploration [[INF-DIAG-01]][[DIAG-008]][[DIAG-009]]. Inflammation after treatment can mimic viable tumor on those scans, which is why exploration remains the reference standard.

glossary.definition: A regular meeting at which specialists from surgery, oncology, radiology and pathology review each patient's case together and agree a plan.
Involving several medical specialties working together on one patient's care.
Repeating scans and blood tests after a period of treatment to see whether the extent of disease has changed.
A keyhole operation to look inside the abdomen for small deposits of cancer that scans cannot see.
A hospital that performs many pancreatic operations each year, which is associated with lower operative mortality.

related.statement: Restaging scans after chemotherapy are the commonest trigger for a change of plan, and they are also where CT is least reliable.
A staging laparoscopy that finds hidden spread converts a surgical plan into a systemic-therapy plan.
Germline and tumor sequencing results that arrive weeks after diagnosis can add a targeted drug to the plan.
A CA 19-9 trend, read after bile-duct drainage, is one of the measurements a tumor board uses to revise a plan.
A second opinion at a high-volume center can move a tumor from one resectability category to another.
Chemotherapy before surgery is partly a test of tumor behavior whose result can change the surgical plan.

faq.q: Should I get a second opinion?
faq.a: For pancreatic cancer a review at a high-volume center is reasonable: operative mortality after pancreatectomy is several-fold lower at hospitals that do many of these operations, and experienced tumor boards are more likely to explore a tumor that still looks unresectable on a post-chemotherapy scan [[SURG-003]][[DIAG-004]].

faq.q: My oncologist changed the plan after my sequencing results came back. Is that normal?
faq.a: Yes. Germline (inherited) and tumor testing are recommended for all treatment-eligible patients precisely because a BRCA mutation, mismatch-repair deficiency or gene fusion can open a different drug, and the results typically arrive weeks after the first plan was made [[SEC-DIAG-01]].

topics.title: Why chemotherapy may come before surgery
topics.orientation: Giving chemotherapy before an operation is called neoadjuvant treatment. In pancreatic cancer it is done for three reasons: to treat the microscopic spread that is usually already present, to see how the tumor behaves before committing to major surgery, and to improve the chance of a clear margin.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: Neoadjuvant means 'before the main treatment'. Chemotherapy given first reaches cancer cells wherever they are in the body, while surgery removes only what the surgeon can see. The months of treatment also act as a trial period: a tumor that spreads during chemotherapy would have spread after surgery too, and that patient is spared an operation that would not have helped. Total neoadjuvant therapy adds radiation before surgery as well.
section1.full: The logic rests on how pancreatic cancer disseminates. Genetic reconstruction of autopsy cases suggests metastatic subclones arise within the primary years before death [[SURG-002]], and growth models infer that most patients already carry microscopic metastases at diagnosis [[SURG-009]]. An operation performed first removes the primary but leaves those cells untreated during the months of recovery, and not everyone recovers in time: in a randomized perioperative trial only 78-79% of resected patients started their planned postoperative chemotherapy [[TX-013]]. Giving the drugs first guarantees that systemic treatment happens. It also selects: in a prospective borderline-resectable trial, 5% of patients progressed during eight cycles of FOLFIRINOX (fluorouracil, leucovorin, irinotecan and oxaliplatin) and were spared surgery, while 65% of everyone enrolled reached a margin-negative resection against a historical expectation of 20% [[TX-011]]. Chemotherapy before surgery changes the specimen as well: node-positive disease fell from 78% to 33% and perineural invasion (cancer growing along nerves) from 73% to 39% in the randomized PREOPANC trial [[TX-004]], and in a FOLFIRINOX series node positivity was 35% against 79% in untreated controls [[DIAG-004]]. The preoperative period is also when a patient's fitness, nutrition and bile drainage are optimized.

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: The evidence supports chemotherapy first for borderline resectable tumors, where it raised margin-negative resection from 40% to 72% and improved five-year survival in a randomized trial. For tumors that are clearly resectable on imaging the picture differs: randomized trials of chemotherapy first have not shown a survival benefit, and one suggested harm, so the choice there is still being settled by phase 3 trials.
section2.full: In the PREOPANC trial of resectable and borderline tumors, preoperative gemcitabine-based chemoradiation (chemotherapy combined with radiation) did not significantly improve survival at first analysis (median 16.0 versus 14.3 months; hazard ratio 0.78, where values below 1 favor the treated group) but did with longer follow-up (hazard ratio 0.73; five-year survival 20.5% versus 6.5%); at the first analysis the benefit was confined to the borderline subgroup, while the long-term report described a consistent effect across both subgroups [[TX-004]][[TX-L10]]. In borderline disease, eight cycles of modified FOLFIRINOX before surgery gave a median survival of 29.8 months with 67% alive at 18 months, whereas adding short-course radiation did not help and that arm was closed [[TX-012]]. For anatomically resectable tumors, the randomized NORPACT-1 trial found 18-month survival of 60% with neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX against 73% with up-front surgery [[TX-L11]], and the SWOG S1505 trial of perioperative chemotherapy reached two-year survival of 47-48%, not above its historical bar [[TX-013]]. The phase 3 trials built to settle the resectable question, Alliance A021806 and PREOPANC-3, had finished enrolling but had posted no results as of 8 October 2026 [[SEC-TX-12]][[SEC-TX-13]]. US guidelines recommend neoadjuvant therapy for borderline resectable disease and list it as an option for selected resectable tumors with high-risk features [[SEC-SURG-11]]. The order of treatment is a decision about risk, and the right answer differs by category.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Two interpretive traps run through this literature. First, survival quoted for patients who reached surgery after neoadjuvant therapy describes a selected group: in the borderline FOLFIRINOX trial two-year survival was 72% among the resected but 56% for everyone who started [[TX-011]], and 18-month survival was 87.5% among resected patients against 66.7% overall [[TX-012]]; the gap is mostly selection and immortal time (patients who reached surgery had already survived the months of chemotherapy), not a treatment effect [[TX-L25]]. Second, the benefit of chemotherapy first appears to scale with how likely an up-front operation was to leave tumor behind, which is why borderline and resectable disease behave differently in trials even though both show pathologic downstaging [[TX-004]][[TX-L11]]. Neither the radiation component nor the ideal number of cycles has been settled by randomization.
research_notes.how_studied: Neoadjuvant strategies are tested in single-arm phase 2 trials with margin-negative resection rate as the primary endpoint, judged against a historical baseline [[TX-011]]; in randomized phase 2 'pick-the-winner' designs where each arm is compared with a fixed historical survival rather than with each other [[TX-012]][[TX-013]]; and in randomized phase 3 trials against immediate surgery with overall survival as the endpoint, analyzed by intention to treat so that patients who never reached surgery still count [[TX-004]]. Pathologic endpoints such as node status and perineural invasion are compared between arms to show what the treatment did to the tumor [[DIAG-004]]. Intention-to-treat analysis is what protects these results from selection.

mechanism_notes.text: Neoadjuvant therapy improves margins and nodal status in both borderline and resectable disease, yet improves survival only in the first. One explanation is that its benefit has two parts: converting a probable positive margin into a clear one, which matters most when the baseline margin risk is high, and delivering early systemic therapy to patients who would otherwise never receive it, which matters most when adjuvant completion is poor [[INF-TX-01]][[TX-004]][[TX-L11]]. In resectable disease both components are small, so the delay and toxicity of preoperative treatment can cancel them.

glossary.definition: Treatment given before the main treatment, usually chemotherapy before surgery.
Treatment given after surgery to destroy cancer cells that may remain.
Giving all planned chemotherapy and radiation before surgery rather than splitting it around the operation.
Analyzing every patient in the group they were assigned to, whether or not they completed the planned treatment.
An operation after which the pathologist finds no cancer at the cut edges of the specimen, also called R0.

related.statement: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is one of the sequencing choices among chemotherapy before, after or instead of surgery.
Modified FOLFIRINOX is the regimen most often given before surgery for borderline resectable pancreatic cancer.
Whether chemotherapy comes first depends on the resectability category assigned at diagnosis.
Chemotherapy before surgery is aimed at the microscopic disease that is usually present at diagnosis.
Adding radiation to preoperative chemotherapy for borderline disease did not improve outcomes in a randomized trial.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is followed by restaging scans that decide whether surgery goes ahead.

faq.q: If chemotherapy first is good for borderline tumors, why not for everyone?
faq.a: Because randomized trials in clearly resectable tumors have not shown a survival benefit: NORPACT-1 found 18-month survival of 60% with neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX versus 73% with surgery first, and the phase 3 trials that will settle the question had not reported as of 8 October 2026 [[TX-L11]][[SEC-TX-12]].

faq.q: Will chemotherapy shrink the tumor away from the vessel?
faq.a: Usually not visibly. In one large series of patients who went on to surgery after total neoadjuvant therapy, radiographic downstaging, meaning an improved resectability category on the scans, had occurred in only 28%, yet 94% had clear margins, because treated tumor is replaced by scar that keeps the same appearance on scans [[TX-L25]][[DIAG-004]].

topics.title: Visible disease and microscopic disease
topics.orientation: Scans show lumps; they do not show cells. Much of what makes pancreatic cancer difficult comes from disease that exists below the resolution of any image, and treatment decisions are built around that invisible fraction.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: A CT (computed tomography) scan can resolve a deposit of a few millimeters, which already contains millions of cells. Cancer cells that have entered the bloodstream or lymphatics and lodged in the liver, peritoneum or lung as single cells or tiny clusters are invisible. These are called micrometastases, and the state of having them after an operation is called minimal residual disease. Blood tests for tumor DNA detect some, but not all, of this hidden disease.
section1.full: In mice, pancreatic cells can enter the circulation and seed the liver before a tumor is even visible under the microscope, often in association with a shift to a more mobile cell state [[SURG-001]]; later work showed that shift is not strictly required for spread but does drive resistance to gemcitabine, a standard chemotherapy drug [[SURG-011]]. In patients, genetic reconstruction of autopsy cases places the birth of metastatic subclones (the cell lineages that went on to spread) years before death [[SURG-002]], and a mathematical model fitted to 228 patients concluded that nearly everyone harbors subclinical metastases at diagnosis [[SURG-009]]. Some of those cells do not grow: single disseminated cancer cells lacking the usual identity markers have been found in the livers of patients and mice, held dormant by an unresolved cell-stress state and by immune pressure, and they can later awaken [[SURG-012]]. The liver is also actively prepared to receive them, through tumor-derived signals that recruit immune cells and lay down fibrous tissue before any metastasis forms [[SURG-010]][[SURG-022]]. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) in blood reflects this hidden burden, but it is detectable in fewer than half of localized cancers because small tumors shed little [[DIAG-006]][[DIAG-011]].

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Microscopic disease is why a margin-negative operation is not the same as a cure, why chemotherapy is given to patients with no visible cancer, and why recurrence usually appears at a distant site rather than where the tumor was. It is also why a tumor-DNA blood test after surgery, if positive, predicts recurrence so strongly, and why a negative test is only partial reassurance.
section2.full: After resection, recurrence occurs in about two-thirds of patients even with adjuvant chemotherapy, and distant recurrence appears earlier than local recurrence, which is the signature of disease that was already elsewhere at the time of surgery [[SURG-014]]. Adjuvant chemotherapy exists to treat that fraction: six months of modified FOLFIRINOX (a four-drug chemotherapy regimen) after surgery lengthened median survival to 53.5 months against 35.5 with gemcitabine in fit patients, an effect that can only be acting on cells no scan could see [[TX-003]]. Tumor DNA in the blood after surgery is the closest thing to a direct measurement: when it persisted or emerged in the first weeks, 10 of 11 patients recurred, with median recurrence-free survival of 5 against 15 months [[DIAG-007]], and with a tumor-informed assay (a test built from the patient's own tumor mutations) a positive test in the postoperative window carried a hazard ratio of 5.45 for recurrence, about a fivefold higher rate [[DIAG-012]]. The negative side is weaker: about half of patients with undetectable postoperative tumor DNA still recur, because detection depends on how much DNA the residual cells shed and how many copies a blood tube can hold [[DIAG-024]][[DIAG-025]]. Even a pathologic complete response in the removed specimen, found in about 3% of neoadjuvant-treated patients, is followed by recurrence in many, since the specimen is only the sampled pancreas [[SURG-018]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Early dissemination is supported by three independent lines of evidence, each with a limitation. The mouse lineage-tracing work shows cells can leave at the precursor stage but cannot show those cells form clinically relevant metastases [[SURG-001]]. The genetic timing study rests on seven autopsy cases and model assumptions, and measures when metastatic competence evolved rather than when cells physically left [[SURG-002]]. The growth model is a computer simulation fitted to patient data rather than a direct observation [[SURG-009]]. The clinical pattern of early distant recurrence after margin-negative surgery is what ties them together [[SURG-014]]. The tumor-DNA studies are small, single-institution cohorts; the strong positive predictive value is consistent across them, while the negative predictive value is limited by how few mutant DNA copies a blood sample contains [[DIAG-007]][[DIAG-024]].
research_notes.how_studied: Lineage tracing labels pancreatic epithelial cells with a fluorescent protein in genetically engineered mice, so that any labeled cell found in blood or liver must have come from the pancreas [[SURG-001]]. Phylogenetic reconstruction sequences the primary tumor and each metastasis from the same patient at autopsy and uses shared versus private mutations, anchored to measured division rates, to estimate when subclones diverged [[SURG-002]]. Circulating tumor DNA assays detect tumor-specific mutations in plasma, either from a fixed KRAS panel or from a panel built from the patient's own tumor sequence, with sensitivity limited by the number of mutant copies in the sample [[DIAG-007]][[DIAG-012]]. Trial and registry follow-up supply the recurrence patterns these methods must explain [[SURG-014]].

mechanism_notes.text: A negative postoperative tumor-DNA test is followed by recurrence in roughly half of patients. At very low tumor fractions the limiting factor is the small number of mutant DNA copies in a standard blood draw, so larger plasma volumes or serial draws should raise sensitivity if the residual cells are shedding at all [[INF-DIAG-02]][[DIAG-025]][[DIAG-011]]. The competing explanation is that residual pancreatic cancer is intrinsically low-shedding, in which case the ceiling is biological rather than a matter of sample size.

Recurrence years after a margin-negative resection is best explained by dormancy: disseminated cells persisting in the liver under immune surveillance and unresolved cell stress until a later shift licenses outgrowth [[INF-SURG-01]][[SURG-012]][[SURG-007]]. The alternative is slow continuous growth below the imaging threshold without true dormancy; serial tumor-DNA sampling with long negative intervals before relapse would favor the dormancy account.

A pathologic complete response in the resected pancreas can be followed by recurrence because neoadjuvant therapy may clear the sampled primary while chemotherapy-tolerant disseminated cells persist elsewhere, making complete response a local rather than systemic finding [[INF-SURG-03]][[SURG-018]][[SURG-005]]. Some such patients are cured, and under-sampling of the specimen can also hide residual primary tumor.

glossary.definition: A deposit of cancer cells at a distant site too small to be seen on any scan.
Cancer cells that remain in the body after treatment has removed everything visible.
Fragments of DNA shed by cancer cells into the blood, detectable by tests that look for tumor-specific mutations.
A state in which disseminated cancer cells survive without dividing, sometimes for years, before resuming growth.
No living cancer cells found in the removed specimen after preoperative treatment.

related.statement: Minimal residual disease after surgery is detected, imperfectly, by circulating tumor DNA tests.
The liver is prepared in advance to receive disseminated pancreatic cancer cells by tumor-derived signals.
Microscopic disease left after treatment is the source of later recurrence.
A clear scan cannot exclude microscopic disease, which lies below imaging resolution.
Adjuvant and neoadjuvant chemotherapy are given to treat microscopic disease that no scan can show.
The liver is the commonest site where microscopic pancreatic cancer deposits later grow into visible metastases.

faq.q: The surgeon said they got it all. Why do I still need chemotherapy?
faq.a: 'Got it all' refers to the visible tumor and clear margins. Recurrence still occurs in about two-thirds of resected patients, mostly at distant sites, and adjuvant FOLFIRINOX raised five-year survival from 31% to 43% in a randomized trial, an effect that can only come from treating cells no scan could see [[SURG-014]][[TX-003]].

faq.q: My tumor-DNA test after surgery was negative. Does that mean I am cured?
faq.a: It lowers the chance of recurrence but does not remove it: about half of patients with a negative postoperative test still recur, because small residual deposits may shed too little DNA to detect in a blood sample [[DIAG-024]][[DIAG-012]].

topics.title: What a clear scan tells you
topics.orientation: 'No evidence of disease' is a precise phrase: it means nothing was seen on this test, at this resolution, on this day. It is good news, and it is also a statement with known limits.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: Every monitoring test has a floor. A CT (computed tomography) or MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scan shows a deposit once it is large and dense enough to differ from the tissue around it; scar tissue, inflammation and tumor can all look alike. A CA 19-9 (carbohydrate antigen 19-9) blood test reflects a sugar molecule the tumor sheds, which some people cannot make. A tumor-DNA blood test detects fragments only if enough are shed into a few milliliters of blood.
section1.full: Imaging resolves structure, not biology. After chemotherapy or radiation, the tumor's fibrous scar keeps the same density and the same contact with vessels as the live tumor it replaced, so in one series the size on CT fell by only about 10% while the metabolically active volume on PET (positron emission tomography) fell by 65%, and PET-based response matched the pathology 73% of the time against 36% for size-based criteria [[DIAG-008]]. Even the pathology yardstick is soft: pathologists agreed only moderately on how much tumor a preoperative treatment had killed, with agreement lowest for intermediate grades [[DIAG-010]]. CA 19-9 rises with stage and falls with response, but bile-duct obstruction and inflammation inflate it, so it must be read as a trend after the bilirubin has normalized [[DIAG-005]][[DIAG-016]], and roughly 5-12% of people are Lewis-antigen-negative (lacking the blood-group enzyme that builds the marker) and make no CA 19-9 regardless of tumor burden [[DIAG-014]][[DIAG-015]]. Tumor DNA in plasma tracks burden in real time, but detection depends on shedding: a foundational study found it in more than 75% of advanced cancers and only 48% of localized ones [[DIAG-006]], and in resectable disease a KRAS-based assay found it in 30% at 99.5% specificity, meaning almost no false-positive results [[DIAG-011]].

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: In pancreatic cancer a clear scan after treatment usually means the visible disease is controlled; it does not mean the microscopic disease is gone. About one in six patients whose scans show localized disease has hidden spread found at laparoscopy, and a negative tumor-DNA test is followed by recurrence in about half of patients. 'Response' and 'remission' describe what tests show, and the tests have floors.
section2.full: Three facts set the limits of a clear scan. First, even after CT, MRI and PET, 18% of 1,004 patients explored by staging laparoscopy had peritoneal or liver deposits the scans had missed, and the figure was 23% among patients who had not yet had chemotherapy [[DIAG-002]]. Second, after resection a clear postoperative scan can coexist with rising tumor DNA, which detected recurrence a mean of 6.5 months before CT in one cohort and had 90% sensitivity for later recurrence (it was positive in 90% of those who went on to recur) in another [[DIAG-013]][[DIAG-007]]. Third, the reverse limit also holds: a scan that still shows tumor against a vessel after chemotherapy is often showing scar, which is why 28 of 40 tumors resected after FOLFIRINOX chemotherapy, most with clear margins, had still looked locally advanced or borderline on their post-treatment scans [[DIAG-004]]. For someone being monitored, this means a stable clear scan is the best available evidence of control, a normal CA 19-9 is reassuring only if that person makes CA 19-9, and a negative tumor-DNA test lowers but does not remove the probability of recurrence, because about half of test-negative patients still recur [[DIAG-024]][[DIAG-012]]. Response on a scan during chemotherapy, measured as shrinkage of the index lesions (the chosen reference deposits), is a different quantity from survival benefit, and the two have come apart in randomized trials [[TME-004]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The imaging-response studies are small, retrospective and single-regimen; the PET-pathology concordance series had 22 patients [[DIAG-008]], and PET restaging remains investigational rather than standard in US guidance [[DIAG-009]]. The laparoscopy yield comes from one high-volume center and was lower after neoadjuvant therapy, so it describes a selected population [[DIAG-002]]. The tumor-DNA lead-time cohort had ten patients per group and was stage II only [[DIAG-013]]. Across assays of rising sophistication, postoperative detectability in resectable disease has plateaued around 30-50%, and two-year survival among test-negative patients was still only 53%, which is the basis for treating a negative test as weak reassurance [[DIAG-024]]. None of these findings is a reason to distrust a clear scan; they are reasons to keep monitoring.
research_notes.how_studied: Response assessment is studied by comparing size-based criteria (RECIST) and metabolic criteria (PERCIST) on the same patients against the pathology of the resected specimen [[DIAG-008]], and pathology grading itself is tested by having several pathologists grade the same slides and measuring agreement with a kappa statistic (a measure of agreement beyond chance) [[DIAG-010]]. Staging-laparoscopy yield is the proportion of radiographically localized patients found to have gross deposits or positive peritoneal washings [[DIAG-002]]. Tumor-DNA lead time is measured by drawing serial plasma samples after surgery and recording the interval between the first positive sample and the first CT showing recurrence [[DIAG-013]]. Lewis-antigen status is determined by genotype or by persistently undetectable CA 19-9 [[DIAG-014]].

mechanism_notes.text: Persistent tumor-vessel contact on CT after treatment is mostly fibrosis, and functional imaging may be able to tell the two apart because viable tumor retains glucose uptake and restricted diffusion while scar does not [[INF-DIAG-01]][[DIAG-008]][[DIAG-009]]. Post-treatment inflammation produces the same functional signals, so these scans can over-call live tumor in the other direction.

A negative tumor-DNA test after surgery is weak reassurance because, at low tumor fractions, the number of mutant DNA copies in a single blood tube is the limiting factor; larger plasma volumes or pooled serial draws should raise sensitivity if the residual cells shed at all [[INF-DIAG-02]][[DIAG-025]][[DIAG-011]]. If residual pancreatic cancer is intrinsically low-shedding, no practical increase in sample volume will close the gap.

glossary.definition: A statement that a test found no detectable cancer, which does not exclude disease below the test's limit of detection.
A standard way of measuring tumor response on scans from changes in the diameters of chosen lesions.
Lacking the blood-group enzyme needed to make CA 19-9, so the marker stays low regardless of tumor burden.
A keyhole operation to look inside the abdomen for small deposits of cancer that scans cannot see.
The interval by which one test detects a change before another test does.

related.statement: A clear or stable scan is the main output of restaging after treatment, and its limits are those of CT.
A CA 19-9 trend complements a clear scan but is uninformative in people who cannot make the marker.
Circulating tumor DNA can reveal recurrence months before a scan but misses about half of residual disease.
Staging laparoscopy finds hidden spread in about one in six patients whose scans appear clear of metastases.
A clear scan says nothing about microscopic disease, which lies below imaging resolution.
PET can distinguish metabolically active tumor from scar better than size on CT, though inflammation also lights up.

faq.q: My scan is clear. Am I in remission?
faq.a: A clear scan means no disease is visible at the resolution of that test, which is the best evidence of control available. It does not exclude microscopic disease: tumor DNA can rise months before a scan shows recurrence, and about half of patients with a negative tumor-DNA test still recur [[DIAG-013]][[DIAG-024]].

faq.q: My CA 19-9 has always been normal. Is that good news?
faq.a: It depends on whether you make the marker. Roughly 5-12% of people are Lewis-antigen-negative and produce no CA 19-9 regardless of tumor burden, in which case a normal value carries no information and CEA or CA-125, two other blood markers, may be followed instead [[DIAG-014]][[DIAG-015]].

topics.title: Recurrence: what it means and why it happens
topics.orientation: Recurrence means cancer has reappeared after a treatment that removed or controlled everything visible. In pancreatic cancer it is common, usually appears at a distant site, and reflects cells that were already present at the time of the original treatment rather than a new cancer.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: A recurrence grows from cells that survived the original treatment. They may have been left at the edge of the operation, which produces a local recurrence in the pancreatic bed, or they may already have traveled to the liver, lung or peritoneum, which produces a distant recurrence. The time to recurrence depends on how many cells remained, how fast they grow, and whether some stayed dormant before resuming growth.
section1.full: Recurrence is a clonal event: the cells that regrow descend from subclones (genetically distinct cell lineages) of the original tumor, and in autopsy studies the metastasis-initiating clones were genetically distinct from the bulk of the primary and kept evolving separately in each organ [[SURG-013]]. Metastatic ability can be acquired without any new driver mutation; in one patient series the distant metastatic subclones shared identical drivers with the primary but had lost a chromatin mark (a chemical tag on DNA packaging that controls which genes are read) across large regions of the genome and had switched to a different glucose-handling pathway [[GENE-008]]. Timing is explained by two mechanisms. Continuous growth below the imaging threshold accounts for most recurrences within the first year [[SURG-009]], whereas recurrences years after surgery are better explained by dormancy: single disseminated cells in the liver that lack the usual identity and immune-display molecules, held in check by cell stress and immune surveillance until a change releases them [[SURG-012]]. In a 957-patient resected series the natural cut between early and late recurrence fell at 12 months, with 51.5% recurring before it, and early recurrence carried a far worse post-recurrence course [[SURG-007]]. Where the cancer reappears is set partly by the organ: the liver is prepared in advance by tumor signals that recruit macrophages (immune scavenger cells) and lay down fibrosis [[SURG-022]][[SURG-023]].

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: After resection, recurrence occurs in about two-thirds of patients even with adjuvant chemotherapy, and distant sites are more common than the pancreatic bed. Survival after recurrence was similar whether it appeared locally or at a distance, which is why pancreatic cancer is treated as a systemic disease from the start. Lung-only recurrence is the exception, with a markedly longer course than liver recurrence.
section2.full: In the ESPAC-4 adjuvant trial, 479 of 730 resected patients (65.6%) recurred, distant recurrence appeared earlier than local (median 9.5 against 11.6 months), and survival after recurrence was almost the same for the two patterns (8.9 against 9.4 months) [[SURG-014]]. Adjuvant chemotherapy delays rather than prevents most recurrence, though the delay translates into survival: modified FOLFIRINOX (a four-drug chemotherapy regimen) gave median disease-free survival of 21.4 against 12.8 months with gemcitabine and raised five-year survival from 31% to 43% [[TX-003]]. The strongest predictors of early recurrence are a high CA 19-9 (carbohydrate antigen 19-9) before or after surgery, a high lymph-node ratio, poor differentiation (cells that look least like normal tissue) and lymphovascular invasion (cancer inside small lymph or blood vessels), each roughly doubling to tripling the odds [[SURG-007]]. Site matters for what follows: in a Swedish series median survival was 30 months after lung recurrence against 13 months after liver recurrence, and lung deposits were favorable even when combined with other spread [[SURG-015]], which is why isolated lung nodules are sometimes resected. A rising tumor-DNA level with a clear scan can be the first sign, months ahead of imaging [[DIAG-013]], and a CA 19-9 that climbs after surgery is likewise a strong predictor [[SURG-007]]. When recurrence is found, the treatment question becomes the one asked of metastatic disease at diagnosis: which systemic therapy, with what goal, and with what support.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The systemic-disease conclusion rests on a secondary analysis of a randomized adjuvant trial in which recurrence was detected by protocol scans rather than autopsy, so site assignment is approximate [[SURG-014]]. The lung-versus-liver hierarchy comes from a single center with imaging-based site assignment, and part of the difference may be lead time, since small lung nodules are found earlier on surveillance CT [[SURG-015]]. The dormancy mechanism is established in mice and descriptively in human liver tissue; no clinical intervention has reversed it [[SURG-012]]. The early-recurrence predictors were derived in patients who had not received neoadjuvant therapy, so they may not transfer to current treatment sequences [[SURG-007]]. SMAD4 loss, once proposed as a marker of widespread versus local failure, showed no association with recurrence pattern in a 127-patient resected series [[GENE-023]].
research_notes.how_studied: Recurrence patterns are studied by following resected patients with scheduled scans and markers, recording the site and date of first recurrence, and comparing survival from that date by site [[SURG-014]][[SURG-015]]. Predictors are found by logistic regression on preoperative and pathological variables, with the early-late cut chosen as the time point that best separates post-recurrence survival [[SURG-007]]. Clonal relationships are reconstructed by sequencing the primary and each metastasis from autopsy cases and building phylogenetic trees [[SURG-013]]. Dormancy is studied by injecting cancer cells into immunized mice and characterizing the single cells that persist in the liver, then testing what triggers their outgrowth [[SURG-012]]. Epigenomic comparison of matched primary and metastatic subclones identifies non-genetic changes that accompany distant spread [[GENE-008]].

mechanism_notes.text: Late recurrence after a clean operation is proposed to arise from disseminated cells that persist dormant in the liver under immune surveillance and unresolved cell stress until a later shift, such as waning immunity or remodeling of the liver niche, licenses outgrowth [[INF-SURG-01]][[SURG-012]][[SURG-007]]. The competing account is slow continuous growth below the imaging threshold, and the two would be separated by serial tumor-DNA sampling showing long negative intervals before relapse.

Lung recurrence may be less lethal than liver recurrence because the liver carries pancreatic-cancer-specific niche programs, including macrophage-driven fibrosis and immune exclusion, that accelerate outgrowth and treatment resistance, whereas the lung lacks an equivalent niche [[INF-SURG-02]][[SURG-015]][[SURG-023]][[SURG-024]]. Lead-time bias from earlier detection of small lung nodules on surveillance CT is a competing explanation that a matched, lead-time-adjusted comparison could test.

glossary.definition: Cancer reappearing in the area where the original tumor was removed.
Cancer reappearing in an organ away from the original site, such as the liver, lung or peritoneum.
The time after treatment during which no recurrence is detected.
A state in which disseminated cancer cells survive without dividing, sometimes for years, before resuming growth.
The number of cancer-containing lymph nodes divided by the number examined, a predictor of early recurrence.

related.statement: Recurrence grows from microscopic disease that was present but invisible at the time of the original treatment.
The liver is the commonest site of recurrence because tumor signals prepare it to receive disseminated cells.
Liver recurrence carries a shorter course than lung recurrence after pancreatic resection.
Rising circulating tumor DNA often signals recurrence months before a scan shows it.
Recurrent and metastatic clones descend from subclones of the original tumor that keep evolving in each organ.
Recurrence after surgery is treated with the systemic therapies used for metastatic disease.

faq.q: Is a recurrence a new cancer?
faq.a: Almost never. Recurrent tumors descend from subclones of the original cancer that had already spread or been left behind, and autopsy genomics shows they share the original driver mutations while continuing to evolve separately in each organ [[SURG-013]][[GENE-008]].

faq.q: The pancreas was removed, so why did the cancer come back in the liver?
faq.a: Because cells had usually already reached the liver before the operation. Distant recurrence appears earlier than local recurrence after surgery, and the liver is actively prepared to receive pancreatic cancer cells by signals the tumor sends ahead of itself [[SURG-014]][[SURG-022]].

topics.title: How to read a treatment result
topics.orientation: Treatment results arrive as a small vocabulary of numbers: response rate, progression-free survival, overall survival, hazard ratio, median. Each measures something different, and pancreatic cancer trials have repeatedly shown that improving one does not guarantee improving another.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: A response rate counts the share of patients whose tumors shrank on scans by a set amount. Progression-free survival is the time until the tumor grows or the patient dies. Overall survival is the time until death from any cause. A median is the point at which half the group has reached the event. A hazard ratio compares the rate of events between two arms over the whole follow-up, so 0.70 means a 30% lower rate on treatment.
section1.full: Each endpoint has a reason to exist and a known weakness. Response rate is quick and needs no comparison group, but it measures the chosen index lesions (the specific tumor deposits selected for measurement) and not the disease elsewhere; a drug can shrink the visible tumor and leave survival untouched. Progression-free survival is less affected by later treatments and needs fewer patients, but it depends on how often scans are done and who reads them: in the adjuvant APACT trial, independently reviewed disease-free survival did not reach significance (hazard ratio 0.88) while investigator-assessed recurrence did, and the difference lay in how recurrence was counted [[TX-006]]. Overall survival is the endpoint that cannot be gamed, but it is diluted by whatever treatments follow progression. The hazard ratio summarizes the whole curve and so can be significant when the medians barely differ: erlotinib, a targeted drug, added to gemcitabine chemotherapy gave a hazard ratio of 0.82 with a median gain of about ten days, and one-year survival of 23% against 17% [[RAS-037]]. Intention-to-treat analysis counts every randomized patient in the arm they were assigned; a per-protocol or 'resected cohort' analysis counts only those who completed the plan, and the two can tell different stories about the same trial [[TX-011]].

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Pancreatic cancer trials supply the clearest examples of endpoints coming apart. Two randomized trials raised the response rate significantly, by 11 and 17 percentage points, and changed survival not at all. Maintenance olaparib doubled progression-free survival without a significant survival gain. Survival among patients who reached surgery after chemotherapy far exceeded survival of everyone who started. And the first RAS inhibitor won approval by improving progression-free and overall survival together in a randomized phase 3 trial.
section2.full: Adding PEGPH20, an enzyme that breaks down hyaluronan, a gel-like component of the tumor's matrix, to chemotherapy raised the response rate from 36% to 47% while the hazard ratio for death was exactly 1.00 [[TME-004]]; adding hydroxychloroquine, a malaria drug repurposed to block the cell's recycling system, raised it from 21.1% to 38.2% while one-year survival was numerically worse, 41% against 49% [[TME-027]]. Both are explained by response measuring the index lesions while survival is set by disease elsewhere.
