Diarrhea in chemotherapy trials is graded by stool frequency above baseline and need for hospital care [[TX-002]]. Pharmacogenomic studies genotype UGT1A1 before treatment and compare toxicity and survival between reduced-dose poor metabolizers and fully dosed others [[GENE-018]]. Enzyme studies score symptoms with the EORTC pancreatic module, a standard patient questionnaire, at fixed weeks [[SUPP-021]].

mechanism_notes.text: Irinotecan's late diarrhea arises because its active metabolite SN-38 is detoxified by UGT1A1 and then reactivated by gut bacteria, injuring the intestinal lining; people with low-activity UGT1A1 therefore carry more SN-38 and suffer more diarrhea and neutropenia, which is why genotype-guided dose reduction equalized toxicity without costing survival [[GENE-018]][[GENE-019]]. The early cholinergic diarrhea is a separate, receptor-mediated effect treated with atropine [[SEC-SUPP-11]].

glossary.definition: Likely to cause nausea and vomiting; chemotherapy drugs are ranked by this risk.
An anti-nausea drug such as ondansetron that blocks serotonin receptors in the gut and brain.
Watery diarrhea with cramping and sweating within a day of irinotecan, treated with atropine.
An over-the-counter drug that slows the bowel, used at the first loose stool for late irinotecan diarrhea.
The gene for the enzyme that clears irinotecan's active metabolite; low-activity variants raise toxicity.
Blockage of the duodenum that stops the stomach emptying, causing vomiting of old food.

related.statement: Irinotecan causes both an early cholinergic diarrhea and a late diarrhea from damage to the intestinal lining.
FOLFIRINOX causes diarrhea in roughly a quarter of patients at severe grade and nausea that standard prevention controls in most.
Inherited UGT1A1 and DPYD variants raise the risk of severe diarrhea and low blood counts from irinotecan and fluorouracil.
Greasy floating stools during chemotherapy are usually enzyme insufficiency rather than drug diarrhea.
Vomiting of food eaten hours earlier signals a blocked duodenum rather than chemotherapy nausea.
Dexamethasone used to prevent chemotherapy nausea raises blood sugar for a day or two each cycle.

faq.q: Should I take loperamide or enzymes for my diarrhea?
faq.a: Watery stools starting a few days after irinotecan are drug diarrhea and call for loperamide at the first loose stool [[SEC-SUPP-11]]. Pale, greasy, floating stools are undigested fat and respond to enzyme capsules with meals, which cut diarrhea scores from 26 to 8 within a week in metastatic disease [[SUPP-021]]. Many people have both and need both.

topics.title: Numbness and tingling (neuropathy)
topics.orientation: Numbness and tingling in the hands and feet are the signature side effect of oxaliplatin, part of FOLFIRINOX and NALIRIFOX, and also occur with nab-paclitaxel. The acute form is startling but brief; the cumulative form is the one that limits treatment.

section1.label: What this experience involves
section1.preview: Oxaliplatin causes two kinds of nerve symptoms. Within hours of each infusion comes an acute, cold-triggered tingling in the hands, feet, lips and throat, sometimes with jaw tightness or cramps; 89% of people had it at the first cycle and it peaked on day three [[TX-022]]. With accumulating doses a persistent numbness and tingling in the toes and fingertips develops that keeps worsening for about three months after the last dose and was still severe in about 1 in 5 people at 18 months [[TX-022]].
section1.full: The acute form is a transient disturbance of nerve-membrane sodium channels by oxaliplatin's oxalate; the chronic form reflects platinum accumulating in the sensory nerve-cell bodies beside the spinal cord, which is why it is dose-dependent and slow to reverse. In the 346-patient natural-history study, cold sensitivity on touching or swallowing cold things affected 71%, throat discomfort 63% and muscle cramps 42% in cycle one, symptoms were about twice as severe in cycles 2-12, and the sensory score on a standard neuropathy questionnaire fell 21 points during treatment, with tingling more prominent than numbness or pain [[TX-022]]. Nab-paclitaxel produces a similar cumulative sensory neuropathy: grade 3 or worse in 17% with gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel versus 1% with gemcitabine alone [[TX-001]], while NALIRIFOX (liposomal irinotecan, oxaliplatin, fluorouracil and leucovorin) caused less neuropathy and neutropenia (low white blood cell counts) than that pairing but more diarrhea [[TX-002]]. The practical consequences are loss of fine touch (buttons, coins, keyboards), unsteadiness in the dark when the feet cannot feel the floor, and burns or cuts that go unnoticed. The label advises avoiding cold drinks, ice and cold air on and around treatment days [[SEC-SUPP-12]]. A typical course: a sharp shock on touching a cold steering wheel after the first cycle, then by the eighth cycle a feeling of walking on pebbles that persists between infusions.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Oxaliplatin is in these regimens because it adds to survival; FOLFIRINOX (fluorouracil, leucovorin, irinotecan and oxaliplatin) extended median survival from 6.8 to 11.1 months over gemcitabine in fit patients with metastatic disease [[TX-L02]]. The trade-off is nerve damage that no drug prevents, so the main protection is adjusting the dose: delaying, reducing or stopping oxaliplatin when symptoms persist between cycles [[SEC-SUPP-07]]. For established painful neuropathy, duloxetine is the one medicine with moderate evidence [[SUPP-026]].
section2.full: Prevention has failed repeatedly, and one attempt caused harm: calmangafodipir, an antioxidant tested in two phase 3 trials, increased moderate-to-severe neuropathy at nine months to 54.3% versus 40.3% on placebo and caused serious hypersensitivity reactions in 3.6%, so the trials were stopped [[SUPP-010]]. The US guideline therefore recommends no agent for prevention and makes dose modification the primary tool [[SEC-SUPP-07]]. Stopping oxaliplatin after a planned number of cycles while continuing the other drugs is a common way to cap exposure, and the fact that most people in the adjuvant FOLFIRINOX trial received reduced dose intensity yet still gained a large survival benefit shows that treatment survives such adjustments [[TX-003]]. Treatment of established symptoms: duloxetine, an antidepressant that also modulates pain pathways, reduced average pain by 0.73 points more than placebo on a 0-10 scale over five weeks, with 59% versus 38% reporting any improvement; it is off-label for this use, and people on oxaliplatin appeared to respond better than those on taxanes, the drug class that includes nab-paclitaxel [[SUPP-026]]. Physical measures such as checking the feet daily, non-slip footwear and night lights address the safety risk. Tumor-related nerve pain in the abdomen and back is a different problem, covered under pain. Neuropathy is also why the care team asks about hands and feet before every cycle: the time to adjust is while symptoms still fade between infusions.

action_note.heading: Before the next infusion
action_note.text: Tell the care team before the next cycle if tingling or numbness no longer clears between infusions, if you are dropping objects, stumbling or cannot feel the floor, or if you have burned or cut yourself without noticing; the guideline's main protection against permanent damage is reducing, delaying or stopping oxaliplatin at that point [[SEC-SUPP-07]][[SEC-SUPP-12]]. Throat tightness during or just after an infusion is usually the cold-triggered acute effect [[TX-022]], but trouble breathing should be treated as an emergency.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The natural-history study [[TX-022]] enrolled colorectal patients on FOLFOX (fluorouracil, leucovorin and oxaliplatin), so its percentages transfer to pancreatic regimens by drug rather than by disease, and it used questionnaires without nerve-conduction tests. The calmangafodipir trials [[SUPP-010]] and the duloxetine trial [[SUPP-026]] were also in mixed or colorectal populations, with the oxaliplatin-specific duloxetine results reported only in a separate subgroup analysis. Pancreatic trials report neuropathy as graded adverse events [[TX-001]][[TX-002]], which understate the day-to-day burden of grade 1-2 symptoms.
research_notes.how_studied: Neuropathy is tracked with the EORTC CIPN20 questionnaire, which scores sensory, motor and autonomic symptoms, and with clinician toxicity grades where grade 3 means symptoms limit self-care [[TX-022]][[TX-001]]. Acute symptoms are captured by daily diaries in the first week of each cycle [[TX-022]]. Prevention trials randomize against placebo and measure the proportion with moderate-to-severe neuropathy at a fixed time after treatment ends, here nine months [[SUPP-010]]. Treatment trials use a crossover design with average pain on a 0-10 scale as the endpoint [[SUPP-026]].

mechanism_notes.text: The two-phase course fits two mechanisms: oxalate released from oxaliplatin transiently alters voltage-gated sodium channels, producing cold-triggered symptoms within hours, while platinum adducts accumulate in dorsal root ganglion neurons over cycles, producing the slow, dose-dependent sensory loss that continues to worsen for months after the last dose [[TX-022]][[SEC-SUPP-12]]. The failure of an antioxidant to prevent it, and its harm, suggests oxidative stress is not the dominant pathway [[SUPP-010]].

glossary.definition: Nerve damage from chemotherapy causing numbness, tingling or pain, usually in the hands and feet.
An unpleasant abnormal sensation such as tingling or burning triggered by touch or cold.
The cluster of sensory nerve-cell bodies beside the spinal cord where platinum drugs accumulate.
An antidepressant that also reduces nerve pain, used off-label for painful chemotherapy neuropathy.
Delaying, reducing or stopping a chemotherapy drug to limit a side effect while continuing treatment.

related.statement: Oxaliplatin causes both the acute cold-triggered tingling and the cumulative numbness of chemotherapy neuropathy.
FOLFIRINOX produces neuropathy through its oxaliplatin component, which is often stopped early to limit it.
Gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel causes a cumulative sensory neuropathy in about 17% at severe grade.
NALIRIFOX caused less neuropathy than gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel in a head-to-head trial.
Chemotherapy neuropathy in the hands and feet is distinct from tumor-related nerve pain in the abdomen and back.
Dose reductions and delays, the main protection against neuropathy, are part of the same dose-adjustment decisions described with growth-factor support.

faq.q: Will the numbness go away?
faq.a: Often partly, slowly. Chronic symptoms kept worsening for about three months after the last oxaliplatin dose before improving, and about 1 in 5 people still had severe sensory symptoms at 18 months [[TX-022]]. Stopping oxaliplatin earlier limits how far it progresses [[SEC-SUPP-07]].

topics.title: Fever and infection during chemotherapy
topics.orientation: Chemotherapy temporarily removes the white blood cells that fight bacteria. During that window a fever can be the only sign of a serious infection, which is why a thermometer reading changes what you do next.

section1.label: What this experience involves
section1.preview: Neutrophils are the white cells that engulf bacteria. Most chemotherapy drugs suppress the bone marrow that makes them, so counts fall to a low point roughly a week or two after each dose and recover before the next. While the count is low, infection may cause no pus, no cough and no redness, only a fever [[SEC-SUPP-02]]. Fever with neutropenia occurred in 31 of 154 people (20.1%) on FOLFIRINOX, mostly within the first four cycles [[SUPP-006]].
section1.full: Risk is not evenly spread. In that cohort, women (hazard ratio 2.20, meaning about twice the rate), people with a performance status of 1 rather than 0 on the fitness scale where 0 is fully active (hazard ratio 2.83) and people carrying low-activity variants of UGT1A1, the gene for the enzyme that clears irinotecan's active metabolite (hazard ratio about 4), were more likely to develop febrile neutropenia, and head tumors were over-represented among those affected (74.2% versus 48.8%), plausibly because a stented bile duct offers bacteria a route in [[SUPP-006]]. The original metastatic trial of FOLFIRINOX (fluorouracil, leucovorin, irinotecan and oxaliplatin) reported febrile neutropenia in 5.4% [[TX-L02]]. Gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel produced grade 3 or higher neutropenia in 38% versus 27% with gemcitabine alone, with febrile neutropenia in 3% versus 1% [[TX-001]]; NALIRIFOX caused less neutropenia than that pairing [[TX-002]]. Two inherited variants change the arithmetic: a 30% starting-dose reduction in UGT1A1 poor metabolizers brought severe toxicity down to the level of others without loss of survival [[GENE-018]], and DPYD variants that impair breakdown of fluorouracil can cause severe early toxicity, which genotype-guided dosing cut from 43.3% to 16.0% [[GENE-019]]. Growth-factor injections (G-CSF, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, such as pegfilgrastim) shorten the neutropenic window and are approved in the US for reducing febrile neutropenia with myelosuppressive (bone-marrow-suppressing) chemotherapy; FOLFIRINOX is classed as a high-risk regimen, although no pancreatic-specific randomized trial of G-CSF exists [[SUPP-006]]. A typical presentation is chills on day ten of a cycle with a temperature of 101 °F and nothing else to find.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: People with pancreatic cancer carry extra infection risks on top of low counts: a biliary stent that can seed bacteria into the bloodstream, undernutrition, diabetes, and steroids given with each infusion. Cholangitis, infection of a blocked or stented bile duct, is the pancreatic-specific emergency and announces itself with fever, chills, jaundice and pain under the right ribs [[SEC-SUPP-14]]. Treatment of febrile neutropenia is urgent antibiotics; the rules for timing are exact.
section2.full: Guidelines define neutropenic fever as a single oral temperature of 38.3 °C (101 °F) or higher, or 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) sustained for an hour, in someone whose neutrophil count is below 500 per microliter or expected to fall below it, and they require assessment and the first dose of antibiotics within an hour of presentation [[SEC-SUPP-01]]. Some people with low-risk features can be treated with oral antibiotics at home after assessment, using validated scoring; most are first assessed in an emergency setting [[SEC-SUPP-01]]. The patient-facing threshold is simpler: 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher counts as a fever during cancer treatment, measured by mouth, never rectally, and chills, breathing trouble, confusion or urinary symptoms warrant a call even without a confirmed fever [[SEC-SUPP-03]]. Infection in a stented bile duct is treated with antibiotics plus urgent drainage or stent exchange, because antibiotics alone cannot clear an obstructed system [[SEC-SUPP-14]]. Prevention is dose planning as much as injections: dose reductions and delays after an episode, growth-factor support for high-risk regimens, and genotype testing where available. An episode of febrile neutropenia is also information; it often leads to a lower dose in later cycles, and the adjuvant FOLFIRINOX trial, in which most people received reduced dose intensity, still showed a large survival benefit [[TX-003]]. Keeping a thermometer at home and knowing the after-hours number turns a frightening night into a manageable one.

action_note.heading: When to call the care team now
action_note.text: A temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher at any time during chemotherapy, or shaking chills even without a measured fever, needs a call to the oncology team or emergency department immediately, day or night, not the next morning [[SEC-SUPP-03]]. With a low neutrophil count, guidelines expect evaluation and the first antibiotic dose within one hour of arrival [[SEC-SUPP-01]]. Fever with jaundice, dark urine or pain under the right ribs, especially with a biliary stent, points to cholangitis and needs urgent drainage as well as antibiotics [[SEC-SUPP-14]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The 20% febrile neutropenia rate [[SUPP-006]] comes from a single Korean center where the UGT1A1*6 variant is common, so the gene effect may differ in US populations where *28 dominates; the rate itself sits within the 5-22% range of other series. Trial adverse-event tables [[TX-001]][[TX-002]][[TX-L02]] report febrile neutropenia in selected, fit patients. The pharmacogenomic studies [[GENE-018]][[GENE-019]] are retrospective and span several cancers. The studies cited here include no pancreatic-specific randomized trial of G-CSF prophylaxis, so its use rests on regimen-class risk.
research_notes.how_studied: Cohorts record every episode of fever with a neutrophil count below 500 per microliter during first-line chemotherapy and use time-to-event models to find predictors such as sex, performance status and UGT1A1 genotype [[SUPP-006]]. Randomized chemotherapy trials grade neutropenia from scheduled blood counts and record febrile neutropenia as a serious adverse event [[TX-001]]. Pharmacogenomic studies genotype patients before treatment and compare toxicity between reduced-dose variant carriers and fully dosed non-carriers [[GENE-018]][[GENE-019]]. Guideline thresholds derive from expert consensus over trials of empiric antibiotics [[SEC-SUPP-01]][[SEC-SUPP-02]].

mechanism_notes.text: The over-representation of head tumors among febrile neutropenia cases (74.2% versus 48.8%) is most simply explained by biliary stents and partial obstruction providing a bacterial reservoir that becomes invasive when neutrophils fall, so that the same chemotherapy carries a higher infection risk in people with stents [[SUPP-006]][[SEC-SUPP-14]]. The cohort did not record stent status directly, so this is inferred from anatomy.

glossary.definition: The most common white blood cell, the first line of defense against bacteria.
A neutrophil count low enough, usually below 500 per microliter, that ordinary infections become dangerous.
Fever occurring while the neutrophil count is low; treated as a medical emergency.
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, an injected growth factor that speeds recovery of neutrophils after chemotherapy.
Bacterial infection of a blocked bile duct, causing fever, chills and jaundice.
The gene for the enzyme that clears irinotecan's active metabolite; low-activity variants raise toxicity.

related.statement: Febrile neutropenia risk with FOLFIRINOX is reduced with growth-factor injections and dose adjustments.
Inherited UGT1A1 and DPYD variants raise the risk of severe neutropenia from irinotecan and fluorouracil.
FOLFIRINOX is classed as a high-risk regimen for febrile neutropenia, which affected 20% of patients in one cohort.
A biliary stent can become a source of bloodstream infection when neutrophils are low.
Fever with jaundice during chemotherapy points to cholangitis in a blocked or stented bile duct.
Fever with new or returning jaundice is the warning sign of cholangitis described under jaundice.

faq.q: My temperature is 99.8 °F and I feel shivery. Do I wait?
faq.a: No. The American Cancer Society page advises contacting the care team for chills even without a measured fever, and 100.4 °F (38 °C) is the threshold at which it becomes an emergency [[SEC-SUPP-03]]. Recheck in 30 minutes if told to, but call first.

topics.title: Blood clots
topics.orientation: Pancreatic cancer is among the cancers most likely to cause blood clots, common enough that prevention is discussed at the start of chemotherapy. Knowing the symptoms matters because many clots are silent until they are not.

section1.label: What this experience involves
section1.preview: Clots form in the deep veins of the leg (deep vein thrombosis), travel to the lungs (pulmonary embolism) or block the veins that drain the gut and liver (visceral vein thrombosis). In 762 people starting chemotherapy, the cumulative incidence was 16.4% within six months and about 1 in 4 over the illness; more than half were found incidentally on routine scans [[SUPP-024]]. The warning signs are one-sided leg swelling or pain, sudden breathlessness, and chest pain that is worse on breathing [[SEC-SUPP-04]].
section1.full: Why this cancer clots: tumor cells and the inflamed tissue around them release tissue factor (a clotting trigger) and mucins (sticky sugar-coated proteins) that activate clotting, the tumor itself can compress the portal or splenic veins, and chemotherapy, central lines, dehydration and immobility add to it. In that French cohort of 762 people, of the clots in the first six months 23% were pulmonary embolism, 23% leg deep vein thrombosis and 31.5% visceral vein thrombosis, and a clot was associated with shorter survival (hazard ratio 2.02), with risk higher in metastatic disease [[SUPP-024]][[SUPP-L11]]. Scores designed to pick out high-risk patients do not work inside this disease: the Khorana, PROTECHT and ONKOTEV scores had a c-index of about 0.50, no better than chance, because 99% of pancreatic patients already score as high risk [[SUPP-024]]. Prevention has been tested. In the pancreatic subgroup of the CASSINI trial, low-dose rivaroxaban, an oral anticoagulant, cut clots while people were taking it (3.7% versus 10.1%, hazard ratio 0.35) with no increase in major bleeding (1.5% versus 2.3%), but 43% stopped the drug within six months and the overall intention-to-treat difference (9.6% versus 13.0%) was not significant [[SUPP-007]]. In the CONKO-004 trial, prophylactic enoxaparin (a low-molecular-weight heparin) injections reduced symptomatic clots in the first three months from 15 of 152 to 2 of 160 (hazard ratio 0.12) without changing survival [[SUPP-L09]]. An example: a calf that is tighter and warmer than the other after a long drive home from an infusion.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Pancreatic cancer alone gives a Khorana score of 2, the threshold at which US guidance says preventive anticoagulation with apixaban, rivaroxaban or low-molecular-weight heparin may be offered to outpatients starting chemotherapy after a discussion of bleeding risk [[SEC-SUPP-04]]. Neither oral drug carries an FDA indication for this prevention as of 8 Oct 2026, so the use is guideline-supported but off-label [[SEC-SUPP-13]]. Once a clot has formed, treatment is months of anticoagulation.
section2.full: Treatment choice balances clot recurrence against bleeding, which matters in a cancer that can erode the duodenum or sit next to a stent. In 433 people with gastrointestinal cancers treated with the oral anticoagulants apixaban or rivaroxaban for at least six months, major bleeding occurred in 3.7%, clinically relevant minor bleeding in 5.3% and recurrent clots in 7.4%, with no difference between the two drugs [[SUPP-025]]; both are approved in the US for treating deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism [[SEC-SUPP-13]]. Guidance allows either a direct oral anticoagulant or low-molecular-weight heparin injections, with caution about oral agents when there is a bleeding lesion in the gut [[SEC-SUPP-04]]. Practical issues decide much of the outcome: an oral drug only works if it is taken, and the 43% discontinuation in CASSINI shows how hard that is during chemotherapy [[SUPP-007]]; injections are reliable but burdensome. Incidental clots found on staging scans are treated the same way as symptomatic ones. Clots also interact with other parts of care: a planned biopsy, stent exchange or operation requires anticoagulation to be paused and restarted on a schedule, and dehydration from diarrhea or vomiting raises risk. Anticoagulation does not treat the cancer and did not change survival in either prevention trial [[SUPP-007]][[SUPP-L09]]; its purpose is to prevent the sudden event.

action_note.heading: When to call the care team now
action_note.text: Sudden breathlessness, chest pain that is worse on breathing in, coughing blood, fainting, or new swelling or pain in one leg or arm need emergency evaluation the same day, because a clot that has reached the lungs can be fatal without treatment [[SEC-SUPP-04]]. On an anticoagulant, black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, a severe headache or bleeding that will not stop are signs of serious bleeding and also need immediate care [[SEC-SUPP-13]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The CASSINI pancreatic result [[SUPP-007]] is a pre-specified subgroup of 273 people and was underpowered; the on-treatment benefit is real but the intention-to-treat null shows that adherence, not pharmacology, limited it. CONKO-004 [[SUPP-L09]] is available to this atlas only as an abstract. Incidence figures [[SUPP-024]] include visceral vein thromboses and incidental events, which many trials exclude, so they run higher than trial endpoints. The bleeding data [[SUPP-025]] are retrospective, lack a heparin comparator and do not separate pancreatic cancer from other gastrointestinal cancers.
research_notes.how_studied: Cohorts follow newly diagnosed patients with scheduled scans and symptom review, count every clot as symptomatic or incidental, and use competing-risk models because death removes people from risk [[SUPP-024]]. Prevention trials randomize against placebo, screen the legs by ultrasound at baseline to exclude existing clots, and adjudicate events blind over 180 days [[SUPP-007]]. Risk scores are judged by the c-index, where 0.5 means no discrimination [[SUPP-024]]. Treatment cohorts record major and clinically relevant non-major bleeding by standard definitions alongside recurrence [[SUPP-025]].

mechanism_notes.text: Risk scores fail within pancreatic cancer because the tumor-driven component of clotting saturates them: nearly every patient scores high, so the remaining variation is set by factors the scores omit, such as adherence to prophylaxis, metastatic burden and visceral vein compression [[SUPP-024]][[SUPP-007]][[SUPP-L11]]. This argues for treating the whole population as high risk rather than screening for whom to protect.

glossary.definition: A clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg, causing swelling and pain.
A clot that has traveled to the lungs, causing breathlessness and chest pain.
A clot in the veins draining the gut, liver or spleen, often found incidentally on scans.
A points system for clot risk in cancer patients; pancreatic cancer alone scores 2, the high-risk threshold.
A medicine that slows clotting, taken as tablets or injections.
An injected anticoagulant such as enoxaparin, long the standard for clots in cancer.

related.statement: Clots in pancreatic cancer are prevented and treated with anticoagulants as described under preventing and treating blood clots.
A tumor pressing on the portal or superior mesenteric vein can cause visceral vein thrombosis.
Dehydration from chemotherapy diarrhea or vomiting raises clot risk in pancreatic cancer.
Clot risk in pancreatic cancer is higher with metastatic disease.
Stent exchanges and other procedures require anticoagulation to be paused and restarted on a schedule.

faq.q: Should I be on a blood thinner from the start of chemotherapy?
faq.a: It is a reasonable question to raise: pancreatic cancer alone meets the guideline threshold at which prophylaxis may be offered after discussing bleeding risk [[SEC-SUPP-04]]. In the pancreatic subgroup of CASSINI, rivaroxaban cut clots from 10.1% to 3.7% while taken, without more major bleeding [[SUPP-007]], but the drug is off-label for this use and the decision depends on bleeding risk and whether you can take it reliably.

topics.title: Blockages: bile duct, stomach outlet and bowel
topics.orientation: The head of the pancreas sits beside three passageways: the bile duct, the duodenum and, through the peritoneum, the rest of the bowel. A tumor can block each, and each blockage has its own warning signs and its own fix.

section1.label: What this experience involves
section1.preview: A blocked bile duct causes jaundice and, if bacteria take hold in stagnant bile, cholangitis with fever and chills. A blocked duodenum (gastric outlet obstruction) causes fullness after a few mouthfuls, then vomiting of food eaten hours earlier. A blocked bowel from disease on the peritoneum causes cramping, a swollen abdomen and no stool or gas. Duodenal blockage is uncommon at diagnosis but developed in roughly 1 in 5 people with unresectable head tumors over the following months [[ANAT-032]].
section1.full: Bile-duct blockage is the most frequent and is usually managed with a self-expanding metal stent placed by endoscopy. Stents fail in predictable ways: in people drained before preoperative chemotherapy, plastic stents re-blocked in 39% versus 7.1% for covered metal stents, at a median of 126 days [[SUPP-013]], and over months of neoadjuvant treatment about 72% of metal stents kept draining, covered ones failing by slipping out of place (6.8%) and uncovered ones by tumor growing through the mesh (16.7%) [[SUPP-012]]. Metal stents also triggered pancreatitis or gallbladder inflammation more often than plastic (43% versus 15%) [[SUPP-013]]. When a stented duct becomes infected, antibiotics alone cannot clear it, and the Tokyo guideline grades severity to decide how urgently drainage must be restored [[SEC-SUPP-14]]. Gastric outlet obstruction is treated by holding the duodenum open with a stent or by creating a bypass. In a randomized trial, an endoscopic ultrasound-guided gastroenterostomy, which connects the stomach to the small bowel through an internal stent, had no recurrences at 12 months versus 15.4% with a duodenal stent, with similar complications [[SUPP-029]]; a second trial found reintervention within six months in 4% versus 29% [[SUPP-L08]]. The internal-bypass device is used off-label for this purpose in the US and is offered at expert centers. In the era before modern chemotherapy, a surgical bypass done preventively during an exploratory operation eliminated later obstruction (0 of 44 versus 8 of 43) without extra complications [[ANAT-032]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: These blockages happen because of where the tumor sits. The bile duct passes through the head of the pancreas; the duodenum wraps around it in a C-shape; and the pancreas lies behind the peritoneal lining, which cancer cells can seed. Growth of the tumor and the scar-like tissue it builds narrow these passages gradually, so the signs usually creep in over days to weeks rather than appearing suddenly, which is why a change in pattern deserves attention.
section2.full: Head tumors are the usual culprits for the first two blockages: 7 of the 8 late duodenal obstructions in the Johns Hopkins trial were from head tumors [[ANAT-032]], and jaundice at presentation marks the head in the large majority of cases [[ANAT-010]]. The sequence often runs jaundice first, then, months later, early fullness and vomiting as the duodenum narrows, which is why some centers consider a preventive bypass or an internal gastroenterostomy before the duodenum closes. A narrowed duodenum also changes how medicines and enzyme capsules move through the gut, so symptoms of maldigestion can worsen at the same time. Bowel obstruction from peritoneal disease is less common, usually later, and is handled differently: chemotherapy is withheld, the liposomal irinotecan label states it must not be given with bowel obstruction [[SEC-SUPP-11]], and treatment may be decompression (a tube to relieve the pressure), a stent or surgery depending on the site and the person's fitness. Each fix has a cost worth knowing in advance: stents can block and infect, bypasses need anesthesia, and the internal gastroenterostomy requires the stomach and bowel to lie close enough together. Draining the bile duct early, before an operation, is overall as safe as early surgery when a metal stent is used (serious adverse events 29.0% versus 26.5%) [[SUPP-008]], but it moves some risk into the waiting period, which is exactly when the warning signs below matter.

action_note.heading: When to call the care team now
action_note.text: Fever or shaking chills with jaundice, dark urine or pain under the right ribs are the signs of cholangitis and need same-day emergency assessment for antibiotics and drainage; this applies especially to anyone with a biliary stent [[SEC-SUPP-14]]. Vomiting food eaten hours earlier, repeated vomiting, or inability to keep fluids down suggests a blocked stomach outlet, and a swollen abdomen with cramping and no stool or gas suggests bowel obstruction; both need prompt evaluation, and chemotherapy should not be given until the blockage is addressed [[SEC-SUPP-11]]. A temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher is a fever during cancer treatment [[SEC-SUPP-03]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The gastric outlet obstruction trial [[SUPP-029]] has reported results only through its registry entry, without a peer-reviewed paper, and the second trial [[SUPP-L08]] was retracted and republished with corrections in 2025, so both should be read as consistent but provisional. Stent-failure figures come from one small retrospective series [[SUPP-013]] and one industry-sponsored trial reported mainly through its registry entry [[SUPP-012]]. The preventive-bypass trial [[ANAT-032]] predates modern chemotherapy, when survival was about eight months in both arms, so its 19% obstruction rate describes that era.
research_notes.how_studied: Stent trials follow patients from placement to surgery or death and record whether drainage was sustained, the mechanism of any failure (migration, ingrowth, occlusion) and complications such as pancreatitis and cholecystitis [[SUPP-012]][[SUPP-013]]. Gastric outlet trials randomize to duodenal stent versus endoscopic gastroenterostomy and measure the ability to eat on a four-point scale, reintervention and recurrence at six and twelve months [[SUPP-029]][[SUPP-L08]]. The preventive-bypass question was tested by randomizing people found unresectable at operation to bypass or no bypass and counting later obstruction [[ANAT-032]]. Cholangitis criteria combine fever, inflammatory blood tests, cholestasis and imaging [[SEC-SUPP-14]].

mechanism_notes.text: Preoperative drainage harmed patients in the plastic-stent era (serious complications 74% versus 39%) but not in the metal-stent trial (29% versus 27%), even though metal stents cause marked duct-wall fibrosis within days, which indicates that the harm came from stent occlusion and cholangitis rather than from the act of stenting or the fibrosis itself [[SUPP-L07]][[SUPP-008]][[SUPP-011]]. Stent caliber and patency, not drainage as such, decide the risk.

glossary.definition: Bacterial infection of a blocked bile duct, causing fever, chills and jaundice.
Blockage of the duodenum that stops the stomach emptying, causing vomiting of old food.
A mesh tube placed by endoscopy that springs open to hold a duct or bowel segment open.
An endoscopic procedure that creates an internal connection between the stomach and small bowel using a short wide stent.
A surgical bypass joining the stomach directly to the jejunum so food can skip a blocked duodenum.
Cancer deposits scattered over the lining of the abdominal cavity, which can kink or narrow the bowel.

related.statement: Gastric outlet obstruction occurs when a pancreatic head tumor narrows the duodenum that wraps around it.
Bile-duct blockage and cholangitis arise where the common bile duct passes through the pancreatic head to the ampulla.
A blocked bile duct is treated with a metal biliary stent, which itself can block or become infected.
Returning jaundice after a stent is the first sign that the stent has blocked.
Tumors in the head of the pancreas cause almost all bile-duct and duodenal blockages.
Cancer deposits on the peritoneum are the usual cause of bowel obstruction in pancreatic cancer.
Fever with a blocked or stented bile duct is cholangitis and is managed as an infection emergency.

faq.q: My stent was placed three months ago and my urine is dark again. Is that the stent?
faq.a: Probably. Plastic stents re-blocked in 39% at a median of 126 days and metal stents in about 7% in one series [[SUPP-013]], and about a quarter of metal stents needed attention over months of chemotherapy [[SUPP-012]]. Dark urine or returning jaundice should be reported the same day; with fever or chills it is an emergency [[SEC-SUPP-14]].

topics.title: Eating and nutrition through treatment
topics.orientation: Eating through pancreatic cancer treatment is a practical engineering problem: getting protein and calories into a body whose appetite, digestion and stomach capacity are all under attack. Dietitian support is part of standard care, not an extra.

section1.label: What this experience involves
section1.preview: Appetite falls, food tastes different during chemotherapy, meals may bring pain or bloating, and even food that is eaten may not be absorbed. US guidance recommends dietary counseling for everyone with cancer-related weight loss and advises against routine tube or intravenous feeding in advanced cancer, while allowing short courses of appetite medicines [[SEC-SUPP-05]]. The working aim is protein and energy in forms the gut can handle, with enzyme capsules whenever fat is passing through undigested.
section1.full: The evidence for specific measures is modest in size but concrete. After pancreatic surgery, a blinded trial gave elderly patients an extra 18 g of protein a day for six weeks: intake rose to 77.3 g versus 56.7 g on placebo, and the supplement group had better quality of life, better nutritional status and faster walking speed, with protein intake tracking muscle mass [[SUPP-016]]. In unresectable cancer, enzyme capsules with meals changed weight by +1.2% versus -3.7% on placebo over eight weeks and raised energy intake [[SUPP-L01]], while an omega-3-enriched protein drink stopped weight loss in both arms of a trial, with people managing on average 1.4 of the 2 cans a day prescribed, which shows how adherence limits supplements [[SUPP-L02]]. Vitamins matter because the fat-soluble ones travel with fat: in advanced disease vitamin D was low in 44% and vitamin A in 18% [[ANAT-021]]. Appetite medicines in US guidance are short courses of a progestin or corticosteroid, with low-dose olanzapine added as an option in 2023; anamorelin, approved in Japan, is not approved in the US [[SEC-SUPP-05]]. The limits are real: after total pancreatectomy, 59% of patients met criteria for malnutrition at 12 months despite care [[SUPP-036]]. A workable day often looks like six small protein-first meals with enzymes at each, rather than three large ones.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Pancreatic cancer undermines eating through several mechanisms at once, which is why ordinary advice to 'eat more' fails. Enzyme insufficiency sends fat and protein through unabsorbed; a narrowed duodenum or a stomach pressed by tumor fills early; signaling proteins such as GDF-15, released by the tumor, switch off appetite in the brain; and chemotherapy alters taste and causes nausea. Muscle can be lost while weight holds, so the scale underestimates the problem [[SUPP-003]]. None of this is a failure of effort.
section2.full: Each mechanism has a matching response. For maldigestion, enzymes are dosed with every meal and snack and increased until stools normalize, with acid suppression added if needed [[SEC-SUPP-09]]; restricting fat is the wrong answer, because fat is the densest calorie source and the enzymes exist to handle it. For early fullness, smaller and more frequent meals, liquids between rather than with meals, and protein first make use of limited capacity; persistent vomiting of old food is a blockage, not a diet problem. For cytokine-driven loss of appetite, no approved US drug treats the cause; the GDF-15 antibody ponsegromab raised weight by up to 2.81 kg over 12 weeks in phase 2 and is in a phase 3 trial for pancreatic cancer cachexia, so this may change [[SUPP-014]]. For chemotherapy effects, anti-nausea prevention and timing meals away from infusion days help. Protein targets are higher than usual because muscle is being broken down; the post-surgical trial's 77 g a day is a reasonable marker of what 'enough' looked like in that setting [[SUPP-016]]. What nutrition cannot do is reverse cachexia by itself, since six months of resistance training did not change CT-measured muscle and supplements arrested rather than reversed weight loss [[SUPP-015]][[SUPP-L02]]. The realistic goal is to slow loss, keep strength for treatment, and preserve the pleasure of eating.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The protein trial [[SUPP-016]] is single-center, six weeks long and in elderly post-surgical patients, and the size of its walking-speed effect is not available to this atlas. The enzyme and omega-3 trials [[SUPP-L01]][[SUPP-L02]] are available to this atlas only as abstracts, from 1998 and 2003. Guideline recommendations [[SEC-SUPP-05]] rest on mixed-cancer evidence. None of the studies cited here tests a particular diet pattern, and the malnutrition rate after total pancreatectomy [[SUPP-036]] comes from 41 patients at one center.
research_notes.how_studied: Nutrition trials randomize a supplement against a placebo drink with the same calories and measure intake by food diary, body composition by bioimpedance (a measurement using a small electrical current), and function by walking speed, over weeks [[SUPP-016]]. Weight trials in advanced cancer weigh patients at fixed intervals and report percentage change [[SUPP-L01]][[SUPP-L02]]. Micronutrient status is measured in blood at dietitian assessment [[ANAT-021]]. Malnutrition after surgery is classified by standard criteria combining weight loss, intake and muscle mass [[SUPP-036]].

mechanism_notes.text: Weight loss despite adequate enzyme replacement in many patients shows that maldigestion and the cytokine-driven muscle-breakdown arm operate independently: enzymes restore absorption but cannot switch off GDF-15 signaling, which suppresses appetite and drives muscle breakdown regardless of calories delivered [[SUPP-002]][[SUPP-014]][[SUPP-003]]. Nutrition therefore works best in combination with treatment of the systemic drive, which is currently investigational.

glossary.definition: A state in which intake or absorption falls short of the body's needs, measured by weight loss, intake and muscle.
A drink or powder providing concentrated protein and calories between or with meals.
Vitamins A, D, E and K, which are absorbed with dietary fat and run low when fat is not digested.
A hormone-like drug such as megestrol used in short courses to stimulate appetite.
Feeling full after only a few mouthfuls.

related.statement: Nutrition slows the weight loss of pancreatic cancer cachexia but cannot by itself reverse its systemic drive.
Nutrition advice in pancreatic cancer depends on enzyme replacement to make eaten fat and protein absorbable.
Enzyme capsules taken with every meal are the first step in nutrition through pancreatic cancer treatment.
Appetite medicines and investigational GDF-15 blockade address the part of weight loss that nutrition cannot.
Protein intake and activity together preserve the muscle and function needed to tolerate treatment.
Persistent vomiting of old food is a blocked stomach outlet rather than a nutrition problem.

faq.q: Should I avoid fat?
faq.a: No. Fat is the densest source of calories, and the problem is undigested fat, not fat itself; enzyme capsules with every meal raised fat absorption by about 26 percentage points in a placebo-controlled trial [[SUPP-002]]. Dose the enzymes to the meal rather than shrinking the meal.

faq.q: Do nutrition drinks help?
faq.a: They help when they are drunk: in a trial of an enriched protein drink, weight loss stopped in both arms but people managed only 1.4 of 2 cans a day [[SUPP-L02]], and after surgery an extra 18 g of protein daily improved walking speed and quality of life [[SUPP-016]]. Small volumes taken between meals work better than large ones that replace them.

topics.title: Activity, exercise and function
topics.orientation: How far you can walk and how easily you can rise from a chair are measures the care team watches, because physical function affects which treatments are offered and how well they are tolerated. It can be improved even during chemotherapy, within limits set by the disease.

section1.label: What this experience involves
section1.preview: Physical function is measured simply: distance walked in six minutes, time to stand from a chair five times, gait speed, and the clinician's performance-status score. In 50 people exercising at home during preoperative chemotherapy, six-minute walk distance rose from 462.5 to 488.2 meters, a gain large enough to matter in daily life, and sit-to-stand time and gait speed also improved [[SUPP-017]]. Exercise during and after treatment is recommended; it does not require a gym or a program.
section1.full: Performance status, the 0-4 scale oncologists use for how much of the day a person is up and active, is both a prognostic factor and an entry ticket: the FOLFIRINOX trial enrolled only people at 0-1 [[TX-L02]], and in the CASSINI pancreatic cohort a status of 2 or worse carried a hazard ratio for death of 5.29 (more than five times the rate) [[SUPP-007]]. That is why function is worth protecting. In the home program, increases in self-reported aerobic and light activity were associated with walking gains, more light activity with better quality of life, and more sedentary time with worse [[SUPP-017]]. A randomized trial of six months of progressive resistance training found that supervised sessions improved arm and knee strength and maximal workload compared with usual care, with adherence of 64% supervised and 78% at home, and no change in body weight [[SUPP-L12]]. The limit is important and is not the patient's doing: the same trial's CT analysis found no effect of training on muscle area or any other body compartment, while muscle area correlated strongly with strength, and people who lost muscle over six months had a median survival of 24.6 months versus 50.8 months for those who gained [[SUPP-015]]. Strength can improve while mass does not, because a body-wide muscle-breakdown signal from the cancer sets mass. A realistic target is daily walking plus two short strength sessions a week, scaled to the week of the chemotherapy cycle.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Exercise is being studied for effects on the tumor itself, and the findings are intriguing but experimental. Tumors removed from people who exercised during preoperative treatment had about twice the blood-vessel density of controls [[SUPP-018]] and more cancer-killing CD8 T cells [[SUPP-019]]. In mice, exercise improved gemcitabine delivery and recruited T cells through IL-15, an immune signaling molecule. Whether this changes survival in people has not been tested, so activity is advised for function and well-being, not as cancer treatment.
section2.full: The vascular finding came from a prehabilitation trial: resected tumors from exercising patients had 7.0 vessels per microscope field versus 3.5 in matched controls and higher microvessel density, with more elongated vessels and open lumens, while in mice exercise remodeled tumor vessels, accelerated regression and delayed regrowth with gemcitabine without changing the drug's uptake transporter [[SUPP-018]]. The immune finding came from a separate program: in mice, treadmill running reduced tumor growth through CD8 (cytotoxic) T cells carrying the IL-15 receptor, cut suppressive myeloid cells (immune cells that dampen T-cell attack), and sensitized tumors to anti-PD-1 checkpoint immunotherapy (a drug that releases a brake on T cells); in patients, preoperative exercise was associated with more CD8 T cells inside the tumor than in historical controls [[SUPP-019]]. Both are hypotheses about delivery and immunity in a tumor known for collapsed vessels and excluded T cells, and both stop short of the question that matters, whether exercising people live longer. Historical controls, small samples and selection (fitter people exercise more) all limit the human data. What is established is the functional and quality-of-life benefit [[SUPP-017]][[SUPP-L12]]. Fatigue, pain, neuropathy and low blood counts legitimately reduce what is possible in a given week; the practical advice is to keep some movement every day, scale rather than stop, and treat a fall in function as a symptom to report rather than a lapse.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The home-exercise study [[SUPP-017]] had no control group and relied partly on self-report, so its walking gains could include practice and regression to the mean. The resistance-training trial [[SUPP-L12]] is available to this atlas only as an abstract; its CT secondary analysis [[SUPP-015]] was small and mixed stages. The tumor-biology studies [[SUPP-018]][[SUPP-019]] compare exercise-trial participants with historical controls, so differences in vessels and T cells may partly reflect who enrolled; the mechanisms come from mice. Performance-status prognostic figures [[SUPP-007]] describe trial populations.
research_notes.how_studied: Function is measured with the six-minute walk test, the five-times sit-to-stand test, gait speed and accelerometers that record minutes of light, moderate and sedentary activity, related to quality-of-life questionnaires by regression [[SUPP-017]]. Body composition is quantified on CT at the third lumbar vertebra before and after a training period [[SUPP-015]]. Tumor vascularity and immune infiltrate are counted on stained sections of resected tumors (CD31 for vessels, CD8 and granzyme B for T cells) and compared with controls, with mouse experiments testing cause by ablating cell types or blocking signals [[SUPP-018]][[SUPP-019]].

mechanism_notes.text: Exercise may improve chemotherapy delivery by remodeling tumor vessels, since exercised mouse tumors had more open vessels and better gemcitabine response, and may recruit cytotoxic T cells through IL-15 signaling; the human tissue findings are consistent but drawn from historical comparisons [[SUPP-018]][[SUPP-019]]. A randomized trial with survival or pathological response as the endpoint would be needed to turn this into advice.

Strength rises with training while CT muscle mass does not because the systemic catabolic drive of cachexia sets mass independently of loading, so function gains come from neural and metabolic adaptation [[SUPP-015]][[SUPP-L12]]. This is why exercise and cytokine-directed treatment are complementary rather than alternatives [[SUPP-014]].

glossary.definition: A 0-4 clinician score of how active and self-sufficient a person is; 0 is fully active, 2 means in bed less than half the day.
A functional test measuring how far a person can walk in six minutes.
Exercise and nutrition before an operation to improve fitness for surgery.
Low skeletal muscle mass, usually measured on a CT scan.
The number of small blood vessels per area of tumor tissue under the microscope.
The cytotoxic T cell that can recognize and kill cancer cells.

related.statement: Cachexia limits muscle mass even when training improves strength and function.
Physical function, scored as performance status, is one of the fitness questions that decides which treatments are offered.
Light regular activity was associated with less fatigue and improved walking capacity during treatment.
Exercise was associated with more open blood vessels inside resected tumors, an experimental finding.
Preoperative exercise was associated with more CD8 T cells inside tumors, an experimental finding.
The months of chemotherapy before surgery are the window in which prehabilitation is offered.

faq.q: Is it safe to exercise during chemotherapy?
faq.a: Home-based walking and strength work during preoperative chemotherapy improved function in 50 patients without reported harm [[SUPP-017]], and supervised resistance training was completed by about two-thirds of participants in a randomized trial [[SUPP-L12]]. Low blood counts, fever, neuropathy or a fresh stent are reasons to scale down for that week and check with the team.

topics.title: Mood, mind and support
topics.orientation: Distress after a pancreatic cancer diagnosis is expected, and depression and anxiety are common, treatable and consequential: they change what treatment people receive. Support for the family is part of the care, not an afterthought.

section1.label: What this experience involves
section1.preview: Shock, fear, anger and grief are normal responses to this diagnosis and do not need a label. Depression and anxiety are different: persistent low mood, loss of interest, hopelessness, or worry that prevents sleep or decisions. They are common enough that US guidance recommends routine distress screening and early referral to palliative care, which includes psychological support [[SEC-SUPP-08]]. At palliative-care admission, distress from appetite loss was strongly linked to psychological and spiritual distress [[SUPP-032]].
section1.full: Mood has measurable consequences for treatment. Among 23,745 US Medicare patients with pancreatic cancer, those with a prior depression diagnosis were less likely to undergo resection for localized disease (odds ratio 0.63, where values below 1 mean lower odds) and less likely to receive chemotherapy for metastatic disease (odds ratio 0.79); their survival was shorter, and adjusting for whether they received treatment removed most of the difference, which points to treatment uptake, not biology, as the main route [[SUPP-009]]. That cohort was elderly and treated before 2005, but the mechanism is plausible today: depression drains the energy needed to attend appointments, tolerate side effects and ask about options, and clinicians may under-offer treatment to people who seem to be struggling. Symptoms and mood feed each other. Among people with pain distress, 79% also had sleep distress and 77% fatigue distress; appetite distress was associated with psychological and spiritual problems (odds ratio 1.78) and with pain severity [[SUPP-032]]. Steroids given with chemotherapy cause insomnia and mood swings for a day or two each cycle, and opioids and poor sleep flatten mood further. Early palliative care in a small prospective study lowered symptom burden in metastatic patients but did not change depression or anxiety scores, which suggests those need their own treatment rather than resolving as symptoms improve [[SUPP-030]]. A person who stops answering calls from the clinic may be depressed rather than disengaged.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Pancreatic cancer brings particular pressures: a diagnosis that arrives late and fast, treatment plans that change, visible weight loss, and statistics that are easy to find and hard to interpret. Caregivers absorb much of this, and the guideline names caregiver support as a component of care [[SEC-SUPP-08]]. Talking, with family, a counselor, a chaplain or a peer, and treating depression when it is present are the evidence-supported responses.
section2.full: What helps, in practice: psychological support from psycho-oncology or counseling services, which many cancer centers provide; antidepressant medicines, which are effective for depression in people with cancer and can be chosen to help sleep or appetite as well; attention to the physical drivers, since untreated pain, nausea and insomnia make mood worse; and structured communication with the care team, so that uncertainty about the plan does not become dread. The randomized trial of systematic early palliative care in pancreatic cancer improved the trial-outcome index of quality of life by 3.83 points (95% confidence interval 0.10-7.57) without changing survival [[SUPP-L10]], and quality-of-life gains in the prospective study were largest in people with metastatic disease [[SUPP-030]]. Family members often need permission to be looked after themselves; caregiver distress is screened under the same guideline [[SEC-SUPP-08]]. Two practical points: distress tends to spike at transitions, at diagnosis, before surgery, at a change of plan and at the end of treatment, so asking for help at those moments is sensible rather than weak; and thoughts of not wanting to go on should be told to the care team the same day, because they are a treatable symptom. Reading survival statistics is best done with someone who can explain which group of people a number describes, since population figures were never built to predict one person.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The depression study [[SUPP-009]] identified depression from insurance claims in people over 65 treated between 1992 and 2005, so it may under-count depression and reflects an era with fewer treatment options; its finding that treatment uptake explains the survival gap is an adjustment result, not a trial. The palliative-care studies [[SUPP-030]][[SUPP-L10]] measured quality of life, not depression, as the primary outcome, and the one that measured depression found no change over 16 weeks. No trial of antidepressants or psychotherapy specific to pancreatic cancer is cited here; those statements rest on general oncology practice.
research_notes.how_studied: Registry studies link cancer diagnoses to claims for depression, resection and chemotherapy, and model survival with and without adjustment for treatment to see how much of the gap treatment explains [[SUPP-009]]. Palliative-care cohorts record patient-rated distress on symptom scales at admission and use logistic regression to find which problems travel together [[SUPP-032]]. Early palliative-care trials randomize to systematic versus on-demand referral and compare quality-of-life questionnaires such as FACT-Hep, a scale for liver and pancreatic cancers, over months [[SUPP-L10]][[SUPP-030]].

mechanism_notes.text: Depression shortens survival in pancreatic cancer mainly through treatment selection: the survival disadvantage largely disappeared once receipt of resection or chemotherapy was accounted for [[SUPP-009]]. This implies that treating depression and ensuring equal access to treatment options could recover much of that gap, a prediction no trial has yet tested.

glossary.definition: A brief routine questionnaire asking about emotional, practical and physical problems at clinic visits.
Psychological and psychiatric care specialized for people with cancer and their families.
Specialist care for symptoms, communication and decisions that runs alongside cancer treatment.
The physical, emotional and practical strain on family members providing care.

related.statement: Distress and depression in pancreatic cancer are addressed by palliative-care teams that include psychological support.
Depression and poor sleep are common contributors to fatigue in pancreatic cancer.
Pain distress and psychological distress travel together in pancreatic cancer and each worsens the other.
Survival statistics are a major source of distress and are best read with someone who can explain which group a number describes.

faq.q: Can depression affect my treatment?
faq.a: Yes, through what gets offered and taken up: in a large US registry, people with a prior depression diagnosis were less likely to have surgery (odds ratio 0.63) or chemotherapy (odds ratio 0.79), and that explained much of their shorter survival [[SUPP-009]]. Treating depression is part of getting the full range of options.

topics.title: Supportive and palliative care alongside treatment
topics.orientation: Palliative care is specialist care for symptoms, communication and decisions that runs alongside cancer treatment from the time of diagnosis. It is not the same as hospice, which is the part reserved for the final phase when disease-directed treatment stops.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: A palliative-care team manages pain, nausea, bowel problems, appetite, breathlessness, sleep and mood, coordinates stents, enzymes and nerve blocks, supports families, and keeps the person's goals in the conversation when plans change. US guidance since 2024 says people with advanced cancer should be referred early, concurrently with active treatment, with distress screening and caregiver support built in [[SEC-SUPP-08]]. It is added to oncology care, not substituted for it.
section1.full: Pancreatic cancer is a strong case for early involvement because the symptom burden is high and arrives in clusters. Across 15,536 people admitted to Australian palliative services, 69% reported distress from pain and 60% from appetite loss, and among those, around 8 in 10 also reported distress from sleep, nausea and bowel problems and about 3 in 4 from fatigue and breathing [[SUPP-032]]. The randomized evidence in this disease is modest but positive: in a multicenter trial of 207 people, systematic early palliative care improved the FACT-Hep trial-outcome index, a quality-of-life score for liver and pancreatic cancers, by 3.83 points (95% confidence interval 0.10-7.57) and the hepatobiliary symptom score by 2.51 points compared with referral on demand, with no difference in survival [[SUPP-L10]]. A 40-patient prospective study found an overall quality-of-life change that did not reach significance (+6.89 points), but a clear gain in people with metastatic disease (+15.3 points) and a fall in symptom burden on the Edmonton scale (-7.4), with no change in depression or anxiety [[SUPP-030]]. In practice the team addresses the pancreatic-specific problems covered elsewhere in this atlas: enzyme replacement that relieved diarrhea within a week and pain within three [[SUPP-021]], nerve blocks for pain [[ANAT-034]], anticoagulation for clots and stents for blockages. Hospice becomes the setting when chemotherapy no longer helps, and the same team usually continues.

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Treatment for pancreatic cancer is intensive, symptoms are often caused by the disease rather than the drugs, and plans change. A team whose job is symptom control and communication makes chemotherapy more tolerable, catches problems such as clots and cholangitis earlier, and helps people decide how much treatment they want. Early referral did not shorten survival in any study here, and quality-of-life gains were largest in metastatic disease [[SUPP-030]][[SUPP-L10]].
section2.full: Three practical reasons stand out. First, many pancreatic symptoms have specific fixes that general oncology visits can miss: undigested fat needs enzymes, not antidiarrheals [[SUPP-021]]; back pain from the celiac plexus may respond to a block when opioids alone fall short [[ANAT-034]]; appetite loss has a cytokine (tumor signaling protein) basis that counseling alone cannot reverse [[SUPP-014]]. Second, depression and distress reduce treatment uptake, and in a large registry depression explained much of a survival gap through lower rates of surgery and chemotherapy [[SUPP-009]]; screening and support are the countermeasure. Third, decisions in this disease are frequent and hard: whether to continue a second-line regimen, whether to accept a stent exchange, when to stop. A palliative team's role is to make those decisions informed rather than to steer them toward less treatment. The limits are worth stating. The quality-of-life effects are modest, measured over months, and come from one randomized trial and small cohorts; no pancreatic study shows a survival benefit, and none shows harm. Access varies, and some people hear 'palliative' as 'giving up'; the guideline's word is 'concurrent', meaning alongside, which is how it is meant. For families, the team is often the first to name caregiver exhaustion and to arrange practical help [[SEC-SUPP-08]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The one randomized pancreatic trial [[SUPP-L10]] is available to this atlas only as an abstract; its 3.83-point gain on a quality-of-life index is small but statistically clear, and it reports no survival difference. The prospective study [[SUPP-030]] was not randomized and its primary endpoint was not met, so the metastatic subgroup gain is hypothesis-generating. Symptom-prevalence figures [[SUPP-032]] describe people already referred to palliative services and are not stratified by stage at diagnosis. The guideline [[SEC-SUPP-08]] draws on trials across cancers, where early palliative care has shown quality-of-life and, in some, survival benefits.
research_notes.how_studied: Early palliative care is tested by randomizing people to systematic referral at diagnosis versus referral when symptoms demand it, then comparing validated quality-of-life questionnaires, such as FACT-Hep and its trial-outcome index, at fixed intervals, with survival as a safety check [[SUPP-L10]]. Prospective cohorts enroll patients at referral and track FACT-Hep and Edmonton Symptom Assessment scores over 16 weeks [[SUPP-030]]. Symptom-burden registries collect patient-rated distress for each symptom at every admission and model which symptoms co-occur [[SUPP-032]].

mechanism_notes.text: Early palliative care improves quality of life in pancreatic cancer mainly by addressing disease-driven symptom clusters with mechanism-specific treatments (enzymes, nerve blocks, stents, anticoagulation) and by removing the barriers to treatment that depression creates, rather than through any direct effect on the tumor [[SUPP-L10]][[SUPP-030]][[SUPP-009]]. This fits the absence of a survival signal in either direction and the larger gains in metastatic disease, where symptom burden is highest.

topics.clinical_status: Guideline-recommended in the US as of 8 Oct 2026: the ASCO 2024 guideline advises early referral of people with advanced cancer to interdisciplinary palliative care, concurrent with active treatment. It is a service, not a drug or device, so no regulatory approval applies.

glossary.definition: Specialist care for symptoms, communication and decisions that runs alongside cancer treatment.
Care focused entirely on comfort in the final phase of illness, after disease-directed treatment stops.
A quality-of-life questionnaire designed for people with liver, bile-duct and pancreatic cancers.
A short scale on which patients rate the severity of nine common symptoms.
Palliative care delivered at the same time as cancer treatment rather than after it.

Palliative care includes distress screening and psychological support for patients and caregivers.
Palliative-care teams coordinate the nutrition, enzyme and appetite measures used for cachexia.
Palliative-care teams help detect and manage the clots that are common in pancreatic cancer.

faq.q: Does seeing palliative care mean my doctors have given up?
faq.a: No. The guideline recommends it early and concurrently with active treatment for anyone with advanced cancer [[SEC-SUPP-08]], and in the pancreatic randomized trial it improved quality of life without any change in survival [[SUPP-L10]]. Hospice is a later and separate decision.

topics.title: Life after a Whipple or pancreatectomy
topics.orientation: A Whipple operation removes the head of the pancreas, the duodenum, the gallbladder and the lower bile duct and reconnects what remains. Recovery is measured in months, and some changes in digestion, blood sugar and weight are permanent but manageable.

section1.label: What this experience involves
section1.preview: The first weeks are about the three new joins healing. The join to the pancreas may leak digestive juice (a pancreatic fistula), the stomach may be slow to empty for days to weeks, and bleeding can occur; in a national series of the highest-risk glands, major complications affected 45.9% and a clinically relevant fistula 30%, with in-hospital mortality around 4% [[SURG-016]]. The following months bring new digestion, often enzyme capsules, sometimes new diabetes, and a weight that may settle below the old one.
section1.full: Delayed gastric emptying, defined by the international surgical group as needing a nasogastric (nose-to-stomach) tube beyond the third day or being unable to tolerate solid food by the end of the first week, is the most common early complaint and resolves with time [[SEC-SURG-02]]; whether the pylorus (the stomach's outlet valve) is preserved makes little difference to it or to survival [[SEC-SURG-09]]. A fistula drives most of the serious trouble: patients with one had major morbidity of 88.0% versus 28.3% and mortality of 6.3% versus 3.5% [[SURG-016]]. Digestion changes permanently because the duodenum and the head's enzyme-producing tissue are gone and the remaining pancreas drains into a jejunal loop (a loop of small intestine): on high-dose enzymes, fat absorption improved by 25.6 percentage points more than placebo, but only 7 of 26 (27%) people with Whipple-type reconstructions reached near-normal absorption, because enzymes and food leave the stomach out of step [[SUPP-002]]. Dumping, in which food enters the small bowel too fast, causes cramps, sweating and faintness after meals and is managed with smaller, lower-sugar meals. New diabetes appeared in 30.2% by six months in one series, predicted by body-mass index rather than by how much pancreas remained [[SUPP-033]]. An extra 18 g of protein a day in the first six weeks improved walking speed and quality of life in elderly patients [[SUPP-016]]. Adjuvant chemotherapy usually starts once recovery allows; most people in the adjuvant FOLFIRINOX trial received it at reduced dose intensity and still benefited [[TX-003]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: These changes follow directly from what the operation removes and rebuilds: no duodenum means no bicarbonate-rich mixing chamber for enzymes; a smaller pancreas means fewer enzymes and islets; a stomach joined to the jejunum means faster, less regulated emptying. More than five years after surgery, overall quality of life was in the normal range, but pancreatic-type pain scores around 40 out of 100 and bowel-habit changes persisted in many, and about half reported bloating [[SUPP-031]].
section2.full: The long view comes from 248 five-year survivors at one US center. Global health and functional scores were similar whether or not people had suffered an early complication, which means a stormy first month does not condemn the years after; those with early complications even reported lower fatigue (21.4 versus 28.1) and diarrhea scores [[SUPP-031]]. What persisted were pancreatic pain, altered bowel habit (30-41 points) and bloating in 42-56%, which track the digestive rebuild rather than the cancer [[SUPP-031]]. The two levers for weight are enzyme dosing, titrated until stools normalize with acid suppression added if needed [[SEC-SUPP-09]], and protein-first eating. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K) deserve monitoring because fat absorption remains subnormal. Blood sugar needs a check at each visit; diabetes after partial resection is driven by weight and the quality of the remnant, so it can appear years later [[SUPP-035]]. Total pancreatectomy, done when the whole gland must go, replaces this picture with immediate insulin-dependent diabetes (HbA1c, the three-month average blood sugar, 8.0% at 12 months on injections or a pump) and a 59% rate of malnutrition at one year [[SUPP-036]]. Surveillance scans and CA 19-9 continue because recurrence remains the main risk after resection; the survival figures that apply are those for people who completed surgery and chemotherapy, not all-comers. A typical year: three months regaining strength, chemotherapy from month two or three, then a new normal of enzymes with every meal.

action_note.heading: In the weeks after surgery
action_note.text: Fever of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher, new or worsening abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, or drain fluid that turns cloudy or bloody can signal a leak, infection or bleeding at one of the new joins and should be reported the same day; bleeding after pancreatic surgery can appear days to weeks later and is a recognized emergency [[SEC-SURG-03]][[SEC-SUPP-03]]. Fever with jaundice or dark urine suggests infection in the rebuilt bile duct and needs urgent assessment [[SEC-SUPP-14]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The national complication figures [[SURG-016]] describe the very highest-risk glands (soft texture, small duct) in a centralized Dutch system, so typical rates are lower; the long-term survey [[SUPP-031]] mixes benign and malignant indications, had no pre-operative baseline and 19% non-response, and survivors by definition exclude those who died early. The enzyme trial [[SUPP-002]] was one week double-blind in 58 patients. Diabetes rates [[SUPP-033]][[SUPP-035]] vary with follow-up length. No study here measures dumping syndrome or vitamin status after a Whipple specifically; those statements rest on established surgical physiology.
research_notes.how_studied: Complications are graded by international consensus definitions: fistula by drain amylase and clinical consequence, delayed gastric emptying by tube duration and diet tolerance, hemorrhage by timing and severity [[SEC-SURG-01]][[SEC-SURG-02]][[SEC-SURG-03]]. Long-term outcomes are surveyed with the EORTC QLQ-C30 and pancreatic PAN26 questionnaires, standard patient-reported instruments, with scores compared against clinical-relevance thresholds [[SUPP-031]]. Fat absorption is measured by stool fat collection on a fixed-fat diet [[SUPP-002]], and post-operative diabetes by scheduled glucose and HbA1c with CT volumetry of the remnant [[SUPP-033]].

mechanism_notes.text: Persistent maldigestion after a Whipple is better explained by mistiming than by enzyme quantity: coated enzyme microspheres and food leave the stomach asynchronously into a jejunal limb that lacks the duodenum's bicarbonate, so lipase is released at the wrong moment and partly inactivated by acid, which is why only about a quarter of patients normalize fat absorption at high doses [[INF-SUPP-01]][[SUPP-002]]. Opened or uncoated enzymes mixed with food plus acid suppression would test this against the alternative of simple remnant insufficiency.

glossary.definition: A leak of enzyme-rich pancreatic juice from the join between the pancreas and the bowel after surgery.
A slow-to-empty stomach after pancreatic surgery, needing a tube or a liquid diet beyond the first week.
Cramps, sweating and faintness after meals when food enters the small bowel too quickly.
A variant of the operation that keeps the stomach's outlet valve.
The part of the pancreas left in place after surgery.
Chemotherapy given after surgery to reduce the chance of recurrence.

related.statement: Life after a Whipple follows from what the Whipple operation removes and rebuilds.
Fistula, delayed gastric emptying and bleeding are the early complications that shape the first weeks after a Whipple.
Enzyme insufficiency after a Whipple persists in most people because the rebuilt anatomy mistimes enzyme and food delivery.
Digestion after a Whipple is supported by enzyme replacement capsules taken with every meal.

Total pancreatectomy replaces the partial-resection picture with immediate insulin-dependent diabetes.
