faq.q: Will I need enzymes forever?
faq.a: Most people do after a Whipple, because the duodenum and part of the gland are gone and the remaining enzymes arrive out of step with food; even on high doses only 27% of Whipple-type patients normalized fat absorption in a trial [[SUPP-002]]. The dose is adjusted to stools and weight rather than stopped [[SEC-SUPP-09]].

faq.q: Will life feel normal again?
faq.a: For most long-term survivors, largely yes: global quality of life more than five years after a Whipple was in the normal range regardless of early complications, though bloating, bowel changes and some pancreatic-type pain persisted in many [[SUPP-031]].

topics.title: The pancreas
topics.orientation: The pancreas is a soft, elongated gland about 15 cm long that lies deep in the upper abdomen, behind the stomach and in front of the spine, with its head tucked into the curve of the duodenum and its tail reaching the spleen.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The pancreas does two jobs with two different cell populations. Most of its bulk is exocrine tissue: acinar cells make digestive enzymes and duct cells add bicarbonate-rich fluid, and together they deliver about 2.5 liters of juice a day into the duodenum through the pancreatic duct [[SEC-ANAT-03]]. Scattered through this tissue, the islets release insulin and glucagon directly into the blood to regulate blood sugar.
section1.full: The gland is described in four parts from right to left. The head sits in the C-shaped curve of the duodenum and includes a hook-like extension, the uncinate process, that curls behind the superior mesenteric vein. The neck is a thin bridge that crosses in front of that vein at the point where it becomes the portal vein. The body runs leftward across the front of the aorta and spine with the splenic vein lying along its back, and the tail ends at the hilum of the spleen. Above the body, the celiac axis leaves the aorta and splits into the hepatic, splenic and left gastric arteries, and the celiac nerve plexus surrounds it. In healthy adults the whole gland occupies roughly 70 cm3 on CT (computed tomography) scans, of which about 45 cm3 is working tissue and the rest is fat that increases with age and body weight [[ANAT-018]]. Function is not spread evenly: islets are about twice as dense in the tail as in the head or body, while a region rich in cells making a minor hormone, pancreatic polypeptide, is confined to the uncinate process [[ANAT-005]]. A meal sets the gland working through hormones released by the duodenum, so the pancreas is coupled to the gut it drains into, and the bile duct from the liver passes down through the head to share the pancreatic duct's opening.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the common pancreatic cancer, and where in the gland it starts largely determines how it is found. About seven in ten arise in the head, where even a small tumor can block the bile duct and cause jaundice; body and tail tumors give no early signal and are more often metastatic when discovered (42% of head versus 69% of body and 84% of tail tumors in a national registry) [[ANAT-003]].
section2.full: The cancer is called "ductal" because its cells form duct-like glands under the microscope, not because every tumor begins in a duct. It is a different disease from the far rarer pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, which arise from islet-type cells, occur at about 2 per million people per year and have a median survival measured in years rather than months [[ANAT-008]], and from acinar cell carcinoma, which is also uncommon and behaves differently [[ANAT-044]]. Location shapes the whole course. Head tumors sit in a crowded plane where the bile duct, the portal and superior mesenteric veins, the hepatic and superior mesenteric arteries, regional lymph node stations and the autonomic nerve plexus all converge, so they produce early symptoms but also involve these structures early [[ANAT-007]][[ANAT-019]]. Body and tail tumors grow in a quieter space and are far less likely to be removable at diagnosis: in the same registry 17% of head tumors were resected versus 4% of body and 7% of tail tumors [[ANAT-003]]. Part of that gap is later detection and part is biology, because body and tail tumors are enriched for the aggressive squamous molecular type, a gene-activity pattern associated with worse outcomes [[ANAT-024]]. The gland's two functions also fail in characteristic ways: enzyme insufficiency is present in about two-thirds of patients with advanced disease [[ANAT-021]], and diabetes is present in roughly 47% at diagnosis, three-quarters of it new [[ANAT-015]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The location figures come from population registries, which include everyone diagnosed rather than only those fit for surgery, so they describe the full distribution of disease [[ANAT-003]][[ANAT-030]]. The survival gap after resection between head and body/tail tumors disappeared after adjustment in the Dutch registry [[ANAT-003]], yet a sequenced surgical cohort found resected body/tail tumors lived about half as long (12.1 versus 22.0 months disease-specific survival), driven by the squamous subtype [[ANAT-024]]. Both lead time and biology contribute, in proportions that differ by cohort. Volumes and islet distributions come from imaging and donor pancreata, not from people with cancer [[ANAT-018]][[ANAT-005]].
research_notes.how_studied: Registry studies classify tumors by site codes recorded at diagnosis and follow survival through national death records; they capture the whole population but lack margin status, chemotherapy detail and, in one series, a definite location for a quarter of cases [[ANAT-030]]. Pancreas volume was measured by tracing the gland on CT scans of people without pancreatic disease and separating fat from working tissue [[ANAT-018]]. Islet distribution was mapped by staining slices of donor pancreata from head, body and tail and counting endocrine area, then confirmed by isolating islets from glands split at the neck [[ANAT-005]]. Incidence and survival of neuroendocrine tumors came from the US SEER registry [[ANAT-008]].

mechanism_notes.text: A tumor of only 1–2 cm3, often in the head far from the islet-rich tail, raises blood sugar across the whole body, and the diabetes often resolves when the tumor is removed even though the operation takes more gland [[INF-ANAT-01]] [[ANAT-015]][[ANAT-016]][[ANAT-006]]. The simplest reading is that the tumor imposes a reversible, mediator-driven suppression on islets everywhere rather than destroying them, which is why the pancreas's endocrine failure in cancer behaves so differently from the failure that follows surgery.

glossary.definition: The part of the pancreas that makes digestive enzymes and fluid and sends them through ducts into the intestine.
The hormone-making part of the pancreas, the islets, which release insulin and glucagon directly into the blood.
A hook-shaped extension of the pancreatic head that curls behind the superior mesenteric vein.
The first part of the small intestine, which wraps around the head of the pancreas.
The notch on an organ where its blood vessels enter and leave; the pancreatic tail reaches the hilum of the spleen.

The pancreas includes the neck, the thin segment that crosses in front of the superior mesenteric and portal veins.

The pancreas is mostly made of acinar cells, which manufacture digestive enzymes.
The pancreas's duct cells line the duct tree and secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid.
The pancreas contains the islets of Langerhans, which release insulin and glucagon.
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma arises within the pancreas, most often in the head.
The pancreas also gives rise to neuroendocrine tumors and acinar cell carcinoma, which are distinct from PDAC.

faq.q: Why is pancreatic cancer so often found late?
faq.a: The gland lies deep behind the stomach, and most of it has no neighbor whose blockage gives an early alarm. Jaundice from a head tumor is the one symptom that strongly points to the diagnosis (positive predictive value 22% in people over 60, meaning about one in five with recorded jaundice had the cancer), whereas pain, weight loss and new diabetes are individually weak signals and often precede diagnosis by many months [[ANAT-010]][[ANAT-022]].

faq.q: Can a person live without a pancreas?
faq.a: Yes. After total pancreatectomy, insulin-requiring diabetes is immediate and universal but usually manageable, with a median HbA1c of about 8% and very little low blood sugar on monitoring; digestive enzymes must be replaced with every meal, and malnutrition persisted in about 6 in 10 patients at one year in one cohort [[SUPP-036]].

topics.title: Head and uncinate process
topics.orientation: The head is the widest part of the pancreas, cradled in the C-shaped loop of the duodenum on the right side of the abdomen, with the lower bile duct running down through it and the uncinate process hooking behind the superior mesenteric vein.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The head holds the largest share of enzyme-making tissue and is where the pancreatic duct and the common bile duct run side by side to a shared opening in the duodenum at the ampulla. Its hook-shaped lower extension, the uncinate process, curls behind the superior mesenteric vein and reaches toward the superior mesenteric artery. The uncinate process contains nearly all of the gland's pancreatic polypeptide cells, a legacy of its separate embryonic origin [[ANAT-005]].
section1.full: Embryologically the pancreas forms from two buds that fuse: a dorsal bud that becomes the body, tail and upper head, and a ventral bud that rotates behind the duodenum to become the lower head and uncinate process. The ventral bud carries the bile duct with it, which is why the duct ends up embedded in the head rather than merely passing beside it. The gastroduodenal artery, a branch of the common hepatic artery, descends along the groove between the head and the neck, and the arcades (looping arterial connections) it forms with branches of the superior mesenteric artery supply both the head and the duodenum as a single unit; this shared blood supply is the reason the head cannot be removed without the duodenum. Behind the head lie the inferior vena cava and the right renal vein, separated from the gland by a thin fibrous plane; in front lies the outlet of the stomach. The uncinate process receives its nerves from the superior mesenteric plexus along the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, whereas the body and tail receive theirs directly from the celiac plexus [[ANAT-039]]. In about 16% of people the right hepatic artery, or an extra one, arises from the superior mesenteric artery instead of its usual origin and runs under the head and bile duct on its way to the liver [[ANAT-007]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Roughly seven in ten pancreatic cancers arise in the head [[ANAT-003]], and head tumors are the ones most likely to be caught while still removable, because even a small tumor here compresses the bile duct and produces jaundice. In a primary-care study jaundice had a positive predictive value for pancreatic cancer of 22% in people over 60 (meaning about one in five with recorded jaundice had the cancer), while no other single symptom reached 1% [[ANAT-010]].
section2.full: The same crowding that gives early warning also sets the limits of surgery. A head tumor grows within millimeters of the superior mesenteric vein and portal vein, the superior mesenteric artery behind the uncinate process, the lymph node stations in front of and behind the head and along the artery, and the nerve plexus around the artery, so it tends to involve these structures early [[ANAT-019]][[ANAT-013]]. In one mapping series of resected head cancers, 55% had node metastases, most often at the superior mesenteric artery station (34%) and the posterior head station (32%) [[ANAT-019]]. Perineural invasion (cancer growing along nerves), present in about 80% of untreated resected tumors, runs mainly along nerves outside the pancreas and is the usual reason a margin behind the uncinate process is positive [[ANAT-013]]. Removal requires the Whipple operation, which takes the head, duodenum, lower bile duct and often part of the stomach as a block; leakage from the join to the remaining pancreas occurs in about 30% of the softest glands and drives most serious complications [[SURG-016]]. Head tumors can also block the duodenum: nausea and vomiting are the presenting complaint in under 10%, but outlet obstruction developed in about one in five patients with unresectable head or periampullary cancer over the following months [[ANAT-032]]. Some small head tumors are invisible as a mass on CT (computed tomography) scans and are found only from the duct dilatation (widening) they cause [[DIAG-022]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The head-versus-body/tail comparisons describe where tumors were found and what happened next, not what a tumor would have done elsewhere; head tumors reach surgery more often (17% versus 4–7%) largely because jaundice forces earlier investigation [[ANAT-003]]. Lymph node and nerve station data come from a center performing extended dissections mostly after neoadjuvant therapy, so the proportions are lower than in historical untreated series, in which 70% of resected head cancers were node-positive [[ANAT-019]][[ANAT-038]]. The arterial-variant prevalence is from a single surgical series and is consistent with a 1,000-case reference study [[ANAT-007]][[SEC-ANAT-01]]. The outlet-obstruction figure predates modern chemotherapy and comes from patients already selected at laparotomy (open operation) [[ANAT-032]].
research_notes.how_studied: Lymphatic routes were mapped by labeling each dissected node with its anatomical station under the Japan Pancreas Society scheme and recording which stations contained cancer [[ANAT-019]][[SEC-ANAT-02]]. Perineural invasion was assessed by reviewing an average of 14 slides per resected specimen and recording whether invaded nerves lay inside or outside the pancreas and whether the margin was involved [[ANAT-013]]. Arterial variants were identified by blinded re-review of preoperative CT and MRI against operative findings [[ANAT-007]]. Nerve pathways to the uncinate process were traced in cadavers with a stain that highlights nerve fibers [[ANAT-039]].

mechanism_notes.text: The meal-stimulated rise in pancreatic polypeptide is blunted in cancer-associated diabetes and, in a small pilot, most blunted when the tumor is in the head [[INF-ANAT-03]] [[ANAT-017]][[ANAT-042]]. Because the pancreatic polypeptide cells are confined to the uncinate process [[ANAT-005]], a blunted response may be a local readout of damage to this part of the head, whereas the high blood sugar itself is a whole-gland effect that does not depend on location.

glossary.definition: The hook-shaped lower part of the pancreatic head that curls behind the superior mesenteric vein toward the superior mesenteric artery.
The small chamber where the bile duct and pancreatic duct join before opening into the duodenum.
Describing the region around the ampulla, where tumors of the pancreatic head, bile duct, ampulla and duodenum all arise.
A branch of the hepatic artery that runs down between the head and neck of the pancreas and supplies the head and duodenum.
A hormone made by cells concentrated in the uncinate process that rises after meals and is a marker of this region's function.

related.statement: The head and uncinate process form the right-hand, widest part of the pancreas.
The lower common bile duct runs down through the back of the pancreatic head to the ampulla.
The duodenum cradles the pancreatic head and shares its blood supply, so the two are removed together.
The uncinate process of the head hooks behind the superior mesenteric vein.
The uncinate process reaches toward the superior mesenteric artery, which lies behind the vein.
Lymph from the head drains to stations in front of and behind the head and along the superior mesenteric artery.
Nerves reach the uncinate process from the superior mesenteric plexus along the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery.
A head tumor is removed by the Whipple operation, which takes the head, duodenum and lower bile duct as one block.
A tumor in the pancreatic head blocks the bile duct and causes jaundice.

faq.q: What does "periampullary" mean on my report?
faq.a: It means the tumor sits in the region where the bile duct and pancreatic duct meet the duodenum, which includes cancers of the pancreatic head, the lower bile duct, the ampulla itself and the duodenal wall. These are different diseases with different outlooks, which is why the pathology report specifies the tissue of origin; symptom studies that group them together include a small share of non-pancreatic tumors [[ANAT-004]].

faq.q: Why does a head tumor have to be removed together with the duodenum?
faq.a: The head and the duodenum share the same arterial arcades from the gastroduodenal and superior mesenteric arteries and the bile duct runs through the head, so neither organ can be separated from the other with its blood supply intact. The Whipple operation removes them as a block, and the main risk afterward is leakage from the join to the remaining pancreas, which occurred in about 30% of the softest glands in a national audit [[SURG-016]].

topics.title: Neck of the pancreas (the genu)
aliases: where the pancreas crosses the vein
topics.orientation: The neck is the narrowest part of the pancreas, a short bridge about 2 cm wide that links the head to the body and lies directly in front of the place where the superior mesenteric vein joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The neck is defined by what lies behind it rather than by anything it does differently: it is the segment of gland draped over the superior mesenteric vein and portal vein, with the gastroduodenal artery marking its right-hand border and the splenic vein joining the portal vein just behind its left. Its tissue is ordinary exocrine pancreas, through which the main duct passes on its way from tail to head.
section1.full: The name "genu", Latin for knee, describes the bend the gland makes as it rises over the vessels. Between the back of the neck and the front of the vein there is normally a plane of loose tissue with no branches crossing it, which is why a surgeon can tunnel a finger or instrument behind the neck to separate gland from vein. This tunnel is the first thing tested at surgery and the point at which most pancreatic operations divide the gland: in the Whipple operation the head is removed to the right of the line, and in distal pancreatectomy the body and tail are removed to the left of it. Because the neck lies in front of the vein confluence and just below the celiac axis and hepatic artery, it is the most crowded crossing in the upper abdomen; the superior mesenteric artery runs behind the vein and a little to its left, so neck, vein and artery are stacked front to back within a few centimeters. The gland is thin here and its duct is small, which matters for reconstruction: a soft gland with a duct of 3 mm or less at this transection line (where the gland is divided) is the main risk factor for leakage after the pancreas is joined to the bowel [[SURG-016]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: A tumor in the neck has almost no room before it touches the superior mesenteric vein or portal vein behind it. Because resectability is judged by how much of a vessel's circumference the tumor contacts on CT (computed tomography) scans, neck tumors are often classified as "borderline resectable". That phrase describes the surgical geometry, not the cancer's behavior: the tumor is fully malignant, and the question is whether it can be removed with a clear margin.
section2.full: The vein behind the neck is the structure most often resected and reconstructed during pancreatic surgery. On CT, the degree of contact predicts whether the vein is truly invaded: in a series of 254 head tumors, histological vein invasion (cancer in the vein wall under the microscope) rose from 3% with no contact to 71–80% when contact exceeded half the circumference or the vein was occluded [[DIAG-001]]. The chance of a clear margin did not differ across those categories once the surgeon planned a vein resection [[DIAG-001]]. Removing a segment of vein and joining the ends did not by itself shorten survival in a series of 117 patients resected after chemotherapy; what mattered was whether the vein wall was actually invaded by cancer (median survival 8.3 versus 24.0 months) [[SURG-017]]. In a second series, invasion of the vein wall replaced margin distance as the only independent predictor of local recurrence [[SURG-006]]. Under US guidelines, vein contact that still permits reconstruction keeps a tumor in the resectable or borderline resectable categories, whereas an occluded vein that cannot be rebuilt makes it locally advanced [[SEC-SURG-11]]. Neck tumors can grow in either direction, so the operation chosen depends on whether the cancer extends toward the head (a Whipple) or the body (a distal pancreatectomy), and some require a central or total pancreatectomy to clear both sides.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The vein-contact data apply to tumors imaged before treatment or after chemoradiation, and the reference standard, tissue examination of the vein, existed only when the vein was removed, so the probabilities are conditional on surgical decisions [[DIAG-001]]. After chemotherapy the relationship loosens: scar tissue at the interface looks like tumor on CT, and 70% of resected tumors in one series were still classified as locally advanced or borderline on their post-treatment scans yet 92% were removed with clear margins [[DIAG-004]]. The venous-resection survival comparisons are from single centers and are shaped by which patients surgeons chose to operate on [[SURG-017]][[SURG-006]].
research_notes.how_studied: Tumor–vein contact was measured by radiologists re-reading pancreas-protocol CT scans blind to the outcome, grouping contact as none, up to 180 degrees, more than 180 degrees, or occlusion, and comparing the groups with what pathologists found in resected vein segments [[DIAG-001]]. The venous-resection studies compared survival between patients whose vein was removed and those whose vein was preserved, then looked within the resected group at whether the vein wall contained cancer [[SURG-017]][[SURG-006]]. Fistula risk at the transection line was recorded in a national audit using the standard international definition of a pancreatic fistula [[SURG-016]][[SEC-SURG-01]].

mechanism_notes.text: After chemotherapy, CT keeps showing the tumor pressed against the vein behind the neck because treated scar has the same density as live cancer, so anatomic imaging over-calls unresectability [[INF-DIAG-01]] [[DIAG-004]][[DIAG-023]]. Live tumor keeps taking up glucose and restricting water diffusion while scar does not, so a functional signal at the vessel interface may separate the two better than contact angle, although inflammation after treatment can mimic tumor on those signals too [[DIAG-008]].

glossary.definition: Latin for knee; the bend the pancreas makes as its neck rises over the portal vein.
A tumor whose contact with nearby vessels makes a clean removal uncertain; it refers to surgical geometry, not to how malignant the cancer is.
The point behind the pancreatic neck where the superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein join to form the portal vein.
The cut edge of a removed specimen; a clear (R0) margin means no cancer cells are found at the edge, which does not by itself mean the cancer is cured.
A leak of pancreatic juice from the join between the cut pancreas and the bowel after surgery.

related.statement: The neck is the thin segment of the pancreas between the head and the body.
The neck of the pancreas crosses directly in front of the superior mesenteric vein–portal vein confluence.
Tumors of the neck are often classified as borderline resectable because of their contact with the vein behind them.
Contact between a neck tumor and the vein is measured on pancreas-protocol CT as degrees of circumference.
A neck tumor involving the vein is removed together with a segment of the vein, which is then reconstructed.
The neck is where the pancreas is divided, and a soft gland with a small duct here is the main risk factor for a pancreatic fistula.

faq.q: Does "borderline resectable" mean the tumor is borderline cancer?
faq.a: No. It describes how closely the tumor touches the vein or artery behind the pancreas and therefore how uncertain a clean removal is; the cancer itself is fully malignant in every category. US guidelines define the categories by degrees of vessel contact on CT, and many borderline tumors are removed with clear margins, often after chemotherapy first [[SEC-SURG-11]][[DIAG-004]].

faq.q: If the tumor touches the vein, can it still be removed?
faq.a: Often yes. When the vein is involved, the surgeon removes that segment with the tumor and rejoins the ends; in one series the chance of a clear margin was the same whether contact was slight or extensive once a vein resection was planned [[DIAG-001]], and patients who needed a vein resection lived as long as those who did not [[SURG-017]].

topics.title: Body and tail
topics.orientation: The body and tail make up the left half of the pancreas: the body crosses the midline in front of the aorta and spine behind the stomach, and the tail continues left to end at the hilum of the spleen, with the splenic artery along its upper edge and the splenic vein running in a groove along its back.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The body and tail hold the same acinar and duct tissue as the head, but their islets are packed about twice as densely, so the tail contributes disproportionately to insulin production [[ANAT-005]]. The main pancreatic duct begins in the tail and gathers side branches as it runs through the body toward the head. They have no bile duct or duodenum beside them; their neighbors are the stomach in front, the splenic vessels behind, and the left kidney and adrenal below.
section1.full: The body lies at the level of the first lumbar vertebra, draped over the aorta at the point where the superior mesenteric artery leaves it, so the artery passes behind the upper border of the body and then runs downward behind the neck. The splenic artery, the largest branch of the celiac axis, takes a tortuous course along the top of the body and tail, and the splenic vein runs straight along the back of the gland to meet the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck; together these vessels tie the body and tail to the spleen. The stomach lies directly in front across a thin space called the lesser sac, which is why upper abdominal and back pain from this region can feel like a stomach complaint. Nerves to the body and tail come straight from the celiac plexus, which sits on the aorta just above the gland, and they distribute around the pancreatic duct [[ANAT-039]]. Endocrine tissue makes up about 2.4% of the tail versus 1.1–1.2% of the head and body, so losing the tail removes more insulin-producing capacity per gram than losing the head [[ANAT-005]], which is one reason diabetes develops in about 28% of people within a few years of a distal pancreatectomy [[SUPP-004]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Cancers of the body and tail are found later than cancers of the head because they cause no jaundice: in a national registry 69% of body and 84% of tail tumors had already spread at diagnosis, compared with 42% of head tumors, and resection rates were 4% and 7% versus 17% [[ANAT-003]]. These tumors more often announce themselves with back pain and weight loss, which are easily attributed to other causes.
section2.full: Back pain is the characteristic symptom because the body lies directly on the celiac plexus and the aorta, and tumor growth backward reaches nerves before anything else, yet in primary care back pain precedes diagnosis by a median of 16 months and only weakly predicts cancer [[ANAT-022]][[ANAT-010]]. The delay is not the whole story. In a sequenced cohort of resected tumors, body and tail cancers lived about half as long as head cancers (median disease-specific survival 12.1 versus 22.0 months) and were more often of the squamous molecular subtype, a gene-activity pattern that carried a median survival of 5.2 months [[ANAT-024]]; adenosquamous histology is also about 1.5 times more frequent here [[ANAT-023]]. Hidden peritoneal spread is likelier: body or tail location nearly tripled the odds of finding metastases at staging laparoscopy that scans had missed [[DIAG-002]]. When surgery is possible, a distal pancreatectomy removes the body and tail together with the spleen and splenic vessels, and a randomized trial found minimally invasive and open approaches gave similar long-term survival [[SURG-004]]. A body tumor can also compress the splenic vein, diverting blood through stomach-wall veins, which can enlarge as a result. Diabetes caused by the cancer, by contrast, is no more common with tail tumors than head tumors despite the tail's islet wealth, which argues that the cancer suppresses islets at a distance rather than by destroying them [[ANAT-015]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The registry proportions describe everyone diagnosed, including those never treated, and the Dutch registry found no residual survival difference after resection once stage and other factors were adjusted, whereas the SEER series found a small residual difference that vanished when the number of nodes examined was included [[ANAT-003]][[ANAT-030]]. The squamous-subtype finding rests on only 92 body/tail tumors and on subtype calls that varied by platform [[ANAT-024]]. Laparoscopy yields come from a single high-volume center with evolving practice [[DIAG-002]]. The post-distal-pancreatectomy diabetes rate includes benign indications and registers the first diabetes visit rather than onset [[SUPP-004]].
research_notes.how_studied: Location effects were studied by comparing stage, treatment and survival across site codes in national cancer registries with thousands of patients [[ANAT-003]][[ANAT-030]], and by sequencing resected tumors to assign molecular subtypes and relate them to location [[ANAT-024]]. Islet distribution was measured in donor pancreata by staining endocrine tissue and comparing head, body and tail slices [[ANAT-005]]. Symptom timing was reconstructed from primary-care records in the two years before diagnosis [[ANAT-022]]. The surgical trial randomized patients with resectable body/tail tumors between minimally invasive and open operations and followed survival [[SURG-004]]. New diabetes after distal pancreatectomy was identified by cross-linking a surgical registry with a national diabetes register [[SUPP-004]].

mechanism_notes.text: Cancer-associated diabetes is just as common with head tumors as with tail tumors, even though the tail holds twice the islet density, and it often resolves after the tumor is removed [[INF-ANAT-01]] [[ANAT-015]][[ANAT-016]][[ANAT-005]]. This pattern fits a circulating or exosome-borne (carried in tiny cell-shed vesicles) mediator that suppresses islets throughout the gland rather than local destruction, which would predict worse diabetes with tail tumors.

Whether diabetes follows a distal pancreatectomy depends less on how much gland was removed than on the balance between the remaining islet capacity and the body's insulin demand: obesity more than doubled the risk after distal resection, and after Whipple operations body-mass index rather than remnant volume predicted new diabetes [[INF-SUPP-02]] [[SUPP-004]][[SUPP-033]].

glossary.definition: The body and tail of the pancreas, the half that lies to the left of the vein crossing.
The thin pocket of the abdominal lining between the back of the stomach and the front of the pancreas.
The notch in the spleen where its artery and vein enter and where the tail of the pancreas ends.
A molecular type of pancreatic cancer, defined by gene activity patterns, that is more frequent in body and tail tumors and behaves aggressively.
A variant of pancreatic cancer in which part of the tumor forms squamous (flat-cell) tissue under the microscope.

related.statement: The body and tail form the left half of the pancreas, from the neck to the spleen.
The tail of the pancreas reaches the hilum of the spleen, which is removed with the tail in cancer surgery.
The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the body and tail and the splenic vein runs along their back.
The body of the pancreas lies directly on the celiac plexus, which supplies its nerves and carries its pain signals.
A tumor of the body or tail is removed by distal pancreatectomy together with the spleen.
Body and tail tumors typically present with back pain rather than jaundice.
Body and tail tumors are more likely than head tumors to have hidden peritoneal spread found at laparoscopy.
Body and tail tumors are often staged by laparoscopy because of their higher rate of imaging-invisible spread.

faq.q: Why was my body or tail tumor found so late?
faq.a: The body and tail have no bile duct to block, so there is no jaundice to prompt an early scan; the first symptoms are usually back pain, weight loss or new diabetes, each of which is common for other reasons and only weakly predicts cancer in primary care [[ANAT-010]][[ANAT-022]]. In a national registry 69% of body and 84% of tail tumors had already spread when found, compared with 42% of head tumors [[ANAT-003]].

faq.q: Will I lose my spleen?
faq.a: For a cancer of the body or tail, yes: the splenic vessels run inside the back of the gland and the lymph nodes drain along them, so the spleen is removed with the specimen. The DIPLOMA trial found that minimally invasive and open versions of this operation gave similar long-term survival [[SURG-004]], and about 28% of people develop diabetes in the years afterward [[SUPP-004]].

topics.title: Pancreatic duct
topics.orientation: The main pancreatic duct is a tube a few millimeters wide that runs the full length of the gland from tail to head, collecting enzyme-rich juice from thousands of side branches and emptying it into the duodenum beside the bile duct.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The duct system is a branching tree: tiny ducts from each acinar cluster join intralobular and then interlobular ducts, which feed the main duct (the duct of Wirsung). In the head the main duct turns downward to meet the common bile duct at the ampulla, and a smaller accessory duct (of Santorini) often drains the upper head separately. Duct cells lining this tree secrete the bicarbonate-rich fluid that carries enzymes and neutralizes stomach acid.
section1.full: In health the main duct is narrow, widest in the head and tapering toward the tail, and it is not seen as a distinct structure on a routine scan unless something downstream blocks it. Its lining is a single layer of cuboidal cells with the CFTR chloride–bicarbonate channel on their duct-facing surface, which drives the secretion of about 2.5 liters of juice a day at bicarbonate concentrations up to 140 mM [[SEC-ANAT-03]][[ANAT-009]]. Flow is pulsatile with meals: secretin released from the duodenum stimulates the ducts, cholecystokinin stimulates the acini (the enzyme-making clusters), and the sphincter at the ampulla relaxes to let juice and bile enter together. Because the duct of the head and the lower bile duct run side by side for their last centimeter or two and share an opening, any process at the ampulla affects both. Nerves to the body and tail distribute around the duct [[ANAT-039]], and the small ducts are where the earliest microscopic precancerous lesions, PanINs, arise; they are found by the hundreds in ordinary adult pancreata and the overwhelming majority never progress [[ORIG-001]]. The diameter of the duct at the neck determines how easily a surgeon can join it to the bowel: a duct of 3 mm or less in a soft gland is the highest-risk configuration for post-operative leak [[SURG-016]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: A tumor anywhere along the duct's course obstructs it, so the duct upstream dilates while the tissue it drains shrinks. This is the sign radiologists look for: an abrupt "duct cutoff" at the tumor and a dilated duct beyond it. It matters because about 12% of pancreatic cancers are invisible as a mass on CT (computed tomography) scans, and in 95% of those the duct changes give the tumor away [[DIAG-022]].
section2.full: Obstruction explains several things at once. In the head, where the pancreatic duct and bile duct converge, a single tumor can dilate both, producing the "double duct sign"; in a series of 103 patients with this sign about half had a malignancy, jaundice was present in 63% of the malignant cases versus 8% of the benign ones, and no cancer was found in the 20 people whose sign was incidental with normal liver tests and a normal blood marker CA 19-9 over a median seven years of follow-up [[ANAT-020]]. Blocked flow of enzymes into the gut is a direct cause of the maldigestion that two-thirds of patients have at diagnosis, and in one prospective series exocrine insufficiency rose from 66% at diagnosis to 92% two months later as obstruction progressed [[ANAT-021]][[ANAT-041]]. Upstream dilatation can itself cause pain and bouts of pancreatitis, one of the presentations that leads to a scan in an older adult. In surgery the duct is the structure that must be reconnected to the bowel after the head or tail is removed, and its caliber, not the tumor, sets the risk of fistula [[SURG-016]]. Separately from PDAC, mucin-producing cysts within the main duct or its branches (intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms) are a distinct, slower precursor pathway; among 53 small branch-duct cysts with nodules observed for a mean of 42 months, none produced a cyst-derived cancer [[ORIG-018]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The data on isoattenuating tumors (those with the same CT density as normal gland) mean that a CT without a visible mass does not exclude cancer when the duct is dilated or abruptly interrupted; all 21 such tumors were in the head and were more often resectable, probably because duct changes brought them to attention early [[DIAG-022]]. The double-duct series shows that the sign is an anatomical statement, that something blocks both ducts where they converge, whose meaning depends on accompanying jaundice, liver tests and CA 19-9 [[ANAT-020]][[SEC-ANAT-05]]. The exocrine-insufficiency progression figure is available to this atlas only as an abstract [[ANAT-041]], while the two-thirds prevalence comes from a prospective dietitian-assessed cohort of advanced disease [[ANAT-021]].
research_notes.how_studied: Radiologists compared multiphase contrast CT with endoscopic ultrasound in 173 patients to identify tumors that could not be seen as a mass and cataloged the indirect signs, duct dilatation, abrupt duct interruption, contour change and atrophy, that revealed them [[DIAG-022]]. The double-duct cohort followed everyone with the sign for at least five years and stratified them by jaundice, liver biochemistry and CA 19-9 [[ANAT-020]]. Duct physiology was studied in isolated animal ducts by measuring intracellular pH changes while blocking CFTR [[ANAT-009]]. Fistula risk by duct diameter came from a national surgical audit [[SURG-016]]. The cyst cohort followed branch-duct lesions with imaging at ten Japanese centers [[ORIG-018]].

mechanism_notes.text: Normal-looking duct tissue in a pancreas that contains a cancer differs by hundreds of proteins from duct tissue in a cancer-free gland, which suggests an organ-wide field state, plausibly chronic low-grade injury with duct obstruction and acinar atrophy, that raises the chance of progression for every one of the hundreds of independent PanIN clones at once [[INF-ORIG-02]] [[ORIG-001]][[ORIG-002]]. If so, duct obstruction is not only a consequence of cancer but part of the soil that favors it.

glossary.definition: The main pancreatic duct, which runs the length of the gland and opens at the ampulla.
An abrupt interruption of the pancreatic duct on a scan, usually at the site of a tumor, with dilatation upstream.
Dilatation of both the bile duct and the pancreatic duct on imaging, which points to a blockage where the two converge in the head.
The small chamber in the duodenal wall where the bile duct and pancreatic duct open together.
Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm, a mucin-producing cyst arising within the pancreatic duct system that is a slow precursor pathway distinct from PanIN.
Shrinkage of tissue, here of the pancreas upstream of a blocked duct.

related.statement: The main pancreatic duct runs the full length of the pancreas from tail to head.
The pancreatic duct is lined by duct cells that secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid.
The pancreatic duct and the common bile duct run side by side through the head and share an opening at the ampulla.
Dilatation or abrupt cutoff of the pancreatic duct on CT is an indirect sign of a tumor that may itself be invisible.
MRI can display the pancreatic duct in detail without contrast, showing dilatation and the level of obstruction.
Obstruction of the pancreatic duct by a tumor cuts off enzyme delivery and causes maldigestion.
IPMN cysts arise within the pancreatic duct system and are a separate, slower precursor pathway.
PanIN precursor lesions arise in the small branches of the pancreatic duct tree.

faq.q: My scan says the pancreatic duct is dilated. Does that mean cancer?
faq.a: Not by itself. A dilated duct means something is slowing flow downstream, which can be a tumor, chronic pancreatitis, a stone or a cyst. When both the bile duct and pancreatic duct are dilated, about half of patients turn out to have a malignancy, but among people whose finding was incidental with normal liver tests and CA 19-9, none developed a head cancer over seven years of follow-up [[ANAT-020]].

faq.q: Why did the radiologist see no mass but still suspect a tumor?
faq.a: About 12% of pancreatic cancers have the same density as normal gland on CT and show no visible mass; in 95% of those the diagnosis was suggested by indirect signs, chiefly duct dilatation and an abrupt duct interruption, and endoscopic ultrasound then visualized every one of them [[DIAG-022]].

topics.title: Acinar cells and digestive enzymes
topics.orientation: Acinar cells are the enzyme factories of the pancreas: grape-like clusters of them make up most of the gland's tissue, and each cell manufactures, stores and releases the proteins that digest fat, protein and starch.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: An acinus is a rounded cluster of acinar cells around a tiny central duct. Each cell packs digestive enzymes into granules, lipase for fat, amylase for starch, and trypsin, chymotrypsin and others for protein, and releases them into the duct when the hormone cholecystokinin (CCK) arrives from the duodenum after a meal [[ANAT-046]]. Protein-digesting enzymes are made as inactive precursors and switched on only once they reach the intestine, which protects the gland from digesting itself.
section1.full: The system has a feedback loop. Trypsin in the duodenum suppresses further CCK release, so enzyme output is matched to what the meal needs: in human volunteers, infusing trypsin into the duodenum cut meal-stimulated enzyme output by about a third and returned CCK to baseline [[ANAT-045]]. CCK and secretin divide the work: secretin raises bicarbonate output from the ducts without changing enzyme output, while CCK raises both [[ANAT-046]]. Acinar cells are among the most protein-productive cells in the body and have correspondingly large reserves, which is why maldigestion becomes obvious only when enzyme delivery falls to a small fraction of normal. Centroacinar cells, which sit at the junction of acinus and duct, carry the CFTR channel (the chloride channel that is faulty in cystic fibrosis) and belong functionally to the duct system [[ANAT-047]]. Acinar tissue is also plastic: under injury, acinar cells can temporarily take on a duct-like appearance, a process called acinar-to-ductal metaplasia, and then return to normal when the injury resolves. That plasticity, useful for repair after pancreatitis, is central to how the cancer begins.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Although the cancer is named "ductal" for its appearance, mouse studies indicate that the commonest route begins in an acinar cell. A mutation in the KRAS gene, the earliest genetic change in most pancreatic cancers, drives the cell through acinar-to-ductal metaplasia into a duct-like state and then into a PanIN precursor; blocking the transcription factor Sox9 (a protein that switches genes on) prevented this entirely [[ORIG-012]]. Acinar cells are also the first casualty of a growing tumor, which cuts off enzyme delivery to the gut.
section2.full: The acinar origin story has texture. In adult mice, acinar cells carrying mutant Kras were largely held in check by a senescence program (a built-in halt on cell division), and episodes of pancreatitis were what released the brake and allowed PanINs and cancer to form [[ORIG-014]]; another model found spontaneous low-grade lesions within two months of activating Kras in adult acinar cells with no injury at all [[ORIG-021]]. Duct cells can also give rise to cancer, by a faster route that skips low-grade PanIN [[ORIG-003]][[ORIG-013]], so the acinar cell is the main but not the only starting point. Once a tumor exists, acinar function fails for two reasons: the duct is obstructed, and the gland upstream atrophies. Exocrine insufficiency is present in about two-thirds of patients with advanced disease, producing weight loss, gas, abdominal discomfort and fatty stools and leaving 44% low in vitamin D [[ANAT-021]]. In mice, loss of enzyme delivery alone drove early fat wasting before the tumor was invasive, and enzyme replacement reversed it [[ANAT-027]]. Enzyme capsules taken with meals raised fat absorption by about 25 percentage points after pancreatic surgery compared with placebo [[SUPP-002]], yet in the United States only about one in five people with pancreatic cancer ever fills such a prescription [[SUPP-001]]. A rare cancer arises directly from acinar cells, acinar cell carcinoma, which affects younger people and has a far longer median survival than PDAC [[ANAT-044]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The cell-of-origin evidence is from engineered mice in which the mutation is switched on in one cell type at a time; in humans the origin is inferred from marker patterns, and the authors of the duct-origin study themselves note that cellular origin is not proven in people [[ORIG-012]][[ORIG-003]]. The two mouse models disagree on whether inflammation is required or merely accelerating, a question that remains open [[ORIG-014]][[ORIG-021]]. The exocrine-insufficiency prevalence was assessed by dietitians rather than by a single laboratory test, and breath testing predicted it poorly [[ANAT-021]]. The fat-wasting mechanism is established in mice; in patients it is associational [[ANAT-027]].
research_notes.how_studied: Lineage tracing marks a chosen cell type with a permanent fluorescent label at the moment the oncogene is activated, so any later lesion can be traced to its cell of origin; deleting Sox9 in the same animals tested whether the acinar-to-ductal step was required [[ORIG-012]]. Feedback regulation of CCK was tested in volunteers by infusing trypsin into the duodenum and measuring enzyme output and plasma hormone levels [[ANAT-045]][[ANAT-046]]. Exocrine insufficiency was assessed prospectively by dietitian evaluation, fecal elastase and nutritional markers [[ANAT-021]]. Enzyme replacement was tested in a placebo-controlled trial measuring the fraction of dietary fat absorbed [[SUPP-002]].

mechanism_notes.text: Hundreds of KRAS-mutant PanINs exist in an ordinary adult pancreas, yet lifetime cancer risk is low, so KRAS plus acinar-to-ductal change cannot be sufficient [[INF-ORIG-01]] [[ORIG-001]][[ORIG-002]]. The proposed rate-limiting step is focal inflammation, which releases a senescent KRAS-mutant lesion from its growth arrest and lets continued division accumulate the chromosomal losses that mark progression; in mice, pancreatitis had exactly this permissive effect [[ORIG-014]], although one model progressed without injury [[ORIG-021]].

glossary.definition: A tiny rounded cluster of enzyme-making cells around a central duct; thousands of them make up the exocrine pancreas.
A hormone released by the duodenum after a meal that tells acinar cells to release enzymes and the gallbladder to contract.
An inactive precursor form of a digestive enzyme that is switched on only after it reaches the intestine.
A reversible change in which injured acinar cells take on the appearance and behavior of duct cells.
A shortage of pancreatic enzymes reaching the intestine, causing poor digestion of fat and weight loss.
Pale, greasy, floating stools caused by undigested fat.

related.statement: Acinar cells make up most of the tissue of the pancreas.
In mouse models, acinar cells are the main cell of origin of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
Acinar cells reprogrammed into a duct-like state give rise to PanIN precursor lesions.
Loss of acinar enzyme delivery to the gut causes the exocrine insufficiency common in pancreatic cancer.
The enzymes acinar cells no longer deliver can be replaced with capsules taken at meals.
Acinar cells deliver enzymes into channels lined by duct cells, which add bicarbonate and water.
A KRAS mutation in an acinar cell is the usual first step toward a PanIN lesion in mouse models.

faq.q: If the cancer starts in acinar cells, why is it called ductal?
faq.a: The name describes what the tumor looks like, not where it came from: PDAC cells arrange themselves into duct-like tubes under the microscope. In mice, an acinar cell carrying mutant Kras first transforms into a duct-like cell, so the cancer that follows looks ductal whatever its origin; duct cells can also be the starting point by a different route [[ORIG-012]][[ORIG-003]].

faq.q: Why are my stools greasy and why am I losing weight?
faq.a: When a tumor blocks the duct or the gland shrinks, too few enzymes reach the intestine to digest fat, so fat passes through and calories are lost; about two-thirds of people with advanced pancreatic cancer have this exocrine insufficiency, with weight loss and gas in 84% [[ANAT-021]]. Enzyme capsules taken with meals raised fat absorption by about 25 percentage points in a placebo-controlled trial [[SUPP-002]].

topics.title: Duct cells and bicarbonate
topics.orientation: Duct cells form the lining of the pancreatic duct tree, from the smallest channels leaving each acinus to the main duct; they are a small fraction of the gland by volume but produce the alkaline fluid that carries enzymes into the intestine.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Duct cells secrete water and bicarbonate. The hormone secretin, released by the duodenum when acid arrives from the stomach, stimulates them to move bicarbonate through the CFTR channel on their duct-facing surface, producing a juice that can reach 140 mM bicarbonate and neutralizes stomach acid so that enzymes can work [[ANAT-009]][[SEC-ANAT-03]]. Secretin raises bicarbonate output without raising enzyme output, so the duct and acinar systems are controlled separately [[ANAT-046]].
section1.full: CFTR is the same channel that is defective in cystic fibrosis, and its location in the pancreas is specific: it sits on the apical (duct-facing) membrane of centroacinar cells and small intralobular duct cells, with no convincing presence in acinar cells [[ANAT-047]]. Experiments in isolated ducts showed that bicarbonate crosses the apical membrane down its electrochemical gradient through CFTR itself, that a CFTR blocker cut the flux by 61%, and that ducts from mice with the common cystic fibrosis mutation secreted none [[ANAT-009]]. This explains why cystic fibrosis thickens pancreatic secretions and destroys the gland: without bicarbonate and water, enzymes stagnate and the ducts plug. Duct cells also express the transcription factor (gene-switching protein) Sox9, which in the healthy gland is restricted to duct and centroacinar cells and maintains their identity [[ORIG-012]]. The duct lining is a renewing epithelium that must repair itself after pancreatitis, and that regenerative capacity, shared with injured acinar cells that transiently become duct-like, is the biological soil in which precancerous change occurs.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: "Ductal adenocarcinoma" is named for the way the cancer cells arrange themselves into gland-like tubes under the microscope, which resemble ducts. Whether the cancer began in a duct cell is a separate question. Mouse models show that duct cells can indeed become PDAC, but by a route that largely skips the low-grade PanIN stage and reaches invasion faster than the acinar route [[ORIG-003]][[ORIG-013]].
section2.full: In one duct-targeted model, carcinoma appeared about two months after the oncogene was switched on, versus about six months in the acinar-targeted comparison, and no mucinous PanIN lesions were seen along the way [[ORIG-003]]; a second model with a different combination of mutations found only high-grade precursor lesions in the duct arm and the full low-to-high spectrum in the acinar arm [[ORIG-013]]. When Kras alone was activated in duct cells, lesions were sparse, no more than ten per mouse and none in several animals, whereas acinar targeting produced abundant PanIN in every animal, which is why the acinar route is considered the main one [[ORIG-012]]. These findings matter because the two routes could produce tumors with different behavior and markers; the duct-derived mouse tumors expressed a protein, AGR2, that was used to look for a duct signature in human tumors, though human proof of origin is lacking [[ORIG-003]]. In the established tumor, cancer cells retain duct-like features, making mucins and expressing duct lineage factors, and the "classical" molecular subtype is the one that most resembles normal duct epithelium. Duct cells are also where the precancerous PanIN lesions live: these microscopic lesions are found in the small ducts of ordinary adult pancreata by the hundreds, nearly all carrying a mutation in the KRAS gene, and the overwhelming majority never progress [[ORIG-001]][[ORIG-002]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The duct-origin findings come from mice with engineered alleles and supraphysiological rates of recombination, which may not reflect how a single human cell acquires a mutation [[ORIG-003]][[ORIG-013]]. The relative contributions of duct and acinar origins in human cancer are unknown; the human arm of the duct study was a marker correlation only [[ORIG-003]]. The CFTR data come from guinea-pig and mouse ducts, with human localization from an immunohistochemistry study available to this atlas only as an abstract [[ANAT-009]][[ANAT-047]]. PanIN prevalence in intact pancreata is an extrapolation reported in an abstract [[ORIG-001]], while the mutation frequencies came from PanINs in resected glands that mostly contained a cancer [[ORIG-002]].
research_notes.how_studied: Bicarbonate transport was studied by loading isolated ducts with a pH-sensitive dye, changing the membrane voltage, and watching how fast intracellular pH shifted with and without a CFTR blocker [[ANAT-009]]. CFTR location was mapped by antibody staining of pancreas sections [[ANAT-047]]. Cell of origin was tested with inducible Cre recombinase lines that activate Kras in either duct cells or acinar cells, combined with a heritable fluorescent label so lesions could be traced back [[ORIG-003]][[ORIG-012]][[ORIG-013]]. PanINs were mapped by three-dimensional reconstruction of pancreas slabs and sequencing of individual lesions [[ORIG-001]][[ORIG-002]].

mechanism_notes.text: Histologically normal ducts in a pancreas that harbors a cancer differ by hundreds of proteins from ducts in a cancer-free gland, which points to an organ-wide field state rather than a single rogue clone [[INF-ORIG-02]] [[ORIG-001]][[ORIG-002]]. Because PanINs arise as hundreds of independent clones, a modest gland-wide shift in duct-cell state, from chronic injury or obstruction, could raise the chance that any one of them progresses.

glossary.definition: The channel on duct cells that moves chloride and bicarbonate into the duct; it is defective in cystic fibrosis.
A hormone released by the duodenum in response to acid that tells duct cells to secrete bicarbonate.
A duct-type cell sitting at the junction between an acinus and its draining duct.
A transcription factor that maintains duct-cell identity and is required for acinar cells to reprogram into a duct-like state.
Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia, a microscopic precancerous lesion in a small pancreatic duct.
The molecular type of pancreatic cancer whose cells most resemble normal duct epithelium.

related.statement: Duct cells form the lining of the pancreatic duct tree.
Duct cells and acinar cells are controlled by different hormones, secretin and cholecystokinin respectively.
Duct cells can give rise to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma by a route that skips low-grade PanIN.
PanIN precursor lesions form within the small ducts lined by duct cells.
The classical molecular subtype of PDAC most resembles normal duct cells.
Activating mutant Kras in duct cells produces few PanIN lesions in mice compared with acinar cells.

faq.q: Does pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma come from duct cells?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The name refers to the tumor's duct-like appearance. In mouse models most PanIN precursors come from acinar cells that reprogram into a duct-like state, while duct cells can also become cancer by a faster route without low-grade PanIN; which route predominates in people is not established [[ORIG-012]][[ORIG-003]][[ORIG-013]].

topics.title: Islets, insulin and glucagon
topics.orientation: The islets of Langerhans are about a million tiny clusters of hormone-producing cells scattered through the pancreas; they make up only 1–2% of the gland but control blood sugar for the whole body by releasing insulin and glucagon directly into the bloodstream.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Each islet contains beta cells that secrete insulin when glucose rises, alpha cells that secrete glucagon when it falls, delta cells that make somatostatin, and PP cells that make pancreatic polypeptide. Islets are not evenly distributed: endocrine tissue makes up about 2.4% of the tail versus 1.1–1.2% of the head and body, and the PP-cell-rich region is confined to the uncinate process [[ANAT-005]].
section1.full: Islets sit embedded among acini and share their blood supply, so the hormones they release pass into the portal vein toward the liver, where insulin exerts much of its effect. The gland carries considerable reserve. When healthy living donors gave roughly half their pancreas, fasting glucose rose only from 83 to 100 mg/dL on average, but 40–55% developed impaired glucose handling or diabetes within a decade [[ANAT-006]], and their maximal insulin response to glucose fell to about a third of that in controls [[ANAT-048]]. Beta cells respond to glucose within minutes; the pancreatic polypeptide cells of the uncinate process respond to a meal through the vagus nerve, and a blunted PP rise after eating marks damage to the head region [[ANAT-017]]. In type 2 diabetes, beta-cell loss is preferentially in the head [[ANAT-005]]. Because islets are perfused by the same vessels as the acini around them, anything a nearby exocrine tumor secretes reaches them at high concentration, and anything it sheds into the portal blood reaches islets throughout the gland.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Pancreatic cancer causes diabetes, usually before it is diagnosed. At diagnosis about 47% of patients have diabetes, three-quarters of it new within two years, compared with 7% of matched controls [[ANAT-015]], and fasting glucose begins to drift upward about 30–36 months before diagnosis [[ANAT-016]]. This is not simply the tumor destroying islets: diabetes is just as common with small tumors and with head tumors far from the islet-rich tail.
section2.full: The evidence that the tumor acts at a distance is the pattern of resolution. After removal of a head tumor by Whipple operation, new-onset diabetes resolved in 57% of patients even though the operation removed more gland, whereas long-standing diabetes never resolved [[ANAT-015]]; by contrast, healthy donors who lost the same amount of pancreas became more diabetic, not less [[ANAT-006]]. Hyperglycemia first appears when the tumor is only 1–2 cm3, several doublings before the typical size at diagnosis [[ANAT-016]]. Laboratory work points to secreted mediators: the tumor-derived peptide adrenomedullin, carried to islets inside exosomes (tiny vesicles shed by cells), suppressed glucose-stimulated insulin release in human islets, and blocking its receptor reversed the effect [[ANAT-014]][[ANAT-025]]; in mice, signaling by the tumor-associated growth factor TGF-beta caused selective beta-cell loss that antibody blockade rescued [[ANAT-026]]. These mechanisms do not yet fully reconcile with the human picture, in which insulin resistance and high insulin levels are prominent. Practically, new diabetes after age 50 is a risk marker rather than a screening test (about 1% of such people are diagnosed with pancreatic cancer within three years, over half within six months [[ORIG-009]]); blood sugar may improve after a successful resection; and surgery changes the balance, since diabetes develops in roughly a quarter to a third of people within one to three years of partial pancreatectomy and in everyone after total pancreatectomy, where it is insulin-requiring but usually manageable [[SUPP-004]][[SUPP-036]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Prevalence figures come from a referral population with histology-confirmed cancer and clinic controls, so they may overstate what a general population would show, but the independence from tumor location and size was consistent [[ANAT-015]]. The pre-diagnostic glucose trajectory was reconstructed retrospectively from stored laboratory values and tumor volumes estimated from imaging, and about 10% of patients never became hyperglycemic [[ANAT-016]]. The mediator studies are cell and mouse work; the TGF-beta model predicts insulin deficiency, which conflicts with the hyperinsulinemic human phenotype, so no single mediator is established [[ANAT-014]][[ANAT-025]][[ANAT-026]]. Donor hemipancreatectomy data are from a small, intensively selected group [[ANAT-006]].
research_notes.how_studied: Diabetes prevalence was measured by fasting glucose and treatment records at diagnosis, before any therapy, and the resection subgroup was retested at a median of 48 days after surgery [[ANAT-015]]. The pre-diagnostic trajectory was built by aligning every stored fasting glucose value from the years before diagnosis against matched controls and against tumor volume at resection [[ANAT-016]]. Islet function was tested in cultured insulin-secreting cells and human islets exposed to tumor-conditioned medium or isolated exosomes, with receptor blockers as controls [[ANAT-014]][[ANAT-025]]. Donors were retested with oral glucose tolerance tests years after surgery [[ANAT-006]].

mechanism_notes.text: New-onset diabetes resolves after a head tumor is removed, whereas donors who lose the same amount of gland develop abnormal blood sugar [[INF-ANAT-01]] [[ANAT-015]][[ANAT-006]]. The tumor appears to impose a functional, mediator-driven suppression on a largely intact beta-cell population, so removing the tumor withdraws the mediator and function recovers, while surgery on a healthy gland removes beta-cell mass permanently. A structural alternative, beta-cell loss driven by TGF-beta, is supported in mice [[ANAT-026]] but predicts a type-1-like picture that is not what is seen in patients.

A blunted pancreatic polypeptide response may report a different lesion from the high blood sugar: PP cells are confined to the uncinate process, so their failure is a local marker of a head tumor, whereas hyperglycemia is a whole-islet effect that is independent of location [[INF-ANAT-03]] [[ANAT-017]][[ANAT-042]][[ANAT-005]]. The competing view is that PP blunting is a general feature of pancreatic-type diabetes, since it is also seen in chronic pancreatitis.

glossary.definition: A microscopic cluster of hormone-producing cells within the pancreas that releases insulin and glucagon into the blood.
The islet cell that makes insulin, the hormone that lowers blood sugar.
A hormone from islet alpha cells that raises blood sugar by releasing glucose from the liver.
A hormone from PP cells in the uncinate process that rises after meals; its response is blunted when the head region is damaged.
Caused by substances a tumor releases rather than by the tumor's physical presence.
Removal of about half the pancreas, as in living-donor pancreas transplantation.

related.statement: Islets are the endocrine component scattered through the pancreas.
Suppression of islet insulin release by the tumor causes the new-onset diabetes that often precedes a pancreatic cancer diagnosis.
Islets are about twice as dense in the tail as in the head or body.
The pancreatic polypeptide cells of the islets are concentrated in the uncinate process of the head.
Loss of islets at pancreatic surgery leads to diabetes that is managed with monitoring and, after total pancreatectomy, insulin.
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from islet-type cells and are a different disease from PDAC.

faq.q: I was just diagnosed with diabetes. Does that mean I have pancreatic cancer?
faq.a: Almost always not. In a population study about 1% of people who developed diabetes after age 50 were diagnosed with pancreatic cancer within three years, roughly eight times the expected rate but still a small absolute number, and over half of those cancers appeared within six months [[ORIG-009]]. New diabetes is treated as a risk marker that may prompt attention to other symptoms, not as a screening test.

faq.q: Will my diabetes go away after surgery?
faq.a: It may, if it was new. In one series new-onset diabetes resolved in 57% of patients after removal of a head tumor, with fasting glucose falling from 174 to 110 mg/dL, whereas long-standing diabetes did not resolve in any [[ANAT-015]]. Surgery can also cause diabetes by removing islets, so the net effect depends on which process dominates [[SUPP-004]].

topics.title: Bile duct and ampulla
topics.orientation: The common bile duct carries bile from the liver and gallbladder down behind the duodenum, through the head of the pancreas, to the ampulla of Vater, where it joins the pancreatic duct and opens into the duodenum through a muscular valve, the sphincter of Oddi.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Bile is made continuously by the liver, stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, and released into the duodenum after meals to emulsify fat so that pancreatic lipase can digest it. Bile also carries bilirubin, the yellow breakdown product of old red blood cells, out of the body. The lower 2–3 cm of the bile duct is embedded in the pancreatic head, which is why a tumor there blocks bile flow so readily.
section1.full: The duct begins where the cystic duct from the gallbladder joins the hepatic duct, runs in the free edge of the hepatoduodenal ligament (the fold of tissue between liver and duodenum) in front of the portal vein and to the right of the hepatic artery, then passes behind the first part of the duodenum and curves down through the back of the pancreatic head. In most people it joins the main pancreatic duct a few millimeters before the ampulla to form a short common channel; in some the two open separately. The sphincter of Oddi controls release of both bile and pancreatic juice in response to cholecystokinin from the duodenum. When flow stops, bilirubin backs up into the blood: the skin and eyes turn yellow, urine darkens, stools become pale because no bile reaches them, and the skin itches. In patients with blocked bile flow the itch tracks the enzyme autotaxin and its product lysophosphatidic acid rather than bile salts themselves, and both fall when bile is drained [[ANAT-043]]. A replaced right hepatic artery (one arising from the superior mesenteric artery instead of its usual origin), present in about 12% of people, runs under the bile duct and pancreatic head and must be identified before surgery here [[ANAT-007]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Jaundice is the symptom that most specifically points to a pancreatic head tumor: in a primary-care study it carried an odds ratio of about 1000 and a positive predictive value of 22% in people over 60 (about one in five with recorded jaundice had the cancer), whereas abdominal pain, back pain and weight loss were individually weak signals [[ANAT-010]]. It appears late, a median of about a month before diagnosis, but it is recognized quickly [[ANAT-022]].
section2.full: Obstruction has consequences beyond color. Bile that cannot drain is prone to infection, and ascending cholangitis, fever and chills with jaundice and right upper abdominal pain, is an emergency because bacteria pass from the stagnant duct into the blood [[SEC-SUPP-14]]. Obstruction also inflates the tumor marker CA 19-9 independent of tumor burden; after drainage, CA 19-9 fell by about three-quarters in benign obstruction and by 39% in malignant obstruction, so a level drawn while jaundiced overstates the cancer [[DIAG-016]]. Dilatation of both the bile duct and pancreatic duct on a scan, the double-duct sign, usually indicates a mass where the two converge; about half of such patients had cancer in one series, 63% of them jaundiced [[ANAT-020]]. Relief is usually endoscopic: a metal stent placed through the ampulla reopens the duct. In a randomized trial, draining the duct with a metal stent before a Whipple operation was as safe overall as operating early (serious complications 29% versus 27%), though it moved some risk into the waiting period, and covered and uncovered designs kept the duct open equally often, about 72%, through months of pre-operative chemotherapy [[SUPP-008]][[SUPP-012]]. Tumors arising at the ampulla itself or from the bile duct lining are different cancers from PDAC, staged and treated on their own terms, which is one reason the pathology report specifies the tissue of origin.

action_note.heading: When to call the care team now
action_note.text: Fever or shaking chills together with jaundice or a biliary stent, especially with pain under the right ribs, can mean cholangitis, an infection of the blocked bile duct that needs same-day assessment and antibiotics [[SEC-SUPP-14]]. Jaundice returning after a stent has been placed, dark urine and pale stools, or intense new itching suggest the stent has blocked; roughly one in four stents needed attention during months of pre-operative chemotherapy in trials [[SUPP-012]][[SUPP-013]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The predictive values for jaundice are from UK primary care and describe the probability of cancer among people presenting with the symptom, not the fraction of cancers that cause it; about 30% of pancreatic cancer patients had jaundice coded in the year before diagnosis [[ANAT-010]]. The drainage trial compared a metal stent with early surgery and found non-inferiority for a composite of serious events, not a benefit, and did not report survival beyond 120 days [[SUPP-008]]; the older plastic-stent trial that found drainage harmful is superseded for metal stents but still informs the caution [[SUPP-L07]]. The itch mechanism is available to this atlas only as an abstract [[ANAT-043]].
research_notes.how_studied: Symptom predictive values were derived by matching thousands of pancreatic cancer patients to controls in a primary-care database and comparing coded symptoms in the year before diagnosis [[ANAT-010]][[ANAT-022]]. The effect of obstruction on CA 19-9 was measured by sampling before and after biliary drainage in benign and malignant obstruction [[DIAG-016]]. Stent strategies were compared in randomized trials with serious adverse events or sustained drainage as the primary endpoint [[SUPP-008]][[SUPP-012]], and the tissue effect of stents was examined histologically in resected duct segments [[SUPP-011]].

glossary.definition: A yellow-green fluid made by the liver that emulsifies dietary fat and carries bilirubin out of the body.
The yellow pigment from broken-down red blood cells that accumulates in the skin and eyes when bile cannot drain.
The chamber in the duodenal wall where the bile duct and pancreatic duct open together.
The ring of muscle at the ampulla that controls the release of bile and pancreatic juice.
Infection of a blocked bile duct, signaled by fever, jaundice and right upper abdominal pain.
A small mesh or plastic tube placed inside a blocked duct to hold it open.
Slowed or stopped flow of bile, whatever the cause.

related.statement: The lower common bile duct runs through the back of the pancreatic head to the ampulla.
Blockage of the bile duct by a head tumor causes jaundice and itching.
A blocked bile duct is reopened with a stent placed endoscopically through the ampulla.
The bile duct carries bile from the liver, and its blockage raises liver enzyme tests and bilirubin.
Bile duct obstruction inflates CA 19-9, so the marker is interpreted after bilirubin falls.
The bile duct opens into the second part of the duodenum at the ampulla.
Fever with jaundice or a biliary stent is a warning sign of cholangitis in a blocked bile duct.
The bile duct and pancreatic duct run side by side through the head and share an opening at the ampulla.

faq.q: Why does a tumor in the pancreas turn my skin yellow?
faq.a: The last few centimeters of the bile duct pass through the pancreatic head, so a tumor there squeezes the duct shut; bilirubin that should leave in bile backs up into the blood and stains the skin and eyes, urine turns dark and stools pale. Jaundice is the one symptom that strongly predicts pancreatic cancer in primary care, with a positive predictive value of 22% over age 60 [[ANAT-010]].

faq.q: Does my CA 19-9 mean anything while I am jaundiced?
faq.a: Less than it will later. Obstruction itself pushes CA 19-9 up: after drainage it fell by about three-quarters in benign blockage and by 39% in malignant blockage, so a value drawn while jaundiced overstates the tumor and is best re-measured once bilirubin has fallen [[DIAG-016]].

topics.title: Duodenum
topics.orientation: The duodenum is the first, C-shaped part of the small intestine, about 25 cm long, which wraps around the head of the pancreas and receives stomach contents, bile and pancreatic juice through the ampulla on its inner wall.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The duodenum is both a conduit and a control center. Its wall senses acid, fat and protein arriving from the stomach and releases secretin and cholecystokinin into the blood; secretin tells the pancreatic ducts to secrete bicarbonate and cholecystokinin tells the acinar cells to release enzymes and the gallbladder to contract [[ANAT-046]]. Mixing of food, bile and enzymes in the duodenum is where fat digestion actually begins.
section1.full: The four parts of the duodenum form a frame around the pancreatic head: the first part runs from the pylorus to the right, the second descends alongside the head and carries the ampulla, the third crosses leftward under the head and uncinate process, passing between the aorta behind and the superior mesenteric vessels in front, and the fourth rises to join the jejunum. The duodenum and pancreatic head share arterial arcades (looping arterial connections) from the gastroduodenal and superior mesenteric arteries, so neither can be removed alone. Enzyme delivery is self-regulating: trypsin reaching the duodenum suppresses cholecystokinin release, matching output to need [[ANAT-045]]. The duodenum's position in front of the uncinate process means that an endoscope passed into it brings an ultrasound probe within millimeters of the head, the bile duct and the vessels; this is the route for endoscopic ultrasound and for passing a needle through the duodenal wall to sample a head tumor, which gives a diagnosis in roughly nine of ten cases and leaves tumor cells along the needle track in about 3% [[DIAG-019]][[DIAG-022]]. The duodenal wall is also where a biliary stent emerges through the ampulla.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: A head tumor can narrow the duodenum where it curves around the gland, so that food cannot leave the stomach. This gastric outlet obstruction is uncommon at presentation, with nausea or vomiting the first complaint in under 10%, but it developed in about one in five people with unresectable head or periampullary cancer over the following months [[ANAT-032]].
section2.full: Obstruction produces early fullness, vomiting of undigested food hours after eating and weight loss, and it takes the oral route to nutrition and medication away. The classic Whipple operation removes the duodenum with the head of the pancreas and the lower bile duct and reconnects the stomach, bile duct and remaining pancreas to a loop of jejunum; a pylorus-preserving variant keeps the stomach intact, and a Cochrane review finds the two equivalent for survival and complications [[SEC-SURG-09]]. Because the duodenum is gone, enzymes and food leave the stomach at different times and enter a limb of bowel that no longer senses them, which is why only about a quarter of people regain near-normal fat absorption after a Whipple even on high-dose enzyme capsules [[SUPP-002]]. When a tumor cannot be removed, the blocked duodenum is bypassed: in a randomized trial a prophylactic surgical bypass prevented all late obstruction (0 of 44 versus 8 of 43) [[ANAT-032]], and an endoscopic bypass that connects stomach to jejunum through the wall had no recurrent obstruction at 12 months versus 15% with a duodenal stent, with similar complications [[SUPP-029]]. Nausea or vomiting with every meal in someone with a head tumor should be reported rather than attributed to chemotherapy, because a mechanical blockage has mechanical solutions.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The one-in-five obstruction figure comes from a 1990s trial in patients found unresectable at operation, before modern chemotherapy, and surgeons had already removed the highest-risk patients from randomization, so it probably understates the lifetime risk in unresected head cancer [[ANAT-032]]. The endoscopic-bypass comparison is from a registry-posted trial result without a peer-reviewed methods section, and the device is used off-label for this purpose in the United States [[SUPP-029]].
