Needle-track seeding was examined mostly in head tumors, where the track is removed at surgery, so the risk for tumors sampled through the stomach is extrapolated [[DIAG-019]].
research_notes.how_studied: The incidence of late obstruction was measured as the natural-history arm of a randomized trial of prophylactic gastrojejunostomy, following both groups until death [[ANAT-032]]. Endoscopic bypass versus duodenal stent was compared in a randomized trial with obstruction recurrence and reintervention at 12 months as outcomes [[SUPP-029]]. Needle-track seeding was looked for histologically in resected specimens along the biopsy path [[DIAG-019]]. Duodenal hormone control was studied in volunteers by infusing nutrients or trypsin into the duodenum while measuring pancreatic output and plasma hormones [[ANAT-045]][[ANAT-046]].

mechanism_notes.text: Fat absorption stays subnormal after a Whipple in about three-quarters of patients despite high enzyme doses, whereas people whose operations preserve the duodenum respond better [[INF-SUPP-01]] [[SUPP-002]]. Without the duodenum, enteric-coated enzyme granules and food leave the stomach out of step and enter a jejunal limb that no longer releases the hormones that time secretion, so the limit is mixing and timing rather than the amount of lipase.

glossary.definition: The first part of the small intestine, which wraps around the head of the pancreas.
A blockage at the exit of the stomach or in the duodenum that stops food from passing onward.
The muscular valve at the outlet of the stomach that controls emptying into the duodenum.
The part of the small intestine after the duodenum, to which the stomach and pancreas are reconnected after a Whipple.
A surgical or endoscopic connection between the stomach and the jejunum that bypasses a blocked duodenum.
A hormone the duodenum releases in response to acid, which stimulates bicarbonate secretion by the pancreas.

related.statement: The duodenum cradles the head of the pancreas and shares its blood supply.
The bile duct and pancreatic duct open into the second part of the duodenum at the ampulla.
The Whipple operation removes the duodenum together with the pancreatic head.
Narrowing of the duodenum by a head tumor causes gastric outlet obstruction with vomiting.
Head tumors are sampled by passing a needle through the duodenal wall under endoscopic ultrasound.
The duodenum receives food from the stomach through the pylorus.
Loss of the duodenum after a Whipple limits how well enzyme capsules mix with food.

faq.q: Why does a Whipple remove part of my intestine?
faq.a: The duodenum and the pancreatic head share the same arterial arcades and the bile duct runs through the head into the duodenal wall, so the head cannot be taken out while leaving the duodenum with a blood supply. The operation removes both and reconnects the stomach, bile duct and remaining pancreas to the jejunum; keeping or removing the pylorus makes no difference to survival [[SEC-SURG-09]].

faq.q: What does it mean if I vomit after every meal?
faq.a: In someone with a tumor of the pancreatic head it can mean the duodenum has narrowed, so food cannot leave the stomach; this developed in about one in five people with unresectable head or periampullary cancer over several months [[ANAT-032]]. It is relieved mechanically, by an endoscopic bypass or a stent, with the bypass having no recurrences at 12 months versus 15% for stents in one trial [[SUPP-029]].

topics.title: Stomach
topics.orientation: The stomach lies directly in front of the pancreas, separated from the body and tail by a thin pocket of peritoneum called the lesser sac, and its outlet, the pylorus, sits just in front of the pancreatic head and neck.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The stomach stores a meal, grinds it, and releases it in portions through the pylorus into the duodenum, where its acid triggers the pancreas to secrete bicarbonate and enzymes. Its position makes the pancreas hard to feel and hard to image from the front, and it also makes the stomach the window through which endoscopes reach the pancreas: an ultrasound probe in the stomach sees the body and tail across a few millimeters of tissue.
section1.full: The back wall of the stomach rests on the pancreas with only the lesser sac between them, so the gland can be examined by passing an ultrasound-tipped endoscope into the stomach and looking backward; a needle passed through the stomach wall samples body and tail tumors, and through the duodenal wall samples head tumors, with a diagnostic yield of roughly 90% in both [[DIAG-022]][[DIAG-019]]. The stomach's blood supply is independent of the pancreas, arriving from branches of the celiac axis along both curvatures and from short gastric arteries that pass from the spleen, which allows the stomach to be left in place when the body and tail are removed and lets it survive even when the splenic artery is divided. Pancreatic back pain is often felt as a stomach complaint because the two organs share nerve routes through the celiac plexus and occupy the same region of the upper abdomen. Enzyme capsules are designed to pass through the stomach intact and release in the duodenum, which is why they are taken with meals and sometimes with acid suppression [[SEC-SUPP-18]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: The stomach is affected by pancreatic cancer in two ways: a tumor at the head can block its outlet, and surgery changes how it empties. Gastric outlet obstruction developed in about one in five patients with unresectable head or periampullary cancer within months [[ANAT-032]], and delayed gastric emptying is one of the three formally defined complications after a Whipple operation [[SEC-SURG-02]].
section2.full: In the classic Whipple operation the lower part of the stomach (the antrum) and the pylorus are removed with the duodenum, and the stomach is joined to the jejunum; the pylorus-preserving variant divides the duodenum just beyond the pylorus and keeps the whole stomach. A Cochrane review found the two approaches equivalent for survival and major complications, with only small differences in delayed gastric emptying [[SEC-SURG-09]]. Delayed emptying, meaning persistent nausea and the need for a nasogastric tube beyond the first week, is graded by an international definition; it slows recovery and feeding but usually resolves [[SEC-SURG-02]]. Five or more years after a Whipple, overall quality of life is in the normal range, but bloating, altered bowel habit and pancreatic-type pain persist in many survivors [[SUPP-031]]. Direct invasion of the stomach wall by a body tumor does occur and is a reason a distal pancreatectomy sometimes includes part of the stomach. When a body or tail tumor compresses the splenic vein behind the stomach, blood from the spleen is rerouted through the short gastric and stomach-wall veins, which can enlarge into varices that bleed; this left-sided portal hypertension (raised pressure in the veins draining the spleen and stomach) is an uncommon but recognized complication of body tumors. For an unresectable tumor blocking the outlet, an endoscopic stomach-to-jejunum bypass placed through the stomach wall had no recurrent obstruction at 12 months versus 15% with a duodenal stent [[SUPP-029]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The obstruction incidence comes from a single-center randomized trial in the 1990s in patients found unresectable at laparotomy, which predates chemotherapy that now prolongs survival, so modern lifetime risk could be higher [[ANAT-032]]. The pylorus-preservation comparison pools trials of mixed quality [[SEC-SURG-09]]. The endoscopic bypass result is registry-posted rather than peer-reviewed and the device is used off-label for this purpose in the US [[SUPP-029]]. The long-term quality-of-life survey had 19% non-response and mixed benign and malignant indications [[SUPP-031]].
research_notes.how_studied: Late outlet obstruction was recorded prospectively in both arms of a randomized trial of prophylactic bypass [[ANAT-032]]. Delayed gastric emptying is graded by the International Study Group of Pancreatic Surgery definition based on nasogastric tube use and tolerance of solid food, so rates can be compared across centers [[SEC-SURG-02]]. Endoscopic sampling accuracy was measured against final histology in consecutive patients [[DIAG-019]][[DIAG-022]]. Long-term symptoms were assessed with validated quality-of-life questionnaires sent to survivors five or more years after surgery [[SUPP-031]].

mechanism_notes.text: After a Whipple the stomach empties enzyme granules and food out of step and into a bowel limb that no longer releases the duodenal hormones that time secretion, which may help explain why fat absorption normalizes in only about a quarter of patients even on high enzyme doses [[INF-SUPP-01]] [[SUPP-002]]. Timing capsules with each mouthful and reducing stomach acid address the mixing problem rather than the dose.

glossary.definition: The muscular valve at the outlet of the stomach.
The lower part of the stomach just before the pylorus, removed in a classic Whipple.
The thin pocket of abdominal lining between the back of the stomach and the front of the pancreas.
Slow emptying of the stomach after pancreatic surgery, causing nausea and prolonged need for a nasogastric tube.
Enlarged veins in the wall of the stomach or esophagus that can bleed when blood is rerouted around a blocked vein.
An ultrasound probe on the tip of an endoscope that images the pancreas from inside the stomach or duodenum.

related.statement: The stomach lies directly in front of the body and tail of the pancreas across the lesser sac.
The stomach empties through the pylorus into the duodenum, which wraps around the pancreatic head.
A classic Whipple removes the antrum of the stomach, while the pylorus-preserving variant keeps it.
Delayed gastric emptying is a defined complication of pancreatic surgery affecting the stomach.
Body and tail tumors are sampled with a needle passed through the stomach wall under endoscopic ultrasound.
Blockage of the splenic vein by a body tumor reroutes blood through stomach-wall veins that can form varices.
A head tumor can block the stomach's outlet, causing vomiting and inability to eat.

faq.q: Will I lose part of my stomach in a Whipple?
faq.a: In the classic version the antrum and pylorus are removed with the duodenum; in the pylorus-preserving version the whole stomach is kept. A Cochrane review found the two equivalent for survival and major complications, with small differences in delayed emptying, so the choice depends on the tumor's position and the surgeon's practice [[SEC-SURG-09]].

faq.q: Why is my pancreatic pain felt in my stomach?
faq.a: The pancreas lies directly behind the stomach and both send pain signals through the same celiac plexus to the same spinal segments, so the brain locates the discomfort in the upper abdomen and often through to the back. In primary care abdominal pain was recorded in 44% of pancreatic cancer patients before diagnosis, usually attributed at first to something else [[ANAT-022]].

topics.title: Liver
topics.orientation: The liver sits in the right upper abdomen above the pancreatic head, receives all the blood draining from the gut through the portal vein, and makes the bile that flows down through the pancreatic head to the duodenum, connections that make it both the organ most affected by a head tumor's blockage and the commonest site of spread.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The liver is the body's chemical plant: it processes nutrients arriving in portal blood, makes proteins, clears bilirubin and toxins, and secretes bile. Portal blood reaches it first: the superior mesenteric and splenic veins, which drain the pancreas and intestine, join behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein, which runs up to the liver in front of the inferior vena cava. The common hepatic artery brings a second, oxygenated supply.
section1.full: The portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct travel together in the hepatoduodenal ligament between the liver and the duodenum, so the liver's three connections all pass close to the pancreatic head; the bile duct then descends through the head to the ampulla. This anatomy explains a cluster of findings in head cancer. Bile backing up from an obstructed duct causes jaundice and abnormal liver enzyme tests, which were present in about half of pancreatic cancer patients in the year before diagnosis versus 9% of controls [[ANAT-010]], and it inflates the blood tumor marker CA 19-9, which falls by about 39% after drainage in malignant obstruction [[DIAG-016]]. Hepatic arterial anatomy varies: in about 16% of people a replaced or accessory right hepatic artery arises from the superior mesenteric artery and runs behind the portal vein and under the pancreatic head, where a tumor can involve it and a surgeon must preserve or reconstruct it [[ANAT-007]]. The liver also holds the cells that first meet anything shed into the portal blood: Kupffer cells, the resident macrophages (immune scavenger cells), line its sinusoids (blood channels), stellate cells sit beside them, and hepatocytes (liver cells) respond to inflammatory signals arriving from the gut.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: The liver is the commonest site of distant spread because tumor cells shed into the pancreatic veins reach it first through the portal vein. After resection, the liver accounted for about half of recurrences (49%), versus 21% in the lungs, and liver recurrence carried the shortest survival, a median of 13 months versus 30 months for lung [[SURG-015]]. A liver metastasis is what most often makes an otherwise removable tumor unresectable.
section2.full: The liver does not receive cancer cells passively. In mouse models the primary tumor prepares it in advance: tumor exosomes (tiny vesicles shed by cells) carrying the protein MIF are taken up by Kupffer cells, which trigger stellate cells to lay down fibronectin and recruit bone-marrow macrophages [[SURG-010]]; separately, the inflammatory messenger IL-6 from the tumor environment makes hepatocytes produce serum amyloid A, which draws in bone-marrow-derived immune cells (myeloid cells) and fibrosis [[SURG-022]]. Blocking either pathway prevented this "pre-metastatic niche" and reduced liver metastasis in mice, and patients whose stage I tumors later spread to the liver had higher exosomal MIF at diagnosis [[SURG-010]]. Once cells arrive, some survive as single dormant cells lacking the surface molecules immune cells use to recognize them, which may help explain recurrence years after surgery [[SURG-012]]. Established metastases are wrapped in a macrophage-driven fibrotic scar that both feeds them and keeps killer T cells out, one reason immunotherapy has not worked here [[SURG-023]][[SURG-024]]. Clinically, scans miss small deposits: liver metastases were the reason for unresectability in 34–47% of patients taken to surgery in one series [[ANAT-032]], and a pre-operative MRI (magnetic resonance imaging), which detects small liver lesions better than CT (computed tomography), was associated with 17% lower mortality after resection in a population study, most plausibly by keeping people with hidden metastases out of futile operations [[DIAG-021]][[SEC-DIAG-07]]. Resecting liver metastases helps only the rare patient whose deposits have been pathologically cleared by chemotherapy [[SURG-021]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The niche biology is established in mice with correlative patient data; no niche-blocking drug has been shown to prevent metastasis in people [[SURG-010]][[SURG-022]][[SURG-023]]. Recurrence-site survival differences come from a single center with sites assigned by imaging, and part of the lung advantage may be lead time from earlier detection on surveillance scans [[SURG-015]]. The MRI survival association is observational and confounded: patients who had MRI were younger, more often stage I and more often received chemotherapy first [[DIAG-021]]. Conversion surgery for metastatic disease is highly selected and non-randomized [[SURG-021]].
research_notes.how_studied: Pre-metastatic niche formation was studied by injecting tumor-derived exosomes or implanting tumors in mice, then examining liver cells, fibrosis and macrophage recruitment, and by genetic or antibody blockade of candidate signals [[SURG-010]][[SURG-022]]. Dormant cells were identified by staining human and mouse livers for single cancer cells lacking the markers CK19 and MHC class I [[SURG-012]]. Recurrence patterns were tracked by surveillance imaging after resection and linked to survival [[SURG-015]]. The MRI question was approached with linked administrative data from an entire province, adjusting for measurable differences between groups [[DIAG-021]]. Arterial variants were cataloged by blinded re-review of pre-operative imaging [[ANAT-007]].

mechanism_notes.text: Recurrence years after a clear-margin resection is best explained by disseminated cells that persist in the liver in a dormant, immune-invisible state under unresolved cell stress, until a later shift, such as waning immunity or remodeling of the niche, licenses outgrowth [[INF-SURG-01]] [[SURG-012]][[SURG-007]]. The competing explanation is slow continuous growth below the detection threshold of scans rather than true dormancy.

Lung recurrence is far less lethal than liver recurrence, which may reflect the liver's PDAC-specific niche programs, MIF, serum amyloid A and granulin-driven fibrosis with immune exclusion, that accelerate outgrowth and resist treatment, whereas the lung lacks an equivalent niche [[INF-SURG-02]] [[SURG-015]][[SURG-023]][[SURG-024]]. Earlier detection of lung nodules on surveillance CT could also contribute.

glossary.definition: The large vein that carries blood from the intestine, pancreas and spleen to the liver.
A macrophage that lives in the liver's blood channels and filters what arrives in portal blood.
Changes in a distant organ, induced by the primary tumor before any cancer cells arrive, that make it more hospitable to metastasis.
A state in which a cancer cell survives in a distant organ without dividing, sometimes for years.
The fold of tissue between the liver and duodenum that carries the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct.
A deposit of cancer growing in an organ distant from where it started.

related.statement: The portal vein delivers blood from the pancreas to the liver, which is why the liver is the first site of spread.
The liver makes the bile that drains through the bile duct and pancreatic head to the duodenum.
The liver is prepared for metastasis by signals from the primary tumor before cancer cells arrive.
Small liver spots found on scans in pancreatic cancer may be metastases or benign and are characterized by MRI.
MRI detects small liver metastases better than CT and is used to characterize indeterminate liver lesions.
The liver is the commonest site of recurrence after pancreatic resection.
The hepatic artery supplies the liver and in about 16% of people has a variant course under the pancreatic head.
Bile backing up into the liver from a blocked duct causes jaundice and abnormal liver tests.

faq.q: Why does pancreatic cancer go to the liver first?
faq.a: Veins from the pancreas drain into the portal vein, which carries blood straight to the liver, so cells shed from a pancreatic tumor meet the liver before any other organ. The liver is also actively prepared by signals from the tumor, such as exosomes carrying MIF, which in mice create a niche that welcomes arriving cells [[SURG-010]]. After resection, 49% of first recurrences were in the liver [[SURG-015]].

faq.q: If a liver spot is found, can the tumor still be removed?
faq.a: A confirmed liver metastasis usually means the cancer is treated as systemic and the pancreas is not resected. Surgery for metastatic disease helped only the small group whose metastases had been completely cleared by chemotherapy on pathology (median survival 25.5 months versus 8.1 without resection), a highly selected result [[SURG-021]]. Small indeterminate spots are characterized by MRI before any decision [[DIAG-021]].

topics.title: Spleen
topics.orientation: The spleen is a fist-sized organ tucked under the left ribs behind the stomach; the tail of the pancreas reaches into its hilum, and the splenic artery and vein run between the two organs along the back of the pancreas.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The spleen filters blood, removing old red cells and bacteria, and houses immune cells that respond to blood-borne infection, particularly encapsulated bacteria (those with a protective outer coat). It has no digestive role, and the body can function without it, but its removal leaves a lifelong vulnerability to certain infections that vaccination reduces. Its connection to the pancreas is anatomical: the two share a vascular corridor.
section1.full: The splenic artery leaves the celiac axis and winds along the upper border of the pancreatic body and tail, giving off branches to the pancreas before splitting at the hilum; the splenic vein forms at the hilum and runs straight along the back of the gland, collecting pancreatic veins and the inferior mesenteric vein before it joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein. The spleen also receives short gastric vessels from the stomach, which can keep it alive if the main artery is divided. Because the tail of the pancreas touches the hilum and the vessels are embedded in the gland's back, a cancer of the tail or body is within millimeters of the spleen's blood supply, and a tumor that occludes the splenic vein makes the spleen swell and diverts its blood through stomach-wall veins. Splenic blood drains through the portal system, so the spleen, like the pancreas, is upstream of the liver. The organ sits against the diaphragm and the left kidney, both of which can be reached by a tail tumor growing outward. The tail that abuts it is the most islet-rich part of the gland, with about twice the endocrine density of the head [[ANAT-005]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: PDAC in the tail reaches the spleen by proximity rather than by selective spread, and the spleen is nearly always removed with the body and tail in a distal pancreatectomy for cancer, because the splenic vessels and the lymph nodes along them must come out with the tumor. In the DIPLOMA randomized trial of left pancreatectomy for cancer, minimally invasive and open operations gave similar long-term survival [[SURG-004]].
section2.full: Removing the spleen with the specimen is standard for cancer because the lymph nodes draining the body and tail lie along the splenic artery and at the hilum, and the vessels themselves are often encased; spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy is reserved for benign and low-grade tumors. Living without a spleen carries a small permanent risk of overwhelming infection from encapsulated bacteria, which is why vaccinations against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus are arranged around the time of surgery and why any fever afterward is treated seriously. Platelet counts often rise after splenectomy, and clotting in the portal and splenic veins is a recognized early complication; pancreatic cancer already carries a high clot risk, with venous thromboembolism (clots in veins) in about 16% of patients within six months of starting chemotherapy and a third of those events in abdominal (visceral) veins [[SUPP-024]]. Diabetes also follows distal resection in about 28% of people over the next few years, driven by loss of the islet-rich tail together with host factors such as obesity, which more than doubled the risk [[SUPP-004]]. Spread to the spleen as a metastasis is unusual; what matters clinically is involvement of the splenic vein, which can cause left-sided portal hypertension (raised pressure in the veins draining the spleen and stomach) with bleeding gastric varices, and of the splenic artery or celiac axis, which determines whether a body tumor can be removed with a clear margin.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The surgical evidence for distal resection concerns the operative approach, not the spleen itself; the trial enrolled upfront-resectable body and tail tumors in experienced centers and found no difference in survival or margin status between approaches [[SURG-004]]. The post-operative diabetes rate includes benign indications and endocrine tumors and dates diabetes from the first registry visit [[SUPP-004]]. The clot incidence is from a French chemotherapy cohort that counted incidental visceral-vein thromboses, which many trials exclude [[SUPP-024]]. No comparative evidence on outcomes of spleen preservation in PDAC is cited here, so the description of practice above rests on surgical convention rather than on trial results.
research_notes.how_studied: The DIPLOMA trial randomized 258 patients across 35 centers between minimally invasive and open left pancreatectomy and followed overall and disease-free survival for years [[SURG-004]]. New diabetes after distal pancreatectomy was identified by cross-linking a national pancreatic surgery registry to a national diabetes register over a median of 45 months [[SUPP-004]]. Venous thromboembolism was recorded prospectively with competing-risk analysis in newly diagnosed patients starting chemotherapy [[SUPP-024]]. Islet density of the tail was measured on stained sections of donor pancreata [[ANAT-005]].

mechanism_notes.text: Diabetes after removal of the tail and spleen depends on whether the remaining islet capacity can meet the body's insulin demand: the tail holds about twice the islet density of the head, so its loss removes a large share of beta cells, and obesity more than doubled the risk after distal resection while remnant volume did not predict diabetes after Whipple operations [[INF-SUPP-02]] [[ANAT-005]][[SUPP-004]][[SUPP-033]].

glossary.definition: The notch in the spleen where its artery and vein enter and where the pancreatic tail ends.
Surgical removal of the spleen.
Bacteria with a protective outer coat, such as pneumococcus, that the spleen is especially important for clearing.
Enlarged veins in the stomach wall that can form when the splenic vein is blocked and may bleed.
Removal of the body and tail of the pancreas, usually with the spleen when done for cancer.
A blood clot in one of the abdominal veins, such as the portal or splenic vein.

related.statement: The tail of the pancreas reaches the hilum of the spleen.
The splenic artery and vein connect the spleen to the celiac axis and portal vein along the back of the pancreas.
The spleen is removed together with the body and tail in a distal pancreatectomy for cancer.
Clots in the splenic and portal veins are a recognized complication after splenectomy and in pancreatic cancer generally.
Removing the islet-rich tail with the spleen leads to diabetes in about 28% of people within a few years.
Lymph nodes draining the body and tail lie along the splenic artery and at the splenic hilum.

faq.q: Will removing my tail and spleen give me diabetes?
faq.a: It raises the chance. In a national cohort 28% of people developed new diabetes after distal pancreatectomy, at a median of about a year, with obesity more than doubling the risk [[SUPP-004]]. The tail carries about twice the islet density of the head, so its removal takes a disproportionate share of insulin-producing cells [[ANAT-005]].

topics.title: Superior mesenteric vein and portal vein
topics.orientation: The superior mesenteric vein (SMV) drains blood from the small intestine and right colon, rises in front of the uncinate process and behind the pancreatic neck, and there joins the splenic vein to become the portal vein (PV), which carries all of that blood to the liver.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The SMV–PV axis is the venous spine of the upper abdomen. It carries nutrient-rich blood from the gut and pancreas to the liver for processing, running directly behind the pancreatic neck with the superior mesenteric artery to its left and behind. Tributaries from the pancreatic head enter from the right, and the splenic vein joins from the left just behind the neck; the portal vein then runs up behind the bile duct to the liver.
section1.full: The vein is thin-walled and low-pressure, and the plane between its front wall and the back of the pancreatic neck is normally free of branches, which is what lets a surgeon pass behind the neck. Along its right side, however, several short pancreaticoduodenal veins and the gastrocolic trunk drain the head directly into it, so the head is tethered to the vein. Because the pancreas drains into this system, anything shed from a pancreatic tumor, including cells, DNA and secreted proteins such as adrenomedullin (a peptide that can suppress insulin release), travels in portal blood to the liver first, which is the anatomical reason the liver is the main site of metastasis and the reason islets throughout the gland are exposed to tumor products [[ANAT-025]]. Sampling portal blood directly during surgery did not detect tumor DNA more often than peripheral blood, but handling the tumor raised circulating tumor DNA about 2.5-fold [[DIAG-025]]. When the vein is narrowed or blocked, blood finds collateral routes through the stomach wall and around the pancreas, and clots can form in it: visceral-vein thromboses made up about a third of venous clots in pancreatic cancer patients within six months of starting chemotherapy [[SUPP-024]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: The SMV–PV is the vessel most often involved by a head or neck tumor and the one whose involvement surgeons can most often deal with. On CT (computed tomography) scans, contact of more than half the circumference predicted true vein invasion in 71–80% of cases and no contact in 3%, yet the chance of a clear margin was the same across categories when a vein resection was planned [[DIAG-001]]. Vein contact alone does not make a tumor unremovable.
section2.full: Under US guidelines, a tumor touching the vein over up to half its circumference without distorting it is still "resectable"; more extensive contact, a distorted contour or a short occlusion that can be reconstructed makes it "borderline resectable"; and an occluded vein that cannot be rebuilt makes it "locally advanced" [[SEC-SURG-11]]. "Borderline resectable" describes the surgical geometry of vessel contact, not the biology of the cancer, which is fully malignant in every category. In 117 patients resected after chemotherapy, those who needed a vein resection lived as long as those who did not (median 16.0 versus 22.0 months, not significantly different), whereas actual invasion of the vein wall on pathology cut survival to 8.3 from 24.0 months [[SURG-017]]; in another series vein-wall invasion was the only independent predictor of local recurrence, outperforming the measured margin distance [[SURG-006]]. After chemotherapy or chemoradiation the picture blurs: scar tissue at the interface looks like tumor, so 70% of tumors later resected, most with clear margins, still looked borderline or locally advanced on their post-treatment CT [[DIAG-004]], and in one small series a clear margin was achieved in all nine patients whose vascular contact had actually progressed on imaging [[DIAG-023]]. Vein resection therefore marks the tumor's local extent rather than adding harm, and it is standard in experienced centers when it achieves a clear margin.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The contact–invasion relationship was measured in head tumors before or after chemoradiation at one center, with the pathological reference available only when the vein was removed, so it is a conditional probability shaped by surgeons' decisions [[DIAG-001]]. The venous-resection survival comparisons are retrospective and single-center; patients needing vein resection may have had more advanced disease, which makes the equivalence more notable but not definitive [[SURG-017]][[SURG-006]]. The post-treatment imaging studies show that CT cannot distinguish fibrosis from live tumor at the vessel, which is why exploration after neoadjuvant therapy is guideline practice even when scans look unchanged [[DIAG-004]][[DIAG-023]][[SEC-DIAG-06]].
research_notes.how_studied: Radiologists re-read pre-operative pancreas-protocol CT blind to outcome and classified vein contact into four grades, which were compared with operative findings, histological vein invasion and margin status [[DIAG-001]]. Pathologists examined resected vein segments for cancer within the wall and related this to recurrence and survival with multivariable models [[SURG-006]][[SURG-017]]. Post-treatment resectability was tested by blinded re-review of scans before and after chemotherapy against what was found at surgery [[DIAG-004]]. Portal-blood tumor DNA was measured by digital PCR from samples drawn during surgery before and after tumor handling [[DIAG-025]].

mechanism_notes.text: After neoadjuvant therapy the vein still looks involved on CT because treated fibrosis has the same density as live tumor, so anatomic imaging over-calls unresectability [[INF-DIAG-01]] [[DIAG-004]][[DIAG-023]]. Viable tumor retains glucose uptake and restricted diffusion while scar does not, so PET or diffusion MRI at the vein interface might separate the two, with the caveat that post-treatment inflammation can also light up on those signals [[DIAG-008]].

glossary.definition: The vein that drains the small intestine and right colon and passes behind the pancreatic neck.
The vein formed behind the pancreatic neck that carries blood from the gut, pancreas and spleen to the liver.
The junction where the superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein meet to form the portal vein.
A tumor whose contact with nearby vessels makes clear removal uncertain; a statement about geometry, not about how malignant the cancer is.
Cancer cells found within the wall of a resected vein under the microscope, as opposed to merely touching it.
An alternative vein that enlarges to carry blood around a blocked one.

related.statement: The neck of the pancreas crosses directly in front of the superior mesenteric vein–portal vein confluence.
The uncinate process of the pancreatic head hooks behind the superior mesenteric vein.
The portal vein carries blood from the pancreas to the liver, which is why the liver is the first site of metastasis.
Contact between a tumor and the superior mesenteric or portal vein is measured on CT in degrees of circumference.
Pancreas-protocol CT shows the relationship of the tumor to the superior mesenteric and portal veins.
An involved segment of the superior mesenteric or portal vein is removed with the tumor and reconstructed.
The degree of superior mesenteric or portal vein contact helps define resectable, borderline resectable and locally advanced disease.
After chemotherapy, scar at the vein interface looks like tumor on CT, so restaging scans over-call vein involvement.
Clots in the portal and mesenteric veins make up about a third of venous clots in pancreatic cancer.

faq.q: My scan says the tumor abuts the portal vein. Is it inoperable?
faq.a: Not by itself. Contact with the vein is common in head and neck tumors, and the segment can be removed with the tumor and reconstructed; in a series of 254 head cancers the chance of a clear margin was the same across contact grades once a vein resection was planned [[DIAG-001]]. US guidelines classify vein contact as resectable or borderline resectable as long as the vein can be reconstructed [[SEC-SURG-11]].

faq.q: What is a vein resection and does it make the operation worse?
faq.a: The surgeon removes the length of vein the tumor touches and rejoins the ends or bridges the gap with a graft. In 117 patients operated on after chemotherapy, those who needed this lived as long as those who did not; what shortened survival was finding cancer actually within the vein wall on pathology [[SURG-017]].

topics.title: Superior mesenteric artery
topics.orientation: The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) leaves the front of the aorta just below the celiac axis, passes behind the pancreatic neck and the splenic vein, and descends in front of the uncinate process and the third part of the duodenum to supply the entire small intestine and right colon.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The SMA is the only artery to most of the small bowel, so it cannot be sacrificed. It runs to the left of and behind the superior mesenteric vein, a few millimeters from the uncinate process, which hooks around behind the vein toward it. From the SMA arise the inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries that supply the head and duodenum, and in about 12% of people a replaced right hepatic artery (a variant in which the artery to the right side of the liver arises here) [[ANAT-007]].
section1.full: The artery is wrapped in a sheath of autonomic nerves, the superior mesenteric plexus, which continues from the celiac plexus above and sends branches to the uncinate process along the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery [[ANAT-039]]. Lymph nodes cluster around it in several basins, along the dorsal pancreatic artery, the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, the gastrocolic trunk and the first jejunal branches, and these form the station numbered #14 in the Japanese classification [[ANAT-019]][[SEC-ANAT-02]]. The tissue between the uncinate process and the artery, roughly a centimeter thick and containing these nerves, lymphatics and small vessels, is the "SMA margin" or retroperitoneal margin of a Whipple specimen, and it is the margin most often found positive because perineural spread (cancer growing along nerves) runs through it [[ANAT-013]]. The artery's position behind the vein means that a tumor reaching it has usually passed the vein first, and because the artery wall is thick and muscular, cancer that encases it tends to follow the nerves on its surface rather than invade the lumen (the channel inside it).

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Contact with the SMA is the main boundary between a tumor that can be removed and one that cannot. Under US guidelines, no arterial contact is "resectable", contact of up to half the circumference (180 degrees) is "borderline resectable", and more than half is "locally advanced" [[SEC-SURG-11]]. Unlike the vein, the artery is rarely resected, because the bowel depends on it.
section2.full: "Borderline resectable" here means the tumor's relationship to the artery makes a clear margin uncertain; it says nothing about how malignant the cancer is. For locally advanced tumors, an anatomic score based on which vessels are involved predicted the chance of eventual resection after chemotherapy: 49% for the least-involved category, 32% for intermediate, 11% for the most involved, and about 20% overall [[SURG-020]][[SURG-019]]. Those who were resected after chemotherapy lived a median of 35.3 months versus 16.3 months for those who were not, though selection by favorable biology explains much of that gap [[SURG-019]]. After chemotherapy the artery often still looks encased on CT (computed tomography) scans because scar replaces tumor at the interface; in one series 70% of tumors that were then resected, most with clear margins, were still radiologically borderline or locally advanced [[DIAG-004]], which is why guidelines favor exploration when the blood marker CA 19-9 falls and there is no progression. Spread along the SMA is also the main lymphatic and neural route out of the head: the SMA station contained cancer in 34% of resected head tumors in one mapping series, and every case with para-aortic node involvement also had SMA nodes, suggesting flow from head to SMA nodes to the aorta [[ANAT-019]][[ANAT-038]]. The SMA margin is where microscopic residual disease most often remains, and it is one reason a complete-looking operation does not equal cure [[ANAT-013]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The resection percentages by anatomic category come from a single high-volume center whose patients overlap between the two reports, and they describe what happened to selected people who received intensive chemotherapy, not what any individual can expect [[SURG-019]][[SURG-020]]. The vein-contact study that underpins degree-of-contact reporting did not analyze arterial contact at all [[DIAG-001]]. Lymph node station data were collected in Japan where circumferential SMA dissection is routine and mostly after neoadjuvant therapy, which lowers node positivity relative to historical series [[ANAT-019]][[ANAT-038]]. The nerve pathway to the uncinate process is from a cadaver study available to this atlas only as an abstract [[ANAT-039]].
research_notes.how_studied: Locally advanced tumors were graded prospectively by the number and degree of involved vessels and followed through chemotherapy to see who reached resection and how long they lived [[SURG-020]][[SURG-019]]. Node mapping labeled each dissected node by anatomical basin around the artery in resected head cancers [[ANAT-019]]. Perineural invasion was quantified on an average of 14 slides per specimen and related to margin status by nerve size and location [[ANAT-013]]. Post-treatment scans were re-read blind and compared with surgical findings [[DIAG-004]]. Arterial variants were counted on blinded review of pre-operative imaging in a consecutive Whipple series [[ANAT-007]].

mechanism_notes.text: Persistent encasement of the SMA on CT after chemotherapy is overwhelmingly fibrosis rather than live tumor, so the contact angle that defined the tumor as locally advanced before treatment loses its meaning afterward [[INF-DIAG-01]] [[DIAG-004]][[DIAG-023]]. A functional signal such as glucose uptake on PET, which fell by 65% in metabolic volume while size fell only 10% in one series, may track viable tumor at the interface better than anatomy, though inflammation can confound it [[DIAG-008]].

glossary.definition: The artery from the aorta that supplies the small intestine and right colon, passing behind the pancreatic neck and in front of the uncinate process.
Tumor surrounding more than half of a vessel's circumference on imaging.
Tumor touching up to half of a vessel's circumference on imaging.
The cut surface of a Whipple specimen facing the superior mesenteric artery, the margin most often found to contain cancer.
Lying behind the peritoneal lining of the abdomen, where the pancreas, aorta and major vessels sit.
A tumor that has grown around nearby arteries to a degree that prevents removal with a clear margin at diagnosis, without distant spread.

related.statement: The uncinate process of the pancreatic head hooks behind the vein toward the superior mesenteric artery.
The superior mesenteric artery runs behind and to the left of the superior mesenteric vein.
The superior mesenteric plexus wraps the artery and carries nerves to the uncinate process.
Lymph node station #14 surrounds the superior mesenteric artery and is involved in about a third of resected head cancers.
Contact between a tumor and the superior mesenteric artery is measured on CT in degrees of circumference.
The degree of superior mesenteric artery contact defines borderline resectable (up to 180 degrees) and locally advanced (more than 180 degrees) disease.
Tumors touching the superior mesenteric artery are usually treated with chemotherapy before any attempt at surgery.
The superior mesenteric artery arises just below the celiac axis and in about 12% of people gives off a replaced right hepatic artery.

faq.q: What does "180 degrees" mean on my scan report?
faq.a: It describes how much of the artery's circumference the tumor touches, as if the vessel were a clock face. Contact of up to half the circumference (180 degrees) with the superior mesenteric artery is classed as borderline resectable under US guidelines and more than half as locally advanced; these are definitions about surgical geometry, not about how aggressive the cancer is [[SEC-SURG-11]].

faq.q: Can the SMA be removed and replaced like the vein?
faq.a: Rarely. The artery is the only blood supply to most of the small intestine, so it is generally preserved and the tumor is dissected off it after chemotherapy has had a chance to shrink or sterilize the tissue around it. In one center's series of locally advanced tumors, about 20% reached resection after chemotherapy, with the chance depending strongly on how many vessels were involved [[SURG-019]][[SURG-020]].

topics.title: Celiac axis and hepatic arteries
topics.orientation: The celiac axis is a short trunk that leaves the front of the aorta just above the pancreas and immediately splits into three: the common hepatic artery to the liver, the splenic artery to the spleen, and the left gastric artery to the stomach; the hepatic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreatic head and neck.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: These arteries supply the liver, stomach, spleen, duodenum and pancreas. The common hepatic artery runs rightward along the top of the pancreas, gives off the gastroduodenal artery, which descends in the groove between head and neck to supply the head and duodenum, and continues as the proper hepatic artery up to the liver beside the bile duct and portal vein. The liver can usually survive on portal blood alone, which gives surgeons some latitude here.
section1.full: The arrangement is variable. In about 16% of people the right lobe of the liver is supplied by a replaced or accessory right hepatic artery that arises from the superior mesenteric artery instead of the celiac axis and runs behind the portal vein, under the pancreatic head and bile duct, into the liver [[ANAT-007]]; in a reference series of 1,000 cases, about a quarter had some departure from the textbook pattern [[SEC-ANAT-01]]. A surgeon who divides such an artery unknowingly can cut off blood to half the liver and to the bile duct join; in the series above the variant was mentioned in only 9 of 26 pre-operative reports but identified in 24 of 25 on blinded re-review, and it was preserved in 24 of 31 cases, reconstructed in 7, and involved by tumor in 3 [[ANAT-007]]. The celiac axis itself is surrounded by the celiac plexus and celiac lymph nodes, and the common hepatic artery carries the lymph node station numbered #8, which contained cancer in 11% of resected head tumors in one series, with the hepatoduodenal ligament station (#12) involved in 5% [[ANAT-019]][[SEC-ANAT-02]]. Tumors arising from the dorsal (upper) part of the head tend to invade the plexus along the common hepatic artery and hepatoduodenal ligament, whereas ventral (lower) tumors follow the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) [[ANAT-040]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Arterial contact sets the limits of surgery. Under US guidelines, contact with the celiac axis or common hepatic artery of up to half the circumference makes a tumor "borderline resectable", while greater contact, or involvement that extends to the aorta or the artery's origin, makes it "locally advanced" [[SEC-SURG-11]]. "Borderline" refers to the surgical geometry, not to how aggressive the cancer is.
section2.full: The hepatic artery is more forgiving than the SMA because the liver has a second blood supply, so a short segment of common hepatic artery can sometimes be removed and reconstructed, and in selected body tumors encasing the celiac axis the trunk itself has been resected together with the body and tail, relying on collateral flow from the SMA through the gastroduodenal artery to reach the liver; these are specialized, non-routine operations. The gastroduodenal artery is divided in every Whipple operation, which makes the remaining hepatic artery the only arterial route to the liver and to the bile duct join, and bleeding from this artery after surgery is one of the three formally defined major complications [[SEC-SURG-03]]. Variant arteries matter because a replaced right hepatic artery runs exactly where a head tumor grows and where the SMA margin is cleared, so it can be involved by cancer or injured during dissection [[ANAT-007]]. After chemotherapy, encasement of an artery on CT (computed tomography) scans often represents scar, which cannot be distinguished from tumor by appearance alone [[DIAG-004]]. Celiac-axis involvement also brings the tumor into the celiac plexus, the source of the deep back pain that body tumors cause and the target of nerve-block procedures for pain.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Variant prevalence comes from one surgical center's consecutive series and agrees with the large reference study; no oncological outcome was reported by variant, so whether tumor contact with a replaced right hepatic artery carries the same meaning as SMA contact is unknown [[ANAT-007]][[SEC-ANAT-01]]. Node station proportions are from a Japanese center practicing extended dissection mostly after neoadjuvant therapy [[ANAT-019]]. The plexus-invasion pattern by embryological origin is available to this atlas only as an abstract [[ANAT-040]]. Resectability categories are guideline definitions that exist to standardize decisions, not measured biological thresholds [[SEC-SURG-11]].
research_notes.how_studied: Arterial anatomy was cataloged by having a radiologist re-review pre-operative CT and MRI from a consecutive Whipple series, blinded to the operative findings, and comparing with what surgeons encountered [[ANAT-007]]. Node station involvement was recorded by labeling every dissected node by its anatomical location [[ANAT-019]][[SEC-ANAT-02]]. Plexus invasion was mapped histologically in resected specimens and related to the part of the head the tumor arose from [[ANAT-040]]. Locally advanced tumors were graded prospectively by vessel involvement and followed to resection [[SURG-020]].

mechanism_notes.text: An artery that still appears encased on CT after chemotherapy is usually wrapped in treated scar rather than live tumor, so the pre-treatment rule that contact angle predicts invasion no longer holds [[INF-DIAG-01]] [[DIAG-004]]. Functional imaging that reads glucose uptake or water diffusion at the arterial interface could in principle separate scar from tumor, although post-treatment inflammation can mimic tumor on those signals as well [[DIAG-008]].

glossary.definition: The short arterial trunk from the aorta above the pancreas that divides into the hepatic, splenic and left gastric arteries.
The branch of the celiac axis that runs along the top of the pancreas toward the liver.
The branch of the hepatic artery that descends between the pancreatic head and neck and is divided during a Whipple.
A common variant in which the artery to the right liver arises from the superior mesenteric artery and runs under the pancreatic head.
Tumor surrounding more than half of a vessel's circumference on imaging.
The fold of tissue between liver and duodenum carrying the hepatic artery, portal vein and bile duct.

related.statement: The hepatic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreatic head, and a variant right hepatic artery passes beneath it.
The celiac axis supplies the liver through the common hepatic artery.
The celiac axis gives rise to the splenic artery, which runs along the pancreatic body and tail.
The celiac plexus surrounds the celiac axis and the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.
Lymph node station #8 lies along the common hepatic artery and is involved in about 11% of resected head cancers.
Tumor contact with the celiac axis and hepatic artery is measured on CT in degrees of circumference.
Contact with the celiac axis or hepatic artery helps define borderline resectable and locally advanced disease.
Bleeding from the hepatic artery stump after a Whipple is a defined major complication.
The celiac axis arises from the aorta just above the superior mesenteric artery, and the two share the celiac plexus.

faq.q: My report mentions a "replaced right hepatic artery". Is that a problem?
faq.a: It is a common variant, present in about 12% of people, in which the artery to the right half of the liver comes from the superior mesenteric artery and runs under the pancreatic head. It matters because the surgeon must find and protect it during a Whipple; in one series it was preserved in most cases and reconstructed in a few, with no liver damage [[ANAT-007]].

faq.q: Can the hepatic artery be removed if the tumor wraps around it?
faq.a: Sometimes, because the liver also receives portal blood; a short segment can be resected and reconstructed in experienced centers, and in selected body tumors the celiac axis itself has been removed with the tumor. These are specialized operations, and under US guidelines arterial contact of more than half the circumference is classed as locally advanced and usually treated with chemotherapy first [[SEC-SURG-11]].

topics.title: Splenic artery and vein
topics.orientation: The splenic artery runs a winding course along the upper border of the pancreatic body and tail from the celiac axis (the short arterial trunk off the aorta that supplies the liver, stomach, spleen and pancreas) to the spleen, and the splenic vein runs straight back the other way, lying in a groove on the back of the gland until it joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck to form the portal vein.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The splenic artery is the largest branch of the celiac axis and supplies the spleen, much of the pancreatic body and tail through short branches, and the upper stomach through short gastric arteries. The splenic vein drains the spleen and the body and tail of the pancreas, receives the inferior mesenteric vein from the left colon, and delivers a substantial share of the liver's portal inflow.
section1.full: Both vessels are embedded in or against the pancreas for most of their length: the artery often loops above and below the upper border, while the vein is fixed in the gland's posterior surface by numerous short pancreatic branches, so the body and tail cannot be separated from the vein without dividing these. This intimacy is why a distal pancreatectomy for cancer removes the vessels and spleen with the specimen, and why spleen-preserving techniques that keep the vessels are reserved for benign disease. The vein's junction with the superior mesenteric vein lies directly behind the pancreatic neck, placing the confluence in the surgical field of both Whipple and distal operations. The splenic vein is a low-pressure, valveless channel; if it is narrowed, splenic blood escapes through the short gastric veins into the stomach wall and down the gastroepiploic veins to reach the portal system by another route. The celiac plexus lies just above the origin of the splenic artery, and the nerves that supply the body and tail travel with the artery into the gland [[ANAT-039]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: A tumor of the body or tail reaches the splenic vein first, because the vein lies in the back of the gland where the tumor grows. Splenic vein involvement does not by itself prevent surgery, since the vein is removed anyway, but occlusion of the vein causes "left-sided portal hypertension": the spleen enlarges and blood rerouted through stomach-wall veins can form varices that bleed.
section2.full: Left-sided portal hypertension is distinctive because the liver is normal and the portal vein is open; the block is confined to the splenic side, so the collaterals run through the stomach rather than the esophagus, and the problem resolves when the spleen is removed with the tumor. Involvement of the splenic artery has different implications: because the artery runs back to the celiac axis, a body tumor that encases it can extend to the celiac trunk and common hepatic artery, which is what moves a body tumor from "resectable" through "borderline resectable" to "locally advanced" under US guidelines [[SEC-SURG-11]]. In a few specialized centers such tumors have been removed by resecting the celiac axis with the body and tail, leaving the liver supplied by collateral flow from the superior mesenteric artery; this is an uncommon operation and not standard. The vein is also a site of cancer-related clots: visceral-vein thromboses accounted for about a third of venous clots within six months of starting chemotherapy in one cohort, most found incidentally on scans [[SUPP-024]]. Because the splenic vein carries blood from the tail into the portal system, cells shed from a tail tumor reach the liver by the same first-pass route as cells from the head, and tail tumors are the most often metastatic at diagnosis (84% in a national registry) [[ANAT-003]]. A distal pancreatectomy for cancer removes both vessels with the spleen, by open or minimally invasive surgery with similar survival in randomized comparison [[SURG-004]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The sources cited here contain no study of splenic-vessel involvement as such; this entry relies on guideline resectability definitions for arterial contact [[SEC-SURG-11]], on registry stage distributions by location [[ANAT-003]], on a randomized trial of operative approach [[SURG-004]] and on a clot cohort that recorded visceral thromboses [[SUPP-024]]. Left-sided portal hypertension is described from established vascular anatomy rather than from a pancreatic cancer series, and the celiac-axis resection described is a specialized procedure whose outcomes are not covered by the sources cited here.
research_notes.how_studied: Resectability definitions are consensus criteria from the US guideline, applied to pancreas-protocol CT, which specify the degree of contact with named arteries and veins [[SEC-SURG-11]]. Clot incidence was recorded prospectively in newly diagnosed patients with scans reviewed for incidental visceral-vein thrombosis [[SUPP-024]]. Stage by location comes from a national registry with site codes [[ANAT-003]]. Nerve routes along the artery were traced by nerve staining in cadavers [[ANAT-039]]. Operative outcomes were compared in a multicenter randomized trial [[SURG-004]].

glossary.definition: The vein that runs along the back of the pancreatic body and tail from the spleen to the portal vein.
The branch of the celiac axis that winds along the top of the pancreatic body and tail to the spleen.
High pressure confined to the splenic venous system when the splenic vein is blocked, with a normal liver and open portal vein.
Enlarged veins in the stomach wall that carry rerouted blood when the splenic vein is blocked and may bleed.
An alternative vein that enlarges to carry blood around a blockage.

related.statement: The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreatic body and tail and the splenic vein along their back.
The splenic artery and vein connect the spleen to the celiac axis and the portal vein.
The splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein.
The splenic artery is the largest branch of the celiac axis.
Blockage of the splenic vein reroutes blood through stomach-wall veins, which can form varices.
The splenic artery and vein are removed with the body, tail and spleen in a distal pancreatectomy for cancer.
The splenic vein is one of the abdominal veins in which cancer-related clots form.

faq.q: Does a tumor touching the splenic vein make it inoperable?
faq.a: No. The splenic vein is removed with the body, tail and spleen in any distal pancreatectomy for cancer, so its involvement is expected rather than disqualifying. What limits surgery for body tumors is extension along the splenic artery to the celiac axis or hepatic artery, which US guidelines grade by the degree of arterial contact [[SEC-SURG-11]].

topics.title: Lymph nodes and lymphatic routes
topics.orientation: Lymph nodes are bean-sized filters strung along the lymphatic vessels that drain tissue fluid from the pancreas; they cluster in named stations in front of and behind the head, along the hepatic and superior mesenteric arteries, around the celiac axis, along the splenic vessels and beside the aorta.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Lymph drains from the pancreas along its arteries. From the head it flows to stations in front of and behind the head, then along the superior mesenteric and hepatic arteries, and finally to para-aortic stations beside the aorta; from the body and tail it flows along the splenic artery to the celiac stations. In the Japanese numbering, station #13 lies behind the head, #17 in front, #14 along the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), #8 along the hepatic artery and #12 in the hepatoduodenal ligament, the band of tissue carrying the bile duct, portal vein and hepatic artery to the liver [[SEC-ANAT-02]].
section1.full: Each node is a filter and an immune meeting place: lymph entering it is screened by macrophages (scavenger cells) and presented to lymphocytes (the immune cells that mount targeted responses), and this is where immune responses to anything arriving from the pancreas, whether infection or tumor antigen, are organized. Because lymphatics follow arteries, the stations a surgeon removes are those along the vessels in the operative field; a standard Whipple takes the stations in front of and behind the head, along the hepatic artery, in the hepatoduodenal ligament and on the right side of the SMA, whereas para-aortic stations lie outside the standard field. The number of lymph nodes retrieved depends partly on how thoroughly the pathologist searches the specimen: more complete sampling finds more of them and changes the stage assigned [[SURG-005]], and body/tail specimens yield fewer than head specimens (7.7 versus 9.7 in one registry) [[ANAT-030]]. The uncinate process and lower head drain along the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery into the SMA basins, which is also the route of its nerves, so lymphatic and neural spread from this region share a corridor [[ANAT-019]][[ANAT-039]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Lymph node involvement is the single strongest measure of how far a resected tumor has spread. In the current staging system (the American Joint Committee on Cancer's 8th edition, AJCC), survival separates sharply by the number of cancer-containing lymph nodes, none, one to three, or four or more, with five-year survival after resection of 35.6%, 20.8% and 10.9% respectively, while tumor size matters little once the nodal count is known [[DIAG-017]][[DIAG-003]].
section2.full: Cancer reaches the lymph nodes early and by predictable routes. In untreated resected head cancers, 70% were node-positive, the posterior head station was involved in 28 of 31 node-positive cases, and every patient with para-aortic involvement also had SMA-station involvement, consistent with flow from head to SMA to aorta [[ANAT-038]]. In a contemporary mapping series, mostly after neoadjuvant therapy, 55% were node-positive, with the SMA station involved in 34% and the posterior head in 32%; median survival was 115.9 months with no positive nodes, 55.6 with one to three and 24.6 with four or more [[ANAT-019]]. Perineural invasion, cancer growing along nerves, travels with nodal spread: untreated tumors with nerve invasion had node metastases in 83% versus 42% without [[ANAT-013]]. After surgery, a high ratio of positive to examined nodes (above 0.2) more than doubled the odds of recurrence within a year [[SURG-007]]. Nodes also mark the limits of surgery: para-aortic involvement is generally treated as distant spread, and the value of removing stations beyond the standard field is debated, with extended dissection practiced in some Japanese centers but not standard elsewhere [[ANAT-019]]. For the reader of a pathology report, "N1" means one to three positive nodes and "N2" four or more; the number examined matters as much as the number involved, because a report based on few nodes may understate the stage [[SURG-005]][[DIAG-003]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Nodal staging figures describe survival after resection in large multi-institutional cohorts; stage explained only a minority of survival variation (concordance about 0.58), so nodal status is the strongest single factor but far from the whole picture [[DIAG-003]][[DIAG-017]]. Station-level data come from Japanese centers practicing extended dissection, mostly after neoadjuvant therapy, which sterilizes some nodes and lowers positivity compared with the 1992 untreated series, which is available only as an abstract [[ANAT-019]][[ANAT-038]]. Sampling intensity confounds node counts and was preferentially applied to specimens with minimal residual tumor [[SURG-005]].
research_notes.how_studied: Nodal staging cut-points were derived by recursive partitioning of survival against the number of positive nodes in thousands of resected patients and validated internationally [[DIAG-003]][[DIAG-017]]. Lymphatic routes were mapped by labeling each dissected node by its numbered station at operation and recording which contained cancer [[ANAT-019]][[ANAT-038]][[SEC-ANAT-02]]. The effect of sampling was tested by comparing specimens submitted entirely for microscopy with those sampled selectively [[SURG-005]]. Early recurrence predictors were identified by logistic regression in 957 resected patients [[SURG-007]].

glossary.definition: A numbered anatomical group of lymph nodes, such as those behind the pancreatic head or along the superior mesenteric artery.
The part of the staging system that counts cancer-containing lymph nodes: N0 none, N1 one to three, N2 four or more.
The number of positive nodes divided by the number examined; a ratio above 0.2 predicts early recurrence.
Lymph nodes beside the aorta, beyond the standard surgical field, whose involvement is generally treated as distant spread.
Removal of lymph node stations beyond the standard field, practiced in some centers but not shown to improve survival.

related.statement: Lymph from the pancreatic head drains to stations in front of and behind the head before reaching the superior mesenteric artery.
Lymph node station #14 surrounds the superior mesenteric artery and is the main route from the head toward the aorta.
Lymph node station #8 lies along the common hepatic artery.
Lymphatic and perineural spread from the uncinate process share the corridor along the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery.
Lymph node involvement is counted and reported as N stage in the pathology report after resection.
Lymph node involvement determines pathological stage but, apart from para-aortic nodes, does not by itself decide resectability.
A high lymph node ratio predicts recurrence within a year of surgery.
The Whipple operation removes the lymph node stations around the head and along the hepatic and superior mesenteric arteries.

faq.q: What does N1 on my pathology report mean?
faq.a: It means one to three of the lymph nodes removed with the tumor contained cancer; N2 means four or more and N0 none. In an international validation of the current staging system, five-year survival after resection was 35.6% for N0, 20.8% for N1 and 10.9% for N2, with the number of nodes examined affecting how reliable the count is [[DIAG-017]][[SURG-005]].

faq.q: Do positive lymph nodes mean the cancer has spread everywhere?
faq.a: Not necessarily, but they show the cancer had begun to travel. Regional lymph node spread is still treated as local disease that surgery and chemotherapy address; para-aortic nodes beside the aorta are the exception and are generally treated as distant spread. Nodal status is the strongest single predictor after resection, yet stage explains only a minority of the variation in survival [[DIAG-003]].

topics.title: Nerves and the celiac plexus
topics.orientation: The pancreas is wrapped in autonomic nerves, the involuntary nervous system: the celiac plexus, a dense web of ganglia on the front of the aorta around the celiac axis and the origin of the superior mesenteric artery just above and behind the gland, sends fibers along every artery into the pancreas and carries pain signals from it back to the spinal cord.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The celiac plexus is the relay station for the upper abdominal organs. Sympathetic fibers from the splanchnic nerves and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus meet in its ganglia, and from there nerves follow the hepatic, splenic and superior mesenteric arteries into the liver, stomach, spleen, intestine and pancreas. The body and tail receive their nerves directly from the celiac plexus; the uncinate process receives them from the superior mesenteric plexus along the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery [[ANAT-039]].
section1.full: Within the gland, nerve fibers run between lobules and distribute around the pancreatic duct, carrying signals that modulate secretion and blood flow [[ANAT-039]]. The vagus supplies the parasympathetic input that, among other things, triggers release of the hormone pancreatic polypeptide from the uncinate process after a meal [[ANAT-017]]. Sensory fibers traveling with the sympathetic nerves are the pain pathway: they pass from the pancreas through the celiac plexus and splanchnic nerves to the lower thoracic spinal cord, which is why pancreatic pain is felt deep in the upper abdomen and through to the back rather than at the surface. Each nerve is sheathed by Schwann cells and surrounded by a perineurium, a layered barrier that normally keeps the nerve's interior separate from surrounding tissue. The plexus sits in the retroperitoneum, behind the peritoneal lining and in front of the spine, immediately above the pancreatic body and behind the neck, so it is within a centimeter or two of any tumor in the body or the posterior head.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Pancreatic cancer grows along nerves. Perineural invasion, cancer cells tracking within or along the nerve sheath, is found in about 80% of untreated resected tumors, mostly in nerves outside the pancreas, and it is the route by which tumors reach the retroperitoneum, leave cancer at the surgical margin and recur locally [[ANAT-013]]. Among patients given neoadjuvant therapy (treatment before surgery), its presence roughly halved median survival (28.5 versus 56.1 months) [[ANAT-013]].
section2.full: Invasion follows the anatomy: tumors of the ventral head (the embryological lower half, including the uncinate process) invade the head plexus and the plexus around the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), whereas tumors of the dorsal head invade along the common hepatic artery and hepatoduodenal ligament [[ANAT-040]]. The involved nerves are typically small, median diameter 0.8 mm, and nerves larger than that were associated with a positive margin in 26% versus 6% [[ANAT-013]]. Nerves are not passive: in mice, nerve density and nerve growth factor were already raised at the precancerous stage, and ablating the pancreas's sensory neurons before disease onset delayed precursor lesions and extended survival from 4.5 to 7.8 months [[ANAT-011]][[TME-030]], while cutting the vagus accelerated tumor development [[TME-031]]. Pain, though, does not simply track invasion. Early lesions recruit Schwann cells that suppress pain through the signaling molecule CXCL12, which may help explain why many cancers are painless until late [[ANAT-012]]; in established tumors, a Schwann-cell population driven by the tumor protein GDF15 promotes pain, and in patients plasma GDF15 tracked pain scores [[ANAT-029]]. Among head tumors, those causing pain had more than twice the mast cells (immune cells that release inflammatory signals) around nerves, a difference that did not follow the grade of invasion [[ANAT-002]]. For persistent pain, the plexus or splanchnic nerves can be destroyed with alcohol: such blocks lowered pain scores for three to six months in several trials [[SUPP-005]][[SUPP-L04]][[ANAT-035]], though a recent randomized comparison with medication alone found no difference [[SUPP-L06]], and destroying the ganglia as well shortened survival without extra benefit [[SUPP-L05]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The perineural-invasion frequency and its survival effect come from one center where most patients had chemoradiation before surgery, which reduced invasion from 80% to 58%, and a literature range of 71–93% is cited for untreated specimens [[ANAT-013]][[SEC-ANAT-06]]. Nerve-ablation and vagotomy results are preventive experiments in mice and do not translate to a treatment; the vagotomy paper later carried an editor's note [[TME-030]][[TME-031]]. The mast-cell and Schwann-cell pain findings are cross-sectional in small human samples with mechanism shown in mice [[ANAT-002]][[ANAT-012]][[ANAT-029]]. Nerve-block trials are small and several are available only as abstracts [[SUPP-L04]][[SUPP-L05]][[SUPP-L06]][[ANAT-035]].
research_notes.how_studied: Perineural invasion was scored by reviewing an average of 14 slides per resected specimen and recording the size and location of invaded nerves [[ANAT-013]]. Plexus anatomy was traced in cadavers with a stain for nerve fibers, and the invasion pattern was mapped in resected head specimens against the embryological origin of the tumor [[ANAT-039]][[ANAT-040]]. Nerve remodeling was quantified by counting labeled nerve fibers in mouse pancreata at successive disease stages [[ANAT-011]], and the contribution of nerves was tested by ablating sensory neurons or cutting the vagus before disease began [[TME-030]][[TME-031]]. Pain mechanisms were studied by comparing immune cells around nerves in painful versus painless human tumors and by deleting candidate molecules in mice [[ANAT-002]][[ANAT-012]][[ANAT-029]].

mechanism_notes.text: The same cell type, the Schwann cell, appears to suppress pain around early lesions and to drive it in established tumors [[INF-ANAT-02]]. As tumor burden and hypoxia rise, tumor secretion shifts toward GDF15, which reprograms recruited Schwann cells from an analgesic CXCL12-responsive state to a pain-promoting CCN3-positive state that sensitizes sensory fibers [[ANAT-012]][[ANAT-029]]. This would explain why pancreatic cancer is painless early, and so diagnosed late, yet severely painful when advanced; an alternative is that late pain is largely non-neural, from capsular stretch, obstruction or metastasis.

glossary.definition: The web of nerve ganglia on the front of the aorta around the celiac axis that supplies the upper abdominal organs and carries their pain signals.
Growth of cancer cells along or within the sheath of a nerve.
The cell that wraps peripheral nerve fibers; in pancreatic cancer it can either dampen or promote pain depending on the signals it receives.
The nerves that carry sympathetic and pain fibers between the celiac plexus and the spinal cord.
Deliberate destruction of nerves, usually by injecting alcohol around the celiac plexus, to relieve pain.
The space behind the abdominal lining and in front of the spine where the pancreas, aorta and celiac plexus lie.
A cluster of nerve cell bodies outside the brain and spinal cord; the celiac ganglia are the largest in the abdomen.

related.statement: The superior mesenteric plexus continues from the celiac plexus and wraps the superior mesenteric artery.
The celiac plexus surrounds the celiac axis and its branches.
The body and tail receive their nerves directly from the celiac plexus, which lies immediately above them.
The uncinate process receives nerves from the superior mesenteric plexus along the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery.
Pain signals from the pancreas travel through the celiac plexus and splanchnic nerves, and the plexus can be blocked to relieve pain.
Nerves inside the tumor are remodeled from the precancerous stage and influence both growth and pain.
Perineural invasion travels with lymph node spread and the two share routes along the arteries.
Perineural invasion is recorded in the pathology report after resection and predicts recurrence.

faq.q: Why does pancreatic cancer cause back pain?
faq.a: The pancreas lies on the celiac plexus and the aorta, and its pain fibers run through the plexus to the lower thoracic spinal cord, so pain is felt deep in the upper abdomen and through to the back. Tumor growth into the nerves and immune changes around them drive the pain; in primary care, back pain was recorded a median of 16 months before diagnosis but only weakly predicted cancer on its own [[ANAT-022]][[ANAT-010]].

faq.q: What is a celiac plexus block?
faq.a: A procedure in which alcohol or another agent is injected around the celiac plexus, through the stomach wall under endoscopic ultrasound or from the back under imaging, to destroy the pain-carrying nerves. Trials show lower pain scores for about three months in many patients, but recent randomized comparisons with medication alone disagree on how much it adds, and destroying the ganglia as well as the plexus shortened survival without extra benefit [[SUPP-L04]][[SUPP-L06]][[SUPP-L05]].

topics.title: Peritoneum and the abdominal cavity
topics.orientation: The peritoneum is the thin, glistening membrane that lines the abdominal cavity and covers most of its organs; the pancreas lies behind it, in the retroperitoneum, so a tumor must grow forward through the gland's front surface to reach the cavity.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The peritoneum has two layers, one lining the abdominal wall and one covering the organs, with a film of fluid between them that lets the bowel glide. It produces and absorbs this fluid continuously, carries blood and lymph vessels, and the fatty apron of the omentum hanging from the stomach is part of it. The pancreas, duodenum, aorta and great vessels sit behind the back layer, outside the cavity.
section1.full: The peritoneal cavity is a closed space in which fluid circulates: it is secreted by the membrane, moved by breathing and gut motion, and drained through lymphatics, especially those under the diaphragm. The front of the pancreatic body and tail is covered by the back wall of the lesser sac, a pocket of peritoneum behind the stomach, and the front of the head is covered by the peritoneum of the right side; the transverse mesocolon, which suspends the colon, attaches along the front of the gland. These are the surfaces a tumor breaches when it grows forward rather than backward. The peritoneum is also a large absorptive surface on which cells shed into the cavity can settle anywhere, favoring the pelvis, the omentum and the undersurface of the diaphragm. Tumor on the membrane irritates it, stimulates fluid secretion and blocks lymphatic drainage, producing ascites, the accumulation of free fluid that causes abdominal swelling and early fullness. The cavity is examined directly by laparoscopy, a camera through small incisions, which can see and biopsy deposits a millimeter or two across that no scan can resolve and can wash the cavity to look for loose cancer cells.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Scans cannot see small peritoneal deposits.
