In more than 1,000 patients whose cancer looked localized on CT (computed tomography), MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) and PET (positron emission tomography) scans, staging laparoscopy found hidden spread in 18%, as visible deposits, cancer cells in washings, or both, and the rate was higher for body and tail tumors and for larger tumors [[DIAG-002]]. Finding spread this way spares a major operation that could not help.
section2.full: Peritoneal spread is one of the three main routes of distant failure, alongside the liver and lungs; sites other than liver and lung accounted for 30% of first recurrences after resection in one series [[SURG-015]]. The likelihood of hidden spread depends on anatomy and size: body or tail location nearly tripled the odds of a positive laparoscopy, tumors over 2 cm more than doubled them, and an indeterminate spot elsewhere on imaging raised them almost sevenfold, so the yield ranged from 1.6% with no risk factors to 42% with all of them [[DIAG-002]]. Chemotherapy before surgery lowered the yield from 22% to 14%, partly by eliminating deposits and partly because patients who progressed never reached laparoscopy [[DIAG-002]]. Positive cytology, cancer cells in washings without visible deposits, is treated as metastatic disease in US practice, though long-term outcome data are limited [[DIAG-002]]. Peritoneal deposits can also follow the biopsy needle: in a series of 73 resected tumors, cancer cells were found along the track in 2.7%, one of whom later recurred on the peritoneum, which is why head tumors are sampled through the duodenal wall, which is removed with the tumor at surgery, rather than through the stomach [[DIAG-019]]. Established peritoneal disease is treated systemically rather than resected, and ascites is drained for comfort. Recurrence anywhere after surgery behaves as systemic disease: survival after recurrence was similar whether the first site was local or distant [[SURG-014]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The laparoscopy yield is from one high-volume center whose practice changed during the study and included patients after neoadjuvant therapy, so the 18% is an average over mixed situations; it establishes that imaging-negative disease is common, not what any individual's probability is [[DIAG-002]]. Positive cytology may include false positives and its long-term meaning was not followed [[DIAG-002]]. Recurrence-site proportions were assigned by imaging without autopsy confirmation [[SURG-015]]. Needle-track seeding was assessed mostly in head tumors, so the risk for transgastric sampling of body/tail tumors is extrapolated [[DIAG-019]].
research_notes.how_studied: Staging laparoscopy was performed in consecutive patients with radiographically localized disease; the surgeon inspected the peritoneal surfaces and liver, biopsied suspicious deposits and washed the cavity for cytology, and logistic regression identified which pre-operative features predicted a positive result [[DIAG-002]]. Recurrence sites were classified from surveillance imaging after resection [[SURG-015]][[SURG-014]]. Needle-track seeding was sought by examining the biopsy path in resected specimens under the microscope [[DIAG-019]]. The effect of pre-operative MRI on futile operations was estimated from linked population data [[SEC-DIAG-07]].

mechanism_notes.text: Even a resected tumor showing complete pathological response can be followed by recurrence, which implies that disease outside the sampled pancreas, in the peritoneum, liver or elsewhere, persisted below the resolution of scans and laparoscopy [[INF-SURG-03]] [[SURG-014]][[DIAG-002]]. The 18% rate of imaging-invisible spread found at laparoscopy is the visible edge of that reservoir; deposits smaller than a laparoscope can see are the rest.

glossary.definition: The thin membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering its organs.
The space behind the peritoneal lining where the pancreas, kidneys, aorta and major vessels lie.
Widespread cancer deposits scattered across the peritoneal surface.
Free fluid accumulating in the abdominal cavity, often from cancer on the peritoneum.
The fatty apron of peritoneum hanging from the stomach, a common site for peritoneal deposits.
A camera examination of the abdominal cavity through small incisions, done to look for spread that scans cannot see.
Examination of loose cells, here from fluid washed through the abdominal cavity, for cancer.

related.statement: Peritoneal spread too small for scans is detected by staging laparoscopy with washings.
Body or tail location nearly tripled the odds of hidden peritoneal spread at laparoscopy compared with head tumors.
The peritoneum is one of the sites where microscopic disease invisible to scans persists.
A clear scan does not exclude peritoneal deposits, which were found at laparoscopy in 18% of imaging-localized cancers.
Peritoneal recurrence is one of the main patterns of distant failure after resection.
The peritoneum and the liver are the two main sites of hidden spread found at staging laparoscopy.
Tumor cells can rarely seed the needle track after endoscopic biopsy and later appear on the peritoneum.
Peritoneal deposits can kink or compress the bowel and cause intestinal blockage.

faq.q: My scans were clear, but laparoscopy found spread. How is that possible?
faq.a: CT, MRI and PET cannot resolve deposits of a millimeter or two on the peritoneal surface or loose cancer cells in abdominal fluid, whereas a laparoscope can see and sample them directly. In more than 1,000 patients with apparently localized disease on modern imaging, 18% had such spread at laparoscopy, ranging from 1.6% with no risk factors to 42% with several [[DIAG-002]].

faq.q: What is ascites and why does it happen?
faq.a: Ascites is free fluid in the abdominal cavity. Cancer deposits on the peritoneum irritate the membrane, increase fluid production and block the lymphatic channels that normally drain it, so fluid accumulates and causes swelling and early fullness; it is drained for comfort and treated by treating the underlying cancer. Peritoneal and other non-liver, non-lung sites made up 30% of first recurrences after resection in one series [[SURG-015]].

topics.title: Desmoplasia: the scar-like stroma
topics.orientation: When a pancreatic tumor is removed and examined, most of what comes out is not cancer. The bulk of the mass is dense, stiff, scar-like tissue that the body itself has built in and around the cancer cells, and pathologists call that reaction desmoplasia; the tissue it produces is the stroma.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Scar-building is a repair program every organ keeps on standby. In the pancreas the main builders are pancreatic stellate cells, star-shaped cells that normally sit quietly between the gland's working units storing fat and vitamin A. An injury switches them into a contractile, collagen-secreting state that seals and strengthens the damaged area, and in ordinary healing the program shuts down again once repair is complete.
section1.full: Activation changes what a stellate cell does rather than what it is. The resting cell is loaded with lipid droplets, and switching on strips out its lipid-storage and lipid-metabolism genes while turning on alpha-smooth-muscle actin, the contractile protein that lets a cell pull on its surroundings [[TME-038]]. What the activated cell secretes is a composite rather than one substance: type I collagen for tensile strength, fibronectin and periostin as attachment scaffolds, and hyaluronan, a sugar polymer that holds water. Low oxygen is one of the triggers, and human stellate cells cultured under hypoxia roughly doubled their output of periostin, type I collagen, fibronectin and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) [[TME-009]]. The switch also runs backwards. The vitamin D receptor turned out to be abundant in stellate cells, including those taken from tumors, and a vitamin D analog pushed activated cells back towards the resting state and reduced inflammation and fibrosis in a mouse model of pancreatitis [[TME-038]]. Fibrosis is therefore a state the tissue actively maintains, not a finished deposit left behind.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) recruits this repair program and never lets it stand down, so the cancer spends its whole existence inside a scar. The consequences point in two opposite directions at once, and holding both in mind is what makes this tissue comprehensible. It obstructs treatment: mouse tumors were so poorly perfused that the active form of the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine could not be detected in them at all [[TME-001]]. It also holds the cancer back.
section2.full: The restraining half was discovered by taking the stroma away. Deleting Sonic hedgehog, a signal the cancer cells send to the fibroblasts, shortened median survival in mice from 6.17 to 3.61 months and raised the rate of visible metastasis from 15.3% to 43.4%, even though blood-vessel density rose roughly threefold [[TME-002]]. Destroying about 80% of the collagen-making myofibroblasts, whether at the precursor stage or in established cancer, produced more invasive, less differentiated and markedly more oxygen-starved tumors, expanded regulatory T cells (immune cells that dampen immune attack) and significantly shortened survival [[TME-012]]. Deleting only the type I collagen those cells make, leaving the cells themselves in place, accelerated the disease as well [[TME-034]]. The earlier drug-delivery experiment had pointed the other way: a short course of a hedgehog-pathway inhibitor raised chemotherapy levels inside the tumor and extended median survival from 11 to 25 days after enrollment, a benefit its authors described as transient [[TME-001]]. Given continuously in the same model at the same dose, the same drug shortened survival from 156 to 121 days [[TME-002]]. Human tissue fits the restraining picture: in resected tumors, low rather than high stromal alpha-smooth-muscle actin went with worse survival [[TME-012]]. As of 8 October 2026 no hedgehog-pathway inhibitor is approved in the US for pancreatic cancer [[TME-013]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: All the depletion results come from mice, and their direction depends on the tool used: removing hedgehog-driven stroma, ablating proliferating myofibroblasts or deleting myofibroblast collagen each shortened survival [[TME-002]][[TME-012]][[TME-034]], while depleting one defined fibroblast subtype did the opposite [[TME-037]]. The single survival gain from stromal depletion was brief and came from one short-course experiment [[TME-001]], and the clinical program built on it failed. The human evidence is observational, stained tissue from people who had surgery related to how long they lived [[TME-012]], which cannot establish cause. The field framed this from the outset as a friend-or-foe problem rather than a settled one [[SEC-TME-01]].
research_notes.how_studied: These experiments use mice that develop pancreatic cancer from their own mutated pancreas rather than from implanted cells, which preserves the scar-like reaction that implanted tumors largely lack [[TME-001]][[TME-002]]. A permanent fluorescent tag on the cancer-cell lineage lets investigators show that the myofibroblasts in the tumor did not arise from cancer cells [[TME-002]]. Ablation works by placing a drug-activated suicide gene in cells expressing alpha-smooth-muscle actin, which kills about 80% of them but spares cells that are not dividing, so quiescent fibroblasts survive the experiment [[TME-012]]. Survival in these studies is measured from enrollment at a defined tumor size rather than from birth, so the medians describe treated animals from a fixed starting point and are not life expectancies [[TME-001]][[TME-003]].

mechanism_notes.text: The opposite results become easier to reconcile if the stroma is read as a mixture rather than a quantity, so that what an intervention does depends on which cells it removes [[INF-TME-01]]. Tools that strip out the restraining population, including hedgehog signaling, bulk myofibroblasts and their collagen, shift the balance towards immune suppression and shorten survival [[TME-002]][[TME-012]][[TME-034]], whereas removing one defined suppressive subset slowed growth and improved the response to immunotherapy in mice [[TME-037]]. A competing explanation is timing rather than composition, since the harmful experiments all began at an early disease stage [[INF-TME-01]]. No subtype-selective stromal treatment has been tested in people.

topics.clinical_status: No stroma-directed therapy is approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 for pancreatic cancer; hedgehog-pathway inhibitors are approved only for basal cell carcinoma, and the pancreatic program was discontinued after negative trials.

glossary.definition: The dense, scar-like tissue reaction that the body builds in and around a tumor, which makes up most of the bulk of a pancreatic cancer.
The supporting tissue between the cells of an organ or tumor, made of matrix, fibroblasts, immune cells and blood vessels.
A star-shaped cell that sits quietly in the normal pancreas storing fat and vitamin A and becomes the main scar-building cell when the organ is injured.
An activated fibroblast that both secretes collagen and contracts, pulling on the tissue around it.
The mesh of proteins and sugars that cells secrete around themselves to give tissue its structure and stiffness.

related.statement: Desmoplasia is built by cancer-associated fibroblasts, which exist in several distinct states within the same tumor.
Desmoplasia includes the collagen and hyaluronan that generate the mechanical pressure measured inside pancreatic tumors.
Desmoplasia is proposed to compress the tumor's blood vessels, contributing to the poor perfusion and low oxygen found in pancreatic cancer.
Desmoplasia is the target of stroma-reprogramming strategies, which aim to change what the scar tissue does instead of removing it.
Desmoplasia is the subject of the stroma-targeting trials whose failures taught the field that less stroma is not the goal.
Desmoplasia shapes where T cells sit in a pancreatic tumor and how well they function once they arrive.

faq.q: If the tumor is mostly scar tissue, can chemotherapy even reach the cancer?
faq.a: It reaches it, but less of it arrives than the dose would suggest. In mouse tumors the active form of gemcitabine was undetectable, while it was measurable in normal tissues and in implanted tumors given the same dose [[TME-001]]. Chemotherapy still produces responses in people, so poor delivery is a limitation rather than a barrier.

faq.q: Could a drug that dissolves the scar tissue help?
faq.a: That idea has been tested and has not worked out. Removing stroma in mice by several different routes made the cancer more aggressive and shortened survival [[TME-002]][[TME-012]][[TME-034]], and the human trials built on the opposite result were negative. Current work aims at changing what the stroma does rather than clearing it away [[TME-038]].

topics.title: Cancer-associated fibroblasts and their states
topics.orientation: Fibroblasts are the connective-tissue cells that build and maintain the scaffolding an organ sits on. The ones found inside a tumor are called cancer-associated fibroblasts, or CAFs, and in pancreatic cancer they are not one cell type doing one job: they exist in several distinct states whose effects on the cancer differ and sometimes oppose each other.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: A fibroblast's ordinary work is structural. It secretes collagen and other matrix proteins, maintains the mesh that holds tissue architecture together, and remodels that mesh after injury. The pancreas has its own resident version, the pancreatic stellate cell. Healthy tissue also keeps a reserve of relatively unspecialized “universal” fibroblasts, which are the source from which the specialized, activated fibroblasts of disease are later generated [[TME-037]].
section1.full: Two facts about fibroblast identity matter before cancer enters the picture. First, the diversity is pre-existing rather than created by a tumor. The surface protein CD105 cleanly separates two discrete and stable fibroblast populations, present in roughly a seven-to-three ratio across most normal and tumor-bearing tissues of both mice and humans, which differ in how fast they divide, in alpha-smooth-muscle actin (a contractile protein) and in the antigen-presenting molecule MHC class II [[TME-036]]. Second, the activated fibroblasts of disease are manufactured from resting ones on demand. Deleting the type 2 receptor for transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) from resting universal fibroblasts in mice prevented the main tumor-associated myofibroblast population from appearing at all, which identifies that receptor as the required input for the conversion [[TME-037]]. Lineage labeling settles what these cells are not: in mice whose cancer cells carry a permanent fluorescent tag, the myofibroblasts around the tumor carry no tag, so they are host cells recruited into service rather than cancer cells that changed shape [[TME-005]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) at least three fibroblast states coexist in the same tumor, and position predicts which is which. Myofibroblastic CAFs form a ring pressed directly against the cancer glands; inflammatory CAFs sit further out and secrete signaling molecules instead of matrix; a third state carries the antigen-presenting machinery normally used by immune cells [[TME-005]][[TME-017]]. The states convert into one another rather than being fixed.
section2.full: What sets the state is the signal received, and distance decides which signal arrives. Growing tumor organoids in direct contact with stellate cells produced the myofibroblastic state, while separating the two by a membrane that passed only soluble factors produced the inflammatory state, secreting the inflammatory signaling molecules interleukin-6, interleukin-11 and LIF [[TME-005]]. The soluble trigger was then identified as interleukin-1 alpha released by the cancer cells and acting on receptors the fibroblasts carry: knocking out either this cytokine (signaling protein) or its receptor pushed the cells back towards the myofibroblastic program, and TGF-beta blocks the inflammatory route by stripping the interleukin-1 receptor from the fibroblast surface [[TME-011]]. Hedgehog signaling operates in the same system, its target genes concentrated in myofibroblastic CAFs; blocking the receptor Smoothened in mice shifted composition towards inflammatory CAFs and left fewer CD8 (killer) T cells and more regulatory (suppressive) T cells behind [[TME-013]]. The antigen-presenting state displays MHC class II and CD74 without the co-stimulatory molecules a professional immune cell uses, yet engages CD4 (helper) T-cell receptors in an antigen-specific way [[TME-017]]. In 43 resected human tumors, four fibroblast programs were resolved, one of which tracked with shorter survival (hazard ratio 1.84, meaning roughly 1.8 times the rate of death over follow-up; 95% confidence interval 1.04-3.25) [[TME-032]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The state definitions rest on mouse tumors, cultured cells and small numbers of human specimens, three to six resections in the founding studies [[TME-005]][[TME-017]], so the human counterpart of each state is established by marker and transcriptional resemblance rather than by matched function. The one human outcome association comes from 43 resected tumors, a relatively favorable subgroup, modeled without any experimental perturbation [[TME-032]]. The functional opposition between the two fibroblast lineages was demonstrated by transplanting equal numbers of cells under the skin rather than into the pancreas [[TME-036]]. What this body of work supports is that fibroblast state is set by signals and is reversible; what it does not yet support is selecting a state to target in a particular person.
research_notes.how_studied: Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing sorts thousands of individual cells by which genes each is transcribing, which is how these states were separated in the first place; because the tissue has to be broken apart first, fragile cell types are under-counted, and fibroblasts came out at only about 2% of all cells recovered [[TME-017]]. Spatial profiling keeps the tissue intact and asks which programs sit beside which, recovering the position information that dissociation destroys [[TME-032]]. The organoid co-culture run with and without a separating membrane is the experiment that isolates physical contact from soluble signaling, and deleting a cytokine or its receptor with CRISPR tests whether a candidate signal is actually necessary [[TME-005]][[TME-011]].

mechanism_notes.text: Because the states differ in what they do, the variable that matters for treatment is probably which fibroblasts are present rather than how many [[INF-TME-01]]. Depleting fibroblasts in bulk by their shared myofibroblast marker shortened survival in mice, while depleting the single LRRC15-marked subtype slowed growth and improved the response to the immunotherapy anti-PD-L1 [[TME-012]][[TME-037]], and two lineages separated by CD105 had opposite effects at matched cell dose, with the restraining effect disappearing entirely in mice lacking adaptive immunity [[TME-036]]. This is an inference drawn across different models and tools rather than a principle anyone has tested directly.

A fibroblast that displays antigen without the second, confirming signal a professional immune cell provides may deactivate the T cell it engages instead of arming it, which would help explain why T cells can sit beside cancer cells in human tumors without killing them [[INF-TME-03]][[TME-017]]. The suppressive myofibroblast subtype shown to blunt CD8 T-cell function directly in mice offers a second, convergent route [[TME-037]]. The authors who found the antigen-presenting state proposed this decoy role explicitly and did not test it, and a competing account, that too few tumor-specific T cells are ever generated, remains open [[INF-TME-03]].

topics.clinical_status: No fibroblast-state-directed or CAF-selective therapy is approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 for pancreatic cancer; LRRC15-directed agents and interleukin-1 blockade remain investigational.

glossary.definition: A fibroblast living inside a tumor, recruited from the host's own connective tissue rather than derived from the cancer.
The fibroblast state found pressed directly against cancer glands, which contracts and secretes most of the collagen.
The fibroblast state found further from the cancer cells, which secretes signaling molecules such as interleukin-6 rather than building matrix.
A surface molecule that displays fragments of protein to CD4 T cells; immune cells normally carry it, and some tumor fibroblasts do too.
A signaling protein that drives fibroblasts towards the contractile, collagen-making state and suppresses the inflammatory one.
A small clump of cells grown in a gel so that it reproduces part of a tissue's three-dimensional structure in the laboratory.

related.statement: Cancer-associated fibroblasts are the cells that build the desmoplastic, scar-like stroma of a pancreatic tumor.
Cancer-associated fibroblasts secrete the collagen and hyaluronan whose swelling generates interstitial pressure inside the tumor.
Cancer-associated fibroblasts influence where T cells go in the tumor and how well they work once they reach the cancer cells.
Changes in cancer-associated fibroblasts are followed by changes in the macrophages and suppressive myeloid cells in the same tumor.
Cancer-associated fibroblasts are the intended target of stroma-reprogramming approaches, which aim to shift their state rather than delete them.
Cancer-associated fibroblast states sit alongside the cancer cells' own states as the two halves of what a tumor region is doing.

faq.q: Are these fibroblasts part of the cancer?
faq.a: No. They are the person's own connective-tissue cells recruited into the tumor. Lineage labeling in mice, which permanently tags cancer cells and everything descended from them, showed the myofibroblasts around the tumor carry no tag [[TME-005]], and the two main fibroblast lineages are already present in normal tissue [[TME-036]].

faq.q: Are some of these fibroblasts helpful?
faq.a: In mice, yes. Two fibroblast lineages separated by the marker CD105 had opposite effects on tumor growth when the same number of cells was transplanted, and the restraining one needed a working immune system to have any effect [[TME-036]]. Whether the human equivalents behave the same way has not been tested.

topics.title: Matrix, hyaluronan and pressure
topics.orientation: Every tissue is held together by a mesh of proteins and sugars that its own cells secrete, the extracellular matrix. In pancreatic cancer that mesh is both abnormally thick and abnormally wet, and the water it holds generates a mechanical pressure inside the tumor that bears on the tumor's blood vessels and on anything the blood is meant to deliver.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The matrix does two mechanical jobs. Fibrous collagen supplies tensile strength, the resistance to being pulled apart that holds a tissue's shape. Hyaluronan, a long unbranched sugar chain, does something close to the opposite: it binds many times its own weight in water, creating the swelling pressure that gives cartilage its cushioning and skin its turgor, and opening the hydrated space that cells crawl through during healing.
section1.full: Pressure is a normal part of tissue physiology, held low and steady. Fluid leaves the capillaries at their arterial end, is reabsorbed or carried off by lymphatics, and the pressure in the space between cells stays close to atmospheric, so the gradient across the capillary wall runs outward and the vessel stays open. Measured directly in mouse pancreas with a needle-mounted transducer, that pressure was 8 to 13 mmHg, mean 10.4, well below arteriolar pressure of 40 to 80 mmHg and capillary pressure of 15 to 40 mmHg [[TME-003]]; measured in the same organ by two other probes, it ranged from about 2.6 mmHg down to slightly below zero [[TME-014]]. The absolute figure depends on the instrument, and the two studies disagree, but every method agrees on the relationship that matters: normal interstitial pressure sits far below the pressure inside the vessels supplying it. Over 80% of the vessels in normal mouse pancreas had open lumens [[TME-003]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) that relationship inverts. Interstitial pressure measured in mouse tumors ran 75 to 130 mmHg, mean about 99, which is above arteriolar and far above capillary pressure, so the tissue presses harder than the blood supplying it pushes back. Only about a quarter of the vessels in those tumors had open lumens [[TME-003]]. The matrix is not merely dense; it is mechanically loaded.
section2.full: Where that load sits was settled by measuring the same mouse tumors two ways: a catheter sensitive to pressure in any form read 76 mmHg, while a wick-in-needle probe that samples only freely mobile fluid read 12 mmHg, and degrading hyaluronan brought the reading down to about 2 mmHg [[TME-014]]. The pressure is carried by a water-swollen gel, not by blood pressure and not by fluid that could simply drain. Collagen supplies the confinement that lets the gel push: across mouse models hyaluronan compressed vessels only where collagen was abundant too, and a drug that lowered both raised the perfused vessel fraction from 21% to 45% [[TME-015]]. An injected enzyme that degrades hyaluronan raised vessel patency from 30% to 70% with no change in vessel number, so existing vessels were reopened rather than new ones grown [[TME-033]], chemotherapy delivery rose more than sixfold, and the enzyme added to gemcitabine lengthened median mouse survival from 55.5 to 91.5 days after enrollment [[TME-003]]. The human test was negative. Among 492 previously untreated people with metastatic PDAC selected for hyaluronan-high tumors and analyzed as randomized, adding the enzyme pegvorhyaluronidase alfa to the chemotherapy pair nab-paclitaxel and gemcitabine shrank tumors more often, 47% versus 36%, while median overall survival was 11.2 versus 11.5 months, a hazard ratio for death of exactly 1.00 (95% confidence interval 0.80-1.27), with musculoskeletal side effects of any grade in 75.4% versus 46.2% [[TME-004]][[SEC-TME-04]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Every pressure and perfusion figure above was measured in mice. The sources cited here include no measurement of interstitial pressure or vessel perfusion in a human pancreatic tumor, and the phase 3 trial took no on-treatment pressure or perfusion readings, so there is no evidence about whether the mechanism was engaged in the patients treated [[TME-003]][[TME-014]][[TME-004]]. The trial is also not a clean refutation: it allocated patients two-to-one, which reduces precision in the comparison arm, and its placebo arm lived longer than the 8.5 months assumed when the trial was powered, so a modest true benefit could have been missed [[TME-004]]. The one human trial of the other matrix-directed adjunct, losartan (a blood-pressure drug) added to the four-drug chemotherapy FOLFIRINOX before chemoradiotherapy in 49 people with locally advanced disease, was single-arm with no matrix or perfusion measurement, so its 31.4-month median survival cannot be attributed to losartan [[TME-016]].
research_notes.how_studied: Interstitial pressure is measured by putting a probe into a living tumor, and the instrument decides what gets measured: a wick-in-needle responds only to freely mobile fluid, while a piezoelectric catheter responds to load held in any phase, so running both in the same tumor is what distinguishes a gel from a reservoir of drainable fluid [[TME-014]]. Perfusion is assessed by injecting a tracer that labels only vessels with blood actually flowing through them and comparing that against all vessels found by staining, which separates how many vessels exist from how many work [[TME-033]][[TME-003]]. Drug delivery is measured as the concentration of active metabolite recovered from tumor tissue rather than the dose given [[TME-003]]. Response rate counts shrinkage on scans and is a different endpoint from survival [[TME-004]].

mechanism_notes.text: Two unrelated drugs, this enzyme and the autophagy inhibitor hydroxychloroquine, each raised the proportion of patients whose tumors shrank without extending life, which suggests that what limits survival in metastatic pancreatic cancer lies largely outside the lesions being measured [[INF-TME-02]][[TME-004]]. On this reading, getting more drug into a visible tumor improves local control while disease already seeded elsewhere sets the outcome, and the added toxicity, musculoskeletal events in roughly three-quarters of treated patients, can reduce the chemotherapy dose actually delivered [[TME-004]]. A simpler competing explanation is that both trials were powered for larger effects than exist, which would make this a statistical rather than a biological finding [[INF-TME-02]].

topics.clinical_status: Pegvorhyaluronidase alfa is not approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 for pancreatic cancer, and its development in this disease was discontinued after the negative phase 3; losartan is approved in the US for high blood pressure only, and its use in pancreatic cancer is investigational on the strength of a single-arm phase 2.

glossary.definition: The mesh of proteins and sugars that cells secrete around themselves to give a tissue structure and stiffness.
A long sugar chain in the matrix that binds large amounts of water, making the tissue swell and press outward.
The pressure in the fluid and gel between cells, which in a tumor can rise high enough to squeeze its own blood vessels shut.
Blood actually flowing through a tissue, as distinct from the number of blood vessels present in it.
The percentage of people whose tumors shrink by a set amount on scans, which is not the same as living longer.
A number comparing the rate of an event between two trial groups, where 1.00 means no difference between them.

related.statement: Matrix and the pressure it generates are the mechanical part of the desmoplastic reaction around a pancreatic tumor.
Matrix pressure is proposed to collapse the tumor's blood vessels, producing the poor perfusion and low oxygen seen in pancreatic cancer.
The amount of collagen and hyaluronan in the tumor is set by which cancer-associated fibroblast states are active.
The hyaluronan-degrading enzyme was tested as an addition to gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel, the regimen it was given alongside in the phase 3 trial.
Matrix-directed treatment is the clearest example of tumor shrinkage on scans without any gain in survival.
The hyaluronidase phase 3 shows why a response rate and a hazard ratio for death have to be read as separate results.

faq.q: If high pressure keeps chemotherapy out, why didn't lowering it help people?
faq.a: That is the open question. In mice, degrading hyaluronan reopened vessels, raised drug levels and extended survival [[TME-003]][[TME-033]]. In the phase 3 trial the same enzyme made tumors shrink more often but left survival identical, hazard ratio 1.00, while adding substantial musculoskeletal side effects [[TME-004]]. No pressure or perfusion was measured in those patients, so it is not known whether the mechanism worked in them.

faq.q: Is my tumor's pressure something that can be measured?
faq.a: Not in practice. Interstitial pressure in pancreatic cancer has been measured with probes placed directly into tumors in anesthetized mice [[TME-003]][[TME-014]]; the sources cited here contain no such measurement in a person, and there is no clinical test for it.

topics.title: Blood supply and oxygen
topics.orientation: Every cell in the body lives within a couple of hundred micrometers of a blood vessel, because that is roughly as far as oxygen diffuses from one. A pancreatic cancer is unusual in having fewer working vessels than the tissue it replaced, and that shortage shapes both how the tumor behaves and how hard it is to treat.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The pancreas is richly supplied by branches of the celiac and superior mesenteric arteries, which divide down into a dense capillary bed. How dense that bed needs to be is set by the diffusion distance of oxygen, and when a tissue outgrows its supply the resulting low oxygen stabilizes a sensor protein that switches on growth factors, chief among them vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), until new vessels restore the balance.
section1.full: That feedback loop is designed to be self-limiting: low oxygen drives vessel growth, the new vessels relieve the shortage, and the signal subsides. Two features of it matter for what happens in cancer. First, a vessel that exists is not necessarily a vessel that works, because flow depends on the pressure difference along it staying positive and on the vessel staying open against whatever the surrounding tissue presses in with. In normal mouse pancreas essentially every vessel identified by staining was also labeled by a tracer injected into the bloodstream, meaning it was carrying blood [[TME-001]], and over 80% had open lumens [[TME-003]]. Second, the cells that build matrix also release vessel-growth signals, so repair and blood supply are normally coupled: pancreatic stellate cells secrete VEGF, and human stellate cells under low oxygen roughly doubled that output [[TME-009]]. In healthy repair the vascular response keeps pace with the fibrotic one.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) the loop does not close. Counted on stained human tissue, pancreatic tumors had about four times fewer microvessels than normal pancreas, and fibrotic chronic pancreatitis about five times fewer [[TME-009]]. The tumor is less vascular than the gland it grew in, which is also why it shows up as a poorly enhancing area on a contrast-enhanced scan.
section2.full: Low vessel number is compounded by low function. In mice whose tumors arise in their own pancreas, only 32% of the vessels present carried a circulating tracer, against 78% in tumors grown from implanted cells and 100% in normal pancreas, and the active triphosphate form of the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine was undetectable in those tumors while measurable in every comparison tissue [[TME-001]]. The resulting tissue is short of oxygen and of fuel at the same time: human tumors compared against each patient's own adjacent pancreas were consistently depleted of both glucose and the amino acid glutamine [[TME-028]]. The deficit then drives its own cause, because low oxygen activates stellate cells and roughly doubles their secretion of periostin, type I collagen and fibronectin, thickening the matrix that compresses the vessels [[TME-009]]. The obvious therapeutic inference does not follow from this. VEGF rose steeply in stellate cells cultured with cancer cells, to 390% of baseline, while vessel density in the tissue fell, and the stellate cells reciprocally raised the cancer cells' output of the vessel-growth inhibitor endostatin to 210% [[TME-009]]. More vessels is not reliably better either: stripping the stroma from mouse tumors raised vessel density roughly threefold and shortened survival [[TME-002]], while ablating myofibroblasts increased low-oxygen tissue sharply and accelerated the disease [[TME-012]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The human part of this picture is vessel counting on stained tissue sections, which records how many vessels are present rather than how much blood flows through them; the study reporting the four- to fivefold deficit did not state its group sizes in the text available to this atlas and predates molecular subtyping of these tumors [[TME-009]]. The perfusion and drug-delivery measurements come from mice, and the sources cited here include no measurement of perfusion or interstitial pressure in a human pancreatic tumor, so the step from few vessels in human tissue to little drug reaching a human tumor is an extrapolation rather than a measured fact [[TME-001]][[TME-003]]. Nutrient depletion was measured in human tumors against each patient's own normal pancreas, although the authors could not assign it to a tissue compartment [[TME-028]].
research_notes.how_studied: Microvessel density is measured by staining endothelial cells for CD31 and counting vessels per microscope field, a method that treats every vessel as equivalent whether or not blood moves through it [[TME-009]]. Perfusion needs a different design: a tracer injected into the bloodstream labels only vessels with flow, so comparing tracer-labeled against stained vessels yields the working fraction [[TME-001]][[TME-033]]. Low oxygen is mapped with a compound that binds covalently to tissue only where oxygen is scarce, leaving a stain whose extent reflects how hypoxic the tissue was [[TME-012]]. Nutrient levels are measured by snap-freezing tumor and adjacent normal tissue in the operating room and analyzing it by mass spectrometry, which captures concentrations at the moment of removal but is not a practicable clinical test [[TME-028]].

mechanism_notes.text: Vessel density behaves here as a consequence rather than a lever: interventions that raised it in mice shortened survival, and one that raised hypoxia also accelerated the disease, so neither oxygen level nor vessel count on its own predicts which way a treatment effect will go [[INF-TME-01]][[TME-002]][[TME-012]]. The more consistent account is that the stromal cells removed in those experiments were also restraining the tumor and supporting an immune response, and the vascular change traveled with that loss rather than producing the outcome [[TME-036]]. Stroma-poor mouse tumors did become sensitive to an antibody against the VEGF receptor that did nothing in stroma-intact tumors, so the vascular compartment is not irrelevant; its effect depends on the tissue around it [[TME-002]].

topics.clinical_status: No antiangiogenic or vessel-directed therapy is approved or standard in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 for pancreatic cancer.

glossary.definition: A shortage of oxygen in a tissue, which changes how its cells behave and which genes they switch on.
Blood actually flowing through a tissue, as distinct from the number of vessels present in it.
The number of small blood vessels counted in a standard area of stained tissue under the microscope.
A signaling protein released by oxygen-starved tissue that instructs nearby blood vessels to grow.
A naturally occurring fragment of a matrix protein that inhibits the growth of new blood vessels.
Having fewer blood vessels than the surrounding tissue, which is how pancreatic cancer typically appears.

related.statement: The pressure generated by matrix and hyaluronan is the proposed cause of the vessel collapse and poor perfusion in pancreatic tumors.
Poor blood supply and low oxygen are features of the tissue created by the desmoplastic reaction around a pancreatic cancer.
Cancer-associated fibroblasts both release vessel-growth signals and build the matrix that compresses vessels, so their state shapes the tumor's blood supply.
The same poor supply that starves a pancreatic tumor of oxygen leaves it short of glucose and glutamine, which is the setting for nutrient scavenging.
A tumor's poorer blood supply is what makes it enhance less than the surrounding pancreas on a contrast-enhanced CT scan.
Low oxygen in the tumor is one of the conditions that shapes the behavior of macrophages and other myeloid cells inside it.

faq.q: Does pancreatic cancer have a lot of blood vessels, like other tumors?
faq.a: The opposite. Human pancreatic tumors had about four times fewer small blood vessels than normal pancreas when counted on stained tissue [[TME-009]], and in mice only about a third of the vessels present were carrying blood at all [[TME-001]]. This is why drugs that block vessel growth, useful in some other cancers, have no established role here.

faq.q: If the tumor is starved of oxygen and nutrients, why doesn't it die?
faq.a: It adapts. Human tumors are depleted of glucose and glutamine relative to the patient's own normal pancreas, and the cancer cells take up and digest extracellular protein to replace what is missing [[TME-028]]. The surrounding stellate cells also feed them, so scarcity selects for cells that handle it well rather than killing the tumor off.

topics.title: Nutrient scarcity, autophagy and scavenging
topics.orientation: A pancreatic tumor is a poorly supplied piece of tissue, and the cancer cells inside it have to find carbon and nitrogen somewhere. This entry covers the ordinary feeding and recycling machinery every cell has, how pancreatic cancer runs that machinery harder, and what happened when a drug was used to try to shut it off.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Cells can feed in two ways. They can import single molecules, such as glucose and individual amino acids, through dedicated transporters in the membrane, or they can swallow bulk material and digest it. Autophagy, literally self-eating, is the second route turned inward: the cell wraps a parcel of its own contents in a membrane and delivers it to the lysosome, the acidic compartment where enzymes cut proteins back into amino acids for reuse.
section1.full: The lysosome is the common destination for both routes. In autophagy, proteins of the ATG family build a double membrane around a region of cytoplasm and any worn-out organelles in it; the resulting autophagosome fuses with a lysosome, and a protein called LC3 embedded in the autophagosome wall is consumed along with the cargo, which is why counting LC3 dots in a cell, or measuring its processed form LC3-II, is how the pathway is read out in a laboratory [[TME-025]]. Macropinocytosis is the outward-facing version of the same idea: the cell throws out a ruffle of membrane, closes it around a gulp of surrounding fluid and whatever protein is dissolved in it, and routes that vesicle to the lysosome as well [[TME-008]]. Both processes idle at a low rate in a well-fed cell and are turned up by starvation, and both are part of how any cell survives a few hours without a meal. The reason bulk feeding is worth the trouble is arithmetic: in blood, the amino acids locked inside proteins such as albumin outnumber the free amino acids floating beside them by roughly two hundred to one [[TME-028]]. Pancreatic stellate cells, the vitamin-A-storing cells of the normal pancreas, use autophagy for their own housekeeping.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Resected human pancreatic tumors are measurably short of both glucose and glutamine compared with the benign pancreas beside them, so the tumor interior is a lean place to live [[TME-028]]. Pancreatic cancer cells make up the shortfall by scavenging: mutant KRAS, the cancer's main driver gene, drives them to drink extracellular protein, neighboring stellate cells hand them a particular amino acid, and they lean on autophagy continuously rather than only under stress.
section2.full: Three supply lines have been described, each resting on a different kind of evidence. Cells carrying mutant RAS take up far more fluid than cells with the normal gene, digest the albumin in it, and use the released amino acids to grow in media too poor in glutamine to support them otherwise; blocking the uptake with the inhibitor EIPA reversed that rescue, and the same gulping was visible in human pancreatic tumor tissue as well as in mice [[TME-008]][[TME-028]]. Pancreatic stellate cells secrete alanine through their own autophagy, and cancer cells burn that alanine in preference to glucose or glutamine; stellate cells engineered to be autophagy-incompetent produced fewer and slower-growing tumors when co-injected into mice [[TME-029]]. Pancreatic cancer cells also run high baseline autophagy, and in a genetic mouse model chloroquine, a drug that blocks the lysosomal step of autophagy, changed survival sharply, with eight of eight control animals dead by 140 days against one of eight treated by about 180 days [[TME-025]]. That mouse result sent the related drug hydroxychloroquine into trials, which did not deliver. Added to the chemotherapy pair gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel as first-line treatment in 112 randomized patients with previously untreated advanced disease, it raised the proportion of tumors that shrank from 21.1 to 38.2 percent while leaving twelve-month survival at 41 percent versus 49 percent, missing the primary endpoint [[TME-027]]. Hydroxychloroquine is not approved in the US for pancreatic cancer as of 8 October 2026.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The negative hydroxychloroquine trials do not show that autophagy is the wrong target, because the drug was never shown to hit it. In the single-arm study, in twenty previously treated patients, only two were free of progression at two months, and LC3-II, a marker first validated in mice given autophagy-inhibiting chloroquine doses, rose inconsistently in patients' blood lymphocytes at 800 or 1,200 mg daily [[TME-026]]. A drug that misses its target and a mechanism that does not matter look identical from the outside and call for opposite next steps. Separately, the human nutrient measurements come from whole tissue, a mixture of cancer cells, fibroblasts, immune cells and matrix, so a low tumor glutamine level cannot be assigned to any one cell type, as those authors state [[TME-028]].
research_notes.how_studied: Nutrient levels were measured by clamping and freezing tumor and adjacent benign pancreas during the operation itself, then quantifying metabolites by mass spectrometry, so the comparison is internal to each patient rather than against a separate control group [[TME-028]]. Which amino acids came from scavenged protein rather than from free monomers was separated by feeding cells heavy-isotope-labeled media [[TME-028]]. Fluid uptake is traced with a labeled dextran that a cell can only acquire by gulping [[TME-008]]. The stellate-cell contribution was narrowed from about two hundred candidate metabolites down to alanine and then tested by disabling autophagy in the supplying cell [[TME-029]]. Autophagy itself is read from LC3 in tissue, or from LC3-II in blood cells when tumor tissue is not available [[TME-025]][[TME-026]].

mechanism_notes.text: Two mechanistically unrelated drugs, a hyaluronan-degrading enzyme and hydroxychloroquine, each raised the proportion of tumors that shrank while leaving survival unchanged or numerically worse [[INF-TME-02]][[TME-004]][[TME-027]]. One reading is that both improve control of the lesions being measured while survival is set by disease outside them and by how much chemotherapy a patient can absorb, with added toxicity canceling the local gain. A simpler explanation is also live: both trials may have been sized for larger effects than exist, so the response gains are real but too small to move survival detectably.

glossary.definition: A cell's recycling route, in which it wraps part of its own contents in a membrane and delivers the parcel to the lysosome to be broken down into reusable building blocks.
Bulk drinking: a cell throws out a ruffle of membrane, closes it around a gulp of surrounding fluid, and digests whatever protein was dissolved in it.
The acidic compartment inside a cell where delivered material is cut back into its component parts.
A resident pancreatic cell that stores vitamin A when quiescent and turns into a matrix-producing myofibroblast when activated.
Direct evidence that a drug actually reached and acted on the molecule it was designed to hit, measured separately from whether the patient improved.
A tumor shrinking by a defined amount on imaging, which is a different measurement from living longer.

related.statement: The nutrient scarcity inside a pancreatic tumor follows from the poor, compressed blood supply and low oxygen described in the entry on blood supply and oxygen.
Mutant KRAS, the gene change covered in the KRAS entry, drives the fluid-gulping uptake route that supplies amino acids to pancreatic cancer cells.
Pancreatic stellate cells, the precursors of the cancer-associated fibroblast states described in that entry, feed alanine to pancreatic cancer cells through their own autophagy.
The same autophagy that feeds pancreatic cancer cells also carries their MHC class I molecules to the lysosome, which is the subject of the antigen presentation entry.
The hydroxychloroquine trials sit alongside the hyaluronidase trials in the entry on lessons from stroma-directed treatments, as the two clearest cases of tumor shrinkage without longer survival.

faq.q: Is hydroxychloroquine a treatment for pancreatic cancer?
faq.a: No, and it is not approved in the US for this disease as of 8 October 2026. Given alone it left two of twenty patients free of progression at two months [[TME-026]], and added to chemotherapy in a randomized trial it did not improve survival [[TME-027]]. Laboratory work has moved to combinations, because blocking the MAPK growth pathway (the signaling chain downstream of KRAS) makes pancreatic cancer cells depend on autophagy much more heavily, so the two blocks are being studied together in cells, organoids and mice [[RAS-016]][[RAS-017]].

faq.q: My scan shows the tumor got smaller. Does that mean I will live longer?
faq.a: Shrinkage and survival are separate measurements, and in pancreatic cancer they have come apart more than once. Hydroxychloroquine nearly doubled the proportion of tumors that shrank, and twelve-month survival was 41 percent with it against 49 percent without [[TME-027]]. Shrinkage can still matter for other reasons, including whether an operation becomes possible, which is worth asking your team about directly.

faq.q: Can I starve the tumor by changing what I eat?
faq.a: None of the studies cited here tested fasting, low-protein diets or sugar restriction in people with pancreatic cancer, so there is no evidence here in either direction. The scarcity described in this entry is a property of the tumor's own tissue, produced by its blood supply and its appetite, rather than of what is on the plate; eating and nutrition through treatment is covered in its own entry.

topics.title: T cells and why they are kept out
topics.orientation: T cells are the part of the immune system that can recognize and kill a cell for what is inside it. In pancreatic cancer they are usually present in the tumor but held away from the cancer cells and switched off, and this entry covers how that happens and why releasing a single brake has not been enough.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: T cells mature in the thymus, each carrying one randomly built receptor. Cytotoxic T cells, marked by a surface protein called CD8, inspect fragments of protein displayed on other cells and kill those showing something no healthy cell makes. Helper T cells, marked by CD4, coordinate the response; regulatory T cells shut it down again. A T cell only becomes a killer after a dendritic cell, the immune system's specialized presenting cell, presents a fragment to it with a second, confirming signal.
section1.full: Two things govern where a T cell goes and what it does once there. Movement is chemical: tissues release small proteins called chemokines, and a T cell crawls up the concentration gradient of whichever chemokine its own receptors can read, so a signal that is strong in one part of a tissue will hold cells in that part. Function is contractual: recognizing a fragment held out on a major histocompatibility complex, or MHC, molecule is only the first signal, and without a second, co-stimulatory signal from a professional antigen-presenting cell the T cell becomes anergic, meaning unresponsive to that target in future, or converts into a regulatory cell that suppresses its neighbors. Becoming an effector killer is also metabolically expensive, so a T cell that arrives in tissue short of glucose and glutamine is handicapped before it begins [[TME-028]]. The normal proportions are reasonably stable and can be measured: in uninvolved human pancreas, CD8 cells make up about 67 percent of all T cells and CD4 cells about 17 percent [[TME-010]]. That baseline matters, because what a tumor does to it can be read against it.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Inside pancreatic tumors the mix inverts: the CD8 share of T cells falls to about 47 percent while CD4 rises to 36 percent, and survival after surgery tracked not how many cytotoxic T cells were present but how many sat within twenty micrometers of a cancer cell [[TME-010]]. What holds them back looks chemical rather than mechanical, and the checkpoint drugs that work elsewhere have found almost nothing here to release.
section2.full: The mechanical story was tested and failed: across 132 resected human tumors, denser collagen-I did not reduce cytotoxic T-cell infiltration, and went with more T-cell subpopulations rather than fewer [[TME-010]]. A chemical account fits better. Sorting tissue by distance from the cancer cells shows CD8 cells abundant in the wider stroma but sparse within 100 micrometers of tumor cells, a pattern seen in pancreatic cancer and not in ampullary or bile-duct tumors; silencing the chemokine CXCL12 in activated stellate cells, or returning them to a resting state, abolished the attraction those cells exerted on patient-derived CD8 cells [[TME-018]]. In mice, cancer cells are coated with CXCL12 made by fibroblasts carrying fibroblast activation protein, and blocking its receptor CXCR4 let antibodies against PD-L1, a brake-releasing checkpoint drug, work in a model where they do nothing alone [[TME-019]]. In people that chain has not converted: a CXCR4 antagonist with the checkpoint antibody pembrolizumab and no chemotherapy produced one objective response in 37 patients [[IMM-010]]; ipilimumab, a checkpoint antibody against CTLA-4, given alone produced none in a 27-patient single-arm trial, with grade 3 or worse immune side effects in three [[TME-035]]; the PD-L1 antibody durvalumab with or without the CTLA-4 antibody tremelimumab gave a 3.1 percent response rate in 65 second-line patients [[TME-007]]; and both added to first-line chemotherapy in 180 randomized patients left median survival at 9.8 months with them against 8.8 without [[IMM-007]]. Among people who lived years after resection, long survival went with having both many predicted neoantigen targets (new protein fragments made by the tumor's mutations) and a dense CD8 infiltrate, neither sufficient alone [[TME-006]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Proximity rather than abundance was the measurement that tracked outcome, and how it was obtained bounds what it means: it was computed with spatial statistics on tissue microarray cores, no functional or exhaustion markers were measured, and resected patients are an earlier-stage group, so cells lying close to cancer cells may mark a permissive tumor rather than active killing, and a slower tumor may simply allow more time for infiltration [[TME-010]]. The long-term-survivor work carries the mirror-image caution: neoantigens were predicted by algorithm rather than measured as peptides on MHC, and exceptional survivors may differ in tumor biology as well as in immunity [[TME-006]]. The trials are sharper in one direction than the other. They exclude a large effect of checkpoint blockade in the populations tested, which were unselected and often second-line, and cannot exclude benefit in a selected subgroup [[TME-007]][[TME-035]].
research_notes.how_studied: T-cell content is read from tissue by staining several markers at once on one slide, which lets CD8, CD4 and regulatory cells be told apart and their coordinates recorded; proximity is then quantified by asking, for every cancer cell, how many cytotoxic T cells lie within a set radius, which is a different question from how many are in the section [[TME-010]]. Compartment analysis is a coarser version of the same idea, drawing a line at 100 micrometers from tumor cells and counting on each side [[TME-018]]. Whether a chemokine causes the pattern is tested by removing it, either by silencing CXCL12 in cultured stellate cells and watching migration stop [[TME-018]], or by depleting the cells that make it in mice and asking whether checkpoint antibodies acquire an effect they did not have [[TME-019]]. Which T cells are tumor-specific is established by sequencing their receptors and testing reactivity against predicted targets [[TME-006]].

mechanism_notes.text: T cells that do reach pancreatic cancer cells may be disarmed in place rather than merely kept out [[INF-TME-03]]. Antigen shown without a co-stimulatory signal drives anergy or conversion to a regulatory state, and the glucose- and glutamine-poor interstitium denies an arriving cell the fuel that effector differentiation needs [[TME-017]][[TME-028]]. Releasing one inhibitory receptor would then have little to act on, which fits the mouse experiments in which checkpoint antibodies acquire activity only after a stromal or myeloid suppressor is removed first [[TME-019]][[TME-037]]. The competing account is that too few tumor-specific T cells are ever primed, in which case improving the local environment alone would not help.

Where tumor-specific T cells have been supplied directly rather than coaxed out, the limiting factors look like the number of effective killer cells delivered and their being switched off locally, rather than their ability to enter the tumor [[INF-IMMUNE-01]]. In mouse models, whether a pancreatic tumor admits transferred T cells is a property of the tumor and not of the cell product, and the innate receptor TLR2 on the T cells themselves restrains their entry, since deleting it only in T cells changed infiltration [[IMM-023]]. The human contribution to that finding is a transcriptional correlation, and no TLR2-directed drug has been tested in this disease.

glossary.definition: A T cell marked by CD8 that inspects protein fragments displayed on other cells and kills a cell showing something it recognizes as abnormal.
A small signaling protein released by tissue that immune cells follow, moving towards wherever its concentration is highest.
A chemokine made by activated fibroblasts and stellate cells that attracts and holds T cells, implicated in keeping them away from pancreatic cancer cells.
The second, confirming signal a T cell needs alongside antigen recognition; without it the cell is switched off rather than switched on.
A lasting unresponsive state a T cell enters when it meets its target without the confirming co-stimulatory signal.
A T cell whose job is to suppress other immune cells, useful for preventing autoimmunity and unhelpful when it suppresses an anti-tumor response.
An antibody that blocks a braking receptor such as PD-1 or CTLA-4 on a T cell, releasing a restraint rather than creating a new response.

related.statement: Activated stellate cells and fibroblasts carrying fibroblast activation protein (FAP), the cell states described in the cancer-associated fibroblasts entry, are the source of the CXCL12 that holds CD8 T cells away from pancreatic cancer cells.
Collagen density in the desmoplastic stroma did not reduce cytotoxic T-cell infiltration in resected human pancreatic tumors, so desmoplasia is not a simple wall keeping T cells out.
A CD8 T cell cannot act on a pancreatic cancer cell unless that cell is displaying MHC class I at its surface, which the antigen presentation entry describes.
Macrophages and myeloid suppressor cells occupy the space immediately around pancreatic cancer cells from which CD8 T cells are largely absent.
The immune combinations entry covers the chemokine blockers and checkpoint pairings built on the T-cell exclusion mechanism described here.
Engineered T cells are an attempt to supply the tumor-specific T cells that pancreatic cancer appears not to generate in sufficient numbers on its own.

faq.q: Does my tumor have immune cells in it?
faq.a: Almost certainly yes. Pancreatic tumors usually contain T cells, and the issue is where they sit and what state they are in rather than whether they arrived at all [[TME-010]][[TME-018]]. A standard pathology report does not quantify this, and apart from mismatch-repair testing no immune measurement on tissue is currently used to choose treatment in this disease.

faq.q: Why do the immunotherapy drugs that work in melanoma do so little here?
faq.a: Those drugs release a brake on T cells that are already primed and functional, and in pancreatic cancer the trials have been close to flat: no responses in 27 patients given ipilimumab [[TME-035]], 3.1 percent with dual blockade in 65 [[TME-007]], and no survival difference when both were added to chemotherapy in 180 randomized patients [[IMM-007]]. The exception is the small group of tumors with mismatch-repair deficiency, which has its own entry.

faq.q: If T cells are already next to the cancer cells, what is stopping them?
faq.a: That is the open question, and two answers are being tested. One is that the cells present have been switched off where they stand, by antigen shown without co-stimulation and by a nutrient-poor interstitium [[TME-017]][[TME-028]]. The other is that too few tumor-specific cells were ever generated, so most of those nearby are bystanders of irrelevant specificity [[TME-006]].

topics.title: Macrophages and myeloid suppressor cells
topics.orientation: Macrophages, monocytes and neutrophils are the immune system's first responders and its clean-up crew. In pancreatic cancer they are the most abundant immune cells present and they sit closest to the cancer cells, and the attempts to redirect them have produced the field's most striking mouse results and some of its most instructive human failures.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Myeloid cells are the branch of white blood cells that eat things. Neutrophils arrive first at an injury and die quickly. Monocytes follow out of the bone marrow and mature into macrophages, which swallow debris and dying cells, digest them, and display the fragments to T cells. Macrophages also run the repair program after an injury: they call in fibroblasts, help build new matrix, and then wind the response down.
section1.full: Three signaling axes recruit and sustain these cells, and all three reappear inside tumors. Colony-stimulating factor 1, acting through its receptor CSF1R, is the survival and differentiation signal for macrophages, so blocking the receptor reduces their numbers and changes the character of those that remain [[TME-020]]. The receptor CCR2 lets inflammatory monocytes leave the bone marrow and enter the blood, which is why blocking it is detected as a shift in the ratio of monocytes held in marrow to monocytes circulating [[IMM-017]]. CXCR2 reads the chemokines that summon neutrophils to a site [[TME-021]]. The repair program is itself a loop: macrophages help activate resident fibroblast-like cells, those cells deposit matrix, and the stiffened tissue signals back through adhesion complexes containing focal adhesion kinase, an enzyme cells use to sense what they are attached to [[TME-022]]. In the liver the resident version of this loop runs through hepatic stellate cells, which sit quiescent until something turns them into matrix-secreting myofibroblasts [[SURG-023]]. In healthy tissue the loop resolves once repair is done.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Myeloid cells dominate the tissue immediately around pancreatic cancer cells, the same space from which CD8 T cells are largely absent. In mice, removing or reprogramming them repeatedly turns a tumor that ignores checkpoint antibodies into one that responds. In people the same maneuvers have produced eye-catching early signals and then failed the randomized test, and one of them failed through a mechanism nobody had predicted.
section2.full: Mouse work makes the point from several directions. Blocking CSF1R cut macrophage numbers and pushed the survivors towards displaying antigen, but also raised the T-cell brake molecules PD-L1 and CTLA-4 and so limited its own benefit; only the combination with both checkpoint antibodies and gemcitabine produced complete regression, in 30 percent of animals [[TME-020]]. Blocking CXCR2, which in human tumors is expressed mainly on neutrophils and myeloid suppressor cells, abolished metastasis and made anti-PD-1 extend survival where it is inert alone [[TME-021]]. Inhibiting focal adhesion kinase, most active in human tumors where collagen is dense and CD8 cells few, doubled median mouse survival by holding tumors still rather than shrinking them, and converted a checkpoint-refractory model [[TME-022]]. In the liver, macrophage-derived granulin activates hepatic stellate cells into a fibrotic niche that supports metastasis and excludes CD8 cells; removing granulin restored the effect of PD-1 blockade [[SURG-023]][[SURG-024]]. Stimulating CD40 was the surprise: it drove regressions in mice that required macrophages and occurred without T cells or chemotherapy, the reverse of the reasoning behind it [[TME-023]]. Human results run the other way. A CCR2 inhibitor with the four-drug chemotherapy FOLFIRINOX gave partial responses in 16 of 33 patients against a prespecified 25 percent benchmark, and was not advanced [[IMM-017]]. In the randomized PRINCE trial, in 105 patients with untreated metastatic disease, only the arm combining chemotherapy with nivolumab, a PD-1 checkpoint antibody, met its one-year survival endpoint, at 57.7 percent; both CD40 arms missed, the triple combination lowest at 41.3 percent [[TME-024]][[SEC-TME-03]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The gap between the mouse and human columns is the main finding rather than a footnote. Every myeloid maneuver that converted a checkpoint-refractory mouse into a responsive one used an implanted or autochthonous (arising in the animal's own pancreas) tumor whose stroma is younger and more immunogenic than established human disease, and most measured tumor volume over days to weeks rather than survival [[TME-020]][[TME-022]]. The single human signal large enough to notice came from 33 patients in one arm of a non-randomized study whose 25 percent comparison rate was an assumption, and whose response rate sits inside the range FOLFIRINOX alone produces when the tumor has not spread beyond the pancreas and the vessels around it [[IMM-017]]. PRINCE is the most informative reading, because its 35 percent one-year benchmark was later shown to be too low: contemporary chemotherapy-alone rates and the trial's own synthetic control were nearer 40 to 45 percent, which narrows any apparent gain in every arm [[TME-024]].
research_notes.how_studied: Macrophage and neutrophil populations are counted by flow cytometry after a tumor is dissociated into single cells, with surface markers separating suppressive states from antigen-presenting ones [[TME-020]]. Whether a cell type is necessary for an effect is tested by removing it and repeating the experiment: depleting macrophages with clodronate-loaded liposomes abolished CD40-driven regression, while depleting CD4 and CD8 T cells did not, which is how the mechanism was pinned to macrophages [[TME-023]]. Target engagement in people is sometimes measured where the drug acts rather than in the tumor, as with the marrow-to-blood monocyte ratio used for a CCR2 inhibitor [[IMM-017]]. Where two tools disagree the gap is informative: deleting CXCR2 from the germline and blocking it with a drug both abolished metastasis in mice, but only the drug slowed the primary tumor [[TME-021]]. Human myeloid biology is otherwise inferred largely from stained sections and expression data, which show where cells are but not what they are doing [[TME-022]].

mechanism_notes.text: A consistent reading of the mouse data is that checkpoint antibodies have little to release until a local suppressor is removed first [[INF-TME-03]]. Depleting FAP-positive fibroblasts, blocking CSF1R and inhibiting focal adhesion kinase each uncovered activity that anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 did not have alone [[TME-019]][[TME-020]][[TME-022]]. On that account myeloid cells are one of two or three convergent brakes, which would explain why adding a single agent to chemotherapy has not worked in people. The competing account is that too few tumor-specific T cells are ever generated, in which case releasing the brakes changes little.

A specific caution falls out of the combination data: regulatory T cells expanded in step with CD8 cells under CSF1R-containing combination therapy, so removing a myeloid brake can recruit a lymphoid one [[INF-IMMUNE-01]]. Blocking CSF1R also raised PD-L1 and CTLA-4 in the same experiments, which is the same shape of problem [[TME-020]]. The practical consequence is that a rise in tumor-infiltrating CD8 cells after a myeloid-directed drug is a pharmacodynamic result, not evidence that patients benefit.

glossary.definition: A long-lived myeloid cell that swallows debris and dying cells, displays fragments of them to T cells, and helps direct tissue repair.
A macrophage inside a tumor, usually in a state that supports tissue building and suppresses T cells rather than one that attacks the cancer.
An immature myeloid cell that accumulates in cancer and actively blunts T-cell responses.
The receptor through which macrophages receive their main survival and differentiation signal, and a drug target for reducing or reprogramming them.
A protein secreted by macrophages in the liver that activates hepatic stellate cells into a scar-forming state supporting metastatic growth.
A receptor on antigen-presenting cells that, when stimulated by an antibody, activates them; in mouse pancreatic tumors the resulting regressions depended on macrophages rather than T cells.
A measurement showing a drug changed the biology it was aimed at, which is separate from showing the patient did better.

related.statement: Macrophage-secreted granulin activates hepatic stellate cells, one of the steps by which the liver is prepared for metastasis.
Myeloid cells fill the space immediately around pancreatic cancer cells where CD8 T cells are sparse, and removing myeloid suppression is what made checkpoint antibodies work in mouse models.
Macrophages help drive the fibroblast activation and matrix deposition that produce desmoplasia, and focal adhesion kinase signaling links the stiffened matrix back to myeloid suppression.
The CD40 agonist and chemokine-receptor blockers described in the immune combinations entry are the clinical expression of the myeloid mechanisms in this entry.
Reprogramming tumor macrophages towards displaying antigen is one route into the antigen presentation problem, since macrophages are among the cells that show fragments to T cells.

faq.q: Is there a drug that targets these cells?
faq.a: Not an approved one. As of 8 October 2026 no CSF1R, CCR2, CXCR2, focal adhesion kinase or CD40-directed agent is approved in the US for pancreatic cancer. The CD40 agonist sotigalimab was the furthest along and missed its one-year survival endpoint in a randomized phase 2 trial [[TME-024]], and the CCR2 inhibitor tested with FOLFIRINOX was not carried forward after its single-arm study [[IMM-017]].

faq.q: A trial report said a drug lowered suppressive immune cells. Is that good news?
faq.a: It is evidence the drug did what it was designed to do, which is a necessary step and not the same as benefit. Blocking CSF1R in mice reduced macrophages and simultaneously raised the checkpoint molecules PD-L1 and CTLA-4, limiting its own effect [[TME-020]], and the human studies that confirmed target engagement most convincingly still did not change survival [[IMM-017]][[TME-024]].

topics.title: Antigen presentation and immune invisibility
topics.orientation: For a T cell to kill a cancer cell, the cancer cell has to show it something. This entry covers how that display works, the precise step at which pancreatic cancer breaks it, why supplying more targets has not been the answer, and the rare exception, well under one tumor in a hundred, in which the whole system does work.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Every nucleated cell in the body continuously advertises what it is making. Proteins are chopped into short peptides, loaded onto MHC class I molecules inside the cell, and carried to the surface, where passing CD8 T cells inspect them. A cell showing a peptide no healthy cell makes is marked for killing. Separately, specialized dendritic cells carry tumor material to lymph nodes and teach new T cells what to look for.
section1.full: MHC class I, short for major histocompatibility complex class I and called HLA class I in people, is assembled in the endoplasmic reticulum from a heavy chain, a small partner protein called beta-2-microglobulin, and a peptide delivered by a transporter from the cell's own protein-recycling machinery. Without beta-2-microglobulin the complex is unstable and never reaches the surface, which is why removing it is the standard way to prove that an effect depends on surface MHC class I [[IMM-009]]. A second class, MHC class II, is carried by professional antigen-presenting cells and shows peptides to CD4 helper T cells, chaperoned by an invariant chain called CD74 [[TME-017]]. Priming is a division of labor. One dendritic-cell subset, the conventional type 1 or cDC1, which depends on the transcription factor BATF3, is specialized for collecting material from dying cells and presenting it to CD8 T cells in the draining lymph node, and mice lacking BATF3 cannot mount a CD8 response against a tumor [[IMM-009]]. Presentation must also come with co-stimulatory molecules. A cell that shows a peptide without them does not activate a T cell; it tolerizes one [[TME-017]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Pancreatic cancer cells do make MHC class I; they destroy it. The molecules are tagged with ubiquitin, a disposal label, collected by a receptor called NBR1, and carried by autophagy to the lysosome, so the surface display is thin while the protein itself is intact inside the cell [[IMM-009]]. Upstream of that, the pancreas is unusually short of the dendritic cells that prime CD8 T cells.
section2.full: In human pancreatic cancer cell lines MHC class I shows up as cytoplasmic dots sitting with lysosomes, where normal ductal cells put it on the membrane, and every human tumor examined contained regions of internalized MHC class I [[IMM-009]]. Blocking autophagy, genetically or with the lysosome-blocking drug chloroquine, moved it back to the surface and let mouse tumors be killed by CD8 T cells; the benefit vanished if CD8 cells were depleted, if the host lacked cDC1, or if beta-2-microglobulin was removed, which places the bottleneck at presentation itself [[IMM-009]]. Targets are not the shortage. When a strong model antigen was engineered into mouse pancreatic tumors, disease accelerated, with higher-grade lesions, more fibrosis, more liver metastases and shorter survival, and checkpoint blockade still did nothing; the pancreas held ten times fewer cDC1 than the lung at the same stage, and mobilizing them reversed the acceleration in a CD8- and interferon-gamma-dependent way [[IMM-011]]. Both come from mice and cell lines with a surrogate antigen stronger than any real pancreatic one. The exception is narrow: of 4,626 pancreatic cancers queried at one center, 55 carried a mismatch-repair gene variant and only about half of those were microsatellite-instability-high [[IMM-027]], and in unselected metastatic disease 172 of 173 patients were microsatellite stable [[IMM-007]]. The checkpoint antibody pembrolizumab is approved in the US for previously treated microsatellite-instability-high or mismatch-repair-deficient solid tumors, pancreatic cancer included [[SEC-TME-02]]; reported response rates there run from 4 of 22 in the labeled registration cohort to 7 of 9 in a small liquid-biopsy series [[SEC-TX-04]][[IMM-021]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Two measurement problems bound what can be claimed about the exception. The first is detection: roughly one in five mismatch-repair-variant cases at one center was classified as microsatellite-instability-high only after orthogonal or computational re-testing, mostly in specimens with few tumor cells, and a plasma assay identified a case that staining of a pancreatic biopsy had called normal [[IMM-027]][[IMM-021]]. Earlier estimates of how common the finding is in pancreatic cancer ranged from 0 to 75 percent across studies for exactly this reason [[IMM-020]]. The second is denominators: reported response rates in microsatellite-instability-high pancreatic cancer run from 4 of 22 in the labeled registration cohort to 7 of 9 in a liquid-biopsy series, with wide intervals around each and the highest figures coming from retrospective series, some combined with chemotherapy [[SEC-TX-04]][[IMM-021]][[IMM-027]].
