Carrying the variant is also not the same as responding: one documented patient progressed through checkpoint blockade and several later chemotherapy lines [[IMM-020]].
research_notes.how_studied: Where a molecule sits inside a cell is established by staining it alongside lysosome markers and by physically separating lysosomes and measuring their contents [[IMM-009]]. Which carrier takes it there was found by attaching to MHC class I an enzyme that labels whatever comes close, then asking which autophagy receptors had been labeled [[IMM-009]]. Necessity is tested by epistasis, meaning that a downstream requirement is removed and the effect is looked for again: deleting CD8 cells, the BATF3 gene that cDC1 need, or beta-2-microglobulin each abolished the benefit of autophagy inhibition [[IMM-009]]. Whether antigen was limiting was tested by engineering a defined antigen into a spontaneous tumor and comparing two organs that differ in dendritic-cell content [[IMM-011]]. Microsatellite status in patients is assigned by combining immunohistochemistry, PCR and sequencing rather than relying on one assay [[IMM-027]].

mechanism_notes.text: Because lysosomal inhibition raises surface MHC class I and the resulting T-cell response needs cDC1, the proposing authors argue the combination worth testing is an autophagy inhibitor with both PD-1 and CTLA-4 blockade rather than either alone, which is what the mouse data showed [[INF-IMMUNE-03]][[IMM-009]]. The weak link is exposure: hydroxychloroquine at doses people tolerate did not consistently inhibit autophagy even by a blood marker [[TME-026]]. No trial has combined an autophagy inhibitor with checkpoint blockade in pancreatic cancer, so this is a reason to watch one specific combination rather than a reason to take the drug.

A second route to invisibility does not involve the cancer cell at all [[INF-TME-03]]. A fibroblast state found in mouse pancreatic tumors carries MHC class II and CD74 but lacks classical co-stimulatory molecules, and it engaged CD4 T-cell receptors in an antigen-specific way in culture while myofibroblasts did not [[TME-017]]. The discovering authors proposed it works as a decoy that anergizes CD4 cells or pushes them towards a regulatory state; that consequence has not been demonstrated, the human counterpart is uncertain, and later work derives these cells from mesothelium (the lining layer of the abdominal cavity) rather than from fibroblasts [[TME-017]].

glossary.definition: The surface molecule, called HLA class I in people, that every nucleated cell uses to display short peptides from the proteins it is making.
The small partner protein without which MHC class I cannot fold properly or reach the cell surface.
A peptide created by a mutation in the cancer, and therefore one that no healthy cell in the body displays.
A specialized dendritic cell that collects material from dying cells and presents it to CD8 T cells in a lymph node, which is the step that starts a killer response.
Loss of the system that corrects copying errors in DNA, which leaves the cancer with large numbers of mutations and therefore many visible targets.
A pattern of shifting lengths in short repeated DNA sequences that indicates mismatch repair has failed, used as the test for that state.
Staining a tissue slide with antibodies to show whether a particular protein is present and where it sits.

related.statement: The same autophagy pathway that supplies pancreatic cancer cells with amino acids also carries their MHC class I molecules to the lysosome to be destroyed.
Antigen presentation is the step that has to work before a CD8 T cell can recognize and kill a pancreatic cancer cell.
Mismatch repair deficiency and microsatellite instability mark the small group of pancreatic cancers that generate enough visible targets for checkpoint blockade to work.
Pembrolizumab is approved in the US for microsatellite-instability-high tumors, which is the only immunotherapy route that antigen presentation currently opens in pancreatic cancer.
Personalized mRNA neoantigen vaccines address the priming step rather than the surface-display step that this entry describes.
One cancer-associated fibroblast state carries MHC class II without co-stimulatory molecules, so it may present antigen to CD4 T cells without activating them.

faq.q: Should my tumor be tested for microsatellite instability or mismatch repair?
faq.a: This is the one immune test in pancreatic cancer that can open an approved treatment, and the answer depends on which assay is run: about a fifth of positive cases at one center were found only after re-testing by a second method, and a blood-based assay has identified a case that tissue staining called normal [[IMM-027]][[IMM-021]]. Which assays are ordered varies between centers; the molecular testing entry covers the usual panel.

faq.q: If the cancer has few mutations, can the immune system ever see it?
faq.a: Sometimes, yes. Pancreatic tumors average about 35 predicted neoantigens against roughly 112 in non-small-cell lung cancer and 370 in melanoma [[IMM-026]], yet rare long-term survivors carry T cells reactive to specific pancreatic neoantigens [[TME-006]]. In mice, adding extra antigen made disease worse rather than better, which points at the priming and display steps rather than at the number of targets [[IMM-011]].

faq.q: Does the cancer lose the HLA genes themselves?
faq.a: Not necessarily, and that distinction matters because a gene that is lost cannot be restored while a protein that is being destroyed can. In pancreatic cancer cells the MHC class I protein is made and then routed to the lysosome, and in a decade-long study of long-term survivors the HLA class I genes were not mutated, deleted or differently expressed compared with short-term survivors [[IMM-009]][[IMM-026]].

topics.title: Nerves inside the tumor
topics.orientation: The pancreas is densely supplied with nerves, and in pancreatic cancer those nerves stop being bystanders: the tumor remodels them, grows along them and receives signals from them. This entry covers that two-way traffic; pain itself has its own entry.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Nerves do two jobs in the healthy pancreas. Sensory fibers run from the gland through the celiac plexus and splanchnic nerves to the spinal cord, reporting stretch, acidity and injury. Parasympathetic fibers of the vagus nerve and sympathetic fibers traveling with the arteries adjust enzyme release and blood flow. Schwann cells insulate every peripheral axon and supply the growth factors that keep it alive and guide repair.
section1.full: Innervation density in a healthy pancreas is low and steady. Control mice carried about 348 nerve profiles across the sampled sections, a density near 2.28 fibers per square millimeter, with a mean fiber length of 33 micrometers [[ANAT-011]]. That steadiness is maintained actively, by a continuing supply of neurotrophins — nerve growth factor, glial-cell-line-derived neurotrophic factor, neurturin and their receptors — on which axons and the cells around them depend; withdraw the supply and axons retract. Schwann cells are the peripheral nervous system's repair crew: after a nerve is damaged they change state, migrate, clear debris and lay down a track that regrowing axons follow, then settle back to rest once repair is finished. Each nerve bundle also travels inside its own sheath, a corridor of loose connective tissue offering little mechanical resistance, running with the arteries out of the pancreas into the retroperitoneum, the space behind the lining of the abdominal cavity. A trophic-factor supply, a mobile repair cell and a ready-made corridor are three ordinary features of nerve biology, and they are the three the cancer later turns to its own use.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Nerves are an active part of the tumor, and they act in two directions at once. In mice, ablating the pancreas's sensory nerves before disease onset delayed precursor lesions and nearly doubled median survival, whereas cutting the vagus nerve did the opposite and sped the disease up. In people, the cancer's main route out of the pancreas is along nerves: perineural invasion is found in roughly four of five untreated resection specimens, mostly in nerves outside the gland.
section2.full: Remodeling begins before there is a cancer. In a mouse model, focal excess innervation appeared at six to eight weeks confined to precursor lesions and fibrotic areas; by ten to twelve weeks fiber density had risen from 2.28 to 3.83 per square millimeter, pancreatic nerve growth factor messenger RNA had risen 2.25-fold, and later the receptor TrkA almost thirtyfold [[ANAT-011]]. Precursor lesions also recruit their own glia (support cells, here Schwann cells): cells within them secrete the signal CXCL12, and Schwann cells covered 75.9 percent of precursor lesions in intact mice against 11.9 percent when that signal was genetically reduced [[ANAT-012]]. In established disease, tumor-derived GDF15 acting on the Schwann-cell receptor GFRAL induces a CCN3-expressing Schwann-cell subset, and human tumors contained more nerve fibers and more S100-beta-positive Schwann cells than adjacent pancreas [[ANAT-029]]. Removing the input changes the disease: ablating pancreas-innervating sensory neurons in newborn mice prevented perineural invasion, delayed precursor formation and raised median survival from 4.5 to 7.8 months, and the most completely ablated animals had no cancer at 18 months [[TME-030]]. Cutting the vagus nerve accelerated tumor development, and a drug mimicking the lost cholinergic (acetylcholine) signal reversed that acceleration [[TME-031]]. The clinical consequence is anatomical: perineural invasion was present in 80 percent of untreated specimens, 91 percent of it in nerves beyond the pancreas, and involved nerves wider than 0.8 millimeters accompanied a positive margin four times as often [[ANAT-013]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The denervation result is prevention, not treatment: nerves were ablated in newborn mice before any lesion existed, and no study has removed nerves from an established tumor [[TME-030]]. Neonatal capsaicin, the chemical used to destroy the sensory nerves, also alters feeding and temperature regulation, which could slow growth without any nerve-to-tumor signal, and the most-ablated subgroup was picked out after the fact. The cholinergic finding rests on a paper that later carried an Editor's Note, and the text available to this atlas reports no numeric survival medians, so the direction of the effect is usable and its size is not [[TME-031]][[SEC-TME-08]]. Vagotomy also changes gastric emptying, nutrition and the gut microbiome. Perineural invasion is scored on a specimen after surgery, so it describes behavior already established rather than forecasting it [[ANAT-013]].
research_notes.how_studied: Three method families carry this topic. Chemical denervation produces a permanent loss of a defined cell population with a dose-response, because the extent of ablation varies between animals and the effect can be graded against how complete it was; a benign pancreatitis comparator separates nerve loss from inflammation [[TME-030]]. Surgical vagotomy paired with a drug that mimics the lost signal is a loss-and-rescue design, stronger than either half alone, because the rescue shows that the missing signal rather than the operation produced the change [[TME-031]]. Nerve counting uses PGP9.5 and S100-beta staining to measure fiber number, density and length at fixed timepoints, which is how remodeling was dated to the precursor stage rather than to invasion [[ANAT-011]][[ANAT-029]].

mechanism_notes.text: Sensory and cholinergic nerves may act on different targets, which would account for their opposite signs. Sensory fibers supply a local trophic environment around precursor lesions together with Schwann cells that provide a migration track, so losing them removes both a growth input and a spread corridor [[TME-030]][[ANAT-012]]; cholinergic signaling instead acts through the muscarinic receptor CHRM1 on the cancer cells themselves, where it damped two growth-signaling pathways (MAPK/EGFR and PI3K/AKT) and the stem-like compartment, and reduced suppressive myeloid cells [[TME-031]]. The competing explanation is systemic rather than local: vagotomy changes gastric emptying, nutrition and the microbiome, and neonatal capsaicin changes feeding and thermoregulation, so either result could reflect whole-animal physiology. Distinguishing them needs selective, reversible silencing of each fiber type in an established tumor, which has not been done.

glossary.definition: Cancer growing in or around the sheath of a nerve, which lets it travel outside the pancreas.
The support cell that wraps peripheral nerve fibers and guides their repair after injury.
The network of nerves behind the stomach through which sensation from the pancreas travels.
The main parasympathetic nerve to the abdominal organs, carrying cholinergic signals to the pancreas.
A growth factor, such as nerve growth factor, that nerve fibers need to survive and extend.
Removing or destroying the nerve supply to a tissue.
The space behind the lining of the abdominal cavity, where the pancreas and its nerves sit.

related.statement: The nerves inside a pancreatic tumor are branches of the celiac plexus and the nerve networks that normally supply the pancreas.
Remodeling of the nerves inside the tumor is one source of the pain pancreatic cancer causes, which is covered in its own entry.
Perineural invasion is one of the findings a pathologist records on the report after pancreatic surgery.
Nerve-associated fibroblasts and a neural-like tumor program occupy one of the recurring neighborhoods found inside pancreatic tumors.
Excess nerve fibers first appear within the fibrotic, scar-like tissue that surrounds precursor lesions.

faq.q: If nerves help the cancer grow, can they be cut?
faq.a: Not as a cancer treatment. The denervation experiments removed nerves from newborn mice before any lesion existed, which is prevention rather than therapy, and nothing equivalent has been tested in people or in established tumors [[TME-030]]. Nerve blocks such as a celiac plexus block are used to relieve pain, not to slow the disease.

faq.q: My report mentions perineural invasion. What does that mean?
faq.a: It means the pathologist saw cancer in or around a nerve sheath, which is the usual way this cancer leaves the pancreas. It is common, found in about 80 percent of untreated resection specimens and mostly in nerves outside the gland, and it is associated with positive margins and shorter survival in large series [[ANAT-013]]. It describes what the tumor has already done, and it is one of several findings a care team weighs together.

topics.title: Tumor neighborhoods and sub-environments
topics.orientation: A pancreatic tumor is not a uniform mass. Sampling many points within one tumor at once shows a small number of recurring neighborhoods, each with a characteristic mix of cancer cells, fibroblasts and immune cells, and which neighborhoods dominate tracks with how the tumor behaves.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Healthy tissues are built from repeating units with a fixed cellular census. The pancreas is organized into lobules, each a cluster of enzyme-making acini draining into a small duct, wrapped in a capillary bed with nerve twigs, a few resident fibroblasts and scattered immune cells in stable proportions. Because most signaling molecules act over tens of micrometers, a cell's behavior is set largely by its immediate neighbors.
section1.full: Position is not incidental in tissue biology; it is part of how a cell's identity is specified. Pancreatic stellate cells make the point directly. In three-dimensional culture, direct contact with epithelial cells drove them into a myofibroblastic state rich in smooth-muscle actin, whereas the same cells separated by a membrane that let only soluble signals pass adopted a different, interleukin-6-secreting inflammatory state [[TME-005]]. Proximity, not merely the presence of a signal, decided which program switched on. Normal tissue holds that geometry steady: each lobule keeps its acini within diffusion distance of a capillary, so oxygen levels across healthy pancreas vary little, the duct runs a fixed distance from the acini it drains, and resident immune cells patrol without accumulating. Repair disturbs the arrangement temporarily — fibroblasts activate, immune cells arrive, the local mixture of cells changes — and then it resolves and the lobular pattern is restored. A tissue therefore has a normal and reproducible neighborhood structure. That is what makes an abnormal one recognizable, and what makes it something to measure rather than merely describe.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: In a study of 43 resected tumors, cancer cells ran fourteen distinguishable gene programs and fibroblasts four, and these co-assembled into three reproducible neighborhoods: one built around the classical tumor program in myofibroblast-rich, immune-poor tissue; one around the squamoid and basaloid programs (the basal-like end of the spectrum) with a varied immune infiltrate and less fibroblast content; and one, enriched after chemotherapy and radiotherapy, around a neural-like progenitor program sitting with nerve-associated fibroblasts and CD8 T cells.
section2.full: What makes these neighborhoods more than a description is that composition and outcome move together, and that the surroundings can change the cancer cell's program. Across those same tumors, profiled as 224,988 individual cell nuclei with matched spatial sampling, an adhesive fibroblast program was associated with shorter overall survival (hazard ratio 1.84, 95% confidence interval 1.04 to 3.25) and the classical tumor program with longer survival (hazard ratio 0.73, 0.56 to 0.95) [[TME-032]]. Those tumor programs are the same classical and basal-like axis seen in bulk tissue, where basal-like tumors had a median survival of 11 months against 19 months for classical [[GENE-004]]. Single-cell work shows why neighborhood and cell state are hard to separate: the two programs are not mutually exclusive, many cells sit in an intermediate state expressing both, and exposing tumor organoids to TGF-beta, a signal abundant in fibroblast-rich tissue, pushed them toward the intermediate and basal states [[GENE-014]]. The neural-like progenitor program is the most clinically pointed finding. It was enriched in tissue removed after chemotherapy and radiotherapy, carried its own neighborhood of nerve-associated fibroblasts, and predicted poorer outcome in independent cohorts [[TME-032]]. Because treated and untreated tumors were not randomized, it may be a program that survives treatment rather than one treatment creates. None of this directs treatment in the US as of 8 October 2026.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The spatial picture here rests on a single study read in full, and that sets the limits of what can be said [[TME-032]]. Two further primary reports bear directly on the topic — one describing spatially confined reactive and deserted sub-microenvironments, the other tracing stromal change into LRRC15-positive myofibroblasts — but only their abstracts were available to this atlas, so no result is taken from them [[SEC-TME-05]][[SEC-TME-06]]. Within the one study, survival modeling used a modest number of patients who had reached surgery, a more favorable group than everyone with this diagnosis, with eighteen programs tested at once and spatial regions chosen by an operator. The neighborhood classification is reproducible and prognostically associated. It is not a validated test, and no treatment decision should turn on it.
research_notes.how_studied: Two measurements are combined because each supplies what the other lacks. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing reads the gene program of individual cells from frozen tissue, since nuclei survive freezing where whole cells do not, and a factorization method then extracts recurring programs instead of forcing each cell into one labeled type — which is what allows a single cell to score for two programs at once [[TME-032]]. Spatial profiling measures the whole transcriptome of selected small regions and keeps the geography that tissue dissociation destroys, so programs found by the first method can be tested for whether they actually sit together. Prognostic associations are then checked in separate bulk cohorts. Culture perturbation adds the causal element: changing the medium changed the state, so plasticity was demonstrated rather than inferred [[GENE-014]].

mechanism_notes.text: The pairing of particular tumor programs with particular fibroblast programs reads most simply as a two-way loop rather than a one-way effect. Fibroblast state depends on how close a fibroblast is to a cancer cell and on what reaches it [[TME-005]], and tumor-cell state shifts toward the basal and intermediate programs under TGF-beta, which fibroblast-rich tissue supplies [[GENE-014]]; the observed co-assembly of classical cells with myofibroblastic fibroblasts, and of squamoid-basaloid cells with a quite different mixture, is what such a loop would produce [[TME-032]]. The competing explanation is that the cancer cell's genome and epigenome fix its program first and determine which stroma it recruits, making the neighborhood a consequence rather than a cause. Separating them requires sampling the same tumor before and after a deliberate change to its surroundings.

glossary.definition: A set of genes a cell switches on together, describing what the cell is currently doing rather than its fixed identity.
A method that reads which genes are active in each cell nucleus separately, usable on frozen tissue.
Measuring gene activity in small defined regions of tissue so that the position of each measurement is preserved.
An activated fibroblast that contracts and produces the dense collagen matrix of scar-like tissue.
A tumor-cell gene program resembling immature nerve tissue, found enriched in tumors removed after chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
A number comparing the rate of an event between two groups, where 1.0 means no difference.

related.statement: The classical and basal-like tumor programs occupy different recurring neighborhoods within the same pancreatic tumor.
Each tumor neighborhood is defined partly by which cancer-associated fibroblast states are present in it.
One neighborhood pairs a neural-like tumor program with nerve-associated fibroblasts, linking tumor neighborhoods to the nerves inside the tumor.
CD8 T cells are abundant in some tumor neighborhoods and nearly absent from others within a single tumor.
A needle biopsy samples one small part of the tumor, so it may not capture every neighborhood present.

faq.q: Does a biopsy represent my whole tumor?
faq.a: Not completely. One tumor contains several distinct neighborhoods with different mixes of cancer cells, fibroblasts and immune cells, and a needle samples a small part of it [[TME-032]]. A biopsy is enough to establish the diagnosis and to run molecular tests, but a single sample can miss programs present elsewhere in the same tumor.

faq.q: Does chemotherapy change the tumor's make-up?
faq.a: The balance of programs differs between tumors removed after chemotherapy and radiotherapy and those removed without it, with a neural-like progenitor program enriched after treatment and associated with poorer outcome in other cohorts [[TME-032]]. Because nobody was randomized and no tumor was sampled both before and after, it is not yet known whether treatment creates that program or simply leaves behind the cells that already carried it.

topics.title: Lessons from stroma-directed treatments
topics.orientation: Much of the mass of a pancreatic tumor is not cancer cells but dense, scar-like tissue. For roughly fifteen years that tissue looked like the obvious obstacle to remove, and the attempts to remove it produced some of the most instructive failures in the field.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: The reasoning was mechanical and well evidenced. Normal mouse pancreas runs at an interstitial fluid pressure of 8 to 13 millimeters of mercury with more than four-fifths of its small vessels open; a mouse pancreatic tumor runs at 75 to 130, above the pressure inside its own arterioles, with only about a quarter of its vessels open. If pressure is collapsing the vessels, chemotherapy cannot arrive — so lower the pressure and the drug should get in.
section1.full: Three independent experiments made that expectation concrete, and each measured the delivery step rather than relying on a growth endpoint alone. In mouse tumors only 32 percent of blood vessels were actually perfused, against 78 percent in transplanted tumors and 100 percent in normal pancreas, and the active metabolite of gemcitabine was undetectable in them while detectable in comparison tissues; a Smoothened inhibitor (a drug blocking the hedgehog pathway) that depletes hedgehog-driven stroma raised vessel density and that metabolite, and extended median survival from 11 to 25 days after enrollment [[TME-001]]. Hyaluronan, the water-binding sugar polymer that holds the pressure, was then stripped out enzymatically: vessel patency rose from about 30 to 70 percent, with existing vessels widening rather than new ones forming, intratumoral drug rose roughly sixfold, and median survival with gemcitabine went from 55.5 to 91.5 days [[TME-003]][[TME-033]]. Losartan, a blood-pressure drug that lowers fibroblast production of TGF-beta1 and collagen, raised the perfused vessel fraction from about 21 to 45 percent and intratumoral levels of the chemotherapy drug fluorouracil by 74 percent [[TME-015]]. Note what none of them measured: benefit in a person, and the effect of removing stroma from the precursor stage onward rather than briefly from a large established tumor.

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Each strand came apart in a different way. In the same mouse model, deleting the hedgehog signal or blocking it over the long term shortened survival instead of extending it, and metastases became more frequent. A randomized phase 3 trial of hyaluronidase in selected patients produced more tumor shrinkage and no survival difference whatever. The losartan evidence is a single-arm trial of 49 people whose own report disagrees with itself about its main result.
section2.full: Deleting the hedgehog ligand cut median survival from 6.17 to 3.61 months and raised gross metastasis from 15.3 to 43.4 percent of animals; long-term drug exposure shortened survival from 156 to 121 days, with roughly 2.9-fold more vessels, not fewer [[TME-002]]. Independently, ablating about 80 percent of proliferating myofibroblasts, at either the precursor or the cancer stage, produced more invasive, less differentiated tumors and shorter survival, with more low-oxygen tissue and expanded regulatory T cells; blocking CTLA-4, an immune checkpoint, reversed the harm, identifying immune suppression as the route [[TME-012]]. Smoothened inhibition does not simply subtract stroma: it shifts myofibroblastic fibroblasts toward the inflammatory state and leaves fewer CD8 T cells behind [[TME-013]]. The hyaluronidase question was then settled in patients. Among 492 people with hyaluronan-high metastatic disease randomized 2 to 1, median overall survival was 11.2 months with pegvorhyaluronidase alfa added to chemotherapy against 11.5 months without (hazard ratio 1.00, 95% confidence interval 0.80 to 1.27), progression-free survival 7.1 months in both arms, response rate 47 against 36 percent, with more leg swelling (61.8 against 33.3 percent) and muscle spasms (51.4 against 9.6 percent) [[TME-004]]. The losartan trial added the drug to the four-drug chemotherapy FOLFIRINOX and chemoradiotherapy in 49 people whose tumors were not removable at presentation, and reported margin-negative resection in either 69 or 61 percent depending on which part of the paper is read, median overall survival 31.4 months among everyone who started, three people stopping losartan for intolerance, and no control group [[TME-016]]. A margin-negative resection is not the same as a cure.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Two of these programs failed in the same instructive way: tumors shrank more often and people did not live longer. Hyaluronidase raised objective response from 36 to 47 percent with a hazard ratio for death of exactly 1.00 [[TME-004]], and in a separate randomized trial hydroxychloroquine raised response from 21.1 to 38.2 percent with 12-month survival of 41 against 49 percent [[TME-027]]. Local tumor control and survival are not interchangeable endpoints in this disease. The losartan result cannot be credited to losartan: total neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX alone achieves high resection rates in selected patients at high-volume centers, and no measurement of tumor stiffness, perfusion or matrix content was made during treatment to confirm the proposed mechanism [[TME-016]]. A fibroblast-targeting trial stopped for disease acceleration is cited as the clinical instance of harm, although that trial's own report was not among the sources available to this atlas [[SEC-TME-07]].
research_notes.how_studied: The decisive methodological distinction is between a brief intervention on a large established tumor and the same intervention applied from the precursor stage. The founding delivery study enrolled mice with established tumors, treated them in a short window, and described the benefit as transient; the contradicting studies deleted the signal genetically from the outset or dosed over the long term, and measured survival from birth or from first detection rather than from enrollment [[TME-001]][[TME-002]]. Comparing their numbers side by side would be an error of time origin. On the clinical side, the hyaluronidase trial used a biomarker-selected population, 2-to-1 allocation and hierarchical endpoint testing, so its negative survival result is interpretable, while its placebo arm outperformed the assumption used to size the trial [[TME-004]]. A single-arm trial cannot separate drug effect from patient selection [[TME-016]].

mechanism_notes.text: The sign of a stromal intervention appears to be set by which fibroblast states are left behind rather than by how much stroma is removed [[INF-TME-01]]. Depleting the pro-tumor LRRC15-positive myofibroblast subtype slowed tumor growth and improved the response to the immunotherapy anti-PD-L1, the opposite direction from depleting myofibroblasts in bulk [[TME-037]], and matched-dose transplants showed CD105-negative pancreatic fibroblasts suppressing growth while CD105-positive fibroblasts permitted it, with the suppression lost entirely in mice lacking adaptive immunity [[TME-036]]. Reprogramming instead of removal points the same way: a vitamin D analog that returns stellate cells toward their resting state raised intratumoral gemcitabine and vessel patency and extended median survival from 14 to 22 days in mice, with no effect given alone [[TME-038]]. A live competing explanation is stage dependence rather than composition, since the transient benefit came from brief treatment of an established tumor and the harm from intervening at the precursor stage [[TME-001]][[TME-002]][[TME-012]].

The response-without-survival pattern may arise because these agents improve control of the lesions being measured while survival in advanced disease is governed by disease outside them, together with nutrition, fitness and delivered chemotherapy dose [[INF-TME-02]]. The simpler competing explanation is statistical: both trials were sized for larger effects than exist, and added toxicity may have cut the dose of the chemotherapy doing the work [[TME-004]][[TME-027]]. A dose-intensity analysis stratified by baseline disease burden would separate the two.

topics.clinical_status: No stroma-directed treatment is approved in the US for pancreatic cancer as of 8 October 2026. Vismodegib and sonidegib are approved in the US only for basal cell carcinoma; pegvorhyaluronidase alfa development in pancreatic cancer was discontinued after the negative phase 3; losartan is approved in the US as of 8 October 2026 for hypertension, its only oncologic evidence being a single-arm phase 2; vitamin D analogs and LRRC15-directed agents remain investigational.

glossary.definition: The non-cancer tissue within a tumor: fibroblasts, matrix, blood vessels, nerves and immune cells.
The dense, scar-like stromal tissue that makes up much of a pancreatic tumor's bulk.
A water-binding sugar polymer in the matrix that holds fluid and generates pressure inside the tumor.
The pressure in the fluid between cells, which can collapse small blood vessels when it exceeds the pressure inside them.
The proportion of patients whose tumor shrank by a defined amount on a scan.
A trial in which everyone receives the treatment, so results cannot be compared with an untreated group drawn at the same time.
An operation in which no tumor is found at the cut edges of the removed specimen; it improves the odds but does not mean cure.
An activated fibroblast that contracts and lays down the collagen matrix of scar-like tissue.
A signaling route by which tumor cells instruct surrounding fibroblasts to build stroma.

related.statement: The scar-like stroma of pancreatic cancer is the tissue every one of these stroma-directed treatments set out to remove or alter.
High interstitial pressure from hyaluronan and collagen was the proposed reason chemotherapy fails to reach pancreatic tumor cells.
Which fibroblast states a treatment leaves behind appears to determine whether removing stroma helps or harms.
The failure of stroma-depleting treatments led to the current research strategy of reprogramming the stroma rather than removing it.
The hyaluronidase trial is a clear example of why a higher tumor response rate does not by itself mean longer survival.
Removing stroma raised the number of blood vessels in mouse tumors yet made the disease more aggressive, separating blood supply from benefit.

faq.q: Why would a drug that shrinks tumors not help people live longer?
faq.a: Shrinkage is measured on the lesions a scan can see, while survival in advanced disease is driven largely by disease outside them and by overall condition. Adding hyaluronidase raised response from 36 to 47 percent with a hazard ratio for death of exactly 1.00, and hydroxychloroquine showed the same pattern in a separate trial [[TME-004]][[TME-027]]. Added side effects can also force reductions in the chemotherapy that is doing the real work [[INF-TME-02]].

faq.q: Should I ask about losartan for my tumor?
faq.a: It is reasonable to ask, but the evidence is thin. Losartan is approved in the US as of 8 October 2026 for high blood pressure only, and its pancreatic evidence is one single-arm trial of 49 people that reported two different figures for its own main result and had no comparison group, so the contribution of losartan itself cannot be separated from the chemotherapy and the selection of patients [[TME-016]].

faq.q: Does this mean the stroma is good and should be left alone?
faq.a: Not quite. Removing it in bulk made mouse tumors more aggressive, but depleting one specific pro-tumor fibroblast subtype slowed growth and improved response to immunotherapy, and reprogramming stellate cells toward their resting state raised chemotherapy levels and survival in mice [[TME-012]][[TME-037]][[TME-038]]. The lesson is about which cells and which operation, not about leaving the tissue untouched.

topics.title: How the liver is prepared for metastasis
topics.orientation: The liver is where pancreatic cancer most often reappears, and it is not simply the organ that happens to be downstream. Signals from the tumor change the liver's resident cells before any metastasis is visible, turning it into tissue that accepts and shelters arriving cancer cells.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: All blood leaving the pancreas and gut passes through the liver first, so the liver samples everything those organs release before the rest of the body sees it. Kupffer cells, the macrophages lining the liver's narrow vessels, clear debris and particles from that stream. Hepatic stellate cells sit alongside storing vitamin A, and hepatocytes mount the acute-phase response that summons immune cells after injury.
section1.full: Each of those cells belongs to a repair program that normally runs and then stops. When the liver is injured, Kupffer cells release TGF-beta among other signals; hepatic stellate cells respond by activating into myofibroblasts and laying down fibronectin and collagen, which stabilizes damaged tissue; and the deposited matrix recruits further macrophages from the bone marrow to clear the damage [[SURG-010]]. In parallel, hepatocytes read circulating interleukin-6 and switch on the transcription factor STAT3, producing acute-phase proteins including serum amyloid A — the same system that raises C-reactive protein during an infection — which draws myeloid cells into the liver [[SURG-022]]. A third strand links macrophages back to stellate cells: macrophage-derived granulin activates resting hepatic stellate cells into myofibroblasts that secrete periostin, an ordinary step in organizing a wound [[SURG-023]]. The liver also filters exosomes, the small membrane-bound packets of protein and RNA that every tissue sheds and that carry material from the cell that made them. In health all of these programs resolve once repair is complete. What follows is a description of the same programs being switched on and then held on.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: The tumor engages each of those repair programs early, by remote signaling rather than by arriving. Pancreatic cancer exosomes are taken up by Kupffer cells and set off the fibronectin-and-macrophage cascade; hepatocytes are switched into acute-phase production while the pancreatic tumor is still small; and recruited monocytes build a fibrotic scar that both feeds arriving cancer cells and keeps killer T cells out of the tissue.
section2.full: The exosome step has been tested by blocking it. Pancreatic cancer exosomes carry high levels of macrophage migration inhibitory factor, or MIF; blocking that single protein prevented the niche forming and reduced liver metastasis in mice, and exosomal MIF was markedly higher in stage I patients who later developed liver metastases than in those who did not [[SURG-010]]. The hepatocyte step was tested the same way: ablating or blocking interleukin-6, STAT3 or serum amyloid A each prevented the niche and inhibited liver metastasis, and hepatocytes in patients with liver metastases overexpressed serum amyloid A [[SURG-022]]. Early recruitment of granulin-secreting inflammatory monocytes is required for metastasis; macrophage granulin activates hepatic stellate cells into periostin-secreting myofibroblasts, and either blocking that recruitment or depleting granulin reduced both stellate activation and metastasis [[SURG-023]]. That same fibrotic barrier excludes CD8 T cells, which is why liver metastases resisted PD-1 blockade (checkpoint immunotherapy) in these models, and depleting granulin let T cells in and restored the response [[SURG-024]]. Some arriving cells then do nothing for a long time: livers of patients and mice contain single cancer cells lacking the usual duct-cell marker CK19 and MHC class I, not dividing and under an unresolved cell-stress state, and in the model both a specific stress-response switch and the removal of T cells were needed to make them grow into visible metastases [[SURG-012]]. These findings describe how recurrence happens. They do not predict whether or when it will happen in a particular person, and none of them is yet a test or a treatment.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Timing is where this topic is most often misread. Lineage-labeled mouse cells circulated and seeded the liver at the precursor stage, before a cancer was visible under the microscope [[SURG-001]], while human genomic reconstruction places full metastatic capacity late in the tumor's genetic evolution, roughly 6.8 years from the founder clone to the subclone that seeded the index metastasis [[SURG-002]]. Physical arrival and the ability to grow are separate clocks. Seeding is also not clonally simple: multicolor tracing showed a substantial share of metastases founded by more than one subclone, with clonality differing by organ [[SURG-026]], and human rearrangement phylogenies show organ-specific branches and continued evolution after dissemination [[SURG-013]]. Estimating the risk that a given person's cancer will recur is a different exercise, done with tumor size, grade, lymphovascular invasion, node ratio and CA 19-9 [[SURG-007]].
research_notes.how_studied: The strength of this work is that most of it is loss-of-function with a rescue rather than correlation. In each case a candidate signal was removed genetically or pharmacologically — MIF, interleukin-6, STAT3, serum amyloid A, granulin — and the question asked was whether the liver still became receptive and whether metastases still formed [[SURG-010]][[SURG-022]][[SURG-023]]. That design can show a signal is necessary in that model, which correlation cannot. The dormancy work pushes the switch the other way: inducing the stress-response factor and depleting T cells together converted silent single cells into growing metastases [[SURG-012]]. The human part of every one of these studies is observational, using tissue or blood from people with and without liver metastases, so it establishes that the same molecules are present and associated, not that blocking them would help a patient.

mechanism_notes.text: Recurrence years after an operation that removed all visible disease is best explained by cells that arrived in the liver early and stayed dormant rather than by cells escaping later [[INF-SURG-01]]. The supporting chain is that cells disseminate before a cancer is visible [[SURG-001]], that livers of patients and mice hold single non-dividing cells with low MHC class I held in check by immunity and an unresolved stress state [[SURG-012]], and that a substantial minority of people recur more than a year after resection [[SURG-007]]. The competing explanation is slow continuous growth below the resolution of a scan rather than true dormancy; long negative intervals on serial blood-based testing before relapse would favor dormancy.

The liver's specific conditioning programs may be why liver recurrence behaves differently from lung recurrence. In one single-center series of 343 resected patients, median survival after recurrence was 13 months for liver, 30 months for isolated lung and 20 months for other sites — cohort figures that describe groups and not any individual [[SURG-015]] — while the niche programs characterized so far, exosomal MIF, hepatocyte serum amyloid A and macrophage granulin fibrosis with T-cell exclusion, are all hepatic [[SURG-010]][[SURG-022]][[SURG-023]][[SURG-024]][[INF-SURG-02]]. The competing explanation is detection: lung nodules are found earlier and smaller on surveillance scans, so part of the difference could be lead time rather than biology.

glossary.definition: Tissue changed by signals from a distant tumor so that it will accept and support cancer cells if they arrive.
A small membrane-bound packet of protein and RNA released by a cell and taken up by other cells.
The resident macrophage lining the liver's small vessels, which clears particles from passing blood.
A liver cell that stores vitamin A at rest and becomes a scar-forming myofibroblast when activated.
An acute-phase protein made by liver cells during inflammation that attracts immune cells.
A protein released by certain macrophages that switches liver stellate cells into scar-forming cells.
A matrix protein secreted by activated stellate cells that helps build the fibrous tissue around a metastasis.
A state in which a disseminated cancer cell survives without dividing, sometimes for years.
The surface display system by which a cell shows fragments of its proteins to killer T cells; losing it makes a cell harder to see.
A deposit of cancer cells too small to be seen on any scan.

related.statement: The pre-metastatic niche forms inside the liver, among its Kupffer cells, stellate cells and hepatocytes.
Liver niche formation and the dormancy of cells already lodged there are a proposed mechanism for recurrence after apparently complete surgery.
The single dormant cells found in the liver are one form of the microscopic disease that imaging cannot show.
Fibrosis built by granulin-activated stellate cells keeps CD8 T cells out of liver metastases.
Kupffer cells, recruited monocytes and bone-marrow-derived macrophages are the myeloid cells that build the liver niche.
Small spots seen in the liver on a scan are evaluated separately, and most of them are not metastases.

faq.q: Does this mean cancer cells are already in my liver?
faq.a: It cannot be known from these studies, and they are not a test. Mouse work shows cells can reach the liver very early, and single dormant cells have been found in livers from patients, but there is no clinical assay that tells a particular person whether such cells are present [[SURG-001]][[SURG-012]]. Whether disease will reappear is estimated from tumor features and markers, which is a separate question from the mechanism described here [[SURG-007]].

faq.q: If the liver is being prepared by signals, can those signals be blocked?
faq.a: Blocking them works in mice. Removing MIF from tumor exosomes, blocking interleukin-6, STAT3 or serum amyloid A in liver cells, or depleting macrophage granulin each prevented the niche and reduced liver metastasis [[SURG-010]][[SURG-022]][[SURG-023]]. None of these has been shown to help a patient, and the human data in those studies are observational, so this is a research direction rather than an available option.

faq.q: Why can recurrence appear years later?
faq.a: One well-supported explanation is dormancy: single cells that reached the liver early survive without dividing and with little MHC class I on their surface, which makes them hard for T cells to see, and in mice it took both an internal stress switch and the loss of T cells to make them grow [[SURG-012]][[INF-SURG-01]]. The competing explanation is very slow growth that stays below what a scan can detect.

topics.title: How normal cells decide to grow
topics.orientation: Every cancer gene in this atlas is a broken part of the machinery that healthy cells use to decide whether to divide. This entry describes that machinery in working order, so that KRAS, CDKN2A, TP53 and the other entries read as specific failures within one system.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: A healthy cell divides only with outside permission. Growth factors from neighboring tissue bind receptors on the cell surface, the receptors switch on a relay protein called RAS, and RAS passes the message inward along two main routes, the MAPK pathway and the PI3K pathway, which prepare the cell to copy its DNA. A separate set of brakes then decides whether the cell may actually enter the division cycle.
section1.full: RAS works as a timed switch. It is active only while bound to the small molecule GTP, and helper proteins called GAPs convert that GTP to GDP within seconds, so the switch turns off unless a receptor keeps re-arming it. Active RAS recruits the kinase RAF, which activates MEK, which activates ERK; ERK enters the nucleus and turns on the genes for cyclin D and other proteins needed for growth. In parallel, active RAS recruits the enzyme PI3K, whose lipid signal activates AKT and mTOR, raising protein synthesis and nutrient uptake and holding off programmed cell death. Neither route commits the cell to divide. That decision belongs to the cycle brake: the retinoblastoma protein RB keeps the E2F transcription factors silent until cyclin D, paired with the kinases CDK4 and CDK6, modifies RB and releases them, and the protein p16, encoded by CDKN2A, blocks CDK4 and CDK6 so that a stressed cell stays parked [[GENE-009]]. A cell with damaged DNA adds a further veto through p53. The system therefore has at least three independent layers, growth signal, cycle brake and damage check, and a tumor generally has to defeat all of them.

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Pancreatic cancer disables each layer of this system in a characteristic way. About nine in ten tumors carry a mutated KRAS that cannot switch itself off, most have physically deleted the CDKN2A brake, and most carry a mutated TP53. A typical tumor holds about 63 genetic alterations, but they concentrate in roughly twelve core pathways, so different tumors reach the same functional result through different genes.
section2.full: The landmark exome (protein-coding gene) sequencing study found a mean of 63 alterations per tumor, found 12 core signaling pathways each disrupted in 67 to 100 percent of the 24 cancers examined, and showed two tumors hitting the same pathways through different genes, one through SMAD4 and one through BMPR2 [[GENE-001]]. KRAS mutation was present in 92 percent of 109 microdissected tumors and 87.4 percent of 317 tumors from a randomized trial [[GENE-002]][[GENE-024]]. Signal strength matters as well as the switch: in mice, tumors that gained extra copies of mutant Kras were far more likely to metastasize, and that gain was tightly linked to complete loss of CDKN2A, with an odds ratio of 15.3 [[GENE-007]]. Established mouse tumors still needed the signal, collapsing within about a week when mutant Kras was switched off [[GENE-012]], yet 70 percent of those mice later relapsed and about half of the relapses had replaced KRAS with an amplified gene called YAP1 [[GENE-013]]. The cycle brake tells the same story of layers: loss of p16 is near universal, but it was retained RB protein, the node below p16, that predicted sensitivity to CDK4/6 inhibitors in patient-derived models and whose loss independently predicted worse survival [[GENE-009]]. A sequencing report lists genes; the biology runs on pathways.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The pathway view explains why pancreatic cancers behave alike while their mutation lists differ, and why blocking a single downstream enzyme has repeatedly disappointed: the network has parallel routes and feedback loops. The KRAS-dependence experiments used mice with an artificial on-off switch, which is cleaner than any drug, so the week-long collapse and the 70 percent relapse rate are proofs of principle rather than forecasts for patients [[GENE-012]][[GENE-013]]. The CDK4/6 result is a caution against reading a deleted CDKN2A as a drug target in itself; no CDK4/6 inhibitor is approved in the US for pancreatic cancer as of 8 October 2026 [[GENE-009]].
research_notes.how_studied: Exome sequencing reads the protein-coding parts of every gene and, with copy-number analysis, finds point mutations, amplifications and homozygous deletions; grouping hits by pathway rather than by gene is what revealed the 12 core processes [[GENE-001]]. Doxycycline-inducible mouse models express mutant Kras only while the animal drinks the antibiotic, so withdrawing it tests whether an established tumor still needs the oncogene, with MRI and FDG-PET tracking regression [[GENE-012]]. Testing drug sensitivity across a panel of patient-derived cell lines whose genomes are known is how a true biomarker such as RB status is separated from a correlated one such as p16 [[GENE-009]].

mechanism_notes.text: When mutant RAS is blocked by a drug, surviving pancreatic cancer cells appear to rebuild output through the growth-factor receptors and wild-type RAS proteins they still possess: PI3K activity recruits the scaffold GAB1 to the membrane and assembles RAS complexes that reactivate MAPK, and in cell experiments blocking PI3K deepened the response to mutant-selective KRAS inhibitors [[INF-RAS-01]][[RAS-027]][[RAS-008]]. This drug-tolerant state, rather than a new mutation, may set the floor of residual disease seen on scans.

glossary.definition: A small protein released by one cell that tells a neighboring cell to grow or divide by binding a receptor on its surface.
A family of switch proteins (KRAS, NRAS, HRAS) that are on when bound to GTP and off when bound to GDP, relaying growth signals into the cell.
The RAF-MEK-ERK relay that carries a RAS signal to the nucleus and turns on growth genes.
The second main RAS output, through PI3K, AKT and mTOR, which boosts nutrient uptake and protein synthesis and suppresses cell death.
The ordered sequence by which a cell copies its DNA and divides, gated by checkpoints that can halt it.
The retinoblastoma protein, a brake that holds a cell out of the division cycle until CDK4/6 releases it.

related.statement: The RAS switch at the center of this growth-signaling system is the protein made by the KRAS gene, which is mutated in about nine in ten pancreatic cancers.
The p16 brake on CDK4 and CDK6 described here is the product of the CDKN2A gene that pancreatic cancers usually delete.
The damage-check layer of growth control is run by p53, the protein mutated in roughly half or more of pancreatic cancers.
Growth control and DNA-damage checkpoints are separate systems that a pancreatic cancer must defeat independently.
The PI3K arm of growth signaling drives the nutrient-scavenging behavior that KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancer cells depend on.
Resistance to RAS-directed drugs arises when the growth-control network described here is rebuilt through receptors, wild-type RAS or alternative genes.

faq.q: If KRAS is stuck on, why does not every cell with the mutation become a cancer?
faq.a: Because a stuck growth signal defeats only one layer. A normal adult pancreas carries on the order of hundreds of tiny KRAS-mutant lesions, the overwhelming majority of which never progress [[ORIG-001]][[ORIG-002]], and in mice such cells stay parked by a senescence brake (a permanent growth arrest) unless inflammation releases it [[ORIG-014]].

faq.q: My tumor report lists a 'pathway'. What does that mean?
faq.a: A pathway is a chain of proteins that pass a signal along; reports group mutated genes by the chain they sit in because the functional result is the same whichever link is broken. In the founding genomic study, 12 such chains were each disrupted in 67 to 100 percent of tumors, often through different genes in different patients [[GENE-001]].

topics.title: DNA damage, repair and checkpoints
topics.orientation: Cells are damaged constantly and survive because they can detect the damage, pause, repair it or remove themselves. This entry explains that defense system in health; the entries on TP53, BRCA, ATM and mismatch repair describe the specific ways pancreatic cancers break it.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: Every time a cell copies its three billion letters of DNA it makes errors, and radiation, chemicals and its own metabolism add breaks on top. Three systems contain the damage: repair enzymes that fix specific kinds of lesion, checkpoints that stop the division cycle until repair is complete, and a last resort in which a cell too damaged to fix either shuts down permanently or dismantles itself.
section1.full: Different lesions call different crews. A mismatch, where the wrong letter was paired during copying, is found and excised by the mismatch-repair proteins MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2, which keep the error rate low in repetitive stretches called microsatellites [[GENE-006]]. A double-strand break, in which both strands are cut, is the most dangerous lesion because the broken ends can be joined to the wrong partner. The accurate fix is homologous recombination, which uses the identical sister copy made during replication as a template; BRCA1, BRCA2 and PALB2 assemble that machinery, while the kinase ATM senses the break and signals through CHEK2 and p53 to halt the cycle [[GENE-016]]. When homologous recombination is unavailable, cells fall back on quicker, error-prone joining that leaves scars. Checkpoints are run largely by p53, which accumulates after damage, switches on genes that arrest the cycle, and if repair fails commits the cell to apoptosis, a tidy self-destruction, or to senescence, a permanent exit from division. A cell that has lost these responses can keep dividing with a damaged genome, and that is the state in which mutations, chromosome losses and amplifications accumulate.

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Pancreatic cancer nearly always disables the main checkpoint, TP53, and in most tumors the genome then goes through catastrophic events, whole-genome doubling or chromosome shattering, that a working checkpoint would have stopped. A smaller group of tumors, roughly one in five in advanced disease, carries an alteration in a gene for accurate double-strand-break repair, and about one in a hundred has lost mismatch repair. Those two deficiencies are the ones current drugs can exploit, and whether one or both gene copies are affected decides how much they matter.
section2.full: TP53 was mutated in 53.6 percent of 317 resected tumors sequenced for point mutations [[GENE-024]], and whole-genome analysis of 107 tumors found that tumors with doubled genomes were enriched for TP53 mutation, that 65 percent had undergone chromosome shattering, and that in 16 percent several driver genes were knocked out in a single event [[GENE-003]]. The repair-deficient minority is defined differently. Among 262 patients with advanced disease, 19 percent carried a damaging alteration in a homologous-recombination gene, 15 percent inherited and 4 percent acquired in the tumor, and the benefit of first-line platinum chemotherapy was concentrated in the 11 percent whose tumors had lost both copies of a gene and the 12 percent with alterations in the core genes BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 [[GENE-016]]. In a trial that enrolled by gene name, every one of six patients with lasting benefit from a PARP inhibitor (a drug that exploits faulty double-strand-break repair) had biallelic loss [[GENE-025]]. Mismatch-repair deficiency was found in 7 of 833 consecutive patients, 0.8 percent [[GENE-006]], and in about 1 to 2 percent across 8,323 patients in a systematic review [[SEC-GENE-03]]. The exit routes are also targets: in adult mice, KRAS-mutant pancreatic cells stayed senescent for a year unless inflammation released them [[ORIG-014]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Two lessons travel across the repair entries. First, frequency and relevance diverge: TP53 loss is common but has no drug, whereas homologous-recombination loss and mismatch-repair loss are rare but change treatment. Second, the unit that predicts response is functional loss, not a gene name. Gene-level annotation pools tumors that have lost repair with carriers whose tumors still repair normally, which is the most economical explanation for why repair-gene status predicted platinum benefit in advanced disease but not the benefit of adjuvant (post-surgery) mFOLFIRINOX chemotherapy in a randomized cohort [[GENE-016]][[GENE-024]][[GENE-025]]. The senescence barrier is a mouse finding and its human counterpart rests on nine stained specimens [[ORIG-014]].
research_notes.how_studied: Targeted panels and exomes find mutations; detecting loss of the second copy needs allele-specific copy-number analysis, which the key repair study performed with a tool called FACETS [[GENE-016]]. Genomic scars of failed homologous recombination are measured as large-scale state transitions or mutational signature 3, though both are hard to read on small panels in a cancer with few mutations [[GENE-016]]. Mismatch repair is assessed by immunostaining for the four proteins, by PCR of microsatellite markers, and by sequencing-based scores, and these can disagree [[GENE-006]]. Whole-genome sequencing reconstructs the order of catastrophic events from the structure of the rearrangements [[GENE-003]].

mechanism_notes.text: The variable that predicts benefit from platinum and PARP inhibitors is probably biallelic loss of repair function rather than the presence of a variant in any listed gene, because biallelic lesions carried higher instability scores than monoallelic ones and only biallelic tumors showed durable PARP-inhibitor benefit [[INF-GENE-02]][[GENE-016]][[GENE-025]]. A competing reading is that repair deficiency mainly marks slower-growing disease, which the randomized adjuvant data would then estimate more fairly than observational platinum comparisons [[GENE-024]].

glossary.definition: A cut through both strands of the DNA helix, the lesion most likely to cause chromosome rearrangement if misrepaired.
The accurate repair of a double-strand break using the matching sister copy of the chromosome as a template.
The proofreading system that corrects wrongly paired letters left behind after DNA copying.
A control point that halts the cell cycle until damage is repaired, run largely by p53.
Programmed, orderly self-destruction of a cell that is too damaged to repair.
A permanent exit from the division cycle that a damaged or oncogene-stressed cell can enter instead of dying.
Affecting both copies of a gene, so that no working version remains in the cell.

related.statement: The p53 checkpoint described here is lost in most pancreatic cancers through TP53 mutation.
BRCA1, BRCA2 and PALB2 are the core components of the homologous-recombination repair machinery described in this entry.
ATM and CHEK2 are the damage-sensing kinases that signal a double-strand break to the checkpoint, not the repair enzymes themselves.
Mismatch-repair deficiency is the loss of the proofreading system described here and is found in about one in a hundred pancreatic cancers.
Loss of the DNA-damage checkpoint is what allows the catastrophic genome events that shape pancreatic cancer evolution.
PARP inhibitors such as olaparib exploit the loss of homologous recombination described here.

faq.q: Does a DNA-repair problem in my tumor mean a targeted drug will work?
faq.a: Only for specific faults. Olaparib, a PARP inhibitor, is approved in the US as maintenance treatment after platinum chemotherapy in patients with an inherited BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation [[TX-005]], and the evidence suggests benefit concentrates in tumors that have lost both copies of a core repair gene rather than in anyone with a repair-gene variant on a report [[GENE-016]][[GENE-025]].

topics.title: KRAS
topics.orientation: KRAS is the gene mutated in about nine out of ten pancreatic cancers and the first change found in the earliest precursor lesions. This entry covers what the normal protein does, what a mutation lets the cell do, and why the mutation is necessary but not sufficient for cancer.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The KRAS gene encodes a small protein anchored to the inside of the cell membrane that relays growth-factor signals inward. It is a molecular switch: on while bound to GTP, off once that GTP is converted to GDP, which happens within seconds. In a normal cell KRAS is on only briefly after a receptor is stimulated, and the growth message it sends is proportionate to the signal the cell received.
section1.full: Three closely related genes, KRAS, NRAS and HRAS, encode RAS proteins, and KRAS is the one that matters in the pancreas. A growth-factor receptor such as EGFR recruits an exchange factor, SOS1, that loads KRAS with GTP; in the on state KRAS changes shape and binds effectors, principally the RAF kinases that start the MAPK cascade and the PI3K enzyme that starts the AKT route. The off step depends on KRAS's own weak ability to hydrolyze GTP, which is accelerated hundreds of times by GAP proteins such as NF1. The whole cycle is designed to be short, so that a cell integrates many brief pulses rather than a continuous command. In the adult pancreas, acinar cells use this signaling for maintenance and for the repair response after injury, during which they can transiently take on a duct-like state and then return to normal [[ORIG-012]]. The positions in the protein that cancer mutates, glycine 12, glycine 13 and glutamine 61, lie exactly where GAPs act and where GTP is hydrolyzed, which is why a single amino-acid change at these sites can jam the switch on.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: A KRAS mutation is present in roughly 90 percent of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas, with G12D the commonest version, and it is already present in over 90 percent of the smallest precursor lesions. Yet an ordinary adult pancreas contains hundreds of such lesions that never progress, so the mutation starts the process without finishing it. Established tumors in mice depend on the continuing signal, and in 2026 the first RAS-directed drug was approved in the US for this disease.
section2.full: KRAS was mutated in 87.4 percent of 317 resected tumors from a randomized trial and 92 percent of 109 microdissected tumors, with G12D in about 43 percent of mutated cases [[GENE-024]][[GENE-002]][[GENE-005]]. Codon-12 mutations were found in 92 to 95 percent of precursor lesions at every grade, at first in only a fraction of each lesion's cells [[ORIG-002]], and 3D mapping estimates hundreds of such lesions per adult pancreas [[ORIG-001]]. What the mutation allows is quantified in mice: switching off mutant Kras in established tumors caused apoptosis from 48 hours and near-complete regression with loss of glucose uptake within about a week [[GENE-012]], but 70 percent of mice relapsed between 9 and 47 weeks and about half of those relapses had become KRAS-independent through amplified YAP1 [[GENE-013]]. A human lung metastasis carrying the identical KRAS G12V as its peritoneal sister subclone had likewise lost ERK activity and its dependence on KRAS [[GENE-008]]. Dosage matters: tumors with extra copies of mutant Kras metastasized far more often, and that gain was licensed by CDKN2A loss [[GENE-007]]. After surgery, adjuvant modified FOLFIRINOX beat gemcitabine only in KRAS-mutant tumors, hazard ratio 0.60 [[GENE-024]]. On 26 August 2026 the FDA approved daraxonrasib for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma after at least one prior therapy, without requiring a RAS mutation test [[SEC-RAS-01]][[RAS-033]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The frequency figures come from two different kinds of cohort and agree closely, which makes about 90 percent a dependable number for this disease; the remaining tenth is covered in the entry on KRAS variants and wild-type disease [[GENE-002]][[GENE-024]]. The dependence experiments establish that KRAS is a maintenance requirement, not only an initiator, but they used an on-off transgene, which is more absolute than any drug, so the relapse routes seen in mice may not be the ones that dominate under partial drug inhibition [[GENE-013]]. The mismatch between hundreds of KRAS-mutant lesions and a rare cancer means the mutation is necessary but conspicuously insufficient, and what supplies the rest is still being worked out [[ORIG-001]][[ORIG-002]].
research_notes.how_studied: Tumor KRAS status is read from DNA sequencing of a biopsy or resection specimen, and increasingly from blood; because the mutation is a single-letter change at a known hotspot it is one of the easiest findings to detect [[GENE-005]]. Precursor lesions are microdissected from resected pancreases and sequenced individually [[ORIG-002]]. Dependence is tested in mice whose mutant Kras gene is controlled by doxycycline, with MRI and FDG-PET documenting regression and relapse [[GENE-012]][[GENE-013]]. Allele dosage is inferred from the fraction of sequencing reads that carry the mutation combined with copy-number data [[GENE-007]].

mechanism_notes.text: Responses to RAS-directed drugs are deep but short, and the most economical explanation is a drug-tolerant persister state established within days, in which receptor ligands drive PI3K and GAB1 to assemble wild-type RAS signaling complexes that keep MAPK partly active [[INF-RAS-01]][[RAS-008]][[RAS-027]]. Progression would then be outgrowth of that pool, which in patients acquires amplified mutant KRAS or RAF and receptor alterations rather than new mutations in the drug-binding site [[RAS-012]].

glossary.definition: A gene encoding a membrane switch protein that relays growth signals; mutated in about 90 percent of pancreatic cancers.
The commonest KRAS mutation in pancreatic cancer, replacing glycine with aspartate at position 12 and jamming the switch on.
The small energy-carrying molecule whose binding switches RAS on; its conversion to GDP switches RAS off.
A gene that, when mutated or over-expressed, actively drives cell growth.
How many copies of the mutant gene a cell carries relative to the normal copy.
A growth-promoting transcription co-activator that some tumors amplify to survive without KRAS.

related.statement: KRAS is the central switch in the growth-signaling system that normal cells use to decide whether to divide.
The specific KRAS variant a tumor carries, and the tenth of tumors with no KRAS mutation, are covered in the entry on KRAS variants and wild-type disease.
A KRAS mutation is already present in over 90 percent of PanIN precursor lesions, the earliest step before pancreatic cancer.
Loss of CDKN2A licenses the gain of extra mutant KRAS copies that drives metastasis in mouse pancreatic cancer.
Daraxonrasib, approved in the US in August 2026, is the first drug directed at RAS proteins for pancreatic cancer.
RAS(ON) inhibitors target the GTP-bound active form of the KRAS protein described here.
Mutant KRAS drives the glucose uptake and nutrient scavenging that pancreatic cancer cells rely on.

faq.q: Is a KRAS mutation good or bad news for me?
faq.a: It is the expected finding in this disease, present in about nine of ten tumors, so by itself it does not set an individual apart [[GENE-024]][[GENE-002]]. It does matter for treatment: adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX benefited KRAS-mutant but not wild-type tumors in a randomized cohort, and the RAS-directed drug daraxonrasib was approved in the US in August 2026 for metastatic disease after prior therapy [[GENE-024]][[SEC-RAS-01]].

faq.q: Are the KRAS drugs I have read about for lung cancer available for pancreatic cancer?
faq.a: Sotorasib and adagrasib target one specific variant, G12C, and their US labels cover lung and colorectal cancer only, with no pancreatic indication [[SEC-RAS-03]][[SEC-RAS-04]]. G12C occurs in only about 1 to 3 percent of pancreatic cancers; see the entry on KRAS variants.

topics.title: KRAS variants and KRAS wild-type disease
topics.orientation: Not every KRAS mutation behaves the same way, and about one tumor in ten has no KRAS mutation at all. This entry explains what the variant names mean, why the differences matter for drugs, and why the wild-type group is where most of the rare targetable findings live.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Variant names such as G12D describe one amino-acid swap in the KRAS protein: the normal glycine at position 12 replaced by aspartate. Positions 12, 13 and 61 sit in the pocket where GTP is hydrolyzed and where GAP proteins dock to switch KRAS off. Each substitution jams the switch differently, and some leave the protein unable to use one of its two effector routes. A KRAS wild-type tumor has a normal KRAS gene and has found another way to drive growth.
section1.full: In the normal protein, glycine 12 and glycine 13 are the smallest possible amino acids and leave room for the catalytic arginine finger of a GAP to reach into the active site, while glutamine 61 positions the water molecule that hydrolyzes GTP. Any bulkier residue at 12 or 13 physically blocks the GAP, and changing glutamine 61 removes the catalytic residue, so all three classes slow or stop the off step. Beyond that shared effect the variants differ in biochemistry: G13D exchanges nucleotide unusually fast, so it cycles on and off faster than other mutants [[GENE-027]], and G12R disturbs the neighboring switch II region of the protein in a way that prevents binding to the PI3K subunit p110-alpha [[GENE-010]]. In mouse fibroblasts, only G12D produced clearly raised MEK, ERK and AKT activity, G12C and G13D were intermediate, and G12R produced signaling close to wild-type levels [[GENE-011]]. These are differences in the shape and strength of the signal that a cell receives, which is why a sequencing report that records the exact variant carries more information than the word mutated.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: In pancreatic cancer G12D accounts for about 43 percent of KRAS mutations, G12V about 31 percent and G12R about 20 percent, while G12C, the one variant with approved drugs in other cancers, is only 1 to 3 percent. Between 10 and 13 percent of tumors are KRAS wild-type, and that group holds most of the gene fusions, the mismatch-repair deficiency and the HER2 amplification that targeted drugs can act on, so it is tested differently.
section2.full: In 2,483 sequenced pancreatic adenocarcinomas, 10.7 percent overall and 10.1 percent of ductal adenocarcinomas were KRAS wild-type, with G12D in 43 percent and G12V in 31 percent of mutated cases [[GENE-005]]; a randomized-trial cohort put wild-type at 12.6 percent [[GENE-024]]. Part of the wild-type enrichment is histology, since 82 percent of acinar cell carcinomas, a distinct and rarer pancreatic tumor type, lacked KRAS mutations [[GENE-005]]. Variant identity carried outcome information in one series: codon-61 tumors showed less ERK activation and better survival than codon-12 tumors [[GENE-002]], and G12R, about one in five pancreatic cancers, cannot engage p110-alpha and does not drive the nutrient-scavenging macropinocytosis that G12D and G12V do [[GENE-010]], yet in mice it was the weakest initiator, stalling for a year before even forming PanIN, the earliest precursor lesion [[GENE-011]]. KRAS G12C occurs in 1 to 3 percent; in single-arm trials sotorasib produced confirmed responses in 21 percent of 38 patients, adagrasib in 7 of 21, and glecirasib in 46.9 percent of 32, with no US pancreatic approval for any of them [[RAS-001]][[RAS-002]][[RAS-009]][[SEC-RAS-03]][[SEC-RAS-04]]. Wild-type tumors carried gene fusions in 21 percent, BRAF mutations in 13 percent, mismatch-repair deficiency in 4.7 percent against 0.7 percent of mutant tumors, and ERBB2 (HER2) amplification in 2.2 percent [[GENE-005]]. After surgery, adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX showed no advantage over gemcitabine in wild-type tumors, interaction P=0.010 [[GENE-024]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The allele frequencies are stable across large series and should be read as fractions of the disease, so a G12C drug can reach at most a few patients in a hundred [[GENE-005]][[RAS-002]]. The G12R story shows that a variant's prevalence and its signaling strength do not line up: the mouse data are initiation models without the TP53 and CDKN2A lesions that accompany human G12R tumors, and no patient-level drug-sensitivity data exist for the allele [[GENE-011]][[GENE-010]]. The wild-type group mixes true ductal adenocarcinomas with distinct tumor types and with cases whose KRAS mutation was present at a level too low for the sequencing to call reliably, which is one reason a confirmatory RNA-based fusion test is reasonable when a first panel reports KRAS wild-type [[GENE-005]][[GENE-024]].
research_notes.how_studied: Variant identity is read from DNA sequencing at the hotspot codons; fusion detection requires RNA sequencing, which commercial panels now include [[GENE-005]]. Blood-based genotyping can miss a tissue-confirmed variant, finding G12C in only 73 to 81 percent of patients whose tumor carried it [[RAS-022]]. Allele biochemistry is studied with purified proteins and crystallography [[GENE-027]][[GENE-010]], and initiation strength with mouse strains in which each variant is engineered into the native Kras gene and switched on in the pancreas [[GENE-011]]. Drug activity by allele comes from single-arm trials with response rate as the main outcome, which cannot be compared across trials as if randomized [[RAS-009]].

mechanism_notes.text: G12R may be common in the pancreas despite weak initiating strength because its lower PI3K output reduces oncogene-induced stress in acinar cells, letting a clone persist quietly until CDKN2A loss both removes the senescence brake and licenses KRAS dosage gain [[INF-GENE-01]][[GENE-010]][[GENE-011]][[GENE-007]]. The competing explanation is that the pancreas simply writes that particular base change more often, in which case the mouse result is the true measure of the allele's strength.

glossary.definition: One particular version of a gene; in this context, which specific KRAS mutation a tumor carries.
A tumor whose KRAS gene has no mutation, found in about one in ten pancreatic cancers.
A KRAS variant with approved drugs in lung and bowel cancer but found in only 1 to 3 percent of pancreatic cancers.
A three-letter unit of DNA that specifies one amino acid; codons 12, 13 and 61 of KRAS are the cancer hotspots.
A process by which cells gulp extracellular fluid and protein to feed themselves, driven by some KRAS variants.
An abnormal joining of two genes that can create a permanently active growth-signaling protein.

related.statement: The variants described here are different versions of the same KRAS mutation that drives about 90 percent of pancreatic cancers.
Gene fusions and other rare drug targets are concentrated in the KRAS wild-type tenth of pancreatic cancers.
Mismatch-repair deficiency is several times more common in KRAS wild-type than in KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancers.
KRAS G12C inhibitors act only on the G12C variant, which occurs in 1 to 3 percent of pancreatic cancers.
Drugs aimed at G12D, the commonest pancreatic KRAS variant, are in trials but none is approved in the US.
Which KRAS variant a tumor carries, and whether it is wild-type, is read from DNA sequencing of tumor tissue or blood.

faq.q: My report says KRAS G12C. Does that mean I can have sotorasib?
faq.a: G12C is the variant those drugs target, but as of 8 October 2026 neither sotorasib nor adagrasib has a US pancreatic indication; their labels cover lung and colorectal cancer [[SEC-RAS-03]][[SEC-RAS-04]]. In single-arm pancreatic trials they produced responses in 21 percent and 33 percent of patients, and a newer agent in 46.9 percent, so access is through trials or off-label discussion with the care team [[RAS-001]][[RAS-002]][[RAS-009]].

faq.q: My tumor is KRAS wild-type. Is that better?
faq.a: It changes what to look for. Wild-type tumors carried gene fusions in 21 percent and mismatch-repair deficiency in 4.7 percent, both of which have US-approved drugs, so RNA-based fusion testing and mismatch-repair testing become more important [[GENE-005]]. In one randomized cohort, wild-type tumors did not gain from adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX over gemcitabine, a finding the authors call hypothesis-generating [[GENE-024]].

faq.q: Is there a drug for G12D, the commonest variant?
faq.a: Not an approved one in the US as of 8 October 2026. The first G12D-selective inhibitor's human trial was stopped for formulation problems, and a successor is in phase 1 and phase 3 trials with no published efficacy results [[SEC-RAS-09]][[SEC-RAS-10]].

topics.title: CDKN2A (p16)
