topics.orientation: CDKN2A encodes p16, the protein that keeps a stressed cell from entering the division cycle. Pancreatic cancers remove it in most cases, typically by deleting the gene outright, and an inherited fault in the same gene is the strongest single-gene risk for this disease.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: CDKN2A lies on chromosome 9 and produces two proteins from overlapping code. The first, p16, binds the kinases CDK4 and CDK6 and prevents them from releasing the brake protein RB, so a cell that has received a growth signal still cannot copy its DNA. The second, p14ARF, shields p53 from destruction. Between them they let a cell under oncogenic stress park itself for good, a state called senescence.
section1.full: In a resting cell p16 is scarcely made and the cycle brake answers to other inputs. Sustained oncogenic signaling, such as a jammed RAS switch, drives p16 up sharply; it holds CDK4 and CDK6 inactive, RB stays bound to the E2F transcription factors, and the DNA-replication genes stay silent [[GENE-009]]. That is the molecular basis of oncogene-induced senescence, a permanent exit from the cycle and one of the body's main defenses against a single activating mutation. p14ARF, read from the same gene in a shifted frame, binds MDM2, the enzyme that normally tags p53 for disposal, so a stressed cell also accumulates p53 and gains its checkpoint and self-destruct functions. One gene therefore feeds both arms of the stress response, the RB arm and the p53 arm, which explains why its loss matters so much and why tumors tend to delete the whole locus rather than mutate it: a deletion removes both proteins at once. In adult mice, pancreatic cells carrying mutant Kras formed only senescent, non-progressing lesions unless inflammation lifted this barrier, and removing p16 together with p19Arf, the mouse counterpart of p14ARF, sped progression and yielded undifferentiated, metastatic tumors [[ORIG-014]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: CDKN2A is one of the four genes that define pancreatic cancer and is lost in most tumors, usually by physical deletion of the chromosome region rather than a spelling change, so panels that detect only spelling changes understate it badly. Losing p16 removes the senescence brake, permits the gain of extra mutant KRAS copies, and marks the step from low-grade to high-grade precursor. An inherited CDKN2A fault is a separate matter and carries a high lifetime risk.
section2.full: In the founding exome study CDKN2A was a recurrent target of homozygous deletion, with tumors averaging 8.3 such deletions across the genome [[GENE-001]], whereas a mutation-only panel applied to 317 trial tumors reported CDKN2A in just 6.6 percent, and the authors said that not calling deletions had produced the undercount [[GENE-024]]. In precursor lesions the gene marks the gate: point mutations appeared in only 11.5 percent of low-grade lesions [[ORIG-002]], but copy-number loss at 9p21, the CDKN2A locus, was present in all 11 high-grade lesions examined [[ORIG-023]]. In mice, extra copies of mutant Kras arose in 23 of 27 tumors with homozygous Cdkn2a deletion against a minority of the rest, odds ratio 15.3, and human tumors showed the same pairing of CDKN2A deletion with high mutant-KRAS allele fraction [[GENE-007]]. The drug consequence is counter-intuitive: in patient-derived models, sensitivity to the CDK4/6 inhibitor palbociclib tracked retained RB protein rather than p16 status, RB loss independently predicted worse survival, and p16 expression was not prognostic at all; no CDK4/6 inhibitor is approved in the US for pancreatic cancer as of 8 October 2026 [[GENE-009]]. Germline (inherited) CDKN2A variants were found in 0.30 percent of 3,030 patients against 0.02 percent of controls, odds ratio 12.33, the highest of any gene tested, and carriers were the only group more likely to have a family history of the disease [[ORIG-006]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Two different facts share the gene name and should not be merged. A deleted CDKN2A in a tumor is an acquired event present in most pancreatic cancers and does not by itself change treatment; an inherited CDKN2A variant is rare, found in about one patient in 300, and is a reason for family counseling and surveillance [[GENE-024]][[ORIG-006]]. The mouse dosage link is causal in mice and correlational in people [[GENE-007]]. For surveillance of carriers, family history and smoking were the only predictors, and a model built on them discriminated no better than chance after validation, so no clinical tool yet tailors surveillance intervals within this genotype [[ORIG-016]].
research_notes.how_studied: Detecting CDKN2A loss requires copy-number analysis, because a deletion leaves nothing for a mutation caller to read; panels that lack it will report the gene as normal [[GENE-024]]. Immunostaining for p16 protein is a surrogate for gene status. Precursor lesions are microdissected from resected tissue and profiled for copy number [[ORIG-023]]. The senescence barrier is studied in mice whose Kras and Cdkn2a genes can be switched independently and whose pancreas can be inflamed on demand [[ORIG-014]]. Germline risk comes from comparing variant frequencies in thousands of patients with population reference databases [[ORIG-006]].

mechanism_notes.text: CDKN2A loss may be the cooperating lesion that lets a weakly signaling KRAS variant such as G12R progress, because it both removes the senescence brake and licenses mutant-KRAS dosage gain [[INF-GENE-01]][[GENE-007]][[GENE-011]]. If so, G12R tumors should show more frequent biallelic CDKN2A loss than G12D tumors, a prediction that existing whole-genome datasets could test.

glossary.definition: The protein made by CDKN2A that blocks CDK4 and CDK6 and keeps a stressed cell out of the division cycle.
Loss of both copies of a stretch of DNA, so the gene is physically absent rather than misspelled.
Kinases that, with cyclin D, release the RB brake and let a cell begin copying its DNA.
The permanent growth arrest a cell enters when a single activating mutation triggers the p16 and p53 stress responses.
A gene change inherited from a parent and present in every cell of the body, as distinct from one acquired by the tumor.

related.statement: The p16 made by CDKN2A is the brake on CDK4 and CDK6 in the cell-cycle layer of growth control.
Loss of CDKN2A licenses the gain of extra mutant KRAS copies that drives metastasis in mouse pancreatic cancer.
Copy-number loss of the CDKN2A region marks the transition from low-grade to high-grade PanIN.
An inherited CDKN2A variant is the strongest known single-gene risk factor for pancreatic cancer and a reason for surveillance.
CDKN2A is often lost in the same catastrophic chromosome event that removes TP53 and SMAD4.
CDKN2A loss is detected only by panels that call deletions, so a report that omits it may reflect the test rather than the tumor.

faq.q: My tumor report does not mention CDKN2A. Does that mean mine is intact?
faq.a: Not necessarily. CDKN2A is usually lost by deletion, and a panel that only calls spelling changes reported it in 6.6 percent of tumors when deletion-aware studies place it far higher [[GENE-024]][[GENE-001]]. Ask whether the test included copy-number analysis.

faq.q: Is a CDKN2A finding something my family should know about?
faq.a: Only if it is germline, meaning inherited and present in blood or saliva as well as the tumor. Inherited CDKN2A variants were found in 0.30 percent of patients and carried a 12-fold odds ratio, so relatives of a carrier are candidates for genetic counseling and high-risk surveillance [[ORIG-006]]. A deletion found only in the tumor is acquired and is not inherited.

topics.title: TP53 (p53)
topics.orientation: TP53 encodes p53, the protein that decides whether a damaged cell pauses, repairs, retires or dies. It is mutated in at least half of pancreatic cancers, and the common mutations do more than remove the checkpoint: the altered protein actively helps cells invade and spread.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: p53 is a transcription factor kept at very low levels in a healthy cell by the enzyme MDM2, which continuously tags it for disposal. DNA damage, oncogenic stress or oxygen shortage interrupt that disposal, p53 accumulates within hours, and it switches on genes that halt the division cycle, promote repair, trigger apoptosis or enforce senescence. It is the cell's most important single decision-maker about whether to continue dividing.
section1.full: The signal that stabilizes p53 arrives through kinases such as ATM, which sense double-strand breaks and phosphorylate p53 so that MDM2 can no longer bind it. Once stable, p53 assembles as a tetramer (a four-part complex) on DNA and activates a program of several hundred genes. The best known is p21, which inhibits the cyclin-dependent kinases and arrests the cycle at the G1 checkpoint, the gate before DNA copying, giving repair enzymes time to work. If damage persists, p53 raises the pro-apoptotic proteins PUMA and NOXA and the cell dismantles itself; alternatively it can lock the cell into senescence. p53 also restrains glucose metabolism and nutrient scavenging and supports several DNA-repair processes directly. Because the protein acts as a four-part assembly, a single mutated copy can poison the complex, which is why most cancer-associated TP53 changes are missense mutations in the DNA-binding domain rather than deletions. These mutant proteins escape MDM2 and accumulate to high levels, which is what pathologists see as strong, diffuse nuclear staining, while a tumor that has lost the gene altogether stains for nothing; both patterns are reported as abnormal p53. In precursor lesions, raised p53 protein appeared specifically in tumors and high-grade lesions, consistent with mutant protein stabilization at that step [[ORIG-025]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: TP53 is mutated in more than half of pancreatic cancers by point mutation alone, and the chromosome region that carries it is lost in every high-grade precursor lesion examined. Its loss opens the door to the catastrophic genome events that shape this disease. The common missense mutations also confer a new ability: in mouse models, mutant p53 drives invasion and metastasis through a growth-factor receptor, and removing the mutant protein reverses that behavior.
section2.full: Point mutations in TP53 were present in 53.6 percent of 317 resected trial tumors, and TP53 status had no prognostic or predictive value for adjuvant chemotherapy in that cohort [[GENE-024]]; the founding exome study listed TP53 among the genes also removed by deletion [[GENE-001]]. Copy-number loss at 17p, the TP53 locus, was found in all 11 high-grade precursor lesions in one series [[ORIG-023]]. Whole-genome sequencing showed that tumors which had doubled their genome were enriched for TP53 mutation and carried about 1.5 times as many copy-number changes [[GENE-003]]. The gain-of-function evidence comes from mouse cells: knocking down mutant p53 in Kras-driven cancer cells cut their motility to the level of p53-null cells and abolished their enhanced invasion through collagen; the mediator was the receptor PDGFR-beta, which mutant p53 switches on by disabling a repressor complex, and a PDGFR inhibitor reduced lung nodules from mutant-p53 cells but not from p53-null cells [[GENE-020]]. In organoids, mutant p53 also gave cells a growth advantage under acute stress and shifted them toward the poor-prognosis basal-like state, a shift that reversed when normal conditions returned [[GENE-015]]. Inherited TP53 variants are rare, 0.20 percent of 3,030 patients, with an odds ratio of 6.70 [[ORIG-006]]. No drug approved in the US as of 8 October 2026 targets mutant p53 in pancreatic cancer.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The frequency and the mechanism rest on different kinds of evidence. The 53.6 percent figure comes from a mutation-only panel and will understate loss by deletion, so the true fraction of tumors without working p53 is higher [[GENE-024]][[GENE-001]]. The PDGFR-beta mechanism is clean because it includes the right control, p53-null cells that did not respond to the inhibitor, but it was shown with mouse cell lines in experimental metastasis assays, and PDGFR inhibition is not an established pancreatic cancer therapy [[GENE-020]]. The reversible basal shift is organoid-only [[GENE-015]]. For a reader, the practical content is that abnormal p53 on a pathology report is expected in this disease and does not by itself alter treatment.
research_notes.how_studied: TP53 status is read by DNA sequencing of the tumor, which identifies the specific change, and by immunostaining, which infers a mutation from either strong diffuse nuclear accumulation or complete absence of protein. Gain-of-function is tested by knocking down the mutant protein with short hairpin RNA in cancer cells and comparing motility, invasion and lung colonization against cells engineered to lack p53 entirely [[GENE-020]]. Organoid models with defined p53 status are exposed to stress and profiled by RNA sequencing before and after recovery [[GENE-015]]. Whole-genome sequencing times genome doubling relative to point mutations [[GENE-003]].

mechanism_notes.text: Mutant p53 appears to be one of the genetic modifiers that sets how readily a tumor cell moves along the classical-to-basal axis in response to its environment, since mutant-p53 organoids switched to the basal program under stress and back again on recovery while comparison organoids did not [[INF-GENE-03]][[GENE-015]]. A measured subtype in a TP53-mutant tumor may therefore report recent conditions as much as a fixed identity.

glossary.definition: The protein made by TP53 that halts a damaged cell, directs repair, or triggers its death or retirement.
A single-letter change that swaps one amino acid for another, producing an altered rather than absent protein.
A new activity acquired by a mutated protein, beyond the loss of its normal role.
The enzyme that keeps p53 levels low in healthy cells by tagging it for destruction.
A pathology pattern, either strong diffuse nuclear staining or complete absence, that indicates a TP53 mutation.

related.statement: p53 is the central decision-maker in the DNA-damage checkpoint system that pancreatic cancers disable.
Loss of TP53 is what permits the genome doubling and chromosome shattering that reshape the pancreatic cancer genome.
Mutant p53 makes tumor cells more prone to switch into the basal-like state under stress.
Loss of the TP53 chromosome region marks the high-grade stage of PanIN precursor lesions.
Abnormal p53 on a pathology report refers to a staining pattern that indicates a TP53 mutation in the tumor.
Inherited TP53 variants are rare but carry a roughly sevenfold increase in pancreatic cancer risk.

faq.q: My pathology report says abnormal p53. Is that a bad sign?
faq.a: It is the expected finding: TP53 was mutated in more than half of resected tumors even by a method that misses deletions, and its status did not predict outcome or chemotherapy benefit in that randomized cohort [[GENE-024]]. The staining pattern tells the pathologist the gene is mutated; it does not change treatment choices.

faq.q: Is there a drug that fixes p53?
faq.a: Not for pancreatic cancer in the US as of 8 October 2026. The mouse finding that mutant p53 works through PDGFR-beta identified a druggable intermediary, but PDGFR inhibition remains preclinical for this disease [[GENE-020]].

topics.title: SMAD4 and TGF-β signaling
topics.orientation: SMAD4 is the relay through which the signaling molecule TGF-β tells an epithelial cell to stop dividing. Roughly a third of pancreatic cancers have lost it, and a long-standing claim that its loss predicts widespread rather than local spread has not held up in resected disease.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Transforming growth factor beta, TGF-β, is a secreted signal that in healthy epithelium restrains growth and maintains differentiation. It binds a pair of receptors on the cell surface, the receptors phosphorylate SMAD2 and SMAD3, and those proteins can only enter the nucleus and change gene activity when partnered with SMAD4. SMAD4 is therefore the single shared relay for the whole pathway, which is why losing it silences the growth-restraining message completely.
section1.full: Inside the nucleus the SMAD complex switches on genes that halt the cycle, including the CDK inhibitors p15 and p21, and switches off growth-promoting genes such as MYC. In the pancreas this is part of how duct and acinar cells are kept quiescent, and the same signal instructs fibroblasts to lay down matrix during wound repair. TGF-β is also a double agent: once a cell has escaped the growth restraint, the remaining branches of the pathway can promote invasion, a change of state toward a mesenchymal or basal-like program, and suppression of immune cells. In pancreatic cancer the stroma is rich in TGF-β, where it drives fibroblasts into the myofibroblast state and blocks the alternative inflammatory fibroblast state by removing the interleukin-1 receptor [[TME-011]]. Exposing patient-derived tumor organoids to TGF-β ligands shifted malignant cells toward intermediate and basal-like states [[GENE-014]]. The founding genomic study treated the TGF-β pathway as one of twelve core processes and showed that different tumors break it at different points, one through SMAD4 and another through the receptor gene BMPR2, with the same functional result [[GENE-001]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: SMAD4 was lost in about a third of resected tumors by protein staining, mostly by deletion of its chromosome region, and that region is lost in every high-grade precursor lesion examined. In tumors whose genomes have shattered, chromosome 18 is a common site, removing SMAD4 while duplicating the nearby gene GATA6, which maintains the better-prognosis classical cell state. A famous autopsy series linked SMAD4 loss to dying of widespread metastases, but the association did not appear in resected patients, and SMAD4 status does not currently guide treatment.
section2.full: Immunostaining found SMAD4 lost in 40 of 127 resected tumors, 32 percent [[GENE-023]], whereas a mutation-only panel reported SMAD4 in just 9.1 percent of 317 tumors and its authors noted that missing deletions caused the shortfall [[GENE-024]]. In whole-genome sequencing, chromosome 18 was a common site of chromothripsis (chromosome shattering), producing SMAD4 loss alongside gain of a segment containing GATA6, and in one tumor a single shattering event removed CDKN2A and SMAD4 together [[GENE-003]]. Loss at 18q was present in all 11 high-grade precursor lesions in a small series [[ORIG-023]]. The clinical claim is contested. In a rapid-autopsy study of 76 patients, 30 percent died of locally destructive disease and 70 percent of widespread metastases, and loss of the SMAD4 protein was highly correlated with the widespread pattern [[GENE-028]]. In 127 resected patients, however, SMAD4 loss occurred in 27 percent of those with isolated local recurrence, 33 percent with distant recurrence, 33 percent with both and 25 percent without recurrence, no association at all, and only lymph-node involvement predicted distant spread, odds ratio 4.7 [[GENE-023]]. SMAD4 status was neither prognostic nor predictive of adjuvant chemotherapy benefit in the randomized cohort [[GENE-024]], and genetic reconstruction of metastatic cases shows all three major suppressors, including SMAD4, already present in the founding clone years before spread [[SURG-002]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The pathway-level consequence of SMAD4 loss, removal of TGF-β growth restraint, is well supported, but the claim that would have changed practice, that SMAD4 status could tell surgeons who needs local versus systemic intensification, failed to reproduce in the setting where it would be used [[GENE-023]][[GENE-028]]. The two studies examined different disease settings, terminal and resected, so either the association is specific to end-stage disease or the original was a small-series artifact; neither has been tested prospectively. The frequency a report gives for SMAD4 depends on whether the assay can see deletions, so a report that omits it may reflect the panel rather than the tumor [[GENE-024]].
research_notes.how_studied: SMAD4 is usually assessed by immunostaining, where complete loss of nuclear protein is a sensitive marker of gene inactivation; sequencing adds the specific change but misses deletions unless copy number is analyzed [[GENE-023]][[GENE-024]]. Pattern-of-failure studies classify recurrences as local, distant or both from records and imaging, which depends on how closely patients were followed [[GENE-023]]. Rapid autopsy captures the distribution of disease at death [[GENE-028]]. Fibroblast responses to TGF-β are studied in co-cultures and mouse tumors [[TME-011]], and state shifts in organoids exposed to the ligand [[GENE-014]].

mechanism_notes.text: Losing SMAD4 removes the cancer cell's own brake, but TGF-β in the surrounding stroma keeps acting on fibroblasts and keeps pushing malignant cells toward the basal-like state through routes that do not all require SMAD4, so a SMAD4-lost tumor sits in an environment it can no longer fully read [[INF-GENE-03]][[GENE-014]][[TME-011]]. Whether such tumors respond differently to that pressure has not been tested with paired specimens.

glossary.definition: Transforming growth factor beta, a secreted signal that restrains epithelial growth and instructs fibroblasts to make scar tissue.
The shared relay protein without which TGF-β signals cannot reach the nucleus; also called DPC4.
An older name for SMAD4, short for 'deleted in pancreatic cancer 4'.
A single catastrophic event in which a chromosome shatters and is stitched back together in the wrong order.
Whether a cancer returns locally, at distant sites, or both after treatment.

related.statement: The TGF-β growth restraint relayed by SMAD4 is one of the twelve core pathways disrupted in pancreatic cancer.
TGF-β in the tumor stroma drives fibroblasts into the myofibroblast state regardless of the cancer cell's SMAD4 status.
TGF-β exposure pushes pancreatic cancer cells toward the basal-like state.
SMAD4 is often removed in a single chromosome-18 shattering event that also duplicates GATA6.
SMAD4 status did not predict whether a resected pancreatic cancer would recur locally or at distant sites.
Loss of the SMAD4 chromosome region is one of the three recurrent copy-number changes in high-grade PanIN.

faq.q: My tumor has lost SMAD4. Does that mean it will spread widely?
faq.a: That idea came from a 76-patient autopsy series in which SMAD4 loss tracked with widespread metastatic disease at death [[GENE-028]], but in 127 patients whose tumors had been removed, SMAD4 loss was equally common whatever the recurrence pattern, and only lymph-node involvement predicted distant spread [[GENE-023]]. SMAD4 status is not used in the US to choose between local and systemic treatment.

topics.title: How the cancer genome changes: punctuated evolution
topics.orientation: A pancreatic cancer is not one genome but a family of related genomes that keeps changing. This entry explains how the final steps to an invasive cancer often happen in bursts rather than one mutation at a time, and why metastases and relapses differ genetically from the tumor that was first sampled.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Every division of a healthy cell copies about three billion DNA letters and then separates two complete chromosome sets, a process guarded by checkpoints that stop division if copying is incomplete or chromosomes are misaligned. Cells that nonetheless end up with doubled, shattered or unevenly shared chromosomes are normally recognized through the p53 checkpoint and either arrested or eliminated, so a stable genome is maintained over a lifetime of divisions.
section1.full: The fidelity of this process is extraordinary: polymerase proofreading and mismatch repair leave roughly one uncorrected error per billion letters per division, and the spindle checkpoint delays separation until every chromosome is attached. Chromosome ends are capped by telomeres, which shorten with each division; when they run out, the exposed ends are read as breaks, and a cell with a working p53 response retires into senescence. If that response is missing, uncapped chromosome ends can fuse, be torn apart at the next division and fuse again, a cycle called breakage-fusion-bridge that scrambles the affected region. A failed division can also leave a cell with two full chromosome sets, tetraploidy, which a working checkpoint would arrest. Chromosome shattering, or chromothripsis, is thought to occur when a lagging chromosome is trapped in a fragile micronucleus, fragments, and is stitched back together in random order within a single cell cycle. In healthy tissue each of these events is rare and each is normally fatal to the cell; their frequency in tumors is a direct consequence of losing the checkpoints described in the entry on DNA damage. The genetic reconstruction of pancreatic cancer suggests the ordinary diploid (normal two-copy) phase of point-mutation accumulation lasts many years before any of this happens [[SURG-002]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Whole-genome sequencing of over a hundred pancreatic cancers overturned the picture of a slow, stepwise accumulation of driver mutations. Nearly half had doubled their genome, two-thirds carried shattered chromosomes, and in one in six the main driver genes were knocked out together in a single event. Point mutations came first, over years; the copy-number losses that complete the cancer came later and often all at once. Metastases are then seeded by distinct subclones that continue to evolve in each organ, and treatment selects new ones.
section2.full: Among 107 whole genomes, 45 percent showed polyploidization, 88 percent of those tetraploid, with most point mutations preceding the doubling and most copy-number changes following it; 65.4 percent carried at least one chromothripsis event, which was associated with worse survival, and 16 percent combined allelic hits to KRAS, CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4 in one rearrangement, in one tumor knocking out CDKN2A and SMAD4 in the same event [[GENE-003]]. Mutational signatures in that cohort were about 80 percent age-related, with 17 percent showing a double-strand-break-repair signature, half of which carried BRCA1 or BRCA2 alterations [[GENE-003]]. Timing estimates from metastatic autopsy cases put about 11.7 years from initiation to the founding clone, 6.8 more years to the subclone that seeded metastasis, and 2.7 years to death [[SURG-002]]. Instability persists after spread: rearrangement analysis of 13 patients showed ongoing parallel evolution with organ-specific branches [[SURG-013]], and in mice a substantial share of metastases were seeded by more than one subclone [[SURG-026]]. Evolution also proceeds without new mutations, since distant metastatic subclones with identical drivers had reprogrammed their chromatin (the packaging that controls which genes are readable) and metabolism [[GENE-008]]. Under RAS-directed therapy, a quarter of patients showed acquired amplification of mutant KRAS or alterations in RAF genes and receptors in blood DNA [[RAS-012]]. Precursor lesions show the same gate: copy-number loss at the CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4 regions in all 11 high-grade lesions examined [[ORIG-023]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Punctuated evolution changes what early detection can hope to achieve: if a diploid precursor can become an invasive genotype within one or a few divisions, the window between a detectable but harmless lesion and a dangerous one may be short, which fits the interval cancers (cancers appearing between scheduled surveillance scans) seen in surveillance cohorts [[GENE-003]][[ORIG-005]]. It also means a single biopsy describes one branch at one time; metastases and relapses can carry drivers, dosages and chromatin states the primary did not [[SURG-013]][[GENE-008]]. The timing figures come from seven autopsy cases and a mathematical model, so they are orders of magnitude rather than schedules [[SURG-002]].
research_notes.how_studied: Whole-genome sequencing captures rearrangements and copy number that exome panels miss; purpose-built algorithms estimate tumor ploidy, distinguish a shattering event from gradually accumulated changes, and time point mutations relative to genome doubling by counting how many copies of each mutation are present [[GENE-003]]. Multi-region and autopsy sequencing builds a family tree of subclones by comparing which mutations are shared and which are private, and molecular-clock assumptions convert branch lengths into years [[SURG-002]][[SURG-013]]. Serial blood DNA under treatment detects emerging resistant clones without re-biopsy [[RAS-012]].

mechanism_notes.text: Local inflammation may be what converts a senescent KRAS-mutant precursor into a dividing one, and continued division in a lesion that has already lost checkpoint restraint is what allows chromosome missegregation and the copy-number losses at CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4 to arise and be selected [[INF-ORIG-01]][[ORIG-023]][[ORIG-014]]. The competing account is that copy-number instability accrues at a fixed low rate per division and the progressing lesion is simply the unlucky one.

glossary.definition: A population of tumor cells descended from one ancestor that carries its own private set of mutations.
A failed division that leaves a cell with two complete sets of chromosomes, after which losses are better tolerated.
A single catastrophic event in which a chromosome shatters and is reassembled in the wrong order.
Gain or loss of whole stretches of DNA, as distinct from a single-letter mutation.
A characteristic pattern of DNA changes that reveals which process, such as aging or failed repair, produced them.
Genetic variation between different cells or regions of the same tumor.

related.statement: The catastrophic genome events described here become possible only after the DNA-damage checkpoints have failed.
Pancreatic cancers that have doubled their genome are enriched for TP53 mutation.
A single chromosome-18 shattering event often removes SMAD4 and duplicates GATA6.
Pancreatic cancer can also evolve toward metastasis through chromatin changes without any new mutation.
The copy-number losses that complete a pancreatic cancer are already present in high-grade PanIN.
Treatment with RAS-directed drugs selects subclones carrying amplified mutant KRAS or new RAF and receptor alterations.
Genetic reconstruction suggests the subclones that seed metastases arise years before diagnosis.

faq.q: If the cancer took years to develop, why was it found so late?
faq.a: The long phase is the accumulation of point mutations in a lesion that is not yet a cancer; the step to an invasive genome can happen in one or a few divisions through genome doubling or chromosome shattering, which is why a harmless-looking precursor and a dangerous one may be separated by a short interval [[GENE-003]][[SURG-002]].

faq.q: Will a biopsy of my metastasis show the same mutations as the original tumor?
faq.a: The main drivers are usually shared, because they were present in the founding clone, but metastases carry additional private changes, keep evolving in each organ, and can change chromatin state and drug dependence without changing their mutations [[SURG-002]][[SURG-013]][[GENE-008]].

topics.title: Classical and basal-like cell states
topics.orientation: Pancreatic cancer cells express one of two broad gene programs, classical or basal-like, and the basal-like program carries a worse outlook. This entry explains what those programs are, why they are better thought of as states than fixed identities, and what a subtype result can and cannot tell a reader.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: A cell's identity is set by transcription factors that hold its lineage program in place. In the pancreatic duct that job falls to factors such as GATA6 and HNF4A, which keep an epithelial, gland-forming, mucus-handling program switched on. Squamous epithelium, the flat protective lining of skin and gullet, uses a different set led by p63. The two programs are normally exclusive, and a mature cell does not drift between them.
section1.full: Lineage factors work by binding thousands of regulatory sites at once and keeping them open, so that the whole gene set of a cell type is expressed together and competing sets stay closed. GATA6 directly supports epithelial genes and represses the transcription factors that would drive a cell toward a mobile, mesenchymal form; experimentally, GATA6 inhibited epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (the shift to a mobile, less structured cell form) in culture and cell dissemination in animals [[GENE-021]]. Identity nonetheless has to be maintained actively, and injury signals can loosen it: acinar cells, for example, transiently adopt a duct-like state after pancreatitis and then return. The squamous program is held by the p63 isoform called delta-N p63 together with YAP and TEAD factors, which respond to mechanical stress and to signals such as TGF-β from the surrounding tissue [[GENE-015]]. In single-cell profiling of pancreatic tumors, the classical program associated with epithelial and pancreatic lineage genes while the basal program associated with TGF-β signaling, WNT signaling and the cell cycle, which places the two states at opposite ends of a response to environmental pressure rather than as two unrelated cell types [[GENE-014]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Tumors whose cells had switched to the basal-like program had a median survival of 11 months against 19 for classical tumors, and the difference reappeared within the mFOLFIRINOX chemotherapy arm of a randomized trial. Low GATA6 marked the basal state and predicted poor survival. Yet single cells can run both programs at once, laboratory conditions alone can flip the reading, mutant p53 makes the switch reversible under stress, and the balance differs by what treatment a patient received. No subtype result currently directs treatment.
section2.full: After computationally removing stromal signal, two tumor-intrinsic subtypes emerged: basal-like, with 44 percent one-year survival, and classical, with 70 percent, P=0.007, validated in an independent cohort [[GENE-004]]. In the PRODIGE-24 trial tissue, classical tumors in the modified FOLFIRINOX arm had better disease-free survival than basal-like tumors, stratified hazard ratio 0.48 [[GENE-024]]. GATA6-low tumors had a median survival of 4.6 months against 12.7 to 13.1 months for medium or high, and in trial specimens low GATA6 predicted poor outcome only in the 5-fluorouracil arm, not the gemcitabine arm, although changing GATA6 levels in cultured cells did not alter 5-fluorouracil sensitivity [[GENE-021]]. Single-cell sequencing of 23 patients' metastases found cells co-expressing both programs, an intermediate state missed by bulk classifiers; organoids grown from the same tumors read almost entirely classical while cell lines read predominantly basal, and adding TGF-β ligands shifted organoids toward the basal state [[GENE-014]]. Organoids with mutant p53 switched to basal under acute stress and back on recovery [[GENE-015]]. In 56 resected patients, tumors that had received FOLFIRINOX plus stereotactic radiotherapy were enriched for classical and depleted of basal-like signatures relative to other exposures, though without paired biopsies [[GENE-026]]. Spatial profiling showed classical cells sitting in fibroblast-rich, immune-poor neighborhoods and squamoid-basaloid cells among diverse immune infiltrates, with the classical program associated with lower mortality, hazard ratio 0.73 [[TME-032]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The prognostic difference is real and reproduced, but its interpretation has shifted from a fixed label to a position on a continuum that the environment, including the measuring environment, can move [[GENE-004]][[GENE-014]]. The GATA6 result is a marker, not a mediator: it indexes a differentiation state that affects chemotherapy response without itself controlling it [[GENE-021]]. The treatment-associated shift toward classical cannot yet separate true state change from preferential killing of basal cells, because no study has profiled the same tumor before and after therapy [[GENE-026]]. As of 8 October 2026, subtyping is a research stratifier in the US and not a standard-of-care basis for choosing treatment [[GENE-024]].
research_notes.how_studied: Bulk RNA profiling of tumor tissue is confounded by the stroma, which can outweigh the cancer cells; the founding study used non-negative matrix factorization to separate tumor from stromal gene sets, and later classifiers such as PurIST score a small set of tumor-specific genes [[GENE-004]][[GENE-024]]. Single-cell RNA sequencing scores each malignant cell separately and reveals mixed states [[GENE-014]]. Organoid and cell-line culture are compared against tissue from the same patient to measure how much the model distorts the reading [[GENE-014]]. GATA6 is scored by immunostaining with assay-dependent cut points [[GENE-021]]. Spatial transcriptomics maps programs onto their tissue neighborhoods [[TME-032]].

mechanism_notes.text: Subtype is best modeled as a reversible position on a classical-to-basal continuum set by the balance between lineage-maintaining factors such as GATA6 and HNF4A and stress- or TGF-β-driven programs such as delta-N p63 and YAP/TEAD, with the intermediate co-expressor state as the transit zone [[INF-GENE-03]][[GENE-014]][[GENE-015]][[GENE-021]]. Prognostic power survives because a tumor measured as basal is one already being pushed there and because the basal program is coupled to dissemination through GATA6 loss. The competing view is that subtypes are clonal and heritable, and that culture and treatment merely select pre-existing subpopulations; lineage barcoding would distinguish the two.

glossary.definition: The tumor-cell program that retains pancreatic epithelial identity and is associated with longer survival.
A tumor-cell program resembling squamous epithelium, associated with shorter survival.
A transcription factor that maintains the classical program; its loss marks the basal-like state.
The ability of a cancer cell to change its gene program in response to its surroundings without changing its DNA.
A three-dimensional miniature tumor grown in the laboratory from a patient's cells.
A classifier that assigns classical or basal-like subtype from a small set of tumor-specific genes.

related.statement: The switch between classical and basal-like programs is an epigenetic change in which genes are used differently without altering the DNA sequence.
Mutant p53 makes tumor cells more prone to switch into the basal-like state under stress.
TGF-β, the signal that SMAD4 normally relays, pushes pancreatic cancer cells toward the basal-like state.
Classical tumor cells tend to sit among myofibroblast-rich stroma while basal-like cells sit among more diverse immune infiltrates.
Classical and basal-like programs occupy different recurring neighborhoods within the same pancreatic tumor.
Classical tumors had better disease-free survival than basal-like tumors within the mFOLFIRINOX arm of a randomized adjuvant trial.

faq.q: My report says basal-like. Does that decide my treatment?
faq.a: Not in current US practice. Basal-like tumors had shorter survival in several cohorts, but single cells can run both programs, the reading shifts with laboratory conditions and treatment, and no trial has selected therapy by subtype, so it remains a research stratifier [[GENE-004]][[GENE-014]][[GENE-024]].

faq.q: Can a tumor change from one subtype to the other?
faq.a: The evidence says yes, at least in part: organoids shifted toward basal when exposed to TGF-β and mutant-p53 organoids switched to basal under stress and back on recovery, and tumors sampled after different treatments showed different balances [[GENE-014]][[GENE-015]][[GENE-026]]. Whether that reflects cells changing state or some cells being killed has not been settled.

topics.title: Epigenetic reprogramming
topics.orientation: Epigenetics describes how a cell decides which of its genes to use without changing the DNA sequence. In pancreatic cancer, these settings can be rewritten during progression and treatment, and a metastasis can acquire new abilities, including independence from KRAS, with no new mutation at all.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Every cell carries the same DNA but reads only part of it. The rest is packed away in chromatin, DNA wound around histone proteins, and chemical tags on those histones and on the DNA itself mark regions as open or closed. A liver cell and a duct cell differ not in sequence but in which regions are open, and the pattern is copied at each division so that identity is inherited by daughter cells.
section1.full: Two classes of mark do most of the work. Methylation of cytosine in DNA, especially at gene promoters, silences the gene; chromatin-remodeling complexes such as SWI/SNF slide histones aside to expose regulatory sequences. Histone tags act as a code: acetylation and some methylations, such as at lysine 4 of histone H3, mark active promoters and enhancers, while di- and tri-methylation at lysine 9 of histone H3, written as H3K9me2 and H3K9me3, mark heterochromatin, the tightly packed and silent fraction. Much of the genome is organized into large blocks of H3K9-modified chromatin, called LOCKs, that keep whole gene neighborhoods switched off in differentiated cells and together with large hypomethylated blocks cover over half the genome [[GENE-008]]. Enhancers, the distant switches that set how strongly a gene is expressed in a given cell type, are the main substrate on which lineage factors such as GATA6 act. The whole system is reversible in principle, because the enzymes that write marks are matched by enzymes that erase them, and metabolism supplies the chemical groups they use; that reversibility is what allows normal cells to respond to injury and what cancer cells exploit.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Distant metastases from one patient shared every driver mutation with the primary tumor yet had lost the silencing mark H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 across huge stretches of the genome, coupled to a new dependence on a branch of glucose metabolism. Three separate interventions on that metabolism reversed the chromatin change. Chromatin-remodeling genes are also mutated in about four in ten tumors, the classical-to-basal switch is an epigenetic change, and some mismatch-repair loss arises from gene silencing rather than mutation.
section2.full: Patients with regional, peritoneal disease showed uniform H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 staining above 80 percent across all tumor sections, whereas those with liver or lung metastases showed progressive loss during subclonal evolution, falling below 20 percent in the metastases [[GENE-008]]. The reprogramming targeted thousands of large chromatin domains, and the distant subclones had become dependent on the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway: glucose deprivation, silencing the enzyme PGD and the inhibitor 6-aminonicotinamide each reversed the chromatin state in distant subclones and not in the peritoneal one, PGD silencing disabled the distant subclones' tumor-forming capacity in 3D assays, and the reversal persisted after the drug was removed [[GENE-008]]. The lung subclone, carrying the same KRAS G12V as its peritoneal sister, had lost active (phosphorylated) ERK, the output of KRAS signaling, and responded minimally to KRAS knockdown [[GENE-008]]. Genes of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex were altered in 42 percent of 109 exome-sequenced tumors [[GENE-002]]. The classical and basal-like programs are themselves epigenetic states that organoids moved between under TGF-β or stress and that GATA6 maintains by direct regulation of its targets [[GENE-014]][[GENE-015]][[GENE-021]]. Silencing of the MLH1 promoter by methylation is a recognized sporadic cause of mismatch-repair deficiency, cited in 6 of 13 sporadic cases in an earlier series [[GENE-006]]. Even histologically normal ducts in a cancer-bearing pancreas differed from donor ducts by 192 proteins [[ORIG-025]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The metastasis finding dissolves the assumption that progression needs new mutations: a cell can gain distant-metastatic fitness and lose KRAS dependence by rewriting its chromatin, and such a change will be invisible to a DNA sequencing report [[GENE-008]]. The work rests heavily on one patient's matched subclones and on 3D culture, so it establishes a route rather than a frequency, and no oxidative pentose phosphate pathway inhibitor is a clinical therapy in pancreatic cancer as of 8 October 2026 [[GENE-008]]. A related tension is unresolved: mouse primary tumors depend on the non-oxidative branch of the same pathway while these human distant subclones depend on the oxidative branch [[GENE-012]].
research_notes.how_studied: Chromatin marks are mapped by immunostaining of tissue sections, which gives a tissue-level percentage, and by chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing, which locates the marks genome-wide and reveals the large organized domains [[GENE-008]]. Metabolic dependence is tested by removing a nutrient, silencing an enzyme with RNA interference, or applying an inhibitor, and then re-measuring the chromatin state and tumor-forming capacity in 3D assays [[GENE-008]]. Mutations in chromatin-remodeling genes are identified by exome sequencing [[GENE-002]]. State plasticity is observed in organoids profiled by RNA sequencing before and after a stimulus [[GENE-014]][[GENE-015]].

mechanism_notes.text: The classical-to-basal switch and the metastatic chromatin reprogramming are probably two views of the same property: malignant cells hold their identity through reversible chromatin states that environmental pressure, nutrient supply and stress can rewrite, so a measured state reports recent conditions as much as inheritance [[INF-GENE-03]][[GENE-008]][[GENE-014]]. If that is right, a chromatin or metabolic state measured in a biopsy would carry a date and a context, and reversing it pharmacologically would be a legitimate aim even where no mutation is targetable.

glossary.definition: DNA wound around histone proteins; its packing determines which genes a cell can read.
The spool proteins around which DNA is wound, carrying chemical tags that mark regions as active or silent.
Methyl tags on lysine 9 of histone H3 that mark tightly packed, silenced chromatin.
A chemical tag on cytosine that, at a gene's promoter, switches the gene off.
A distant regulatory DNA switch that sets how strongly a gene is expressed in a given cell type.
A branch of glucose metabolism that makes building blocks for DNA and the antioxidant NADPH.

related.statement: The classical and basal-like programs are epigenetic states, held by chromatin settings rather than mutations.
Pancreatic cancer can evolve toward metastasis by epigenetic reprogramming as well as by genetic change.
The chromatin state of distant metastatic subclones depends on glucose flowing through the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway.
Subclones that colonize the liver and lung had lost silencing chromatin marks that peritoneal subclones retained.
Methylation that silences the MLH1 gene is one way a pancreatic cancer can lose mismatch repair without a mutation.
A human lung metastasis had lost its dependence on KRAS through chromatin reprogramming while keeping the mutation.

faq.q: If my metastasis has the same mutations as the primary tumor, why does it behave differently?
faq.a: Because behavior is set by which genes are in use, not only by which are mutated. Distant metastatic subclones with identical drivers had erased silencing marks across half the genome, rewired their glucose metabolism and in one case stopped depending on KRAS [[GENE-008]].

topics.title: PanIN: microscopic precursor lesions
topics.orientation: PanIN is the microscopic lesion from which most pancreatic cancers are thought to arise. This entry explains what it is, why ordinary adult pancreases contain hundreds of them, and why finding a low-grade one says very little about any individual's future.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The smallest pancreatic ducts are lined by a single layer of low cuboidal cells that secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid and carry enzymes from the acinar clusters toward the main duct. A PanIN, short for pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia, is a patch of that lining, under five millimeters across, where the cells have become taller, mucus-filled and piled up. Pathologists grade it low or high by how disordered the cells and their nuclei have become.
section1.full: Low-grade PanIN keeps an orderly architecture: columnar cells with abundant mucin and nuclei still lined up at the base. High-grade PanIN, also called carcinoma in situ, shows crowded, irregular nuclei, loss of polarity and budding into the duct lumen, but the cells remain within the duct wall; invasion through the basement membrane is what defines cancer. These lesions are far more common than the cancer. A three-dimensional mapping study estimated a mean of 13 PanINs per cubic centimeter of grossly normal pancreas, extrapolating to hundreds per adult organ, and found that most arose as independent clones with distinct mutations [[ORIG-001]]. In 147 microdissected lesions, KRAS codon-12 mutations were present in 92 to 95 percent at every grade, over 99 percent of the lowest-grade lesions carried at least one driver mutation, and in the earliest lesions the mutant cells made up only a fraction of the lesion [[ORIG-002]]. Even in its earliest form a PanIN is the most inflamed structure in an otherwise normal pancreas, and the immune reaction around it is so patchy that local immune density fell by half within 40 micrometers [[ORIG-024]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Because hundreds of KRAS-mutant PanINs exist in a normal pancreas and cancer is rare, the overwhelming majority never progress. What distinguishes the few that do is not a new point mutation but chromosomal loss of the CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4 regions, found in every high-grade lesion examined. Some PanIN-like lesions beside a cancer are not its ancestors at all but normal tissue reacting to the tumor, and in mice a duct-cell origin can skip the low-grade stage entirely.
section2.full: Copy-number changes were present in all 11 high-grade PanINs profiled, averaging 2.7 gains and 4.3 losses per lesion with recurrent involvement of 9p21, 17p and 18q, the chromosome regions carrying CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4, whereas CDKN2A point mutations occurred in only 11.5 percent of low-grade lesions [[ORIG-023]][[ORIG-002]]. Proteomically, high-grade PanIN sat between low-grade PanIN and tumor, and raised p53 protein appeared only from the high-grade stage [[ORIG-025]]. In mice the brake is senescence: adult acinar cells carrying mutant Kras, even with p16 or Trp53 (the mouse TP53) removed, produced no lesions in a year unless episodic pancreatitis released them [[ORIG-014]], although in a different model mutant Kras alone in adult acinar cells produced low-grade lesions by two months and high-grade by twelve without any injury [[ORIG-021]]. When Kras and Trp53 loss were targeted to duct cells, mice developed only high-grade lesions and reached cancer sooner, with no low-grade stage [[ORIG-013]]. Lineage tracing also showed that an established tumor induces PanIN-like lesions in genetically normal neighboring tissue, so lesion counts from resection specimens include bystanders [[ORIG-003]]. Immune hotspots around larger PanINs carried regulatory T cells at 40 percent of T cells against 9 percent around small ones [[ORIG-024]]. The practical consequence shows in surveillance: five of eight cyst resections in one program and seven of seventeen operations in another found only low-grade dysplasia [[ORIG-015]][[ORIG-005]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The headline prevalence figures rest on an abstract and on resection specimens from pancreases that mostly contained a cancer, a sampling frame that both the bystander finding and the field-effect finding (that even normal-looking ducts in a cancer-bearing pancreas are altered) show is biased; no study of organ donors is among the sources cited here, so true prevalence in cancer-free pancreases is not directly measured [[ORIG-001]][[ORIG-003]][[ORIG-025]]. All three progression studies are cross-sectional, so whether copy-number loss, immune hotspots or field change cause progression or follow it cannot be settled from them [[ORIG-023]][[ORIG-024]]. The firm conclusion is negative and useful: a low-grade PanIN carries almost no information about an individual's fate, which is why surveillance programs remove some that prove harmless [[ORIG-015]].
research_notes.how_studied: PanINs are identified on stained sections and microdissected for sequencing, which is how mutation frequencies by grade are obtained [[ORIG-002]]; array-based copy-number profiling of the same lesions reveals chromosomal losses that sequencing panels miss [[ORIG-023]]. Serial-section three-dimensional reconstruction counts lesions per volume and maps immune cells around each one, revealing heterogeneity that two-dimensional slides average away [[ORIG-001]][[ORIG-024]]. Lineage tracing in mice tags acinar or duct cells with a fluorescent protein so that each lesion's cell of origin can be read, and chimeric embryos distinguish tumor-derived from host-derived lesions [[ORIG-003]].

mechanism_notes.text: Focal inflammation may be the gate: a hotspot of immune activity could release a senescent KRAS-mutant PanIN into division, and continued division in a lesion that has lost checkpoint restraint is what allows the chromosomal losses at CDKN2A, TP53 and SMAD4 to arise and be selected [[INF-ORIG-01]][[ORIG-024]][[ORIG-014]][[ORIG-023]]. The extreme patchiness of inflammation would then explain why only a few lesions in a field of hundreds progress. The competing account is cell-intrinsic chance, with the hotspot recruited by a lesion that has already advanced.

glossary.definition: Pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia, a microscopic precursor lesion in a small duct that can, rarely, progress to cancer.
Mildly disordered but orderly-looking precursor cells that are extremely common and rarely progress.
Severely disordered precursor cells still confined to the duct, also called carcinoma in situ.
Cancer-like cells that have not yet broken through the duct wall into surrounding tissue.
A PanIN-like change in normal tissue induced by a nearby tumor rather than being its ancestor.
A group of cells descended from a single ancestor that share its mutations.

related.statement: A KRAS mutation is present in over 90 percent of PanINs at every grade, making it the earliest change in the sequence.
Loss of the CDKN2A chromosome region marks the transition from low-grade to high-grade PanIN.
In mice the classic PanIN sequence arises from acinar cells, while a duct-cell origin can skip the low-grade stage.
PanIN is the microscopic precursor; IPMN and MCN are the larger cystic precursors visible on imaging.
A PanIN is an altered patch of the epithelium lining the smallest pancreatic ducts.
The chromosomal losses that complete a pancreatic cancer are already present in high-grade PanIN.
Surveillance of high-risk people sometimes removes PanIN that proves to be only low-grade.

faq.q: My pathology report mentions PanIN next to the tumor. Does that mean the cancer will come back?
faq.a: No. PanINs are present by the hundreds in ordinary adult pancreases, nearly all carry KRAS mutations and almost none progress, and some lesions beside a tumor are normal tissue reacting to it rather than precursors [[ORIG-001]][[ORIG-002]][[ORIG-003]]. Recurrence risk is judged from stage, nodes and margins, not from nearby PanIN.

faq.q: Can PanIN be seen on a scan?
faq.a: No; the lesions are under five millimeters and detected only under the microscope. What surveillance imaging can see are cysts and solid lesions, and when such findings are removed the pathology sometimes shows only low-grade PanIN or cyst dysplasia [[ORIG-015]][[ORIG-005]].

topics.title: Cysts: IPMN and MCN
topics.orientation: Pancreatic cysts are common incidental findings, and two kinds, IPMN and MCN, are precursors that can occasionally become cancer. This entry explains what they are, how slowly most observed cysts progress, and why the pancreas around a cyst can matter as much as the cyst itself.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The pancreatic duct system is a branching tree lined by cells that normally secrete watery, bicarbonate-rich fluid. An intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm, IPMN, is a growth of this lining that switches to producing thick mucin, forms finger-like fronds and dilates the duct it occupies, either the main duct or a side branch. A mucinous cystic neoplasm, MCN, is a mucin-filled cyst that does not connect to the duct and has a distinctive ovarian-type tissue in its wall.
section1.full: Main-duct IPMN dilates the central duct, which is why it can present with pancreatitis or enzyme problems, while branch-duct IPMN appears as one or more grape-like cysts off a side branch and is the kind most often found by chance on scans done for other reasons. Both carry a lining that is graded, like PanIN, from low-grade to high-grade dysplasia, and the lining comes in several epithelial subtypes, gastric, intestinal, pancreatobiliary and oncocytic, that behave differently if an invasive cancer ever develops [[ORIG-017]]. The dilated duct and the mucin it contains are what imaging detects, so IPMN is the one precursor in this disease that can be followed over time [[ORIG-018]]. MCN arises almost exclusively in women, usually in the body or tail of the gland, and its wall of ovarian-type stroma is the feature that defines it under the microscope; it does not communicate with the duct system. Both lesions are considered neoplastic, meaning clonal growths rather than reactive changes, but a cyst being neoplastic does not mean it is on its way to cancer, and the measured rates below should be read with that in mind. The sources cited here contain no study of the natural history or genetics of MCN, so the numbers that follow concern IPMN.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Observed branch-duct IPMNs progress slowly: among 53 with small mural nodules followed for a mean of 42 months, none produced an IPMN-derived cancer, although about 2 percent of patients developed a separate cancer elsewhere in the gland. When invasive cancer does arise within an IPMN it carries a markedly better outlook than ordinary pancreatic cancer, stage for stage. Surveillance programs nonetheless remove cysts that prove to contain only low-grade change, and the sequence from cyst to cancer is neither universal nor linear.
section2.full: In a ten-center Japanese registry, 12 of 53 cysts with mural nodules under 10 mm showed nodule growth, six were resected for that reason and one contained high-grade dysplasia; no IPMN-derived cancer occurred, one patient (1.9 percent) developed a separate concomitant cancer, and among 349 nodule-free patients the figures were 0.3 percent IPMN-derived and 2.0 percent separate cancer, with no cyst feature predicting the separate cancers [[ORIG-018]]. Invasive carcinoma arising in an IPMN had a median survival after resection of 58 months against 18 for conventional cancer, with the advantage persisting stage-matched, hazard ratio 0.58, and medians of 35, 95 and 132 months for tubular, colloid and oncocytic histology respectively [[ORIG-017]]. In the US CAPS5 surveillance program, eight patients had resections for concerning cysts, three with high-grade dysplasia and five with only low-grade [[ORIG-015]]. In the Dutch program, three of four symptomatic interval cancers arose in people whose last visit had shown presumed-unchanged multifocal branch-duct IPMN, and of 11 people operated on without cancer being found, 64 percent developed exocrine insufficiency (loss of digestive-enzyme output needing enzyme replacement) [[ORIG-005]]. In that cohort a cyst mattered for cancer risk only with a solid component or mural nodule or growth over 5 mm per year, while MRI detected cystic lesions better and endoscopic ultrasound detected solid lesions better [[ORIG-005]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The registry data invert the usual emphasis: in guideline-selected low-risk branch-duct IPMN, the pancreas developed a separate cancer more often than the watched cyst became one, which localizes risk to the organ rather than the lesion and also explains how an interval cancer can appear in someone whose cyst looked stable [[ORIG-018]][[ORIG-005]]. Part of the favorable survival of surveillance-detected cancers reflects the better biology of IPMN-derived tumors rather than earlier detection alone [[ORIG-017]]. Follow-up of about three and a half years is short against the natural history of these lesions, and the harms of resection, exocrine insufficiency in nearly two-thirds, are not trivial [[ORIG-018]][[ORIG-005]].
research_notes.how_studied: IPMN natural history is measured in registries where patients with low-risk features are followed with MRI, CT or endoscopic ultrasound at intervals set by each institution, recording nodule height, cyst size and main-duct diameter, and recording whether any cancer arose inside the cyst or elsewhere [[ORIG-018]]. Outcome comparisons between IPMN-derived and conventional cancer use resection series with stage-matched multivariable models [[ORIG-017]]. Surveillance cohorts report what each resection contained, which is how the rate of operations for low-grade change is known [[ORIG-015]][[ORIG-005]]. No primary study of MCN is among the sources cited here.

mechanism_notes.text: An IPMN may be a visible marker of an organ-wide field state, chronic low-grade injury with duct obstruction and stromal remodeling, that raises the transformation probability of every independent clone across the gland, which would explain why no cyst feature predicted the separate concomitant cancers [[INF-ORIG-02]][[ORIG-018]][[ORIG-025]]. The competing reading is that the field differences are a consequence of a tumor already present, in which case they carry no predictive value.

glossary.definition: Intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm, a mucin-producing growth within a pancreatic duct that dilates it into a cyst.
Mucinous cystic neoplasm, a mucin-filled cyst with ovarian-type wall tissue, usually in the body or tail and almost always in women.
An IPMN in a side branch of the duct system, the kind most often found incidentally and most often observed rather than removed.
A solid lump on the inner wall of a cyst, a feature that raises concern on imaging.
A pancreatic cancer that arises elsewhere in the gland, separate from the cyst being watched.
A mucin-rich type of invasive cancer arising from IPMN with a comparatively favorable course.

related.statement: IPMN and MCN are the larger cystic precursors, while PanIN is the microscopic precursor of most pancreatic cancers.
An IPMN arises from the lining of the main pancreatic duct or one of its branches and dilates it.
MRI detected cystic pancreatic lesions better than endoscopic ultrasound in a high-risk surveillance cohort.
Endoscopic ultrasound detected solid components and small solid lesions better than MRI in a surveillance cohort.
Cysts are the most frequent findings in surveillance of high-risk people and the usual reason for operations that find no cancer.
Nearly two-thirds of people who had pancreatic resections for cysts that proved benign developed exocrine insufficiency needing enzyme replacement.

faq.q: A scan found a cyst on my pancreas. Does that mean I will get cancer?
faq.a: Most observed cysts do not become cancer. Among 53 branch-duct IPMNs with small nodules followed for a mean of 42 months, none produced an IPMN-derived cancer, and the risk that mattered was a separate cancer elsewhere in the gland in about 2 percent [[ORIG-018]]. Features that raise concern are a solid component, a mural nodule, main-duct dilation or growth over 5 mm a year [[ORIG-005]].

faq.q: If my cancer arose from an IPMN, is that different from ordinary pancreatic cancer?
faq.a: Yes, in outcome: median survival after resection was 58 months for IPMN-derived cancer against 18 for conventional cancer, and the advantage held stage for stage, with colloid and oncocytic types doing best [[ORIG-017]].

topics.title: Which cell becomes the cancer cell
topics.orientation: Pancreatic cancer looks like a duct cancer under the microscope, but the cell it starts from is not settled, and in mice it can be more than one. This entry explains the two routes, why a digestive-enzyme cell can turn into a duct-like one, and why the cell of origin shapes how the cancer behaves.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: The exocrine pancreas has two main cell types. Acinar cells, the great majority, are packed with digestive enzymes and release them into tiny ducts. Duct cells line those channels and add bicarbonate-rich fluid. Acinar cells are not permanently fixed in their identity: after injury they can temporarily take on a duct-like form, a process called acinar-to-ductal metaplasia, and normally change back once the tissue heals.
section1.full: Acinar-to-ductal metaplasia is a genuine change of cell state, not just a change of shape. A damaged acinar cell switches off its enzyme-making program and switches on duct genes, which lets it survive while the tissue is repaired and then revert. The transcription factor Sox9, normally restricted to duct and centroacinar cells, is the switch: in mice, oncogenic Kras drives this reprogramming, deleting Sox9 blocks Kras-driven metaplasia and precursor formation completely, and forcing Sox9 expression induces duct genes in acinar cells and promotes lesions [[ORIG-012]]. Injury can produce metaplasia without Sox9, but those lesions do not progress [[ORIG-012]]. The reason this matters is that the flexibility built into acinar cells for repair is the same flexibility a cancer exploits: a cell that can already switch toward a duct-like state is one step closer to forming a duct-like neoplasm. Duct cells, by contrast, are already in the state the cancer resembles, so they would not need this reprogramming step. Which of these starting points a tumor takes changes the route it follows and, in mice, the markers it carries and how fast it reaches invasion [[ORIG-003]][[ORIG-013]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: In mice, both acinar and duct cells can give rise to pancreatic cancer, but by different routes. The acinar route reprograms through metaplasia into the classic low-grade-to-high-grade PanIN sequence and is held in check by senescence. The duct route largely skips the low-grade stage and reaches invasion faster. There is no single linear origin story, and proof of the cell of origin in human tumors is not yet possible.
section2.full: When oncogenic Kras was targeted to mouse acinar cells they developed low-grade PanIN-like lesions within a month and the full spectrum over time, with most lesions lineage-traced back to the acinar compartment [[ORIG-003]]. When Kras plus loss of Trp53 (the mouse TP53) was targeted to duct cells, those mice reached carcinoma in about two months, developed only high-grade lesions with no low-grade PanIN, and none of the PanIN-like lesions traced back to the duct lineage [[ORIG-003]][[ORIG-013]]; duct-derived and acinar-derived tumors reached equivalent final burden but differed in timing and in the marker AGR2 [[ORIG-003]][[ORIG-013]]. The acinar route is gated by senescence and inflammation: adult acinar cells with mutant Kras and p16 or Trp53 loss made no lesions in a year unless episodic pancreatitis released the brake [[ORIG-014]], though a separate model produced lesions from adult acinar Kras with no injury, so the requirement is a threshold rather than an absolute [[ORIG-021]]. Lineage tracing also showed that some PanIN-like lesions beside a tumor are genetically normal host tissue reacting to the cancer, not its ancestors [[ORIG-003]]. The human arm of these studies is marker correlation only, and the authors state that proof of cellular origin in human pancreatic cancer is not yet possible [[ORIG-003]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Two independent laboratories agree that a duct-cell origin can bypass the low-grade PanIN stage and reach invasion faster, which offers one explanation for how an interval cancer can appear months after reassuring imaging that showed no precursor [[ORIG-003]][[ORIG-013]]. The acinar-senescence gate suggests why chronic pancreatitis is a risk factor, but the evidence that inflammation is strictly necessary is contradicted by a model in which adult acinar Kras sufficed, so the most economical reading is a dose-and-allele threshold rather than an on-off requirement [[ORIG-014]][[ORIG-021]]. All of this is mouse biology; the human data are correlative and the cell of origin of any individual tumor cannot be read from the specimen [[ORIG-003]].
research_notes.how_studied: The method is genetic lineage tracing: a cell-type-specific switch turns on a fluorescent protein in acinar or duct cells at the same time as the Kras mutation, so every lesion can be scored for whether it descended from the labeled cell [[ORIG-003]][[ORIG-013]]. Transplanting sorted labeled tumor cells and making chimeric embryos distinguishes tumor-derived lesions from host-derived bystanders [[ORIG-003]]. Deleting or over-expressing Sox9 tests whether the metaplasia switch is required [[ORIG-012]]. Inducing pancreatitis on demand with a drug such as cerulein, and timing oncogene activation to adulthood, tests the senescence gate [[ORIG-014]][[ORIG-021]].

mechanism_notes.text: The acinar route and the duct route may not be rivals but two entries into the same disease whose balance depends on genotype and injury: a strong genotype or duct origin reaches invasion through a short high-grade path, while a weaker acinar genotype runs the long PanIN sequence and is held by senescence until inflammation releases it [[INF-ORIG-01]][[ORIG-013]][[ORIG-014]][[ORIG-003]]. No experiment has yet varied cell of origin, genotype strength and inflammation together, so this reconciliation remains a hypothesis.

glossary.definition: The enzyme-making cell that forms the bulk of the exocrine pancreas.
The cell lining the pancreatic ducts, whose appearance the cancer resembles.
A reversible switch in which an acinar cell takes on a duct-like state, normally part of injury repair.
A transcription factor that drives the acinar-to-ductal switch and is required for Kras-driven precursor formation in mice.
A technique that permanently labels one cell type so its descendants, including any tumor, can be identified.
The normal cell type from which a cancer first arose.

related.statement: Acinar cells can reprogram into a duct-like state and are the origin of the classic PanIN sequence in mice.
Duct cells can give rise to pancreatic cancer by a route that largely skips low-grade PanIN.
Acinar-to-ductal metaplasia is the first step of the acinar route that leads into the PanIN sequence.
Oncogenic KRAS is the change that drives acinar-to-ductal metaplasia and starts both routes to cancer.
Chronic pancreatitis may raise risk by releasing the senescence brake that holds acinar-route lesions in check.
The cell of origin shapes the markers and behavior a tumor carries, echoing the classical and basal-like states.

faq.q: Does it matter which cell my cancer came from?
faq.a: In mice it changes the route and speed to invasion and the markers the tumor carries, but it cannot be determined for an individual human tumor, and the researchers themselves say proof of cell of origin in human pancreatic cancer is not yet possible [[ORIG-003]][[ORIG-013]].

faq.q: Does every pancreatic cancer go through the PanIN sequence?
faq.a: No. The acinar route runs through the classic low-grade-to-high-grade PanIN sequence, but in mice a duct-cell origin reaches cancer largely without a low-grade stage, so there is no single linear origin story [[ORIG-003]][[ORIG-013]].

topics.title: Risk factors
topics.orientation: People reasonably ask what caused their pancreatic cancer. This entry lays out the measured risk factors and their sizes, distinguishes a cause from a consequence, and is honest that for most individuals no single factor explains the disease.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: A risk factor is anything that raises the average chance of a disease across a population; it is not a cause in any single person, and most people with a risk factor never develop the cancer. The factors below act on the same biology described elsewhere in this section: they add DNA damage, sustain inflammation, or change the metabolic environment in which a KRAS-mutant cell sits, nudging the long odds against progression slightly less long.
section1.full: Relative risk is the ratio of a disease's rate in people with a factor to its rate in people without; an odds ratio approximates it. Because pancreatic cancer is uncommon, even a doubling of relative risk leaves the absolute lifetime chance of most exposed people low, which is why no common risk factor justifies screening the general public. The factors cluster into a few mechanisms. Tobacco smoke delivers carcinogens that damage DNA directly. Excess body fat and heavy alcohol use sustain low-grade inflammation and metabolic stress. Chronic inflammation of the pancreas, from any cause, can release the senescence brake that holds early lesions in check, which is the mechanism worked out in mice [[ORIG-014]]. Common inherited variation, such as at the ABO blood-group locus, shifts risk by amounts far too small to matter for an individual. Set against these is a relationship that runs the other way: when pancreatic cancer follows new-onset diabetes after middle age, the diabetes is often an early effect of the occult cancer rather than a cause of it, and reading it as a cause would be a mistake. Inherited high-risk syndromes are covered separately in the entries on inherited risk and specific genes.

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: The best-measured modifiable factors are tobacco, which roughly doubles risk, and excess weight and alcohol, which each add smaller amounts. When pancreatic cancer is found soon after new-onset diabetes in someone over 50, the diabetes was usually caused by the cancer, not the reverse; new diabetes on its own is rarely a sign of cancer. Inherited variants in a handful of genes are found in about one patient in eighteen, usually without a family history. For most people the honest answer is that no single factor accounts for the disease.
section2.full: Pooled case-control data put current smoking at an odds ratio of 2.20 against never-smokers, rising to about 3.4 at 35 or more cigarettes a day, with former smokers carrying only a small residual excess [[ORIG-010]]. Highest-versus-lowest body-mass-index quartile gave an odds ratio of 1.33, with central adiposity adding more [[ORIG-008]], and alcohol raised risk by about 3 percent per 10 grams per day, becoming apparent above roughly 15 grams a day in women and 30 in men, independently of smoking and with no excess for wine [[ORIG-020]]. New-onset diabetes is the clearest cause-versus-consequence trap: about 0.85 percent of people over 50 who met diabetes criteria were diagnosed with pancreatic cancer within three years, an observed-to-expected ratio of 7.94 (nearly eight times the rate expected in the general population), but over half of those cancers appeared within six months, so the diabetes was usually the cancer's effect [[ORIG-009]]. Inherited variants in CDKN2A, BRCA2, ATM, TP53, MLH1 or BRCA1 were present in 5.5 percent of 3,030 patients, most of whom had no family history [[ORIG-006]]. The ABO blood-group variant shifts risk with an odds ratio near 1.2, far too small to be useful individually [[ORIG-007]]. Carrying certain gum-disease bacteria was associated with higher risk and one bacterial group with lower risk, an association only [[ORIG-011]]. US incidence under age 50 has risen, faster in women, but remains under 10 percent of cases [[ORIG-019]]. The US Preventive Services Task Force recommends against screening average-risk adults, a Grade D recommendation dated 6 August 2019 [[SEC-ORIG-01]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: These are population averages and do not explain any single person's cancer; a doubling of a small risk is still a small risk, which is why the US Preventive Services Task Force recommends against screening average-risk adults even when they smoke, are overweight or have diabetes [[SEC-ORIG-01]][[ORIG-009]]. The new-onset-diabetes finding is the one most often misread: the large relative risk is real, but because most of those cancers surface within six months the diabetes is the alarm, not the arsonist [[ORIG-009]]. Several associations, the oral bacteria and the ABO variant among them, are associations only, with no established mechanism or individual predictive value [[ORIG-011]][[ORIG-007]].
research_notes.how_studied: Modifiable factors are measured in pooled case-control consortia and large prospective cohorts that compare exposure between people who did and did not develop the cancer, adjusting for confounders such as smoking; dose-response gradients strengthen a causal reading [[ORIG-010]][[ORIG-008]][[ORIG-020]]. The diabetes relationship was studied by following a community cohort from the date they met diabetes criteria and counting cancers by interval, which is how the clustering within six months was seen [[ORIG-009]]. Germline prevalence comes from sequencing thousands of patients against reference databases [[ORIG-006]], and common-variant risk from genome-wide association studies [[ORIG-007]].

mechanism_notes.text: Chronic inflammation may be the common thread linking several environmental risk factors to the cancer, because in mice episodic pancreatitis released the oncogene-induced senescence that otherwise held KRAS-mutant lesions dormant, and an anti-inflammatory drug reduced lesion development [[INF-ORIG-01]][[ORIG-014]]. The human evidence for anti-inflammatory prevention is a nine-patient staining comparison, and no such agent is approved or recommended in the US for pancreatic cancer prevention [[ORIG-014]].

glossary.definition: Something that raises the average chance of a disease across a population without causing it in any one person.
How many times more common a disease is in people with a factor than in people without it.
A measure that approximates relative risk, comparing the odds of exposure in people with and without the disease.
Diabetes appearing for the first time, which after middle age can be an early sign of an occult pancreatic cancer.
