Long-standing inflammation of the pancreas, which can raise cancer risk by sustaining tissue damage.
A US Preventive Services Task Force rating that a service should not be offered because harms outweigh benefits.

related.statement: In people who develop pancreatic cancer, new-onset diabetes after middle age is more often an early effect of pancreatic cancer than a cause of it.
Inherited gene variants are a distinct category of risk, covered in the entry on inherited risk and family surveillance.
Chronic inflammation may raise risk by releasing the senescence brake on acinar-route precursor lesions.
Risk factors act on the long odds that one of the many KRAS-mutant PanINs in a pancreas will progress.
These risk factors modestly raise the chance of developing the pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma this atlas describes.
The recommendation against screening average-risk adults does not apply to people at high inherited risk.

faq.q: I did not smoke and I am not overweight. Why did I get this?
faq.a: For most people no single factor explains the disease. The measured risk factors are modest, a doubling at most for the strongest, and inherited variants are found in only about 5.5 percent of patients, most without any family history, so a cancer with no identifiable cause is the common situation [[ORIG-010]][[ORIG-006]].

faq.q: I was recently diagnosed with diabetes and then cancer. Did the diabetes cause it?
faq.a: Most likely the other way round. About 1 percent of people over 50 with new-onset diabetes are found to have pancreatic cancer within three years, but more than half of those cancers appear within six months, meaning the tumor caused the diabetes [[ORIG-009]].

faq.q: Should I be screened because I have these risk factors?
faq.a: No, if you are at average risk. The US Preventive Services Task Force recommends against screening asymptomatic average-risk adults, and specifically notes that diabetes, older age, smoking and obesity raise risk only modestly, leaving such people within the recommendation against screening [[SEC-ORIG-01]].

topics.title: Inherited risk and family surveillance
topics.orientation: A minority of pancreatic cancers occur in people who inherited a risk gene or come from a family with several cases. This entry explains how much such risk raises the odds, who is offered imaging surveillance, and why surveillance of high-risk people is a different question from screening the public.

section1.label: What this means
section1.preview: Everyone inherits two copies of each gene, one from each parent. The genes that matter here normally protect against cancer by repairing DNA or restraining cell growth. Inheriting one faulty copy does not cause cancer by itself, but it means every cell starts one step closer to losing that protection, so the lifetime odds rise. How much they rise depends on which gene is affected, and the absolute risk stays below certainty even for the strongest.
section1.full: A germline variant is present in every cell from birth, unlike the mutations a tumor acquires. For a tumor-suppressor gene, one inherited faulty copy usually has little effect until the second, working copy is lost in a single cell during life, a two-step process that explains why carriers develop cancer at higher rates and often younger, but not inevitably. The genes implicated in pancreatic risk fall into familiar groups: DNA double-strand-break repair (BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, ATM), the cell-cycle brake (CDKN2A), the damage checkpoint (TP53), and mismatch repair (the Lynch-syndrome genes MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2). A separate category is familial pancreatic cancer, defined by two or more affected first-degree relatives, where no causative gene is identified in most families but the clustering itself raises risk. Importantly, most carriers identified in unselected patient series had no family history of pancreatic cancer, so family history and gene status are overlapping but not interchangeable ways of defining risk [[ORIG-006]]. The size of the inherited contribution is modest at the population level: variants in the main risk genes were found in 5.5 percent of all patients [[ORIG-006]].

section2.label: In pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Specific inherited variants raise risk by amounts ranging from roughly two-fold to twelve-fold, and absolute lifetime risk is genotype-specific. People who meet high-risk criteria, generally an estimated lifetime risk around 5 percent or higher, are offered imaging surveillance with MRI and endoscopic ultrasound. That is guideline-recommended for high-risk groups, whereas the US Preventive Services Task Force recommends against screening average-risk adults. Surveillance shifts stage but its mortality benefit is inferred, not proven, and lead-time bias, the apparent gain in survival that comes simply from diagnosing earlier, must be kept in mind.
section2.full: In 3,030 patients, six genes were significantly associated with the disease, with odds ratios from 2.58 for BRCA1 to 12.33 for CDKN2A, and together present in 5.5 percent [[ORIG-006]]. Absolute risk varies by genotype: Lynch-syndrome families carried roughly a 4 percent cumulative risk by age 70, which sits below the threshold normally used to justify imaging, so Lynch alone is not a standard surveillance indication [[ORIG-022]]. Surveillance results diverge sharply between programs using the same two modalities. A US program detected 77.8 percent of screen-detected cancers at stage I with 73.3 percent five-year survival and a hazard ratio of 0.13 against cancers found outside surveillance [[ORIG-015]], while a Dutch program found only 30 percent at the earliest stage, saw four of ten cancers present as symptomatic metastatic interval cancers within months of a reassuring visit, and operated on 11 people who proved not to have cancer, 64 percent of whom developed exocrine insufficiency (loss of digestive-enzyme output) [[ORIG-005]]. Over 16 years another US cohort found a 7 percent progression rate, 1.6 percent per year, with 9 of 10 surveillance-detected cancers resectable [[ORIG-004]]. Both sets of authors concede lead-time bias, and no randomized trial of surveillance exists. Within a single high-penetrance genotype, CDKN2A, family history and smoking predicted who progressed only weakly, a model discriminating no better than chance after validation [[ORIG-016]]. The contrast with the public is set by the Task Force Grade D recommendation against screening average-risk adults, dated 6 August 2019 [[SEC-ORIG-01]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Surveillance of high-risk people demonstrably shifts stage and demonstrably causes some non-therapeutic surgery; a mortality benefit is inferred from non-randomized comparisons rather than proven, and the component least vulnerable to that criticism is resecting high-grade dysplasia before invasion [[ORIG-015]][[ORIG-005]][[ORIG-004]]. Lead-time bias, the apparent lengthening of survival simply from diagnosing earlier, plausibly runs to years in these cohorts, the same order as the survival differences claimed, which is why the programs disagree [[ORIG-015]]. The divergence is most likely case mix, especially the proportion of aggressive CDKN2A carriers, but that cannot be confirmed because within-genotype models do not discriminate [[ORIG-016]].
research_notes.how_studied: Germline risk is estimated by sequencing panels in thousands of patients and comparing variant frequencies with population databases, yielding odds ratios, and by following gene-defined families to estimate absolute risk by age [[ORIG-006]][[ORIG-022]]. Surveillance is studied in prospective cohorts of high-risk people imaged at intervals with MRI and endoscopic ultrasound, reporting stage at detection, interval cancers, operations performed and their pathology, and survival from diagnosis; none has a randomized unscreened comparator, so survival-from-diagnosis cannot separate real benefit from lead time [[ORIG-015]][[ORIG-005]][[ORIG-004]].

mechanism_notes.text: The headline survival figure of a surveillance program sums at least three things: genuine stage shift with averted death, lead-time and length-time bias (earlier diagnosis, and the preferential catching of slower-growing tumors) that lengthen measured survival without moving the date of death, and a case mix enriched for the less lethal cystic and IPMN-derived cancers that surveillance preferentially catches [[INF-ORIG-03]][[ORIG-015]][[ORIG-017]]. Separating them needs cumulative-mortality rather than survival-from-diagnosis analysis, which no study provides. Resection of high-grade dysplasia before invasion is the one component not subject to lead-time bias.

topics.clinical_status: Imaging surveillance (MRI and endoscopic ultrasound) is guideline-recommended for individuals at high inherited risk (generally about 5 percent or higher estimated lifetime risk); the US Preventive Services Task Force recommends against screening average-risk adults (Grade D, 6 August 2019). Checked 2026-10-08.

glossary.definition: A gene change inherited from a parent and present in every cell, as distinct from one the tumor acquires.
A family with two or more first-degree relatives affected, often with no identified causative gene.
Regular imaging of people at high risk to find cancer early, distinct from screening the general public.
A cancer that appears, often advanced, between scheduled surveillance visits.
The apparent lengthening of survival that comes simply from diagnosing a cancer earlier, without delaying death.
The proportion of people carrying a risk variant who actually develop the associated cancer.

related.statement: Inherited risk is a distinct category from the modifiable risk factors such as smoking and obesity.
BRCA1, BRCA2 and PALB2 are among the inherited genes that raise pancreatic cancer risk and also change treatment.
An inherited CDKN2A variant carries the highest single-gene odds ratio and defines a high-risk group for surveillance.
The Lynch-syndrome mismatch-repair genes raise pancreatic risk modestly, to about 4 percent by age 70.
Endoscopic ultrasound is one of the two imaging methods used to survey people at high inherited risk.
MRI is the other main imaging method used for surveillance of high-risk individuals.
Germline testing of a patient identifies inherited variants that have implications for relatives as well as treatment.

faq.q: My relative had pancreatic cancer. Should I be scanned?
faq.a: It depends on how strong the inherited risk is. Surveillance with MRI and endoscopic ultrasound is recommended for people whose estimated lifetime risk is around 5 percent or higher, typically from a known high-risk gene or multiple affected close relatives, but the Task Force recommends against screening average-risk adults [[SEC-ORIG-01]][[ORIG-015]]. A genetics evaluation is the usual first step.

faq.q: Does surveillance actually save lives?
faq.a: It reliably finds some cancers earlier and at a resectable stage, and resecting high-grade dysplasia before it becomes invasive is genuine prevention, but a mortality benefit has not been proven in a randomized trial and the programs differ sharply, partly because of lead-time bias and the mix of tumor types caught [[ORIG-015]][[ORIG-005]][[ORIG-004]].

faq.q: I have Lynch syndrome. Does that mean pancreatic surveillance?
faq.a: Not on its own. Lynch-syndrome families carried about a 4 percent cumulative risk by age 70, which is below the threshold usually used to justify imaging, so Lynch alone is not a standard surveillance indication absent additional family history [[ORIG-022]].

topics.title: BRCA1/2, PALB2 and homologous recombination deficiency
topics.orientation: BRCA1, BRCA2 and PALB2 are the core genes of accurate double-strand-break repair. When a tumor loses them it becomes sensitive to platinum chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors, which is one of the few places in pancreatic cancer where a genetic finding changes treatment. What matters is loss of function, not merely a variant on a report.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: When both strands of DNA are cut, the safest repair copies the missing information from the identical sister chromosome made during replication, a process called homologous recombination. BRCA1, PALB2 and BRCA2 work in sequence to load the repair enzyme RAD51 onto the broken ends so this templated copying can happen. Without them a cell must fall back on quicker, error-prone joining that scrambles the genome.
section1.full: The three proteins form a relay. BRCA1 helps detect the break and commits the cell to accurate repair; PALB2, as its name (partner and localizer of BRCA2) indicates, bridges BRCA1 to BRCA2; and BRCA2 delivers RAD51 onto the exposed single-stranded DNA so it can search the sister chromosome for a match. This machinery works only where a sister copy exists, which is during and just after DNA replication, so it is the system a dividing cell relies on. A cell that loses it is not defenseless but is forced onto error-prone backup pathways, and over many divisions that leaves a characteristic scar of large rearrangements across the genome, which can be measured as a score. Because the protection requires both gene copies to be working, a person who inherits one faulty copy still repairs normally until the second copy is lost in a tumor cell; this is why inherited carriers are at risk yet most of their cells are fine, and why the tumor, not the blood, is where the functional deficiency becomes complete. That same dependence on backup repair is the vulnerability drugs exploit: platinum chemotherapy makes cross-links that need homologous recombination to resolve, and PARP inhibitors block an alternative repair route so that cells lacking homologous recombination accumulate lethal breaks [[GENE-016]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: About 19 percent of advanced pancreatic cancers have a damaging alteration in a homologous-recombination gene, with the benefit of platinum chemotherapy concentrated in those that have lost both copies or that affect the core genes BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2. These tumors respond better to platinum, and after platinum, maintenance treatment with the PARP inhibitor olaparib doubles time without progression in inherited BRCA carriers. The predictive signal is functional loss, not the mere presence of a variant, which is why gene-level reports can mislead.
section2.full: Among 262 patients with advanced disease, 19 percent carried a damaging alteration in a homologous-recombination gene, 15 percent inherited and 4 percent acquired, and first-line platinum improved progression-free survival only in that group, hazard ratio 0.44, with no such benefit from non-platinum therapy; the benefit concentrated in the 11 percent with biallelic loss and the 12 percent with core-gene alterations, and germline (inherited) and somatic (tumor-acquired) origin behaved identically [[GENE-016]]. In the founding BRCA cohort of 71 carriers, platinum-exposed patients lived a median 22 months against 9, but this reached significance only when stages 3 and 4 were pooled [[GENE-017]]. Maintenance olaparib, approved in the US on 27 December 2019 for inherited BRCA carriers whose metastatic disease had not progressed after at least 16 weeks of platinum, doubled progression-free survival, 7.4 against 3.8 months, hazard ratio 0.53, but did not significantly extend overall survival, 19.0 against 19.2 months, although three-year survival was 34 against 18 percent [[TX-005]][[TX-L24]][[SEC-TX-03]]. Maintenance rucaparib, not approved for this disease, produced responses in germline PALB2 and somatic BRCA2 carriers as well [[TX-017]]. The warning sign for over-reading gene lists comes from the adjuvant setting: in a randomized trial of 317 resected tumors, repair-gene and BRCA status did not predict benefit from modified FOLFIRINOX, interaction P=0.568 and 0.785, whereas KRAS status did [[GENE-024]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The evidence most strongly supports biallelic loss of a core homologous-recombination gene as the predictive marker; gene-level annotation pools true deficiency with carriers whose tumors still repair, which is the simplest explanation for why repair-gene status predicted platinum benefit in advanced disease but not adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX benefit in a randomized cohort [[GENE-016]][[GENE-024]]. The olaparib result is honest about its limits: a doubling of progression-free time and a better three-year tail without a significant overall-survival difference, plausibly because placebo patients crossed to effective later therapy [[TX-005]][[TX-L24]]. The approval is germline-only, although somatic and germline deficiency behaved alike in the biology [[SEC-TX-03]][[GENE-016]].
research_notes.how_studied: Germline status is tested from blood or saliva, somatic status from the tumor; distinguishing one working copy from none requires allele-specific copy-number analysis, performed in the key study with a tool called FACETS, because biallelic status is what tracks instability and benefit [[GENE-016]]. The genomic scar of failed repair is quantified as large-scale state transitions or mutational signature 3, both difficult to read on small panels in a cancer with few mutations [[GENE-016]]. Treatment effect is measured in a randomized maintenance trial, progression-free survival as the primary endpoint and overall survival as a secondary one [[TX-005]][[TX-L24]].

mechanism_notes.text: The variable that predicts platinum and PARP-inhibitor benefit is probably biallelic loss of homologous-recombination function rather than a variant in any listed gene, since biallelic tumors carried higher instability scores than monoallelic ones and, in a separate trial, every durable PARP-inhibitor responder had biallelic loss [[INF-GENE-02]][[GENE-016]][[GENE-025]]. The competing reading is that the deficiency mainly marks more indolent, chemosensitive disease, which would make the randomized adjuvant result the more trustworthy estimate [[GENE-024]].

topics.clinical_status: Maintenance olaparib is FDA-approved (US, 27 December 2019) for germline BRCA1/2-mutated metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma without progression after at least 16 weeks of first-line platinum, with a required companion diagnostic; rucaparib and niraparib are not approved for this disease. Checked 2026-10-08.

glossary.definition: The accurate repair of a double-strand break using the matching sister copy of the chromosome as a template.
A core repair gene that loads the RAD51 enzyme onto broken DNA; its loss sensitizes a tumor to platinum and PARP inhibitors.
A core repair gene that bridges BRCA1 and BRCA2 in the double-strand-break repair relay.
Homologous recombination deficiency, the functional loss of accurate double-strand-break repair.
A drug that blocks a backup DNA-repair route, killing cells that already lack homologous recombination.
Treatment given to hold disease in check after initial chemotherapy has controlled it.

related.statement: BRCA1, BRCA2 and PALB2 are the core machinery of the homologous-recombination repair system.
ATM and other non-core repair genes are listed alongside BRCA but do not reliably confer the same drug sensitivity.
Maintenance olaparib is approved for inherited BRCA carriers whose metastatic disease has not progressed after platinum.
Inherited BRCA and PALB2 variants raise pancreatic cancer risk and are identified by germline testing.
Distinguishing loss of one gene copy from loss of both requires allele-specific analysis beyond a standard mutation report.
The platinum drug oxaliplatin in FOLFIRINOX is the chemotherapy that homologous-recombination-deficient tumors respond to best.

faq.q: My report lists a BRCA2 mutation. Does that mean olaparib will work for me?
faq.a: It makes you a candidate under the right conditions. Olaparib is approved in the US as maintenance for inherited BRCA carriers whose metastatic disease has not progressed after at least 16 weeks of platinum chemotherapy, where it doubled time without progression though it did not significantly extend overall survival [[TX-005]][[TX-L24]][[SEC-TX-03]]. The benefit is greatest when both gene copies are lost in the tumor [[GENE-016]].

faq.q: Does it matter whether the BRCA mutation is inherited or in the tumor only?
faq.a: For the biology, no: germline and somatic homologous-recombination deficiency behaved identically for instability and platinum benefit [[GENE-016]]. For the approved drug, yes: the olaparib pancreatic indication is restricted to germline BRCA carriers [[SEC-TX-03]].

faq.q: Why did my doctor say the repair-gene finding would not change my post-surgery chemotherapy?
faq.a: Because in a randomized trial of resected tumors, repair-gene and BRCA status did not predict benefit from modified FOLFIRINOX, whereas KRAS status did; the platinum benefit is established in advanced disease, not the adjuvant setting [[GENE-024]][[GENE-016]].

topics.title: ATM and other repair genes that are not BRCA
topics.orientation: Many sequencing reports list a variant in ATM, CHEK2 or another repair gene that is not BRCA. These findings do not behave like a BRCA mutation, and treating them as equivalent is a common error. This entry explains what these genes do and why a single-copy variant in one of them is weak evidence for a targeted drug.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: ATM is the alarm kinase for a double-strand break: it senses the broken DNA and phosphorylates a cascade of targets, including CHEK2 and p53, that halt the cell cycle and mobilize repair. ATM and CHEK2 are therefore signaling and checkpoint genes rather than the repair enzymes themselves. The dozen or so other genes on a homologous-recombination panel play supporting roles distinct from the core BRCA1, BRCA2 and PALB2.
section1.full: When a double-strand break forms, ATM is recruited to the break within minutes and triggers two responses at once: it stops the cell dividing, by activating CHEK2 and p53 so the cycle arrests, and it marks the surrounding chromatin to recruit repair factors. It does not itself copy DNA from the sister chromosome; that is the job of the BRCA-PALB2-RAD51 core. This division of labor is why losing ATM is not the same as losing BRCA2. A cell without ATM has a weaker alarm and checkpoint but may retain much of its accurate repair capacity, so it does not develop the deep dependence on backup pathways that makes a BRCA-deficient cell vulnerable to platinum and PARP inhibitors. The wider panel of non-core genes, which includes CHEK2, BARD1, BRIP1, RAD50, RAD51C, NBN and others, spans sensing, signaling and accessory functions, and their individual contributions to repair, and to drug sensitivity, differ and are mostly weaker than the core genes. As with BRCA, the protection generally requires both copies of a gene, so whether one or both copies are lost in the tumor matters more than the gene's name on a report [[GENE-016]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: ATM is one of the commonest inherited risk genes in pancreatic cancer, but a single-copy ATM variant does not predict response to PARP inhibitors (drugs that exploit faulty DNA repair) the way a BRCA mutation does. In a trial that enrolled by gene name, median benefit was brief, yet the few patients who did well had all lost both copies of a repair gene, including some with biallelic ATM loss. Function, specifically loss of both copies, carries the signal that a gene label alone does not.
section2.full: Inherited ATM variants were the single commonest finding in a 3,030-patient germline study, 2.28 percent, with an odds ratio of 5.71, ahead of BRCA2 at 1.95 percent [[ORIG-006]]. But in a phase 2 trial of the PARP inhibitor niraparib that enrolled patients across BRCA1/2, PALB2, ATM and CHEK2, median progression-free survival was only 2.0 months and the objective response rate 14 percent; the striking finding was that all six patients with six months or more of benefit and assessable tumors had biallelic inactivation of a repair gene, including three with biallelic ATM loss who stayed on treatment beyond a year [[GENE-025]]. This fits the core-versus-non-core and monoallelic-versus-biallelic (one-copy versus both-copy) hierarchy from the larger homologous-recombination study, in which biallelic lesions carried higher instability scores than monoallelic ones and core-gene alterations tracked platinum benefit [[GENE-016]]. The non-core genes therefore do not license the same treatment inferences as BRCA: a monoallelic ATM finding should not be presented as equivalent to a biallelic BRCA2 loss. Consistent with that, repair-gene status including these genes did not predict adjuvant modified FOLFIRINOX benefit in a randomized cohort [[GENE-024]]. Niraparib is not approved in the US for pancreatic cancer [[GENE-025]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The practical content is a caution: an ATM or CHEK2 variant on a report is a risk gene and a reason for family counseling, but it is weak evidence for a PARP inhibitor unless the tumor has lost both copies [[ORIG-006]][[GENE-025]]. The biallelic-ATM signal that did show durable benefit rests on just three patients in a single-arm trial, so it is a lead worth pursuing, not an established indication [[GENE-025]]. The larger lesson, shared with the BRCA entry, is that the reportable unit should be allelic status rather than gene name, since gene-level pooling is the most economical explanation for the weak and setting-dependent predictive value [[GENE-016]][[GENE-024]].
research_notes.how_studied: Trials such as the niraparib study enroll by gene label, then analyze zygosity afterward, which is how the association of benefit with biallelic loss emerged from an otherwise modest overall result [[GENE-025]]. Distinguishing loss of one copy from both requires allele-specific copy-number analysis of the tumor, not just a mutation report [[GENE-016]]. Germline prevalence and risk come from sequencing thousands of patients against population references [[ORIG-006]]. The adjuvant analysis nested gene testing within a randomized trial, the strongest design for separating a predictive from a prognostic marker [[GENE-024]].

mechanism_notes.text: ATM and other non-core findings probably confer drug sensitivity only when both copies are lost, because the durable responders in a gene-labeled trial were uniformly biallelic and biallelic lesions carried the higher instability scores [[INF-GENE-02]][[GENE-025]][[GENE-016]]. If so, a report should state allelic status, and a monoallelic non-core variant should not be read as a BRCA-equivalent. The competing possibility is that these genes are mainly risk markers with little treatment meaning in pancreatic cancer.

topics.clinical_status: No PARP inhibitor is FDA-approved for ATM- or CHEK2-associated pancreatic cancer; niraparib remains investigational for this disease. Checked 2026-10-08.

glossary.definition: The alarm kinase that senses a double-strand break and triggers cell-cycle arrest and repair, distinct from the repair enzymes themselves.
A checkpoint kinase activated by ATM that helps halt the cell cycle after DNA damage.
A homologous-recombination-related gene other than BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2, generally conferring weaker drug sensitivity.
Loss of both copies of a gene in the tumor, which is what tracks drug sensitivity for these genes.
The loss of the second, working copy of a gene in a cell that started with one faulty copy.
Whether one or both copies of a gene are affected in a cell.

related.statement: ATM and CHEK2 are listed with BRCA and PALB2 on repair panels but do not reliably confer the same drug sensitivity.
ATM is the damage-sensing kinase of the double-strand-break checkpoint rather than a repair enzyme.
Inherited ATM variants are among the commonest pancreatic cancer risk findings and a reason for family counseling.
Whether both copies of ATM are lost, which is what matters for treatment, requires allele-specific analysis beyond a mutation report.
The approved PARP inhibitor is restricted to germline BRCA carriers and does not cover ATM findings.
ATM signals a double-strand break partly through p53, the checkpoint protein mutated in most pancreatic cancers.

faq.q: My report shows an ATM mutation. Is that like having a BRCA mutation?
faq.a: No. ATM is a risk gene but a single-copy ATM variant does not predict PARP-inhibitor benefit the way a BRCA mutation does; in a gene-labeled trial the durable responders had all lost both copies of a repair gene [[GENE-025]][[GENE-016]]. A monoallelic ATM finding should not be treated as a BRCA-equivalent.

faq.q: Could a PARP inhibitor still help me with an ATM finding?
faq.a: Possibly, if the tumor has lost both ATM copies: three such patients stayed on niraparib beyond a year in one trial, but that rests on very few patients, niraparib is not approved for pancreatic cancer, and the finding is a lead rather than a standard of care [[GENE-025]].

topics.title: Mismatch repair deficiency and microsatellite instability
topics.orientation: Mismatch repair proofreads DNA after copying. A tumor that has lost it accumulates thousands of mutations and becomes visible to the immune system, which is why it can respond to immunotherapy. In pancreatic cancer this is real but rare, under one in a hundred, and the test that identifies it can miss cases.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: After DNA is copied, the mismatch-repair proteins MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2 scan the new strand for wrongly paired letters and small insertions or deletions, cut them out and let the correct sequence be restored. They work hardest in microsatellites, short repeated sequences that slip easily during copying. A cell that loses this system cannot correct those errors, so its mutation count climbs steadily with every division.
section1.full: The repair proteins act in pairs: MSH2 with MSH6 recognizes the mismatch, and MLH1 with PMS2 coordinates its excision and resynthesis. Because microsatellites are prone to copying errors, they are where loss of repair shows first, producing changes in their length that can be detected and that give the condition its name, microsatellite instability. A cell with intact repair keeps its mutation burden low; a cell without it becomes hypermutated, accumulating tens of thousands of changes, many of which alter proteins. Those altered proteins are displayed on the cell surface as neoantigens, fragments the immune system has never been taught to tolerate, which is why mismatch-repair-deficient tumors attract T cells and respond to drugs that release the immune brakes. Loss can be inherited, as in Lynch syndrome, where one faulty copy of a repair gene is passed down and the second is lost in a tumor cell, or sporadic, most often through chemical silencing of the MLH1 gene by promoter methylation rather than by mutation [[GENE-006]]. Either way the functional result is the same hypermutated, immunogenic state, and the mutation count, called tumor mutational burden, is one way it is measured.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Mismatch-repair deficiency occurs in under 1 percent of pancreatic cancers at most centers, about 1 to 2 percent across large reviews, and is several times more common in KRAS wild-type tumors. It is the one change that makes a pancreatic cancer eligible for the approved immunotherapy pembrolizumab, so despite its rarity it is worth finding, and because a tissue test can come back falsely normal, a blood test sometimes catches cases that staining misses.
section2.full: Confirmed mismatch-repair deficiency was found in 7 of 833 consecutive patients, 0.8 percent, all with Lynch syndrome [[GENE-006]], and a systematic review of 8,323 patients placed the pooled rate at about 1 to 2 percent, strongly associated with medullary and mucinous histology and a KRAS/TP53 wild-type background [[SEC-GENE-03]]. It was several times more common among KRAS wild-type tumors, 4.7 percent against 0.7 percent, and tumor mutational burden was high in 4.5 percent of wild-type against 1 percent of mutant tumors [[GENE-005]]. Carrying a mismatch-repair variant is not the same as having an immunotherapy-responsive tumor: in one series a mismatch-repair (MMR) variant conferred high microsatellite instability in only about half of carriers [[IMM-027]]. Where the tumor is truly deficient, response can be substantial: pembrolizumab, FDA-approved on a tissue-agnostic basis (for any tumor type) for mismatch-repair-deficient solid tumors, produced an objective response in 18 percent of 22 pancreatic patients in the pivotal basket trial (one enrolling many tumor types), lower than in some other tumors but far above the near-zero response of unselected pancreatic cancer [[TX-016]][[C-TX-21]]. Detection is the practical obstacle: tissue immunostaining was falsely negative in 1 of 6 cases in one series, and a blood test identified a mismatch-repair-deficient cancer that a pancreatic-body biopsy had missed, after which the patient received and responded to immunotherapy [[IMM-021]][[GENE-006]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Mismatch-repair deficiency is rare in pancreatic cancer but it is the only route by which a patient can reach an approved immunotherapy, so the small yield is clinically worth the test, especially in KRAS wild-type tumors where it clusters [[GENE-005]][[SEC-GENE-03]]. The assays disagree: immunohistochemistry, microsatellite PCR and sequencing-based scores can each miss or over-call cases, and because a variant confers instability in only about half of carriers, finding the variant is not the end of the question [[GENE-006]][[IMM-027]]. Blood testing adds a safety net when tissue is scant or falsely normal [[IMM-021]]. The response rate in confirmed-deficient pancreatic tumors, 18 percent, is lower than the roughly 50 percent seen across deficient tumors generally, so the biomarker is necessary but not sufficient [[TX-016]].
research_notes.how_studied: Mismatch-repair status is assessed four ways that can disagree: immunostaining for the four proteins, PCR of microsatellite markers, a sequencing-derived instability score, and tumor mutational burden; concordance studies quantify the disagreement [[GENE-006]]. Prevalence comes from consecutive single-center series and from systematic reviews pooling thousands of patients [[GENE-006]][[SEC-GENE-03]]. Treatment response is measured in tissue-agnostic basket trials with objective response and duration as endpoints [[TX-016]]. Liquid-biopsy detection is evaluated by comparing blood results against tissue in real-world cohorts [[IMM-021]].

mechanism_notes.text: Even where neoantigens, antigen-presentation machinery and interferon signaling are intact, pancreatic tumors may blunt the immune response by degrading their own surface MHC class I through autophagy, a process reversible with an available drug, which could help explain why the pancreatic response rate to checkpoint blockade lags other mismatch-repair-deficient cancers [[INF-IMMUNE-03]]. No trial has yet combined an autophagy inhibitor with checkpoint blockade in this disease.

topics.clinical_status: Pembrolizumab is FDA-approved (US) on a tissue-agnostic basis for unresectable or metastatic mismatch-repair-deficient or microsatellite-instability-high solid tumors after prior therapy, which includes the roughly 1 percent of pancreatic cancers that qualify; no immunotherapy is approved for pancreatic cancer as a disease. Checked 2026-10-08.

glossary.definition: The proofreading system that corrects wrongly paired letters left after DNA copying.
Changes in the length of short repeated DNA sequences that signal loss of mismatch repair.
Deficient mismatch repair, the loss of the proofreading system, detected by staining or testing.
The total number of mutations in a tumor, raised sharply when mismatch repair is lost.
A new protein fragment made by a mutation and displayed on a cell, which the immune system can recognize as foreign.
An inherited loss of one mismatch-repair gene copy that raises the risk of several cancers.

related.statement: Mismatch-repair deficiency is the loss of the DNA-proofreading system described in the DNA-repair entry.
Mismatch-repair deficiency is several times more common in KRAS wild-type than in KRAS-mutant pancreatic cancers.
Pembrolizumab is approved for mismatch-repair-deficient tumors, the only immunotherapy route open to pancreatic cancer patients.
Lynch syndrome, an inherited cause of mismatch-repair deficiency, modestly raises pancreatic cancer risk.
Mismatch-repair status is assessed by staining, microsatellite PCR, sequencing scores or a blood test, which can disagree.
The neoantigens produced by mismatch-repair loss must be displayed to T cells for immunotherapy to work.

faq.q: My tumor is mismatch-repair deficient. Does immunotherapy work for pancreatic cancer?
faq.a: It can, and this is the one setting where an approved immunotherapy is available: pembrolizumab is approved for mismatch-repair-deficient solid tumors and produced responses in 18 percent of pancreatic patients in the pivotal trial, far above the near-zero rate in unselected disease, though lower than in some other cancers [[TX-016]][[C-TX-21]].

faq.q: The test was normal but my relatives had Lynch syndrome. Could it have been missed?
faq.a: Yes. Tissue immunostaining was falsely negative in 1 of 6 cases in one series, and a blood test identified a deficient cancer that a tissue biopsy missed, so repeat or blood-based testing is reasonable when suspicion is high [[GENE-006]][[IMM-021]].

topics.title: Gene fusions and other rare targets
topics.orientation: A small group of pancreatic cancers, nearly all without a KRAS mutation, carry a gene fusion or another uncommon alteration that a matched drug can target. These findings are rare individually but together define the patients most likely to benefit from a precision therapy, which is why KRAS wild-type tumors are tested thoroughly.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: A gene fusion is an accidental joining of two genes after a chromosome breaks and rejoins the wrong way, so that part of one gene is spliced onto another. When the resulting hybrid contains a growth-signaling kinase, that kinase is often left permanently switched on, driving the cell as a mutated KRAS would. The genes involved, such as NTRK, RET, ALK, ROS1, FGFR2 and NRG1, normally encode receptors or signaling proteins used in development and tissue maintenance.
section1.full: In a healthy cell these genes are tightly controlled. The NTRK genes encode nerve-growth-factor receptors, RET and ALK and ROS1 encode other receptor kinases, and NRG1 encodes a ligand that activates the HER family of receptors. Each is normally switched on only by the right signal at the right time. A fusion removes that control in one of two ways: it can fuse a kinase to a partner gene that is always expressed, so the kinase is made constantly, or to a partner that forces the kinase proteins to cluster and activate each other without a signal. BRAF, which sits just below RAS in the growth pathway, is activated instead by a point mutation, most often V600E, that locks the kinase on; HER2, encoded by ERBB2, is driven by amplification, extra copies of the gene that flood the surface with receptor. The common thread is that each of these alterations switches on the same growth machinery that KRAS does, which is also why they almost never coexist with a KRAS mutation: one jammed switch in the pathway is enough, so a tumor that has a fusion generally has a normal KRAS, and vice versa [[GENE-005]].

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Gene fusions were present in about one in five KRAS wild-type tumors and essentially absent from KRAS-mutant ones. Individually each target is rare, a few percent or less, but several now have matched drugs, some with pancreatic-specific evidence and some approved for any tumor type on the basis of basket trials, which enroll many cancer types by shared alteration and included few or no pancreatic patients. HER2 amplification affects about 2 percent of wild-type tumors and has no approved pancreatic indication.
section2.full: In 2,483 sequenced tumors, fusions were found in 21 percent of KRAS wild-type cases, involving BRAF 6.6 percent, FGFR2 5.2 percent, ALK 2.6 percent, RET 1.3 percent, NRG1 1.3 percent and RAF1 1.3 percent, against essentially none of the KRAS-mutant tumors; BRAF was mutated in 13 percent of wild-type tumors, though only about 37 percent of those were the class 1 V600 type (the kind the approved BRAF drugs act on) [[GENE-005]][[GENE-002]]. Matched drugs carry different kinds of evidence. Zenocutuzumab is FDA-approved for NRG1-fusion pancreatic adenocarcinoma and produced a 42 percent response in 36 pancreatic patients [[TX-020]][[SEC-TX-08]]. Selpercatinib is approved tissue-agnostically for RET-fusion solid tumors, with 6 of 11 pancreatic patients responding [[TX-019]][[SEC-TX-06]]. Larotrectinib and entrectinib are approved for NTRK-fusion solid tumors on baskets that did not enumerate pancreatic cases [[TX-018]][[SEC-TX-05]], and the BRAF-plus-MEK inhibitor combination dabrafenib plus trametinib for BRAF V600E solid tumors on a trial with no pancreatic cohort [[TX-021]][[SEC-TX-07]]. HER2/ERBB2 amplification was found in 2.2 percent of wild-type tumors, alongside FGF3 at 3 percent, FGFR3 1.8 percent, NTRK amplification 1.8 percent and MET 1.3 percent, and has no approved pancreatic indication [[GENE-005]][[C-GENE-16]]. Because the fusions carrying the clearest drugs also carry the clearest need for RNA-based detection, a KRAS wild-type result is a signal to test more deeply [[GENE-005]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: These targets matter out of proportion to their frequency because they are where a durable, sometimes dramatic response is achievable in a disease that rarely offers one, and because they cluster in the testable KRAS wild-type tenth [[GENE-005]]. The evidence base is uneven: zenocutuzumab and selpercatinib have pancreatic response data, whereas the NTRK and BRAF approvals rest on tissue-agnostic baskets with few or no pancreatic patients, so the expected benefit is extrapolated [[TX-020]][[TX-019]][[TX-018]][[TX-021]]. HER2 amplification is a target in other cancers but has no pancreatic approval, and the only frequency available is within the wild-type subset, so it should not be read as an all-comers rate [[C-GENE-16]].
research_notes.how_studied: Fusions are detected by RNA sequencing, which reads the hybrid transcript directly, because DNA panels can miss the breakpoint; the large prevalence figures come from commercial sequencing of thousands of tumors [[GENE-005]]. Drug activity is measured in single-arm or tissue-agnostic basket trials with objective response and duration as endpoints, which is why some approvals cover pancreatic cancer explicitly and others cover it only as part of all solid tumors [[TX-020]][[TX-019]][[TX-018]][[TX-021]]. Amplifications are counted from copy-number data in the same sequencing series [[GENE-005]].

mechanism_notes.text: Fusions and KRAS mutations are near-mutually exclusive because each independently jams the same growth pathway, so a tumor selects one driver and does not need the other, which is the practical reason KRAS wild-type status is the trigger for deep fusion testing [[INF-GENE-01]][[GENE-005]][[GENE-002]]. The same logic predicts that resistance to a fusion-targeted drug will often come from reactivating the shared pathway downstream, as is seen with RAS-directed drugs.

topics.clinical_status: Zenocutuzumab is FDA-approved (US, accelerated, 4 December 2024) for NRG1-fusion pancreatic adenocarcinoma; selpercatinib (RET), larotrectinib and entrectinib (NTRK), and dabrafenib plus trametinib (BRAF V600E) are approved tissue-agnostically; HER2-directed therapy has no approved pancreatic indication. Checked 2026-10-08.

glossary.definition: An abnormal joining of two genes that can create a permanently active growth-signaling protein.
An enzyme that adds phosphate groups to other proteins to switch signaling pathways on.
A fusion involving the NRG1 gene that activates HER-family receptors and is targetable with zenocutuzumab in pancreatic cancer.
A drug approval based on a molecular alteration regardless of where the cancer started.
Extra copies of a gene, which can flood a cell with a growth-driving protein such as HER2.
A point mutation that locks the BRAF kinase on, targetable with a BRAF-plus-MEK inhibitor combination.

related.statement: Gene fusions and other rare targets are concentrated in the KRAS wild-type tenth of pancreatic cancers.
Fusions, BRAF mutation and HER2 amplification all switch on the same growth pathway that KRAS normally controls.
Matched drugs target the specific fusion or alteration a tumor carries, several of them approved tissue-agnostically.
Fusions are reliably detected only by RNA-based sequencing, which is why KRAS wild-type tumors are tested deeply.
Unlike these rare targets, daraxonrasib acts on the common RAS pathway that drives most pancreatic cancers.
Like these fusion drugs, pembrolizumab reaches pancreatic cancer through a tissue-agnostic rather than a pancreatic-specific approval.

faq.q: My tumor has an NRG1 fusion. Is there a drug?
faq.a: Yes. Zenocutuzumab is FDA-approved for NRG1-fusion pancreatic adenocarcinoma after prior therapy and produced responses in 42 percent of pancreatic patients in its trial, a notable result for this disease [[TX-020]][[SEC-TX-08]].

faq.q: These drugs were approved for 'solid tumors'. Do they have pancreatic data?
faq.a: It varies. Zenocutuzumab and selpercatinib have pancreatic response data, but the NTRK drugs and the BRAF combination were approved on baskets with few or no pancreatic patients, so their benefit in pancreatic cancer is extrapolated from other tumor types [[TX-020]][[TX-019]][[TX-018]][[TX-021]].

faq.q: Why test for these if they are so rare?
faq.a: Because they cluster in the KRAS wild-type tenth of tumors and offer some of the few chances of a durable response, so a KRAS wild-type result is a reason to test deeply with RNA-based sequencing for fusions [[GENE-005]].

topics.title: UGT1A1 and DPYD: inherited drug-toxicity variants
topics.orientation: Two inherited variants matter not because they drive the cancer but because they govern how a patient breaks down two common chemotherapy drugs. A slow-metabolizing version of UGT1A1 or DPYD can turn a standard dose into a dangerous one, so these are host-safety findings, entirely separate from the tumor alterations in the rest of this section.

section1.label: Normal biological role
section1.preview: Every person inherits versions of the enzymes that clear drugs from the body. UGT1A1 attaches a sugar to the active form of irinotecan so it can be excreted. DPYD makes the enzyme DPD, which breaks down fluorouracil and its tablet form capecitabine. Some inherited versions of these genes work slowly, so a person with them clears the drug less well and reaches higher, more toxic levels at a standard dose.
section1.full: These genes are not cancer genes; they are part of normal metabolism, and the relevant variants are present from birth in healthy cells throughout the body. UGT1A1 adds a glucuronide group to SN-38, the active metabolite of irinotecan, converting it to a form the body can dispose of; the reduced-function versions, named by stars such as *28 and *6, slow that step so SN-38 lingers and damages the bone marrow and gut lining [[SEC-GENE-01]]. DPD, the product of DPYD, performs the first and rate-limiting step in degrading fluorouracil; roughly 80 percent of a fluorouracil dose is normally broken down this way, so a person with reduced DPD activity accumulates the drug and can suffer severe early toxicity. Several DPYD variants reduce activity by different amounts, from the near-complete loss caused by c.1905+1G>A to partial reductions, and a person can carry one faulty copy or, rarely, two. Because the consequence falls on the patient rather than the tumor, the goal of testing is not to choose a drug but to adjust its dose, and the variants are measured in blood or saliva, not in the cancer.

section2.label: Connection to pancreatic cancer
section2.preview: Both drugs are mainstays of pancreatic cancer treatment: irinotecan is part of the four-drug combination FOLFIRINOX and is also used in a liposomal form, and fluorouracil or capecitabine appears in most regimens. Reduced-function UGT1A1 or DPYD variants raise the risk of severe, occasionally fatal early toxicity, and pre-emptive dose reduction lowers that risk without clearly sacrificing effectiveness. US labels now address both, and the capecitabine label reveals a gap: it directs DPYD testing while noting no FDA-authorized test exists.
section2.full: For irinotecan, a 30 percent starting-dose reduction in UGT1A1 poor metabolizers brought severe toxicity down to the level of normal metabolizers across 779 patients, about half with pancreatic cancer, with no detectable cost in progression-free or overall survival, hazard ratios 1.02 and 1.10 [[GENE-018]]. The US irinotecan label (Camptosar, SPL version 37, published 13 May 2026) states in Warnings and Precautions 5.3 that individuals homozygous for UGT1A1*28 or *6 (carrying two copies), or compound heterozygous *6/*28 (one of each), are poor metabolizers at increased risk of severe or life-threatening neutropenia (a dangerous drop in infection-fighting white cells), directs that genotype testing for *28 and *6 be considered, and advises considering a starting-dose reduction of at least one level while stating the precise reduction is not known [[SEC-GENE-01]]. On the side of febrile neutropenia (fever with low white cells), UGT1A1 intermediate and poor metabolizers had roughly a fourfold higher risk on FOLFIRINOX [[SUPP-006]]. For fluoropyrimidines (fluorouracil and capecitabine), genotype-guided dosing cut clinically relevant toxicity from 43.3 percent to 16.0 percent overall, but the benefit was variant-specific: clear for c.1905+1G>A and c.2846A>T carriers, while for the common HapB3 variant the guideline reduction produced no clear toxicity benefit yet substantially lowered the delivered dose [[GENE-019]]. The US capecitabine label (NorthStar RxLLC, SPL version 2, published 23 July 2026) now directs testing for DPYD variants before starting treatment unless immediate treatment is necessary, states that no FDA-authorized DPYD test is currently available and that available tests vary, and advises against the drug in complete DPD deficiency, with no dose proven safe [[SEC-GENE-02]].

action_note.heading: When to call the care team now
action_note.text: A fever of 38.0 degrees Celsius or 100.4 Fahrenheit or higher during chemotherapy can be the only sign of dangerously low white cells and needs urgent evaluation and antibiotics within an hour [[SEC-SUPP-03]][[SEC-SUPP-01]]. Severe mouth sores, heavy diarrhea or profound weakness in the first days of a fluorouracil, capecitabine or irinotecan cycle can signal an inherited inability to clear the drug and should prompt an immediate call rather than waiting for the next visit [[SEC-GENE-02]][[SEC-GENE-01]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: These are the best-evidenced pharmacogenomic actions in the whole atlas, and the practical message is that a safety test can prevent harm at no clear cost to effectiveness, at least for the clearly actionable variants [[GENE-018]][[GENE-019]]. The important nuance is that one dose rule does not fit every variant: for HapB3 the guideline reduction lowered exposure without lowering toxicity, suggesting a more individualized approach [[GENE-019]]. The capecitabine label's combination, a directive to test with an admission that no authorized test exists, is the single most consequential regulatory fact here and should be read with both halves, because it means testing relies on laboratory tests that vary in which variants they detect [[SEC-GENE-02]].
research_notes.how_studied: UGT1A1 evidence comes from a multicenter cohort in which poor metabolizers received a pre-specified 30 percent reduction and were compared with fully dosed normal metabolizers for toxicity and survival [[GENE-018]], and from a pancreatic cohort relating genotype to febrile neutropenia [[SUPP-006]]. DPYD evidence comes from a real-world study comparing patients genotyped before treatment with those genotyped only afterward, analyzed variant by variant, using delivered dose intensity as a proxy for exposure [[GENE-019]]. The regulatory statements are taken from the US product labels current on 8 October 2026 [[SEC-GENE-01]][[SEC-GENE-02]].

topics.clinical_status: The US irinotecan label (Camptosar, 13 May 2026) directs considering UGT1A1 *28 and *6 genotyping and a starting-dose reduction in poor metabolizers; the US capecitabine label (23 July 2026) directs DPYD testing before treatment unless immediate treatment is necessary, while stating no FDA-authorized DPYD test is currently available. Checked 2026-10-08.

glossary.definition: The study of how inherited gene variants change a person's response to, and handling of, drugs.
An enzyme that clears the active metabolite of irinotecan; slow-working versions raise the risk of severe toxicity.
The gene for DPD, the enzyme that breaks down fluorouracil and capecitabine; reduced-function versions cause drug build-up.
A person whose inherited enzyme versions clear a drug slowly, reaching higher and more toxic levels.
Reduced or absent activity of the DPD enzyme, which makes standard fluoropyrimidine doses dangerous.
A named version of a drug-metabolism gene, such as UGT1A1*28, defining its activity level.

related.statement: UGT1A1 genotype governs how a patient clears irinotecan and so how toxic a standard dose will be.
DPYD genotype governs how a patient breaks down fluorouracil and capecitabine.
UGT1A1 slow metabolizers face a higher risk of febrile neutropenia on FOLFIRINOX, which contains irinotecan.
Drug-toxicity genotyping is done on blood or saliva and is separate from the tumor sequencing that guides targeted therapy.
Recognizing a slow-metabolizer genotype helps anticipate the neutropenia that growth-factor support is used to manage.
The severe neutropenia these variants predispose to is the reason a fever during chemotherapy is an emergency.

faq.q: Is a UGT1A1 or DPYD result something my family should worry about for cancer?
faq.a: No. These are drug-handling genes, not cancer-driving ones; a reduced-function result affects how safely you can take certain chemotherapy, not your family's cancer risk [[SEC-GENE-01]][[SEC-GENE-02]].

faq.q: If I test positive, does a lower dose mean weaker treatment?
faq.a: Not detectably for the clearly actionable variants: a 30 percent irinotecan reduction in UGT1A1 poor metabolizers equalized toxicity with no measurable loss of survival [[GENE-018]]. For fluoropyrimidines the picture is variant-specific, and for the HapB3 variant the standard reduction lowered dose without a clear safety gain, which is why dosing is being individualized [[GENE-019]].

faq.q: My oncologist wants a DPYD test but mentioned test limitations. Why?
faq.a: Because the US capecitabine label directs testing before treatment yet also states that no FDA-authorized DPYD test currently exists and that available tests vary in which variants they detect, so a normal result does not rule out every risk variant [[SEC-GENE-02]].

topics.title: Molecular testing: what is tested and what it yields
topics.orientation: Molecular testing reads a cancer's genes, from the tumor or from blood, to find alterations that could guide treatment or identify inherited risk. This entry explains what the tests measure, how often they change what happens, and what tissue and blood can and cannot each find.

section1.label: What it measures
section1.preview: Comprehensive genomic profiling sequences a panel of cancer genes, or the whole exome (all protein-coding genes), to catalog a tumor's mutations, deletions, amplifications and fusions, plus summary measures such as microsatellite instability and mutational burden. A separate germline test, on blood or saliva, reads inherited variants. Tumor testing uses a tissue biopsy or, when that is hard to obtain, cell-free DNA shed into the blood.
section1.full: The tests differ in what they can see. A DNA panel finds point mutations and, if designed for it, copy-number changes such as the CDKN2A and SMAD4 deletions that dominate this disease; a panel that reads only mutations will under-report those genes badly [[GENE-024]]. Detecting a gene fusion reliably needs RNA sequencing, because the DNA breakpoint can fall anywhere in a large intron (a non-coding stretch of the gene) and be missed [[GENE-005]]. Microsatellite instability and tumor mutational burden are computed from the same sequencing data. A single endoscopic-ultrasound needle pass usually yields enough DNA (about 90 percent of samples were adequate for sequencing), so the diagnostic biopsy can often serve for molecular testing too [[DIAG-020]]. When tissue is insufficient, plasma cell-free DNA can substitute: in pancreatic and bile-duct cancers, 90 percent of mutations found in tissue were also found in plasma, and plasma recovered a genotype in 78 percent of cases where the tissue sample was inadequate [[DIAG-026]]. Germline testing is run separately and is recommended for patients with pancreatic cancer because it identifies inherited variants with implications for both treatment and relatives [[SEC-DIAG-01]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Testing matters because it finds the uncommon alterations that change treatment: mismatch-repair deficiency for immunotherapy, BRCA for platinum and olaparib, and fusions for matched drugs. But the arithmetic is sobering. When advanced tumors are sequenced, roughly half carry something called relevant, yet in one large program only 2 percent of referred patients actually received a matched therapy, and the oft-quoted survival advantage comes from that select 2 percent.
section2.full: Prospective sequencing of advanced disease found a therapeutically relevant alteration in 48 percent and an inherited damaging variant in 18 percent [[GENE-022]]. In the Know Your Tumor registry, a molecular tumor board judged 26 percent of profiles actionable, but only 1,082 of 1,856 referred patients (58 percent) ever received a report and only 46 (2 percent) received a matched therapy [[GENE-029]]. The widely cited figure that matched therapy was associated with longer survival, 2.58 against 1.51 years, comes from that non-randomized 2 percent, so it measures who reached matched therapy at least as much as what the therapy did, and no randomized trial has shown a survival benefit of matched therapy in this disease [[GENE-029]]. Tissue and blood have complementary blind spots: a tissue biopsy can be falsely normal for mismatch-repair deficiency that a blood test then catches [[IMM-021]], while blood genotyping can miss a tumor-confirmed alteration, finding a known KRAS G12C in only 73 to 81 percent of patients whose tumor carried it, so tissue remains the reference for assigning a targeted mutation [[RAS-022]]. Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is also detectable in only about 48 percent of localized cancers against over 75 percent of metastatic ones, so a negative blood result in early disease is weak [[DIAG-006]]. The practical reading is that testing is worthwhile for the minority it helps decisively, that a report omitting deletions or fusions may reflect the panel rather than the tumor, and that tissue and blood are best used to cover each other.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The yield-versus-benefit gap is the central honest point: a high rate of relevant findings does not translate into a high rate of patients helped, because reporting delays, access barriers and disease tempo intervene, leaving the 2.58-year figure a description of a selected 2 percent rather than a treatment effect [[GENE-029]][[GENE-022]]. This argues for testing but against over-reading a single headline number. The tissue-versus-blood comparison is equally practical: neither is complete alone, blood misses a fraction of targetable mutations and is insensitive in localized disease, while tissue can be falsely normal for mismatch-repair deficiency, so the two are complementary [[RAS-022]][[IMM-021]][[DIAG-006]][[DIAG-026]].
research_notes.how_studied: Yield is measured in prospective sequencing programs that report how many patients had relevant or actionable alterations and how many received matched therapy, which is how the drop from 48 percent relevant to 2 percent treated was documented [[GENE-022]][[GENE-029]]. Tissue adequacy is tested by measuring DNA from endoscopic-ultrasound needle passes against sequencing thresholds [[DIAG-020]]. Plasma-versus-tissue concordance is measured by sequencing both from the same patients [[DIAG-026]], and detection rates by stage by counting how often ctDNA is found in localized versus metastatic disease [[DIAG-006]]. Blood false-negative rates come from trials where every patient's tumor was known to carry the target [[RAS-022]].

mechanism_notes.text: A negative post-operative or early-stage blood test is weak reassurance because at low tumor fraction the limiting factor is the small number of mutant DNA copies in a standard blood draw, so a draw can miss them by chance; larger plasma volumes or serial draws could partly overcome this if the tumor sheds at all [[INF-DIAG-02]][[DIAG-006]]. This is a statistical-sampling limit, not evidence that the cancer is gone.

topics.clinical_status: Germline and somatic molecular profiling of advanced pancreatic cancer is guideline-recommended practice in the US (ASCO 2020), and plasma testing is accepted when tissue is inadequate; no randomized trial has shown a survival benefit of matched therapy in pancreatic cancer. Checked 2026-10-08.

glossary.definition: High-throughput reading of many genes at once to catalog a tumor's DNA changes.
Sequencing of the tumor itself to find alterations it has acquired.
Sequencing of blood or saliva to find inherited variants present in every cell.
Fragments of DNA, some from the tumor, that circulate in the blood and can be sequenced as a liquid biopsy.
A genetic change that points to a specific available or investigational treatment.
A broad panel test that reports mutations, copy-number changes, fusions and summary biomarkers together.

related.statement: Molecular testing identifies the KRAS variant or wild-type status that directs further testing.
Germline and somatic testing find the BRCA and PALB2 alterations that guide platinum and olaparib use.
Molecular and immunohistochemical testing identify the mismatch-repair deficiency that qualifies a tumor for immunotherapy.
RNA-based sequencing is needed to detect the gene fusions that matched drugs target.
Circulating tumor DNA is the blood-based form of molecular testing, complementary to tissue sequencing.
A single endoscopic-ultrasound biopsy usually yields enough DNA to serve both diagnosis and molecular testing.

faq.q: Should my tumor be sequenced even though targeted options are rare?
faq.a: Guidelines recommend germline and somatic testing for treatment-eligible patients, because the uncommon findings it catches, mismatch-repair deficiency, BRCA, fusions, are exactly the ones that change treatment [[SEC-DIAG-01]][[GENE-022]]. The caution is that a high rate of relevant findings does not mean a high rate of patients helped; in one program only 2 percent received a matched therapy [[GENE-029]].

faq.q: Is a blood test as good as a tissue biopsy?
faq.a: They are complementary. Blood can substitute when tissue is inadequate, matching 90 percent of tissue mutations, but it missed a tumor-confirmed KRAS G12C in up to a quarter of patients and is insensitive in localized disease, while tissue can be falsely normal for mismatch-repair deficiency that blood then catches [[DIAG-026]][[RAS-022]][[DIAG-006]][[IMM-021]].

faq.q: My report did not list CDKN2A or any fusion. Does that mean they are absent?
faq.a: Not necessarily. CDKN2A and SMAD4 are usually lost by deletion, which a mutation-only panel misses, and fusions need RNA sequencing to detect, so an omission may reflect the test's design rather than the tumor [[GENE-024]][[GENE-005]].

topics.title: Pancreas-protocol CT
topics.orientation: Pancreas-protocol CT (computed tomography) is the workhorse scan of pancreatic cancer: it is usually the first test to show the tumor, and its pictures of the arteries and veins decide which resectability category a tumor is placed in.

section1.label: What it measures
section1.preview: A CT scanner records how much X-ray each small block of tissue absorbs. A pancreas protocol injects iodine contrast and images the gland at timed moments as the dye passes through the arteries, then the pancreas, then the veins. A pancreatic cancer usually appears as a region that takes up less contrast than the gland around it, and the timed phases map the tumor against the vessels that run beside it.
section1.full: The pancreatic phase is timed for the moment when normal pancreas enhances most strongly, because that is when the difference between gland and tumor is widest; the later portal-venous phase fills the superior mesenteric and portal veins so that contact between tumor and vein can be measured in degrees of the vessel's circumference. That measurement is the backbone of resectability reporting: in 254 head tumors, the chance that the vein was truly invaded on pathology rose from 3% with no contact to 71-80% when contact exceeded half the circumference or the vein was occluded [[DIAG-001]]. What CT cannot do is see a tumor whose density matches the gland. About 12% of pancreatic carcinomas are isoattenuating, invisible as a mass, and in 95% of those cases the radiologist infers the tumor from indirect signs such as a dilated or interrupted pancreatic duct, a dilated bile duct or shrinkage of the gland beyond the blockage; endoscopic ultrasound then finds the tumor itself [[DIAG-022]]. CT also maps the arteries a surgeon must preserve. A variant right hepatic artery (replaced or accessory, arising from the superior mesenteric artery) running behind the pancreatic head was present in 16% of one surgical series, and a blinded re-read of the scans found it in 24 of 25 cases whereas the original reports had mentioned it in 9 of 26 [[ANAT-007]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: CT answers the first question in pancreatic cancer, where the tumor sits relative to the vessels, well enough to drive the resectable, borderline resectable and locally advanced categories. It answers two other questions poorly. It cannot see deposits below its resolution, so a scan that shows no spread does not exclude it, and after chemotherapy it cannot tell scar tissue from living tumor at a vessel wall.
section2.full: The contact angle is a probability, not a verdict. It predicts whether the vein will need to be removed far better than whether the margin will be clear: in the same 254-patient series the clear-margin rate was the same across every contact category, because surgeons planned a vein resection when the scan showed extensive contact [[DIAG-001]]. Reading is observer-dependent as well. When a national trial re-reviewed scans centrally, 29% of patients enrolled as resectable were judged ineligible, most often for suspected metastases, arterial contact or venous contact of half the circumference or more [[TX-013]]. The resolution floor shows up at staging laparoscopy, where 18% of 1,004 patients whose CT, often with MRI and PET as well, showed localized disease turned out to have peritoneal or liver deposits [[DIAG-002]]. The largest problem appears after treatment. Chemotherapy and radiation replace tumor at the vessel wall with fibrous scar of the same density, so in one series 70% of tumors removed after FOLFIRINOX chemotherapy still looked locally advanced or borderline on their post-treatment scans, yet 92% came out with clear margins and the pathology showed fibrosis where the scan showed tumor [[DIAG-004]]. CT alone therefore identifies a resectable tumor after chemotherapy only about two-thirds of the time, which is why restaging leans on the blood marker CA 19-9 and sometimes PET rather than on anatomy alone [[DIAG-009]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The contact-angle data come from a single high-volume center whose surgeons could see the imaging, so the apparent accuracy for 'need for vein resection' is partly self-fulfilling, and arterial contact was not analyzed [[DIAG-001]]. The isoattenuating-tumor series is retrospective and two-center, and isoattenuation depends partly on how well the contrast phase was timed [[DIAG-022]]. The central-review figure shows that resectability labels assigned in routine practice shift under expert reading, which affects how trial results transfer to community settings [[TX-013]]. US resectability categories are built on these CT descriptors [[SEC-SURG-11]], so the uncertainty in the measurement passes directly into the category.
research_notes.how_studied: Vessel-contact accuracy is studied by having readers blinded to outcome grade the tumor-vein interface on the preoperative scan and then comparing that grade with the pathologist's finding in the resected vein, which is only available when the vein was removed [[DIAG-001]]. Invisible tumors are identified by comparing multiphase CT with subsequent endoscopic ultrasound and biopsy in the same patients, with the indirect ductal signs tallied separately [[DIAG-022]]. Post-treatment accuracy is tested by blinded re-reading of pre- and post-chemotherapy scans against what the surgeon found and what the pathologist reported [[DIAG-004]]. Arterial variants are counted by re-reviewing preoperative scans against the anatomy found at operation [[ANAT-007]].

mechanism_notes.text: Persistent tumor-vessel contact on CT after treatment is mostly fibrosis, and a functional signal such as PET uptake or MRI diffusion at the contact may be able to separate living tumor from scar because viable tumor keeps its glucose metabolism and cell density while treated fibrosis loses both [[INF-DIAG-01]][[DIAG-008]][[DIAG-009]]. Post-treatment inflammation produces the same functional signals, so the functional scan can over-call tumor in the direction opposite to CT's over-call of contact.

glossary.definition: A CT scan with thin slices and contrast injection timed to show the pancreas, its arteries and its veins in separate phases.
One of the timed sets of images taken as injected dye passes through arteries, organs and veins.
Having the same density as the surrounding gland on CT, so the tumor casts no visible shadow.
Tumor touching a vessel over half its circumference or less.
Tumor wrapping around more than half of a vessel's circumference.

related.statement: Tumor-vessel contact is measured on the portal-venous phase of a pancreas-protocol CT as degrees of the vessel's circumference.
A baseline pancreas-protocol CT is the reference against which restaging scans after chemotherapy are compared.
Endoscopic ultrasound finds the roughly one in eight tumors that a pancreas-protocol CT cannot see as a mass.
The portal-venous phase of CT shows the superior mesenteric and portal veins against which the tumor is graded.
The resectable, borderline resectable and locally advanced categories are assigned from CT vessel-contact measurements.
A dilated or interrupted pancreatic duct on CT is the indirect sign that reveals a tumor the scan cannot see directly.
CT finds small liver spots that it often cannot characterize, which MRI is then asked to resolve.

faq.q: I already had a CT in the emergency department. Why do I need another one?
faq.a: An emergency CT is usually a single-phase scan done to find a cause for pain or jaundice, whereas a pancreas protocol uses thin slices and contrast timed to the pancreas and its vessels. The pancreatic phase is what separates a tumor from the gland and the venous phase is what grades vessel contact, and about one tumor in eight is invisible even on a dedicated scan and is inferred from duct changes [[DIAG-022]].

faq.q: The scan says the tumor touches the vein. Does that mean it cannot be removed?
faq.a: Contact is a probability about invasion, not a verdict. With contact of half the circumference or less the vein was invaded in 23% of cases in a large series, and even with greater contact the margin was clear as often as without contact because the surgeon planned to remove and reconstruct the vein [[DIAG-001]].

topics.title: MRI and diffusion imaging
topics.orientation: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) builds its pictures from the behavior of water in tissue rather than from X-ray absorption, which gives it a different set of strengths: it is the best non-invasive test for small liver deposits, it shows the ducts without contrast, and its diffusion images read the density of cells.

section1.label: What it measures
section1.preview: An MRI scanner aligns the hydrogen nuclei of water in a strong magnetic field, nudges them with radio pulses and listens to the signal they give back as they relax; tissues relax at different rates, and that difference is the contrast in the pictures. Three kinds of image matter in pancreatic cancer: T2 and MRCP images that show fluid and ducts, contrast-enhanced images timed like a CT, and diffusion-weighted images that measure how freely water molecules move.
section1.full: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) adds a pair of magnetic gradients that cancel for water that stays put but not for water that has wandered between them, so tissue where water moves freely loses signal and tissue where movement is hindered stays bright. Water is hindered in densely packed cells, so a cellular tumor or metastasis stands out as a bright spot on DWI with a low apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), the number that quantifies the restriction, while a fluid-filled cyst does the opposite. MRCP (magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography) uses heavily T2-weighted images in which only stationary fluid is bright, drawing the bile duct and pancreatic duct without any injection. Contrast-enhanced phases work as on CT, with gadolinium in place of iodine, but each phase is captured during a short breath-hold, so a patient who cannot hold still blurs exactly those images; diffusion and pre-contrast sequences are usually acquired with free breathing or respiratory triggering and often remain readable when the contrast phases do not. In a reader study of resectability after chemotherapy, adding PET/MRI to CT raised sensitivity for a removable tumor from 66% to 86%, and the study could not separate how much of that gain came from the metabolic signal and how much from diffusion [[DIAG-009]]. In high-risk surveillance, MRI/MRCP found cystic lesions far better than endoscopic ultrasound but solid lesions far worse, 22% against 100% [[ORIG-005]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: In pancreatic cancer MRI is mainly used for the liver and for problem-solving. Small liver spots that CT cannot characterize are usually settled by MRI, and in a population study patients who had an MRI before their pancreatectomy had fewer futile operations (ones that find disease that cannot be removed) and lived longer, a difference that probably reflects better selection of who should be operated on rather than any effect of the scan itself.
section2.full: The liver is where pancreatic cancer most often spreads: in a resected cohort 49% of recurrences appeared there first [[SURG-015]]. Deposits a few millimeters across sit below CT's ability to tell them from cysts, and MRI's combination of T2 brightness, diffusion restriction and contrast behavior classifies many of them. The consequence is visible at the population level. Among 4,579 patients who had a pancreatectomy in Ontario, those who had a preoperative abdominal MRI had a median survival of 33.1 months against 21.1 months, an adjusted hazard ratio (relative death rate) of 0.83 [[DIAG-021]], and a companion analysis found a futile operation (a laparotomy or staging laparoscopy that ended without resection) in 6.4% with MRI against 9.7% without [[SEC-DIAG-07]]. MRI did not treat anyone; the plausible reading is that it found liver metastases before surgery in patients who would otherwise have had an operation that could not help them, and the MRI group was also younger and more often treated with chemotherapy first, so part of the gap is selection [[DIAG-021]]. On the pancreas itself, MRI meets the same wall as CT after treatment, because scar and tumor share the same contact with vessels; whether diffusion can separate them is open, since viable tumor should restrict water movement while acellular fibrosis should not, yet post-treatment inflammation restricts it too [[INF-DIAG-01]]. In a 1,004-patient laparoscopy series an indeterminate lesion outside the pancreas raised the odds of finding hidden spread nearly seven-fold, which is the situation MRI is most often asked to resolve [[DIAG-002]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The Ontario survival association is observational with confounding by indication (the patients chosen for MRI differed from those not chosen): MRI recipients were younger, more often stage I and more often had neoadjuvant therapy, and the administrative data cannot confirm that the patients spared surgery had liver metastases [[DIAG-021]][[SEC-DIAG-07]]. Routine preoperative MRI is not mandated in US guidance, which endorses it for indeterminate liver lesions [[DIAG-021]]. The PET/MRI restaging study was single-center, and the PET/MRI was ordered as a problem-solving test in patients already thought to have responded, which biases toward resectable cases [[DIAG-009]]. The surveillance comparison of MRI with endoscopic ultrasound concerns asymptomatic high-risk individuals, not people with a known tumor [[ORIG-005]].
research_notes.how_studied: Population studies link administrative records of who had an MRI to survival and to futile-surgery rates after adjusting for measured differences, which can show association but not cause [[DIAG-021]][[SEC-DIAG-07]]. Reader studies have several radiologists score the same patients in separate sessions, first with CT alone and then with the added modality, and compare each session against surgical and pathological findings [[DIAG-009]]. Modality sensitivity in surveillance is measured by performing both tests at every visit and counting which one saw each lesion that was later confirmed [[ORIG-005]]. The physics of diffusion imaging is established; what remains under study is whether restriction at a treated vessel interface marks viable tumor [[INF-DIAG-01]].

mechanism_notes.text: Diffusion restriction at a treated tumor-vessel interface may mark viable tumor where anatomic contact cannot, because living cancer cells hinder water movement and acellular fibrosis does not [[INF-DIAG-01]][[DIAG-009]]. Inflammation and edema after treatment also restrict diffusion, and desmoplastic density may do so independently of cellularity, so the signal could over-call tumor; the discriminating test is matching the MRI signal point by point against the resected specimen.

glossary.definition: An MRI sequence that is bright where water molecules are hindered by densely packed cells and dark where they move freely.
