The number derived from diffusion images that quantifies how freely water moves; low values mean restricted movement.
An MRI technique that shows the bile and pancreatic ducts as bright fluid-filled tubes without any contrast injection.
The metal in MRI contrast agents, which brightens tissues according to their blood supply.
A late set of images with a liver-specific contrast agent in which normal liver cells take up the agent and metastases do not.

related.statement: Small liver spots left indeterminate by CT are usually characterized by MRI using T2 brightness, diffusion and contrast behavior.
MRI complements pancreas-protocol CT, which remains the preferred scan for mapping vessel contact.
PET/MRI combines metabolic uptake with diffusion imaging, and which signal carries the information after chemotherapy is unresolved.
After chemotherapy MRI faces the same problem as CT, since scar and tumor share the same vessel contact.
MRI is the best non-invasive test for small deposits in the liver, the most common site of pancreatic cancer spread.
MRCP draws the pancreatic duct and bile duct as fluid-filled channels, showing where a tumor interrupts them.
MRI/MRCP sees pancreatic cysts better than endoscopic ultrasound does, though it sees solid lesions worse.

faq.q: My MRI report says the contrast images were degraded by motion. Was the scan wasted?
faq.a: Usually not. The contrast phases are captured in short breath-holds and are the sequences most easily blurred, whereas diffusion and pre-contrast images are acquired with free breathing or respiratory triggering and are often still readable, and diffusion is the sequence that matters most for small liver spots. The radiologist's report will say which questions the readable sequences could answer.

faq.q: Why did I need an MRI when I already had a CT?
faq.a: Most often because the CT showed a small liver spot it could not characterize, or because the care team wanted the liver checked carefully before committing to a major operation. In one population, patients who had a preoperative MRI had fewer futile operations and longer survival, most plausibly because metastases were found before surgery rather than after [[DIAG-021]][[SEC-DIAG-07]].

topics.title: Endoscopic ultrasound and biopsy
topics.orientation: Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) puts a small ultrasound probe on the tip of an endoscope and places it in the stomach or duodenum, a few millimeters from the pancreas, which lets a doctor see small tumors and pass a needle into them for a tissue diagnosis.

section1.label: What it measures
section1.preview: Ultrasound records echoes of high-frequency sound reflected by boundaries between tissues. From outside the body the pancreas is hidden behind gas and fat, but from inside the stomach or duodenum the probe sits directly against it, so EUS resolves lesions smaller than CT can and shows the tumor's edge against the duct and the vessels. A fine needle passed through the gut wall under ultrasound view collects cells or a core of tissue.
section1.full: The two needle types differ in what they bring back: fine-needle aspiration (FNA) draws up loose cells that a cytologist reads as single cells and clusters, while fine-needle biopsy (FNB) cuts a small core that preserves tissue architecture and gives more material for molecular tests. Either way the sample is small, and the diagnosis rests on finding malignant cells in it, so a negative result means no malignant cells were seen in that sample rather than no cancer. In 173 patients who had both CT and EUS, EUS visualized every tumor including the 12% that were invisible on CT, and needle sampling had a sensitivity of about 90% in both groups, with false-negative cytology in 2 of 21 CT-invisible tumors [[DIAG-022]]. In 73 consecutive resected patients, diagnostic accuracy was 98.6% and clinical adverse events, two bleeds and one pancreatitis, occurred in 4.1% [[DIAG-019]]. The same sample feeds molecular testing: a single dedicated FNA pass yielded enough DNA for any tier of sequencing in about 90% of 105 patients [[DIAG-020]]. In a surveillance program for high-risk relatives, EUS saw 100% of solid lesions where MRI/MRCP saw 22%, while MRI was better for cysts [[ORIG-005]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Pancreatic cancer is treated on the basis of a tissue diagnosis whenever chemotherapy is to come before surgery, because the drugs are chosen for adenocarcinoma specifically and other pancreatic tumors need different treatment. EUS is the usual way to get that tissue, it finds the small tumors CT misses, and its risks are small and measurable: bleeding or pancreatitis in a few percent, and tumor cells left along the needle track in under 3% of resected specimens.
section2.full: Three facts shape how the biopsy is used. First, the sample is the gateway to treatment selection: US guidance recommends germline and tumor testing for mismatch-repair deficiency, BRCA and NTRK fusions in every treatment-eligible patient, and the needle sample is the tissue those tests usually run on [[SEC-DIAG-01]]. DNA quantity is rarely the limit; what fails is tumor fraction, the proportion of the sample that is cancer cells, because a pancreatic cancer sample is mostly stroma, and in a prospective biopsy protocol pathologists' estimates of tumor cellularity correlated only moderately with sequencing-based estimates [[GENE-022]]. When tissue is insufficient, plasma sequencing recovered the genotype in 78% of such cases in a small advanced-disease series [[DIAG-026]], and in one case a tissue stain missed mismatch-repair deficiency that a blood assay detected [[IMM-021]]. Second, seeding is real but rare: histologic tumor continuity along the needle track was found in 2 of 73 resected specimens, both large tumors, and for head tumors the track is removed with the specimen at a Whipple, whereas a transgastric route to a body or tail tumor leaves the track in place, which is why the route is chosen with the planned operation in mind [[DIAG-019]]. Third, a negative biopsy of a mass that looks like cancer on imaging is generally treated as inconclusive and repeated, because sensitivity is about 90%, not 100% [[DIAG-022]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The seeding series is single-center with 73 cases, mostly head tumors where the track was removed, so the risk for body and tail tumors biopsied through the stomach is extrapolated, and tumor along the track may sometimes be pre-existing extension rather than implantation [[DIAG-019]]. No head-to-head randomized comparison of FNA and FNB needles is among the sources cited here; needle adequacy rests on the DNA-yield cohort, which measured DNA mass rather than sequencing success and did not compare with core biopsy [[DIAG-020]]. The CT-invisible-tumor series is retrospective and limited to patients referred for EUS [[DIAG-022]]. The surveillance comparison concerns asymptomatic high-risk people rather than symptomatic patients [[ORIG-005]].
research_notes.how_studied: Diagnostic accuracy is measured against the resected specimen or against clinical follow-up, counting the biopsies that called cancer when cancer was present [[DIAG-019]][[DIAG-022]]. Needle-track seeding is assessed by having the pathologist examine the puncture route in the resected specimen for a continuum of tumor between track and mass [[DIAG-019]]. DNA adequacy is measured by spectrophotometry of a pass set aside for extraction, against thresholds for amplicon, exome and genome sequencing [[DIAG-020]]. Tumor cellularity is estimated both by the pathologist's visual count and from the sequencing data, and the two are compared [[GENE-022]].

glossary.definition: An ultrasound probe on the tip of an endoscope placed in the stomach or duodenum to image the pancreas from a few millimeters away.
Drawing loose cells into a thin needle for a cytologist to examine.
Cutting a small core of tissue with a needle so that the tissue's structure is preserved.
Cancer cells carried along the path of a biopsy needle and left behind in the tissue it passed through.
The fraction of a sample that is cancer cells rather than scar, blood or normal tissue.

related.statement: Endoscopic ultrasound finds the tumors that pancreas-protocol CT cannot see as a mass.
The EUS needle sample is usually the tissue on which molecular testing for mismatch repair, BRCA and fusions is run.
An EUS biopsy distinguishes ductal adenocarcinoma from neuroendocrine and other pancreatic tumors that need different treatment.
A tissue diagnosis by EUS biopsy is required before chemotherapy is given ahead of surgery.
The EUS probe images the pancreatic head through the wall of the duodenum, and the biopsy needle passes through that wall.
When an EUS sample is too sparse for sequencing, plasma tumor DNA can sometimes supply the genotype instead.

faq.q: Can the biopsy spread the cancer?
faq.a: Tumor cells along the needle track were found in 2 of 73 resected specimens, both large tumors, and no study has shown that this changes survival. For head tumors the track is removed with the Whipple specimen; for body and tail tumors the endoscopist chooses the route with the planned operation in mind [[DIAG-019]].

faq.q: The biopsy came back negative but my doctors still think it is cancer. Why?
faq.a: A negative needle sample means no malignant cells were found in that small sample, and sensitivity is about 90%, so roughly one cancer in ten gives a negative first biopsy [[DIAG-022]]. When the scan looks like cancer the biopsy is usually repeated rather than taken as reassurance.

topics.title: PET scan
topics.orientation: A PET (positron emission tomography) scan images metabolism rather than anatomy: it shows where in the body cells are taking up a radioactive sugar, and in pancreatic cancer it is used selectively, to look for spread and to judge whether treated tissue is still alive.

section1.label: What it measures
section1.preview: FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) is glucose with a radioactive fluorine atom attached. Cells take it up through the same transporters as glucose and trap it after the first step of metabolism, so tissue that burns a lot of sugar accumulates the tracer, and the scanner, detecting the paired gamma rays released when the fluorine decays, maps where the tracer collected. The CT or MRI acquired at the same time places that map on the anatomy.
section1.full: Pancreatic cancer cells take up glucose avidly: in mice, switching off the mutant KRAS gene that drives the cancer abolished FDG uptake within a week as the tumor regressed, because KRAS itself programs the glucose uptake [[GENE-012]]. The signal is quantified as a standardized uptake value and, more informatively, as the metabolic tumor volume, the volume of tissue above an uptake threshold. Those quantities behave differently from size. In 22 patients scanned before and after preoperative chemotherapy, the tumor's diameter fell by a median of 9.6% while its metabolic volume fell by 65%, and the PET-based response criteria agreed with the pathologist's assessment of the resected tumor in 73% of cases against 36% for size-based criteria [[DIAG-008]]. The tracer is not specific to cancer. Inflamed tissue, healing tissue and infection take it up, high blood glucose competes with it, and a prospective multicenter study found PET/CT of limited value in distinguishing cancer from chronic pancreatitis, while raising sensitivity for pancreatic cancer from 88.5% with CT to 92.7% [[SEC-DIAG-05]]. Resolution is also coarse: deposits of a few millimeters hold too little tracer to register, so a negative PET does not exclude small-volume spread, and 18% of patients whose work-up usually included PET still had occult deposits found at laparoscopy [[DIAG-002]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: PET earns its place in pancreatic cancer at two decision points. Before surgery it can reveal a distant deposit that changes the plan, and in a prospective study it changed management in about 45% of patients and stopped a planned resection in one in five. After chemotherapy it can report whether tissue still pressed against a vessel is metabolically alive, which CT cannot, at the cost of sometimes mistaking inflammation for tumor.
section2.full: The post-treatment use rests on the mismatch between anatomy and viability. Chemotherapy leaves scar that keeps the tumor's size and vessel contact, so a scan that still shows contact does not say whether anything alive remains there. In a reader study of 120 patients restaged after chemotherapy, CT alone recognized a resectable tumor 66% of the time; adding PET/MRI raised that to 86%, but specificity, the proportion of truly unresectable tumors correctly identified, fell from 67% to 59% because inflamed treated tissue also takes up tracer [[DIAG-009]]. The same study found that residual FDG uptake at the tumor-vessel contact predicted recurrence after resection with a hazard ratio (relative recurrence rate) of 4.37, the kind of viability signal anatomy cannot give [[DIAG-009]]. In the 22-patient paired-PET series, a metabolic-volume reduction below 50% independently predicted both recurrence and death [[DIAG-008]], and in a resected cohort given all chemotherapy and radiation before surgery, a complete metabolic response on interval PET tracked major pathologic response (little viable tumor left in the specimen) [[TX-L25]]. The limits run in both directions. Early PET responses have occurred in trials without any survival benefit, as when 88% of patients had a metabolic response to a CD40 antibody plus gemcitabine while 4 of 21 had a size response and median survival was 7.4 months [[TME-023]]. PET restaging is not standard in US guidance for pancreatic cancer and CT remains the preferred restaging modality, so PET is ordered when a specific question needs its answer [[DIAG-008]][[DIAG-009]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The paired-PET series had 22 patients, was retrospective and used a pathologic reference whose own reproducibility is moderate [[DIAG-008]][[DIAG-010]]. The reader study was single-center, PET/MRI was ordered as a problem-solving test in patients already thought to have responded, which biases the sample toward resectable disease, and the reference standard was partly a multidisciplinary decision rather than pathology [[DIAG-009]]. The prospective PET-PANC results are available to this atlas only as a study summary, so the numbers are stated without the detail of the full monograph [[SEC-DIAG-05]]. The total-neoadjuvant cohort is available only as an abstract and describes resected patients, not everyone who started treatment [[TX-L25]].
research_notes.how_studied: Metabolic response is scored by PERCIST, which compares the peak lean-body-mass-corrected uptake before and after therapy, and anatomic response by RECIST, the standard size-based criteria, which compare diameters; both are then matched against the regression grade assigned to the resected tumor [[DIAG-008]]. Diagnostic accuracy is measured prospectively by scanning consecutive patients with suspected pancreatic cancer and comparing CT and PET/CT reads with the final diagnosis [[SEC-DIAG-05]]. The viability inference is tested by asking whether uptake at the vessel interface predicts recurrence after resection [[DIAG-009]], and in mice by switching the driver gene off and watching tracer uptake vanish [[GENE-012]].

mechanism_notes.text: Residual FDG uptake at a treated tumor-vessel interface may mark the viable tumor that CT contact cannot distinguish from scar, because living cancer keeps its glucose metabolism while treated fibrosis is hypometabolic [[INF-DIAG-01]][[DIAG-008]][[DIAG-009]]. Post-treatment inflammation and high blood glucose both alter uptake, so the signal can over-call tumor, and the discriminating test is a point-by-point comparison of PET signal with viable tumor in the resected specimen.

glossary.definition: Fluorodeoxyglucose, a radioactive sugar that accumulates in cells with high glucose use and is imaged by PET.
A number describing how concentrated the tracer is in a region relative to the dose and body size.
The volume of tissue whose tracer uptake exceeds a chosen threshold.
Standard criteria for scoring treatment response from changes in PET tracer uptake rather than size.
A fall in tracer uptake after treatment, which can occur without any change in size.

related.statement: PET adds a viability reading to restaging after chemotherapy, where CT size and vessel contact barely change.
PET is read together with a CT acquired at the same time, which supplies the anatomy the tracer map lacks.
Residual FDG uptake at the tumor-vessel contact after chemotherapy predicted recurrence where the contact angle could not.
Mutant KRAS programs the glucose uptake that makes pancreatic cancer visible on FDG-PET.
PET cannot see millimeter-scale deposits, so staging laparoscopy still finds hidden spread in a sixth of patients scanned with it.
A PET response can occur without any survival benefit, so metabolic improvement is not the same as a clear scan.

faq.q: Why doesn't everyone with pancreatic cancer get a PET scan?
faq.a: PET is not part of the standard work-up in US guidance; CT remains the preferred scan for staging and restaging. PET adds a few points of sensitivity for distant disease, changes management in a sizeable minority, and after chemotherapy makes reads more sensitive but less specific because inflamed tissue also takes up tracer, so it is ordered when a specific question needs that answer [[SEC-DIAG-05]][[DIAG-009]].

topics.title: Staging laparoscopy
topics.orientation: Staging laparoscopy is a short keyhole operation, often done under the same anesthetic as a planned resection or before chemotherapy begins, in which the surgeon looks directly at the liver surface and the peritoneum for deposits too small for any scan to show.

section1.label: What it measures
section1.preview: Through one or two small incisions a camera is passed into the abdomen and the surgeon inspects the surfaces of the liver, the peritoneal lining and the omentum, biopsies anything suspicious, and often rinses the cavity with saline and sends the fluid for cytology, a search for free cancer cells. The test records what is visible to the eye at a scale of a millimeter or two, which is finer than a scan, on surfaces that scans see poorly.
section1.full: The yield is the fraction of patients whose scans showed disease confined to the pancreas but whose laparoscopy found otherwise. In 1,004 consecutive patients at one center, all of whom had CT and most of whom also had MRI and PET, laparoscopy was positive in 18%: visible deposits in 140 and malignant cells in the washings in 96 [[DIAG-002]]. The yield was not uniform. It was 23% in patients who had not yet received chemotherapy and 14% in those who had, and it rose with tumor size above 2 cm, with a tumor in the body or tail rather than the head, with age 60 or under, and most sharply with an indeterminate lesion outside the pancreas on imaging, which raised the odds nearly seven-fold; patients with none of the risk factors had a 1.6% yield and those with all four had 42% [[DIAG-002]]. The washings add a second measurement: malignant cells in the fluid count as hidden disease even without a visible deposit, raised CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) in the fluid raised the odds of occult metastases nearly three-fold, and CA 19-9 (the blood tumor marker) measured in the fluid reached 60% sensitivity and 77% specificity [[DIAG-002]]. A preoperative MRI reduces the number of futile operations somewhat: in a population of 4,579 pancreatectomies, futile laparotomy or staging laparoscopy occurred in 6.4% of patients who had MRI first against 9.7% who did not [[SEC-DIAG-07]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: The laparoscopy exists because pancreatic cancer spreads early and in small amounts. Modeling anchored to autopsy data suggests most patients already carry microscopic deposits at diagnosis, and the liver and peritoneum are where those deposits first become visible. Finding them before a major operation spares the patient a Whipple that could not have helped and redirects treatment to the whole body.
section2.full: Scans have a volume floor and the peritoneum is nearly flat, so a sheet of tumor a cell or two thick on the surface of the liver or the lining of the abdomen produces no mass for CT to find. That is the disease staging laparoscopy is built to catch, and the 18% figure is a direct measurement of how often the floor is crossed [[DIAG-002]]. The biology underneath is early dissemination: a branching-process model fitted to 228 patients predicted near-universal subclinical (undetectable) metastatic burden at diagnosis [[SURG-009]], and single dormant cancer cells, lacking the markers that would let a pathologist or the immune system recognize them, have been found in the livers of patients and mice [[SURG-012]]. Laparoscopy does not see those single cells either; it sees deposits that have grown large enough to be visible on a surface. What it changes is the plan: a patient found to have peritoneal deposits is treated for metastatic disease and spared a pancreatectomy with its recovery, whereas a patient whose laparoscopy is clean proceeds knowing that one more layer of hidden disease has been excluded, though not the microscopic layer. The lower yield after chemotherapy is ambiguous, since it may mean chemotherapy eradicated small deposits or that patients who progressed during chemotherapy never reached laparoscopy, and the study could not separate the two [[DIAG-002]]. US guidelines recommend the procedure selectively, for patients whose risk factors make hidden disease likely, rather than for everyone [[DIAG-002]][[SEC-SURG-11]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The yield study is retrospective and from one high-volume referral center whose practice changed over the study period, and it has no long-term outcome data for patients whose only positive finding was cytology, so the clinical meaning of cells in washings without visible disease remains uncertain [[DIAG-002]]. The futile-surgery comparison is an administrative population analysis that cannot confirm what the MRI found [[SEC-DIAG-07]][[DIAG-021]]. The dissemination model is mathematical and anchored to late-stage autopsy data, so it generates the hypothesis rather than proves it [[SURG-009]]. No multicenter prospective yield study is among the sources cited here.
research_notes.how_studied: Yield is measured as the proportion of radiographically localized patients in whom laparoscopy finds gross metastases or positive cytology, and risk factors are identified by multivariable regression against that outcome [[DIAG-002]]. Peritoneal fluid markers are evaluated by measuring CEA and CA 19-9 in the washings and computing sensitivity and specificity against the laparoscopic finding [[DIAG-002]]. Futile surgery is identified in administrative data as a laparotomy or laparoscopy without resection and compared between patients with and without preoperative MRI after propensity weighting (statistical balancing of the two groups' measured characteristics) [[SEC-DIAG-07]]. Dormant cells in the liver are identified by immunostaining for the markers the cells have lost [[SURG-012]].

mechanism_notes.text: Cancer cells that reach the liver can persist as single dormant cells under immune surveillance and later awaken, which would explain recurrences years after a clean staging and a margin-negative operation [[INF-SURG-01]][[SURG-012]]. These cells lie below the resolution of laparoscopy, scans and blood tests, so a negative staging excludes visible deposits and not the dormant layer; the competing explanation is slow continuous growth below imaging thresholds rather than true dormancy.

glossary.definition: A keyhole operation to look inside the abdomen for small deposits of cancer that scans cannot see.
Saline rinsed over the abdominal lining and collected so that any free cancer cells can be found under the microscope.
The examination of loose cells, rather than a block of tissue, for signs of cancer.
A deposit of cancer that exists but was not detected by the tests used.
An open operation begun with the intention of removing the tumor but abandoned because spread is found.

related.statement: Staging laparoscopy inspects the peritoneum directly, the surface where tiny pancreatic cancer deposits escape every scan.
Staging laparoscopy examines the surface of the liver for small deposits that CT and MRI may not show.
Staging laparoscopy finds visible deposits but not the microscopic disease that most pancreatic cancer patients carry at diagnosis.
Staging laparoscopy finds hidden spread in about one in six patients whose pancreas-protocol CT showed localized disease.
A preoperative MRI reduces, without eliminating, the number of patients whose laparoscopy or laparotomy proves futile.
An elevated CA 19-9 raises the odds that staging laparoscopy will find hidden spread.
An indeterminate lesion on imaging is the strongest single predictor that staging laparoscopy will find hidden spread.

faq.q: My scans are clear. Why does the surgeon want to do a laparoscopy first?
faq.a: Because scans cannot see thin deposits on the surface of the liver or the peritoneum, and in a large series 18% of patients with clear scans had such deposits, rising to 42% in those with several risk factors such as a body or tail tumor, a larger tumor or an ambiguous spot on imaging [[DIAG-002]]. Finding them first spares a major operation that could not have helped.

topics.title: Tumor–vessel contact and what it predicts
topics.orientation: How far a tumor wraps around the superior mesenteric vein, portal vein, superior mesenteric artery or celiac arteries is the measurement that places a pancreatic cancer in the resectable, borderline resectable or locally advanced category, and it is a probability about what the surgeon will find, not a fact about it.

section1.label: What it measures
section1.preview: On the portal-venous phase of a pancreas-protocol CT, the radiologist reports how many degrees of each vessel's circumference the tumor touches: none, 180 degrees or less (abutment), more than 180 degrees (encasement), or occlusion of the vein. The number stands in for a question the scan cannot answer directly, which is whether cancer cells have grown into the vessel wall.
section1.full: The relationship between the angle and the truth was measured in 254 head tumors with a blinded re-read of the preoperative scan and the pathology of the resected vein. Histologic invasion of the vein rose from 3% with no contact to 23% with contact of 180 degrees or less, 71% beyond 180 degrees and 80% with occlusion; the more-than-180-degree threshold predicted the need for vein resection with a positive predictive value of 89.5% (when the scan showed that much contact, the vein needed resection in 89.5% of cases) and a specificity of 97.4%, while 'any contact' was sensitive but unspecific [[DIAG-001]]. The clear-margin rate did not differ across the four categories, 92-100% in each, because surgeons who saw extensive contact planned a vein resection and took the vein with the tumor [[DIAG-001]]. The angle is read by people, and readers disagree: when a national trial re-reviewed scans centrally, 29% of patients enrolled as resectable were reclassified, with venous contact of 180 degrees or more in 35% of those and any arterial contact in 51% [[TX-013]]. Arteries are judged more strictly than veins, because an artery usually cannot be replaced the way a vein segment can and because the arteries near the pancreatic head vary: a variant right hepatic artery (replaced in about 12% of people, accessory in a further few percent) runs behind the head in about 16% of people and is itself sometimes involved by tumor [[ANAT-007]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: 'Borderline resectable' describes the tumor's relationship to vessels, not its malignancy: a borderline resectable tumor is a fully malignant adenocarcinoma whose removal with clear margins is uncertain because of vessel contact. The categories matter because they steer the sequence of treatment, and they matter less after chemotherapy, when scar at the vessel wall looks identical to tumor.
section2.full: What outcome tracks is whether cancer has invaded the vein wall, which is a pathology finding, not an imaging one. In 372 patients with resectable or venous-borderline disease, vein-wall invasion independently predicted survival and local recurrence while the measured distance to the vein margin did not [[SURG-006]], and in 117 patients resected after chemotherapy, removing the vein made no difference to survival whereas histologic venous invasion within the resected group cut median survival from 24.0 to 8.3 months [[SURG-017]]. The CT angle is the best preoperative proxy for that invasion, which is why it defines the categories, and in locally advanced disease a formal anatomic score predicted who would eventually reach resection: 49% in the most favorable group, 32% in the middle and 11% in the least favorable [[SURG-020]]. The categories lose much of their meaning after treatment. Chemotherapy or chemoradiation replaces tumor at the interface with fibrous tissue of identical density, so 70% of tumors resected after FOLFIRINOX chemotherapy still looked locally advanced or borderline, yet 92% came out with clear margins and fibrosis where the scan showed contact [[DIAG-004]], and in a chemoradiation series all nine patients whose CT showed progression of vascular contact had clear margins [[DIAG-023]]. The working rule in current practice is that persistent contact after chemotherapy is not by itself a reason to withhold exploration [[DIAG-004]][[SEC-SURG-11]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Studies disagree on whether needing a vein resection itself predicts worse survival: in the 254-patient contact series it did, 27.8 against 44.5 months, while in the post-chemotherapy series it did not and only histologic invasion mattered, a difference that likely reflects the proportion of resected veins that were truly invaded and the treatment era [[DIAG-001]][[SURG-017]]. Arterial contact was not analyzed in the main contact series, so the angle-to-invasion relationship for arteries is assumed rather than measured here [[DIAG-001]]. The central-review figure comes from a trial in which community-labeled resectable tumors were often borderline on expert reading [[TX-013]]. The locally advanced scoring series overlaps the same center's conversion-surgery cohort, so the two should not be read as independent confirmation [[SURG-020]].
research_notes.how_studied: Contact accuracy is studied by grading the tumor-vein interface on the preoperative scan, blinded to outcome, and comparing it with the pathologist's examination of the resected vein, which exists only when the vein was removed, so the reference is incomplete by design [[DIAG-001]]. Invasion versus margin distance is separated in multivariable survival models that enter both [[SURG-006]][[SURG-017]]. Reader variability is measured by central re-review of scans submitted with a local resectability label [[TX-013]]. Post-treatment discordance is measured by blinded re-reading of post-chemotherapy scans against operative and pathological findings [[DIAG-004]][[DIAG-023]].

mechanism_notes.text: Persistent tumor-vessel contact after chemotherapy is overwhelmingly fibrosis, and a functional signal at the interface, PET uptake or diffusion restriction, may separate viable tumor from scar where the contact angle cannot [[INF-DIAG-01]][[DIAG-004]][[DIAG-009]]. Post-treatment inflammation produces the same signals, so the functional read can over-call tumor just as the anatomic read over-calls contact.

The degree of vessel contact may stand in for the risk of a positive margin, which would explain why chemotherapy before surgery improves survival more clearly in borderline resectable than in cleanly resectable disease even though it improves margins and node status in both [[INF-TX-01]][[TX-004]][[TX-013]]. A chance split within an underpowered trial is the competing explanation, and the pending phase 3 trials stratified by vessel contact are the test.

glossary.definition: Tumor touching a vessel over half its circumference or less.
Tumor wrapping around more than half of a vessel's circumference.
A fully malignant tumor whose contact with vessels makes removal with clear margins uncertain; the word borderline describes the anatomy, not the cancer.
Cancer cells found growing into the wall of a vein under the microscope, as opposed to merely touching it on a scan.
A resection in which no tumor is found at the inked edges of the specimen, which does not mean no cancer remains in the body.

related.statement: Tumor contact with the superior mesenteric and portal veins is graded in degrees of circumference and predicts whether the vein will need resection.
Contact with the superior mesenteric artery is judged more strictly than venous contact because an artery usually cannot be replaced.
Variant hepatic arteries running behind the pancreatic head complicate how arterial contact is read and managed.
The degree of tumor-vessel contact is what assigns a tumor to the resectable, borderline resectable or locally advanced category.
Extensive vein contact leads the surgeon to plan a vein resection, which is why margin rates do not fall as contact rises.
After chemotherapy, persistent vessel contact on restaging scans is usually fibrosis and no longer predicts an unclear margin.
Vessel contact is the main reason chemotherapy is given before surgery, since it marks the tumors most likely to leave a positive margin.

faq.q: Does 'borderline resectable' mean the cancer is borderline, or not very malignant?
faq.a: No. The word describes the tumor's relationship to blood vessels, not its biology; a borderline resectable tumor is a fully malignant adenocarcinoma whose removal with clear margins is uncertain because it touches a vein or artery. The category is assigned from the CT contact angle, which predicts vein invasion probabilistically [[DIAG-001]].

faq.q: The scan after chemotherapy still shows the tumor against the vein. Did the chemotherapy fail?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Treated tumor at the vessel wall is replaced by fibrous scar that looks identical on CT, and in one series 70% of resected tumors still looked locally advanced or borderline after FOLFIRINOX, yet 92% were removed with clear margins [[DIAG-004]]. Persistent contact without progression elsewhere is generally a reason to explore, not to stop [[SEC-SURG-11]].

topics.title: Restaging after chemotherapy
topics.orientation: Restaging is the set of tests repeated after a course of chemotherapy, usually a pancreas-protocol CT with the blood marker CA 19-9 and sometimes PET, to decide whether the plan still holds; in pancreatic cancer it is complicated by the fact that treated tumor rarely shrinks away on the scan even when it has been largely killed.

section1.label: What it measures
section1.preview: Restaging compares a new scan with the baseline scan on three axes: has the tumor grown or shrunk, has its contact with vessels changed, and has anything appeared elsewhere. RECIST, the standard response vocabulary, scores the first axis from the change in diameter of chosen lesions. CA 19-9 adds a blood measurement that tracks tumor burden in people who make the marker, and PET adds a reading of whether the remaining tissue is metabolically active.
section1.full: In pancreatic cancer the three axes come apart. After FOLFIRINOX chemotherapy in 40 patients who went on to resection, the median diameter fell from 3.6 to 2.2 cm and the median CA 19-9 fell from 169 to 16 U/mL, yet a blinded re-read still classified 70% of the tumors as locally advanced or borderline because the contact with vessels had not changed [[DIAG-004]]. In 22 patients scanned with PET before and after preoperative therapy, diameter fell by 9.6% while metabolic volume fell by 65%; by RECIST 20 of 22 were 'stable disease', by PET criteria 14 had responded, and the PET criteria matched the pathology of the resected tumor in 73% against 36% for RECIST [[DIAG-008]]. The phrase 'not well visualized' on a restaging report usually describes this state: the tumor's edge has blurred into treated tissue and no discrete mass can be measured. In a three-reader study of 120 patients, CT alone identified a resectable tumor after therapy 66% of the time; adding PET and CA 19-9 raised sensitivity to about 85% while specificity fell from 67% to about 60%, and the CT failure was partly a reading bias, persistent contact being called unresectable [[DIAG-009]]. In a large cohort given all chemotherapy and radiation before surgery (total neoadjuvant therapy), radiologic downstaging occurred in only 28% of patients who were nonetheless resected with 94% clear margins [[TX-L25]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: The decision restaging informs is whether to operate, and after chemotherapy the answer depends less on the scan's picture of the tumor than on whether the disease has spread, whether CA 19-9 has fallen, and whether the patient is fit. A scan that looks unchanged is compatible with a tumor that is mostly scar, which is why 'no progression' rather than 'shrinkage' has become the threshold for exploring.
section2.full: The reason is histological. Treated pancreatic cancer leaves a dense fibrous bed with scattered or absent cancer cells, with the same X-ray density and the same vessel contact as the tumor it replaced; in a chemoradiation series all nine patients whose CT showed vascular contact progressing had clear margins at surgery [[DIAG-023]]. Progression elsewhere is read with more confidence, because a new liver or peritoneal deposit is a new finding rather than a reinterpretation. Blood tests carry much of the weight: CA 19-9 fell below 40 U/mL in 72% of resected patients after FOLFIRINOX against 31% before [[DIAG-004]], and in a resected cohort an 'optimal' CA 19-9 response was one of three factors independently predicting survival, with six or more cycles completed and a major pathologic response [[TX-L25]]. Chemotherapy also changes what other tests find: laparoscopy yield fell from 22% to 14% after preoperative therapy [[DIAG-002]] and tumor DNA was detectable in 21% of treated patients against 69% of untreated [[DIAG-007]], which may reflect eradication, selection of responders or suppressed shedding. Even the reference the scans are judged against is soft: pathologists grading how much tumor the treatment killed agreed only moderately, with kappa values (1 is perfect agreement, 0 is chance) of 0.33 to 0.65 and the poorest agreement for intermediate grades [[DIAG-010]][[DIAG-018]]. Where the anatomic score did improve on imaging, median survival after resection was 60.7 months against 29.8 without change [[SURG-020]]: visible improvement means something; its absence means much less.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The FOLFIRINOX series is small, single-center and limited to patients judged fit for exploration; the blinded reviewer was a surgeon, follow-up was short, and the fibrosis-versus-tumor finding is described rather than quantified [[DIAG-004]]. The paired-PET study had 22 patients [[DIAG-008]], and the reader study ordered PET/MRI as a problem-solving test in patients already thought to have responded [[DIAG-009]]. The chemoradiation series used a regimen not standard in the US, though the imaging finding generalizes, and radiation may be especially prone to producing perivascular change that mimics progression [[DIAG-023]]. Resected-cohort survival figures describe patients selected by having responded, not everyone who started chemotherapy [[TX-L25]][[SURG-020]]. The landmark statement that radiographic downstaging rarely occurs after neoadjuvant therapy is available to this atlas only as an abstract [[SEC-DIAG-06]].
research_notes.how_studied: Restaging accuracy is studied by re-reading pre- and post-treatment scans blinded to timing and comparing the assigned category with what surgery and pathology found [[DIAG-004]][[DIAG-023]]. Response criteria are compared within the same patients, RECIST from diameters and PERCIST from tracer uptake, against the regression grade of the resected specimen [[DIAG-008]]. Reader studies add modalities in sequential sessions and measure the change in sensitivity and specificity for resectability [[DIAG-009]]. Pathologic regression grading is tested by having two pathologists grade the same slides under several systems and computing agreement statistics [[DIAG-010]][[DIAG-018]]. Laparoscopy yield and tumor-DNA detection are compared between treated and untreated patients as a natural experiment [[DIAG-002]][[DIAG-007]].

mechanism_notes.text: Because treated fibrosis keeps the size and vessel contact of the tumor it replaced, restaging after chemotherapy may be better judged by functional viability at the interface, from PET uptake or diffusion restriction, than by anatomic contact [[INF-DIAG-01]][[DIAG-008]][[DIAG-009]]. Inflammation after treatment produces the same functional signals, so this is an interpretation under test, and the reference it would be tested against, pathologic regression grading, is itself only moderately reproducible [[DIAG-010]].

glossary.definition: A standard way of measuring tumor response on scans from changes in the diameters of chosen lesions.
Standard criteria for scoring treatment response from changes in PET tracer uptake rather than size.
A report phrase meaning the tumor's edge has blurred into treated tissue so that no discrete mass can be measured.
A pathologist's estimate of how much of a treated tumor is scar rather than living cancer.
A change in a tumor's category after treatment, which on scans happens far less often than clearance of the margin does.

related.statement: Restaging after chemotherapy relies on a pancreas-protocol CT compared with the baseline scan, which underestimates response.
PET measures metabolic volume at restaging, which falls far more than diameter when chemotherapy has worked.
CA 19-9 at restaging often moves when the scan does not, in people who make the marker.
Persistent vessel contact on restaging scans is usually fibrosis and no longer predicts an unclear margin.
Restaging decides whether chemotherapy given before surgery has left the tumor explorable, with no progression as the threshold.
Restaging precedes the pathology report, whose regression grade is the imperfect reference restaging scans are judged against.
Restaging is the point at which a treatment plan most often changes, in either direction.

faq.q: My restaging scan says 'stable disease'. Is the chemotherapy not working?
faq.a: Stable disease on CT is the most common finding after effective chemotherapy in pancreatic cancer, because treated tumor is replaced by scar of the same size and density. In one series 20 of 22 patients were 'stable' by size while 14 had responded by PET and most had substantial tumor kill on pathology [[DIAG-008]]; a falling CA 19-9 and the absence of new deposits are the signals that carry more weight [[DIAG-004]].

topics.title: CA 19-9
topics.orientation: CA 19-9 (carbohydrate antigen 19-9) is the blood marker followed most closely in pancreatic cancer; it rises with the amount of tumor, falls with effective treatment, and carries two traps, a group of people who cannot make it at all and a bile-duct blockage that inflates it.

section1.label: What it measures
section1.preview: CA 19-9 is not a protein but a sugar structure, sialyl Lewis-a, attached to mucins and other glycoproteins on the surface of duct cells in the pancreas, bile ducts and gut. Making it requires a working copy of the FUT3 gene, the Lewis blood-group enzyme. Pancreatic cancer cells produce the structure in large amounts and shed it into blood, where a laboratory antibody test measures it in units per milliliter.
section1.full: Because normal bile-duct cells also make CA 19-9 and clear it into bile, anything that blocks bile flow backs it up into blood. The size of that effect was measured by draining the obstruction: in patients with benign obstructive jaundice the CA 19-9 fell by a mean of 76% after drainage, while in patients with malignant obstruction it fell by 39%, the part attributable to the blockage rather than the tumor [[DIAG-016]]. The second trap is genetic. People who inherit two non-functional FUT3 alleles are Lewis-negative and make no CA 19-9 regardless of tumor burden; they were 5% of one resected cohort, defined by persistently undetectable values [[DIAG-014]], 6.6% of a 1,004-patient surgical series [[DIAG-002]] and 11.7% of 853 patients in a Chinese center, where their median survival was shorter and their CA-125 higher [[DIAG-015]]. In people who make it, the level scales with stage: median preoperative values rose from 20.5 U/mL in stage IA to 182 U/mL in stage IV among patients without jaundice [[DIAG-005]]. As a single screening-type measurement it is weak, detecting 49% of resectable cancers at a fixed threshold [[DIAG-011]], and its value lies in the trend within one person over time.

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: In someone who makes the marker and whose bile duct is not blocked, CA 19-9 is the cheapest real-time estimate of tumor burden available. Its baseline predicts how a resection is likely to go, its fall after surgery or chemotherapy is one of the strongest signs the treatment reached the disease, and its rise during follow-up often precedes a scan. None of this applies to a Lewis-negative person, whose normal value carries no information.
section2.full: The numbers behind each use come from resected cohorts. A preoperative level of 1,000 U/mL or more was associated with a median survival of 1.0 year against 2.3 years below that, and a postoperative level under 200 U/mL was the strongest single predictor of survival independent of stage [[DIAG-005]]. Normalization below 37 U/mL within six months of surgery doubled median disease-specific survival, 29.9 against 14.8 months, and patients whose level before adjuvant chemotherapy was 90 U/mL or less gained from that chemotherapy whereas those above showed no measurable benefit in that retrospective comparison [[DIAG-014]]. Before surgery, a level above 210 U/mL raised the odds of recurrence within a year 2.3-fold [[SURG-007]], and a model reading CA 19-9 together with tumor size found that about one in five up-front resections for anatomically resectable disease was futile, defined as death or recurrence within six months [[SURG-008]]. During chemotherapy before surgery the marker often moves when the scan does not: it fell from a median of 169 to 16 U/mL in patients later resected after FOLFIRINOX chemotherapy while their scans still showed vessel contact [[DIAG-004]], and adding CA 19-9 to CT improved the identification of resectable tumors after treatment [[DIAG-009]]. An elevated CA 19-9 also raised the odds of hidden spread at laparoscopy 1.7-fold [[DIAG-002]], so a high value before surgery is a reason to look harder before operating. It is measured after the bilirubin has come down, because until then the blockage and the tumor cannot be separated [[DIAG-016]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: All of the prognostic thresholds come from retrospective cohorts, and some measured survival from a postoperative draw, which excludes early deaths and flatters the apparent benefit [[DIAG-005]][[DIAG-014]]. Non-expressor status was inferred from persistently low values rather than genotype, so some low-burden secretors were misclassified, and the Lewis-negative frequency differs by ancestry, around 5-7% in European-ancestry cohorts against 11.7% in the Chinese series [[DIAG-014]][[DIAG-015]]. The drainage study's correction formula was derived and tested in the same 121 patients [[DIAG-016]]. In tumor-DNA cohorts, CA 19-9 above 90 U/mL was not an independent predictor once tumor DNA was in the model, and elevated CA 19-9 did not predict disease-free survival in a tumor-informed assay cohort [[DIAG-024]][[DIAG-012]]. The adjuvant-benefit stratification is hypothesis-generating, not randomized [[DIAG-014]].
research_notes.how_studied: The obstruction effect is measured as a before-and-after natural experiment, drawing CA 19-9 before and after biliary drainage in benign and malignant obstruction and comparing the percentage fall [[DIAG-016]]. Prognostic value is studied by dividing resected cohorts at thresholds and comparing survival by Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox models that include stage and nodes [[DIAG-005]][[DIAG-014]][[SURG-007]]. Non-secretion is identified by values persistently below 5 U/mL or by Lewis antigen testing [[DIAG-014]][[DIAG-015]]. Screening-type sensitivity is estimated case-control, comparing resectable cancers with people without known cancer at a fixed cut-off [[DIAG-011]].

glossary.definition: A sugar structure shed by pancreatic and bile-duct cells into blood, measured as a marker of pancreatic cancer burden in people who can make it.
Lacking the blood-group enzyme needed to make CA 19-9, so the marker stays low regardless of tumor burden.
A person whose CA 19-9 stays undetectable even with cancer present, usually because of Lewis-negative genotype.
The bile pigment that rises in blood when the bile duct is blocked and causes jaundice.
A fall of a tumor marker back into the reference range after treatment.

related.statement: A blocked bile duct backs CA 19-9 into the blood, inflating the value until the obstruction is relieved.
CA 19-9 is interpreted only after jaundice has resolved, because obstruction and tumor both raise it.
CEA and CA-125 are the markers followed instead of CA 19-9 in people who are Lewis-negative.
A falling CA 19-9 during preoperative chemotherapy often signals response when the restaging scan looks unchanged.
Tumor DNA in blood tracks burden independently of CA 19-9 and does not depend on Lewis genotype.
A rising CA 19-9 after surgery often precedes the scan that shows recurrence.
After a biliary stent relieves obstruction, CA 19-9 falls and the remaining value better reflects the tumor.

faq.q: My CA 19-9 was in the thousands at diagnosis. Does that mean the cancer is advanced?
faq.a: Not by itself. If you were jaundiced, a large part of the value came from the blocked bile duct; in benign obstruction three-quarters of the elevation disappears after drainage [[DIAG-016]]. The level does rise with stage in people without jaundice, so the value measured after the bilirubin has fallen is the one that carries information [[DIAG-005]].

faq.q: Is it true some people cannot make CA 19-9?
faq.a: Yes. Roughly 5-12% of people, depending on ancestry, are Lewis-negative and make none regardless of tumor burden, so their normal value carries no information [[DIAG-014]][[DIAG-015]][[DIAG-002]]. The status is usually inferred from values that stay undetectable, and CEA or CA-125 may be followed instead.

topics.title: CEA and CA-125 as alternative markers
topics.orientation: CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) and CA-125 are blood markers borrowed from other cancers; in pancreatic cancer they are followed mainly in the people who cannot make CA 19-9, and CA-125 in particular tends to track disease on the peritoneum.

section1.label: What it measures
section1.preview: CEA is a cell-surface glycoprotein that the fetal gut makes in quantity and that many adult gut cancers switch back on; it is shed into blood and measured by antibody. CA-125 is a fragment of MUC16, a very large mucin produced by the cells lining the peritoneum, pleura and pericardium and by some cancers. Neither depends on the Lewis blood-group enzyme, which is why they remain measurable in people whose CA 19-9 is undetectable from birth.
section1.full: Each marker has sources other than tumor, which sets its noise floor. CEA rises with smoking, with liver disease that slows its clearance and with inflammation of the bowel; CA-125 rises whenever the peritoneal lining is irritated, by fluid in the abdomen, by infection or by surgery, and physiologically in menstruation and pregnancy, so a single raised value has several explanations. Their relationship to pancreatic cancer was measured in a series of 853 patients: the 11.7% who were Lewis-negative had serum CA 19-9 about five-fold lower than Lewis-positive patients, as expected, but CA-125 roughly 1.9-fold higher, and their tumors stained more strongly for MUC16, 16 of 20 against 9 of 19 [[DIAG-015]]. The same patients were more often metastatic at diagnosis and had shorter survival, 7.4 against 13.3 months, so part of the higher CA-125 may reflect peritoneal disease rather than a property of Lewis-negative tumors [[DIAG-015]]. CEA appears in combination panels: in 221 resectable cancers, adding protein markers including CEA to tumor-DNA detection raised sensitivity from 30% for DNA alone to 64% for the combination, at 99.5% specificity in controls [[DIAG-011]]. In fluid washed from the abdominal cavity at staging laparoscopy, an elevated CEA raised the odds of hidden metastases nearly three-fold [[DIAG-002]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: The practical place of these markers is as substitutes and supplements. When CA 19-9 is uninformative because a person is Lewis-negative, a care team may follow CEA or CA-125 instead, reading the trend rather than any single value. Neither is endorsed in guidelines as a pancreatic monitoring marker, and no study has yet shown that following them changes outcomes.
section2.full: The case for CA-125 in Lewis-negative patients rests on biology and cross-sectional data rather than on monitoring performance: the Shanghai series showed higher serum CA-125 and higher MUC16 expression in Lewis-negative tumors but had no longitudinal CA-125 data, so whether its trajectory predicts recurrence after resection is untested [[DIAG-015]]. CA-125's origin in the peritoneal lining gives it a particular meaning in pancreatic cancer: peritoneal spread is common, is poorly seen on scans, and irritates the mesothelial cells that make MUC16, so a rising CA-125 with a clear scan raises the question of peritoneal disease specifically [[DIAG-002]]. CEA's meaning is less specific. It is one of the markers used to define minimal residual disease in trials: a phase 1 vaccine study enrolled patients with no disease on imaging who were positive for residual disease by tumor DNA or by CA 19-9 or CEA, with 7 of 25 qualifying on the serum markers alone [[IMM-003]]. Long-term survivors of pancreatic cancer have been found enriched for immune responses against MUC16-derived neoantigens, the new protein fragments created by tumor mutations, which places the CA-125 molecule on the tumor cell as well as in the blood [[TME-006]]. For a person reading their own results, the useful questions are whether they make CA 19-9, which marker their team has chosen to follow and why, and whether a change is a trend across several draws or a single value with another explanation.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The evidence here is thin and indirect. The Lewis-negative series is single-center, did not separate low-secretor Lewis-positive patients, and offers no monitoring data, so CA-125's value as a substitute is an inference from its higher baseline rather than a demonstrated performance [[DIAG-015]]. The combination-panel sensitivity comes from a case-control design that inflates specificity relative to a screening population and did not report CEA's own contribution [[DIAG-011]]. The washings CEA finding is from one center [[DIAG-002]]. The vaccine trial defined residual disease inconsistently across tumor DNA and serum markers in a 25-patient phase 1 [[IMM-003]]. CA-125 is not guideline-endorsed as a pancreatic monitoring marker and is used empirically [[DIAG-015]].
research_notes.how_studied: Marker levels are compared between Lewis-negative and Lewis-positive patients, and tumor expression of MUC16 is checked by immunohistochemistry on resected tissue to see whether the serum difference reflects the tumor [[DIAG-015]]. Panel performance is measured by thresholding each protein and tumor-DNA assay in cases and controls and reporting sensitivity at a fixed specificity [[DIAG-011]]. Peritoneal-fluid markers are measured in laparoscopic washings and related to the laparoscopic finding [[DIAG-002]]. Neoantigen immunity against MUC16 was identified by predicting neoantigens from tumor sequencing and testing T-cell reactivity in long-term survivors [[TME-006]].

glossary.definition: Carcinoembryonic antigen, a glycoprotein made by fetal gut and by many adult gut cancers, measured in blood as a tumor marker.
A fragment of the mucin MUC16 shed by the lining of the abdominal cavity and by some cancers, measured in blood.
The very large mucin molecule whose shed fragment is measured as CA-125.
The single layer of cells lining the peritoneum, pleura and pericardium, which makes MUC16.
A substance measurable in blood whose level tends to track the amount of cancer present.

related.statement: CEA and CA-125 are followed in place of CA 19-9 in people who are Lewis-negative and cannot make it.
CA-125 is made by the cells lining the peritoneum, so it tends to rise with peritoneal spread of pancreatic cancer.
Elevated CEA in the fluid washed from the abdomen at staging laparoscopy predicts hidden metastases.
Serum markers such as CEA are combined with tumor DNA in detection panels and in trial definitions of residual disease.
MUC16, the source of CA-125, carries neoantigens that long-term survivors' T cells have been found to recognize.

faq.q: I am Lewis-negative. Which marker should be followed instead of CA 19-9?
faq.a: There is no guideline-endorsed substitute. CA-125 was about twice as high in Lewis-negative as in Lewis-positive patients in one series and their tumors expressed more of its parent molecule, which is the basis for following it, but no study has shown that its trend predicts recurrence [[DIAG-015]]. CEA is the other common choice; whichever is used, the trend across draws matters more than any single value.

topics.title: Circulating tumor DNA and minimal residual disease
topics.orientation: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is the fraction of the DNA fragments floating in blood plasma that came from cancer cells; a test that looks for it after surgery is called a minimal residual disease (MRD) test, and in pancreatic cancer its positive results are strong while its negative results are weak.

section1.label: What it measures
section1.preview: Dying cells release short DNA fragments into the blood, where they circulate for a matter of hours before being cleared. Most come from blood cells; a tumor contributes a small fraction, identifiable because the fragments carry the tumor's mutations, most often in the KRAS gene. A ctDNA test sequences the plasma DNA and counts fragments carrying those mutations, either in a fixed set of hotspots or, in tumor-informed designs, in a panel of variants chosen from the patient's own tumor.
section1.full: The quantity measured is the number of mutant fragments in a few milliliters of plasma, and that number sets the test's limit. Detection scales with tumor burden: a foundational survey found ctDNA in more than 75% of patients with advanced pancreatic cancer and in 48% with localized disease [[DIAG-006]], and in 221 resectable cancers a KRAS assay sensitive to one mutant template in 10,000 detected ctDNA in 30%, ranging from 0% in stage IB to 35% in stage IIB, while every mutation found in plasma matched the tumor [[DIAG-011]]. A tumor-informed 16-variant assay, which removes the blind spot for tumors without a hotspot mutation, was still positive in only 29% of patients in the window two to twelve weeks after surgery [[DIAG-012]]. The floor has a physical component. In 34 patients sampled during their operation, mechanically mobilizing the tumor raised peripheral ctDNA 2.5-fold and converted a negative sample to a positive one, and sampling the portal vein did not improve detection over an arm vein [[DIAG-025]]. Plasma can also carry mutations that are not from the tumor: clonal hematopoiesis, the expansion of mutated blood-cell clones with age, produced one plasma-only mutation in a concordance series, a source of false positives for assays that are not tumor-informed [[DIAG-026]]. When tissue is scarce, plasma recovered the genotype in 78% of cases whose biopsy had failed sequencing [[DIAG-026]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: After a pancreatic resection, finding ctDNA means recurrence is very likely and usually arrives months before a scan shows it. Not finding it means the test found nothing, which is different from nothing being there: in one cohort only about half of test-negative patients were alive two years later. No ctDNA test is approved in the US for pancreatic cancer as of 8 October 2026; those in use are laboratory-developed tests, and treatment changes based on them are being studied in trials.
section2.full: The positive side is consistent across cohorts. In 41 patients sampled a median of 24 days after surgery, ctDNA was present in 11, and 10 of those 11 recurred, with median recurrence-free survival of 5 months against 15; during surveillance the test caught 90% of recurrences a median of 84 days before the clinic did [[DIAG-007]]. In the tumor-informed cohort a positive postoperative test carried a hazard ratio (relative recurrence rate) of 5.45, and during surveillance 12.38 [[DIAG-012]], and in a stage II series ctDNA flagged progression a mean of 6.5 months before CT [[DIAG-013]]. The negative side is the problem. Among 72 patients negative by a three-allele KRAS assay, one that checks only three KRAS mutations, two-year survival was 53% [[DIAG-024]], and in the surveillance cohort the negative predictive value was 82%, with 3 of 17 patients who stayed negative still recurring [[DIAG-007]]. Three explanations compete: residual disease that sheds little DNA, too few mutant copies in a blood draw even when shedding occurs, and assays blind to a particular tumor's mutations [[DIAG-024]][[DIAG-025]][[DIAG-011]]; in other tumor types plasma missed a tissue-confirmed KRAS allele in 7% to 27% of patients depending on the cancer [[RAS-022]]. In research, ctDNA selects patients with residual disease for trials, as in a vaccine study whose entrants had clear scans but positive ctDNA or serum markers [[IMM-003]], and serial plasma sequencing during KRAS-directed treatment has revealed resistance mutations [[RAS-015]][[RAS-012]]. No ctDNA assay is FDA-approved for pancreatic cancer; the only approved MRD companion diagnostic is for bladder cancer [[SEC-DIAG-04]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The prognostic cohorts are small, single-institution or commercial-database based, recurrence was defined radiographically, and follow-up is short relative to how late pancreatic cancer can recur [[DIAG-007]][[DIAG-012]][[DIAG-013]]. The two-year survival among test-negative patients was measured with a three-allele assay that misses the 18% of tumors in that cohort without a hotspot mutation, so some negatives were assay blind spots rather than low shedding [[DIAG-024]]. The plasma-tissue concordance series was in advanced disease, where ctDNA is abundant; concordance is expected to fall in resectable disease near the detection floor [[DIAG-026]]. Whether acting on a positive result, by starting or changing treatment earlier, improves survival has not been shown and is a trial question [[DIAG-013]]. Lower detectability after preoperative chemotherapy, 21% against 69%, cannot be separated into eradication and suppressed shedding [[DIAG-007]].
research_notes.how_studied: Detection studies sequence plasma from patients of known stage and report the fraction positive, with specificity measured in people without cancer [[DIAG-006]][[DIAG-011]]. Prognostic studies draw plasma at fixed times after surgery, blind the clinicians to the result, and compare recurrence-free survival by status [[DIAG-007]][[DIAG-012]]. Lead time is the interval between the first positive plasma sample and the first scan showing recurrence [[DIAG-013]]. The physical limit is probed by sampling before and after the tumor is handled during surgery and by comparing portal and peripheral blood [[DIAG-025]]. Concordance is tested by sequencing paired tissue and plasma from the same patients [[DIAG-026]]. Tumor-informed assays are built by sequencing the resected tumor first and then tracking a personal set of variants [[DIAG-012]].

mechanism_notes.text: A negative ctDNA test after surgery is weak reassurance partly for physical reasons: at low tumor fractions the limiting factor is the handful of mutant DNA copies that a standard blood tube can contain, so larger plasma volumes, pooled serial draws or better-timed draws should raise sensitivity if the residual cells shed at all [[INF-DIAG-02]][[DIAG-025]][[DIAG-011]]. If residual pancreatic cancer is intrinsically low-shedding, as a desmoplastic (scar-rich), low-cellularity tumor might be, no practical increase in sample volume will close the gap, and the 53% two-year survival among test-negative patients marks how wide it is [[DIAG-024]].

Disseminated cells can persist in the liver as single dormant cells that neither divide nor shed, which would produce long ctDNA-negative intervals before a late relapse [[INF-SURG-01]][[SURG-012]]. The competing explanation is slow continuous growth below detection thresholds; serial ctDNA sampling with profiling of relapsing lesions is the test.

When preoperative chemotherapy leaves no viable tumor in the resected pancreas, recurrence can still follow because chemo-tolerant disseminated cells persist elsewhere, and ctDNA at the time of such a resection should predict recurrence better than the pathology alone [[INF-SURG-03]][[SURG-018]]. The competing explanations are that some such patients are cured and that other recurrences arise from under-sampled residual primary; correlating ctDNA at resection with the site of first recurrence would separate them.

glossary.definition: Fragments of DNA shed by cancer cells into the blood, identified by the tumor's mutations.
All the DNA fragments floating in blood plasma, most of which come from normal blood cells.
Cancer that remains after treatment in amounts too small for scans to show.
A ctDNA test designed around mutations first found by sequencing the patient's own tumor.
Age-related growth of blood-cell clones carrying mutations, which can appear in plasma and mimic tumor DNA.
The proportion of people with a negative test who truly do not have the condition being tested for.

related.statement: Circulating tumor DNA is the only routine test that can register microscopic disease, and it detects less than half of it.
A rise in circulating tumor DNA precedes the scan that shows recurrence by a median of three to six months.
Circulating tumor DNA can be positive while the scan is clear, and negative while microscopic disease remains.
Tumor DNA and CA 19-9 are independent blood markers, and tumor DNA works in people who cannot make CA 19-9.
Most ctDNA tests in pancreatic cancer look for the KRAS mutations that nearly all these tumors carry.
Plasma sequencing can supply the tumor's genotype when a biopsy sample is too sparse for molecular testing.
KRAS vaccine trials have used circulating tumor DNA to select patients with residual disease and to follow their response.
Serial plasma sequencing during RAS inhibitor treatment has identified the mutations that drive resistance.

faq.q: My ctDNA test after surgery was negative. Does that mean the cancer is gone?
faq.a: It means the test found no tumor DNA in that blood sample, which lowers but does not remove the chance of recurrence. In one cohort two-year survival among test-negative patients was 53%, and in another 3 of 17 patients who stayed negative throughout follow-up still recurred, because residual disease can shed too little DNA for a single tube of blood to capture [[DIAG-024]][[DIAG-007]].

faq.q: Is Signatera or any ctDNA test approved for pancreatic cancer?
faq.a: No ctDNA assay is FDA-approved as a companion diagnostic for pancreatic cancer as of 8 October 2026; the one approved MRD assay is for bladder cancer, and pancreatic use is as a laboratory-developed test [[SEC-DIAG-04]]. The evidence that a positive result predicts recurrence is strong, but whether changing treatment because of it improves survival is still being tested [[DIAG-012]][[DIAG-013]].

topics.title: The pathology report: margins, nodes and regression
topics.orientation: The pathology report is the examination of the removed pancreas, nodes and vessels under the microscope; it fixes the stage that scans could only estimate, and the three lines read most closely are the margin, the lymph nodes and, after preoperative treatment, how much tumor the treatment killed.

section1.label: What it measures
section1.preview: The pathologist inks the surfaces of the specimen, slices it, and records for each slice whether tumor reaches the ink, how many lymph nodes were found and how many contain cancer, how the tumor cells are built (differentiation), whether they have entered small vessels, lymphatics or nerves, and the T and N stage that follow. After chemotherapy, a regression grade estimates the fraction of the tumor bed that is scar rather than living cancer.
section1.full: The margin rule in common use calls a resection R1 when tumor lies within 1 millimeter of an inked surface and R0 when it does not, a standard that, once adopted, reclassified many 'clear' resections as R1 [[SEC-SURG-04]], with wider clearance associated with better survival in later series [[SEC-SURG-05]][[SEC-SURG-06]]. Nodes carry more prognostic weight than the tumor's size. In 1,525 resected head cancers, five-year survival was 35.6% with no positive nodes, 20.8% with one to three (N1) and 10.9% with four or more (N2), and once nodes were negative the tumor's size no longer separated survival [[DIAG-017]]; a 2,318-patient validation found the same size and node cut-offs and a concordance of only 0.58, meaning stage explains a minority of the variation in outcome [[DIAG-003]]. The lymph node ratio, positive nodes divided by nodes examined, above 0.2 raised the odds of recurrence within a year 2.5-fold, poor differentiation 1.7-fold and lymphovascular invasion 1.7-fold [[SURG-007]]. For a tumor on the vein, whether cancer has invaded the vein wall predicted survival and local recurrence better than the distance to the vein margin [[SURG-006]]. The report also depends on how much of the specimen was examined: submitting the entire tumor and pancreas found more nodes and assigned lower ypT and ypN stages (the T and N stages assigned after preoperative treatment) than partial sampling, partly because thorough submission was reserved for near-complete responders [[SURG-005]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: In pancreatic cancer the report explains why an operation that removed everything visible is followed by chemotherapy: at diagnosis microscopic spread is usually already present, so R0 describes the specimen's edges, not the body. Preoperative chemotherapy changes the report, lowering node positivity and nerve invasion, and in about 3% of cases leaves no cancer at all, a finding associated with much longer survival but not with cure.
section2.full: Two comparisons show what chemotherapy before surgery does to the specimen. After FOLFIRINOX chemotherapy, 35% of resected tumors had positive nodes against 79% with surgery first, and perineural invasion (cancer growing along nerves) fell from 95% to 72% [[DIAG-004]]; in a randomized trial of preoperative chemoradiation, node positivity was 33% against 78%, perineural invasion 39% against 73% and venous invasion 19% against 36% [[TX-004]]. A pathologic complete response, no viable tumor found, occurred in 3.3% of 5,402 patients resected after neoadjuvant (preoperative) therapy in a US national database, more often after total neoadjuvant therapy (all planned chemotherapy given before surgery), and carried a median survival of 64.9 against 21.6 months; it marks favorable biology, may partly reflect sampling, and recurrence still follows it in some patients [[SURG-018]]. Regression grading is the least reproducible line on the report: two pathologists grading 97 specimens agreed with kappa values (1 is perfect agreement, 0 is chance) from 0.33 to 0.65 depending on the system, worst for intermediate grades, and only an area-based measure of residual tumor related to survival [[DIAG-010]]; a FOLFIRINOX series found concordance of 0.52 to 0.64 and no relationship between grade and survival [[DIAG-018]]. Node stations matter anatomically as well as numerically: head cancers most often involve the posterior-head and superior-mesenteric-artery stations, and median survival fell from 115.9 months with no positive nodes to 24.6 with four or more in one Japanese series [[ANAT-019]]. Node-negative, margin-negative patients still recur at distant sites, the clearest sign that the report describes the specimen and not the disease [[SURG-007]][[DIAG-017]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The margin thresholds rest on sources available only as abstracts [[SEC-SURG-04]][[SEC-SURG-05]][[SEC-SURG-06]], and the margin's independent effect shrinks once vein-wall invasion is in the model [[SURG-006]]. Staging validations used R0-only, high-volume cohorts, with cut-offs found by partitioning the same data they validate [[DIAG-003]][[DIAG-017]]. The sampling study is confounded because complete submission was chosen for the specimens with least residual tumor [[SURG-005]]. The complete-response figure comes from registry coding without central review [[SURG-018]]. The regression-grading studies had two observers each, and the Japanese cohort used gemcitabine-based regimens that may regress tumors differently from FOLFIRINOX [[DIAG-010]][[DIAG-018]]. A stain for the SMAD4 tumor-suppressor protein on the specimen correlated with widespread rather than local failure in an autopsy series, but in 127 resected patients it showed no relationship to the pattern of recurrence, so it is not a routine prognostic line [[GENE-028]][[GENE-023]].
research_notes.how_studied: Margins are studied by inking surfaces under a standardized protocol and measuring the distance from tumor to ink in millimeters, then relating categories to survival [[SEC-SURG-04]]. Staging systems are validated by applying old and new editions to the same resected cohorts and comparing how well each separates survival, using concordance statistics [[DIAG-003]][[DIAG-017]]. Regression grading reproducibility is measured by having pathologists grade the same slides independently under several systems and computing kappa or Kendall agreement [[DIAG-010]][[DIAG-018]]. Vein-wall invasion and margin distance are entered together in multivariable models to see which carries independent information [[SURG-006]]. Sampling effects are measured by comparing stage assignments between entirely and partially submitted specimens [[SURG-005]].

mechanism_notes.text: A pathologic complete response can be followed by recurrence because preoperative chemotherapy clears the sampled primary while chemo-tolerant disseminated cells persist in the liver and elsewhere, so the response is a local finding with residual systemic disease [[INF-SURG-03]][[SURG-018]][[SURG-005]]. Some such patients are cured, and some recurrences may arise from under-sampled residual primary; ctDNA at the time of resection is the test that would separate these.

glossary.definition: A resection in which no tumor lies within 1 millimeter of the inked edge of the specimen, which does not mean no cancer remains in the body.
A resection in which tumor lies at or within 1 millimeter of an inked edge of the specimen.
The number of cancer-containing lymph nodes divided by the number of nodes examined.
The tumor stage assigned by the pathologist after preoperative treatment, the y marking that treatment came first.
A pathologist's estimate of how much of a treated tumor is scar rather than living cancer.
No living cancer cells found anywhere in the examined specimen after preoperative treatment.
How closely the cancer cells resemble normal cells; poorly differentiated tumors look least like their tissue of origin.
Cancer cells found growing along or within nerves in the specimen.

related.statement: The pathology report counts the lymph nodes removed and the number containing cancer, which separates survival more strongly than tumor size.
The Whipple specimen is what the pathology report examines, with the vein margin and the retroperitoneal margin inked separately.
The pathology report describes the specimen's edges, and microscopic disease beyond them is why R0 is not cure.
Whether cancer has invaded the wall of a resected vein predicts outcome better than the distance to the vein margin.
The regression grade on the pathology report is the reference restaging scans are judged against, and pathologists agree on it only moderately.
The pathology report assigns the final T and N stage that scans could only estimate.
Perineural invasion recorded on the pathology report marks cancer growing along the nerves around the pancreas.
Chemotherapy before surgery lowers node positivity and nerve invasion in the specimen, which the pathology report records as ypN and ypT.

faq.q: My report says R0. Does that mean they got it all?
faq.a: R0 means no tumor was found within 1 millimeter of the inked edges of the specimen, which is the best result an operation can produce. It describes the specimen, not the body: patients with negative margins and negative nodes still recur at distant sites because microscopic spread is usually present before surgery, which is why chemotherapy follows [[SURG-007]][[DIAG-017]].

faq.q: What does a lymph node ratio of 0.3 mean?
faq.a: It means that 30% of the lymph nodes the pathologist examined contained cancer, for example 6 of 20. A ratio above 0.2 raised the odds of recurrence within a year about 2.5-fold in a large series, and the number of positive nodes separates survival more strongly than the tumor's size [[SURG-007]][[DIAG-017]].

topics.title: Small liver spots and what they can be
topics.orientation: A report that mentions a small spot in the liver that is 'too small to characterize' or 'indeterminate' is common in pancreatic cancer, and most such spots are not metastases; what settles them is usually MRI and, failing that, a repeat scan after an interval.

section1.label: What it measures
section1.preview: A liver 'lesion' is anything in the liver that differs from the surrounding tissue on a scan. Small cysts, which are fluid-filled, and hemangiomas, which are tangles of blood vessels, are common in healthy adults and are the usual cause of an incidental spot. A metastasis is a cluster of cancer cells with its own blood supply. Each has a signature on MRI that CT cannot always read when the spot is only a few millimeters across.
section1.full: On CT a tiny spot is a few pixels of lower density, which a cyst, a hemangioma and a metastasis all produce, and the scanner's slice thickness blurs the edges of anything smaller than the slice. MRI reads the same spot with several independent properties.
