action_note.text: For several days after each infusion, avoid cold drinks, cold air on bare skin and handling cold objects; the acute cold-triggered symptoms, including a frightening sense of throat tightness, are expected and pass within days [[SEC-SUPP-12]][[TX-022]]. Tell the care team before the next cycle if tingling or numbness no longer clears between cycles, or if you start dropping objects, struggling with buttons or feeling unsteady, because dose adjustment at that point is what limits permanent damage [[SEC-SUPP-07]]. A temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher during chemotherapy needs a same-day call, since low white cells can turn an infection dangerous within hours [[SEC-SUPP-03]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The neuropathy time course [[TX-022]] comes from people with colon cancer receiving 12 cycles of FOLFOX, nested in a trial whose calcium and magnesium intervention failed; it transfers to pancreatic cancer on the assumption that the toxicity depends on the drug rather than the tumor, and cumulative doses differ between regimens. The prevention trials [[SUPP-010]] and the duloxetine trial [[SUPP-026]] likewise enrolled mostly colorectal and breast cancer patients. The adjuvant discontinuation figures [[TX-003]] describe fit patients under 80 with good recovery after surgery. Second-line oxaliplatin after gemcitabine gave conflicting randomized results, better survival in one trial (5.9 versus 3.3 months) and worse in another (6.1 versus 9.9 months), so its place after gemcitabine depends on schedule, fitness and what treatment follows [[TX-L04]][[TX-L05]].
research_notes.how_studied: Acute neuropathy was captured with daily 0 to 10 symptom diaries for five days after each infusion, and chronic neuropathy with a standard chemotherapy-neuropathy questionnaire (EORTC CIPN20) before each cycle and for 18 months afterwards, giving within-person trajectories rather than a single severity grade [[TX-022]]. Prevention trials randomize a candidate protector against placebo and count patient-reported moderate-to-severe neuropathy at a fixed time, here nine months [[SUPP-010]]. The duloxetine trial used a blinded crossover design with the Brief Pain Inventory, so each participant's pain on the drug could be compared with their own pain on placebo [[SUPP-026]]. Dose-intensity reporting in the adjuvant trial, the fraction of the planned dose actually delivered, is what reveals how often oxaliplatin is dropped [[TX-003]].

mechanism_notes.text: The acute cold-triggered symptoms and the chronic numbness are thought to arise differently: the acute form behaves like a transient disturbance of nerve-membrane ion channels that resolves as the drug clears, whereas the chronic form tracks cumulative platinum accumulation in sensory nerve cell bodies, which lack the barrier that shields the brain [[TX-022]]. The observation that first-cycle acute severity predicted later chronic damage suggests shared susceptibility, and the failure of an antioxidant strategy, which made neuropathy worse, argues that oxidative stress alone does not explain the injury [[SUPP-010]].

topics.clinical_status: Oxaliplatin is approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 for colorectal cancer only. In pancreatic cancer its use is off-label for the drug but guideline-recommended practice within FOLFIRINOX, and it is a named partner drug in the FDA-approved NALIRIFOX regimen (liposomal irinotecan label, 13 Feb 2024) for first-line metastatic disease.

glossary.definition: A platinum atom chemically bonded to DNA bases, distorting the helix and blocking copying.
Damage to the nerves of the hands and feet causing tingling, numbness or pain.
An unpleasant tingling or tightness triggered by touching or swallowing something cold.
The share of the planned chemotherapy dose actually delivered over the planned time.
A DNA repair system that fixes double-strand breaks using the matching chromosome as a template.
Chemotherapy given after surgery to reduce the chance of recurrence.

related.statement: Oxaliplatin is one of the four drugs in FOLFIRINOX and the usual reason the regimen is modified over time.
Oxaliplatin is given at a lower dose in NALIRIFOX than in FOLFIRINOX, with less neuropathy reported.
Oxaliplatin causes the cold-triggered and chronic sensory neuropathy described under neuropathy.
Oxaliplatin was added to fluorouracil and leucovorin in the trial design that FOLFIRINOX builds on.
Oxaliplatin and irinotecan are the two partner drugs that distinguish FOLFIRINOX from fluorouracil alone.
Homologous-recombination defects such as BRCA or PALB2 loss make tumors more sensitive to oxaliplatin and other platinum drugs.
Oxaliplatin-based second-line chemotherapy after gemcitabine has conflicting randomized results.
Oxaliplatin works by creating DNA crosslinks that the cell’s repair and checkpoint systems must resolve or die.
Oxaliplatin lowers white cells, so fever during treatment with it is handled as a possible neutropenic infection.

faq.q: Will the numbness go away?
faq.a: For many people it improves but slowly: in a prospective study, numbness kept worsening for about three months after the last dose, and at 18 months half had near-complete recovery, a third had mild residual symptoms, and one in five still had severe symptoms [[TX-022]]. How bad the first-cycle symptoms were predicted the long-term outcome.

faq.q: Why would my oncologist drop oxaliplatin but keep the other drugs?
faq.a: Because the nerve damage is cumulative and the rest of the regimen keeps working without it. In the adjuvant trial 55% of patients stopped oxaliplatin before completing all cycles and the regimen still improved survival over gemcitabine [[TX-003]]; guideline advice is that dose reduction or stopping is the only proven way to limit permanent neuropathy [[SEC-SUPP-07]].

faq.q: Why do I have to avoid cold after an infusion?
faq.a: Cold triggers an acute nerve reaction in most people on oxaliplatin, with tingling in the hands, throat discomfort on swallowing cold drinks and cramps, peaking around day three [[TX-022]]. The label advises avoiding cold exposure in the days after each dose; the reaction is unpleasant and alarming but passes [[SEC-SUPP-12]].

topics.title: Irinotecan
topics.orientation: Irinotecan is a chemotherapy drug that works by trapping an enzyme on DNA; it is part of FOLFIRINOX, and a liposome-wrapped form is approved in the US for metastatic pancreatic cancer. Its two main harms, low white cells and diarrhea, both depend on how quickly a person's liver enzyme UGT1A1 clears its active metabolite.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: Irinotecan is a prodrug: enzymes in the liver and in tumor convert it to SN-38, a far more potent molecule. SN-38 binds topoisomerase I, the enzyme that nicks one DNA strand to relieve twisting while DNA is copied, and freezes it on the DNA so the nick cannot be resealed [[TX-L21]]. When the DNA-copying machinery, the replication fork, runs into the trapped complex, the single-strand nick becomes a double-strand break, and a dividing cell that accumulates such breaks dies.
section1.full: SN-38 is inactivated when the liver enzyme UGT1A1 attaches a sugar group to it and sends it into bile; bacteria in the gut can strip that sugar off again, releasing active SN-38 onto the intestinal lining, which is why diarrhea arrives days after a dose and tends to be worse in people who clear SN-38 slowly. A separate early diarrhea, with sweating and cramps during or just after the infusion, comes from irinotecan's stimulation of the nerves that drive gut secretion and is treated with atropine rather than loperamide [[SEC-SUPP-11]]. In FOLFIRINOX, irinotecan joins oxaliplatin, fluorouracil and leucovorin; the adjuvant trial lowered its dose after an early safety review and still produced median overall survival of 53.5 versus 35.5 months with gemcitabine [[TX-003]]. Liposomal irinotecan wraps the drug in a lipid shell that keeps it circulating longer, and it holds the only US approvals for pancreatic cancer among irinotecan products: with fluorouracil and leucovorin after gemcitabine-based therapy, where median survival was 6.1 versus 4.2 months and the liposomal drug alone did nothing (hazard ratio 0.99), and in the first-line NALIRIFOX regimen, which beat gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel by 11.1 versus 9.2 months [[TX-014]][[TX-002]][[SEC-TX-02]]. Conventional irinotecan's own label still lists only colorectal cancer, so its FOLFIRINOX use is guideline-based rather than labeled [[SEC-GENE-01]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: The dose of SN-38 a person actually experiences depends on inherited versions of UGT1A1. The current US irinotecan label, revised 13 May 2026, states that people with two low-activity copies (UGT1A1*28/*28, *6/*6 or *6/*28) are poor metabolizers at increased risk of severe or life-threatening neutropenia (a shortage of infection-fighting white cells), advises considering genotype testing, and advises considering a lower starting dose for them while noting that the precise reduction is not known [[SEC-GENE-01]].
section2.full: Two kinds of evidence fill in what the label leaves open. Among 154 Korean patients on FOLFIRINOX, febrile neutropenia, fever with dangerously low white cells, struck 20.1%, mostly within the first four cycles, and intermediate or poor UGT1A1 metabolizers had about four times the hazard, with women and less fit people also at higher risk [[SUPP-006]]. In six Dutch hospitals where poor metabolizers routinely start at 70% of the dose, 779 patients were followed, 396 of them with pancreatic cancer: the dose-reduced poor metabolizers had severe toxicity no more often than fully dosed others, and their progression-free and overall survival were indistinguishable (adjusted hazard ratios 1.02 and 1.10), which bounds any survival cost of the reduction as small [[GENE-018]]. A smaller real-world comparison found genotype-guided dosing cut clinically relevant toxicity from 43.3% to 16.0% across variants of UGT1A1 and of DPYD, the gene that governs fluorouracil clearance [[GENE-019]]. Diarrhea is the other decision-relevant harm: grade 3 to 4 (severe) diarrhea affected 20% on NALIRIFOX versus 5% on gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, and 13% with liposomal irinotecan plus fluorouracil second line [[TX-002]][[TX-014]]. The liposomal label carries boxed warnings for severe neutropenia and diarrhea and names loperamide for late diarrhea of any severity [[SEC-SUPP-11]]. US guidelines class FOLFIRINOX as high risk for febrile neutropenia, which is why preventive white-cell growth factor is often considered from the first cycle [[SUPP-006]].

action_note.heading: When to call the care team now
action_note.text: A temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher at any time during irinotecan-containing chemotherapy is treated as an emergency until the white-cell count is known, because neutropenic infection can become life-threatening within hours and antibiotics are meant to start within an hour of arrival [[SEC-SUPP-03]][[SEC-SUPP-01]]. Diarrhea that begins more than a day after the infusion should be reported at the first loose stool so the loperamide plan on the label can start, and diarrhea with fever, dizziness or blood, or that persists despite loperamide, needs same-day contact; the next dose is withheld for grade 2 (moderate) or worse diarrhea [[SEC-SUPP-11]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The febrile-neutropenia cohort [[SUPP-006]] is single-center, retrospective and Korean, where the *6 allele is common while *28 predominates in people of European ancestry, so its hazard ratios transfer as direction more than magnitude. The Dutch survival cohort [[GENE-018]] compared poor metabolizers on reduced doses with others on full doses rather than randomizing dose, so it cannot prove equivalence, and toxicity was recorded only for three cycles. The mixed-variant toxicity comparison [[GENE-019]] had small per-variant subgroups and several non-significant contrasts. The NAPOLI-1 figures [[TX-014]] are available only from the abstract and trial registry, and the comparator fluorouracil schedule was not stated. None of the sources cited here compares liposomal with conventional irinotecan head to head in pancreatic cancer.
research_notes.how_studied: UGT1A1 status is determined by genotyping the promoter repeat (*28) and the coding variant (*6) and assigning a predicted metabolizer phenotype, which studies then relate to measured SN-38 exposure and to toxicity graded by the Common Terminology Criteria [[SEC-GENE-01]][[GENE-018]]. Febrile neutropenia is defined by a temperature threshold together with a neutrophil count below 500 per microliter, which makes it a reproducible endpoint across cohorts [[SEC-SUPP-01]]. Randomized regimen trials report grade 3 to 4 diarrhea and neutropenia in the safety population alongside survival in everyone randomized, so toxicity and benefit can be read against the same denominators [[TX-002]]. The topoisomerase mechanism was established biochemically with purified enzyme and DNA, showing protein-linked strand breaks only when the enzyme was present [[TX-L21]].

mechanism_notes.text: The label's advice to consider but not require genotyping, and to reduce the dose by an unspecified amount, reflects a gap that the Dutch cohort partly fills: a 30% starting-dose reduction in poor metabolizers equalized severe toxicity without a detectable survival penalty, consistent with toxicity tracking SN-38 exposure while anti-tumor effect saturates within the usual dose range [[GENE-018]][[SEC-GENE-01]]. The competing explanation is that poor metabolizers who did well were a selected fit subgroup; a randomized comparison of dosing strategies would settle it.

topics.clinical_status: Conventional irinotecan is approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 for colorectal cancer only; its use in FOLFIRINOX for pancreatic cancer is off-label for the drug but guideline-recommended. Liposomal irinotecan (Onivyde) is approved in the US for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma with fluorouracil and leucovorin after gemcitabine-based therapy (22 Oct 2015) and with oxaliplatin, fluorouracil and leucovorin as first-line treatment (13 Feb 2024); it is not approved as a single agent.

glossary.definition: An enzyme that cuts and reseals one DNA strand to relieve twisting during copying.
The active metabolite of irinotecan, many times more potent than the parent drug.
A liver enzyme that inactivates SN-38; inherited low-activity versions raise toxicity.
A person who inherits two low-activity copies of a drug-clearing gene and so has higher drug exposure.
Fever occurring while the infection-fighting white cells are dangerously low.
A drug enclosed in a tiny fat bubble so that it circulates longer and is released slowly.
Diarrhea beginning more than a day after an irinotecan dose, caused by SN-38 released in the gut.

related.statement: Irinotecan is one of the four drugs in FOLFIRINOX and the main source of its diarrhea and neutropenia.
Liposomal irinotecan is the irinotecan component of NALIRIFOX, the regimen approved first line in 2024.
Liposomal irinotecan with fluorouracil and leucovorin is an approved second-line option after gemcitabine-based therapy.
Inherited UGT1A1 variants slow the clearance of irinotecan’s active metabolite and raise the risk of severe neutropenia.
Irinotecan-containing regimens carry a high risk of febrile neutropenia, which is why fever during treatment is an emergency.
Irinotecan causes an early cholinergic diarrhea and a late diarrhea from SN-38 released in the gut.
The neutropenia risk of irinotecan-containing FOLFIRINOX is one reason white-cell growth factors are considered from the first cycle.
Irinotecan and oxaliplatin are the two partner drugs that distinguish FOLFIRINOX from fluorouracil alone.
Liposomal irinotecan works only when combined with fluorouracil and leucovorin, not on its own.

faq.q: Should I be tested for UGT1A1 before starting FOLFIRINOX?
faq.a: The US irinotecan label advises considering UGT1A1 testing to identify poor metabolizers, who face a higher risk of severe neutropenia, but it does not require it [[SEC-GENE-01]]. Dutch centers test routinely and reduce the starting dose by 30% in poor metabolizers, with no detectable survival penalty in a large cohort [[GENE-018]]; whether a US center tests is worth asking before the first cycle.

faq.q: Is liposomal irinotecan better than regular irinotecan?
faq.a: None of the sources cited here compares them head to head in pancreatic cancer. The liposomal form has the pancreatic approvals because its trials were run in pancreatic cancer, second line with fluorouracil and first line in NALIRIFOX [[TX-014]][[TX-002]], whereas conventional irinotecan's pancreatic use rests on the FOLFIRINOX trials.

faq.q: What should I do when diarrhea starts?
faq.a: Diarrhea beginning more than a day after a dose is the type the label addresses with loperamide at the first loose stool, and the care team should be told it has started; diarrhea with fever, dizziness or blood, or that does not settle, needs same-day contact, and the next dose is withheld for grade 2 (moderate) or worse diarrhea [[SEC-SUPP-11]].

topics.title: Gemcitabine
topics.orientation: Gemcitabine (brand name Gemzar) has been the reference chemotherapy for pancreatic cancer since 1997. Every later regimen was measured against it, and it remains a partner drug in combinations and a treatment on its own for people who cannot tolerate more.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: Gemcitabine is a counterfeit nucleoside: it resembles deoxycytidine, one of the four building blocks of DNA, but carries two fluorine atoms. Cells take it up, add phosphate groups to activate it, and insert it into growing DNA strands, where it halts further building. It also depletes the real building blocks by inhibiting the enzyme that makes them. It is infused over about 30 minutes, usually weekly for three weeks of every four.
section1.full: Gemcitabine's activity depends on how a cell handles it. Nucleoside transporters such as ENT1 carry it inside, and lowering Ent1 in mouse tumor cells made them resistant [[TX-008]]. Deoxycytidine kinase adds the first phosphate, and the triphosphate form competes with the natural base for incorporation into DNA; once in place it permits one more nucleotide before copying stops, a masked termination that repair enzymes handle poorly. The diphosphate form also inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, which makes the building blocks of DNA, so the drug poisons the product and starves the supply. Cytidine deaminase inactivates gemcitabine; lowering that enzyme raised the active metabolite in mouse tumors and sensitized cells, the best current explanation for why nab-paclitaxel improves it [[TX-008]]. Gemcitabine clears from the blood quickly, but its phosphorylated forms persist inside cells for many hours, so a short weekly infusion is enough. The original schedule was 1,000 mg/m² weekly for seven of eight weeks, then three of four; trials now use days 1, 8 and 15 of a 28-day cycle [[TX-L03]][[TX-001]]. Its toxicity is comparatively mild: in the gemcitabine-alone arm of the MPACT trial, grade 3 or worse neutropenia (a shortage of infection-fighting white cells) occurred in 27%, fatigue in 7% and neuropathy in 1% [[TX-001]], and in the gemcitabine-alone arm of the adjuvant APACT trial neutropenia in 43% [[TX-006]]. Its nausea-provoking potential is classed as low [[SEC-SUPP-06]]. Rare lung inflammation (interstitial pneumonitis) caused the one toxic death in the gemcitabine arm of the PRODIGE 24 trial [[TX-L01]], and liver-enzyme rises were more frequent than with S-1, an oral fluorouracil-type drug, in a Japanese trial [[TX-L09]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Gemcitabine earned its place in a 126-patient trial in which 23.8% of people had a sustained improvement in pain, function or weight versus 4.8% with weekly fluorouracil, and median survival was 5.65 versus 4.41 months. The FDA approved it as a single agent for pancreatic cancer on 15 May 1996. After surgery, six months of gemcitabine doubled the time to recurrence compared with observation.
section2.full: The 1997 trial's primary measure was clinical benefit response, a composite of pain, performance status and weight sustained for at least four weeks, which captured what the drug did best; 12-month survival was 18% versus 2% [[TX-L03]]. In the CONKO-001 adjuvant trial, 368 patients with resected pancreatic cancer were randomized to six cycles of gemcitabine or observation; median disease-free survival was 13.4 versus 6.9 months, and after more than 11 years of follow-up, overall survival favored gemcitabine (hazard ratio 0.76), with 20.7% versus 10.4% alive at five years [[TX-L07]][[TX-L08]]. That result made adjuvant chemotherapy standard and made gemcitabine the control arm of the trials that followed: adding capecitabine gave 28.0 versus 25.5 months [[TX-L06]], and modified FOLFIRINOX gave 53.5 versus 35.5 months in fitter, more selected patients [[TX-003]]. In metastatic disease, gemcitabine alone was the comparator for nab-paclitaxel (8.5 versus 6.7 months) and for FOLFIRINOX (11.1 versus 6.8 months) [[TX-001]][[TX-L02]]. It is also the chemotherapy given with radiation in the PREOPANC trials [[TX-004]][[TX-L13]]. Its roles today are three: partner in gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel; comparator that every new treatment must beat; and single agent for people whose fitness or organ function rules out combinations. A fall in CA 19-9 during the first cycles is the earliest sign that it is working, and restaging scans confirm it; in the MPACT trial of nab-paclitaxel, a 90% fall marked a group with median survival of 13.5 months [[TX-001]].

action_note.heading: When to call the care team now
action_note.text: A temperature of 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) or higher during gemcitabine can be the only sign of infection while neutrophils are low and needs same-day evaluation, with antibiotics within an hour of arrival [[SEC-SUPP-03]][[SEC-SUPP-01]]. New breathlessness or a dry cough that worsens over days should be reported promptly, because gemcitabine can rarely inflame the lungs [[TX-L01]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Gemcitabine's own benefit is small in survival terms, about 1.2 months in the median over weekly bolus fluorouracil, and its lasting importance is as the yardstick: a new regimen's hazard ratio against gemcitabine (0.72 for nab-paclitaxel, 0.57 for FOLFIRINOX in different trials) is the number that places it [[TX-L03]][[TX-001]][[TX-L02]]. The adjuvant evidence is the clearest demonstration in pancreatic cancer that chemotherapy after surgery changes long-term outcomes, with five-year survival doubled from 10% to 21% [[TX-L08]]. The nab-paclitaxel mechanism work also explains gemcitabine's main weakness, rapid inactivation by cytidine deaminase inside tumors [[TX-008]].
research_notes.how_studied: The pivotal 1997 trial used clinical benefit response, a composite of pain, function and weight, as its primary endpoint, a choice that fitted a drug whose survival effect was small and whose symptom effect was real; survival was secondary [[TX-L03]]. CONKO-001 randomized resected patients to chemotherapy or observation, the only design that can show adjuvant chemotherapy works at all, and followed them for a median of 136 months [[TX-L07]][[TX-L08]]. Both are available to this atlas only as abstracts. The cellular pharmacology comes from mouse tumors in which drug metabolites were measured directly and transporter and enzyme levels were manipulated [[TX-008]]. Later trials supply gemcitabine's toxicity profile from their control arms [[TX-001]][[TX-006]].

mechanism_notes.text: The amount of active gemcitabine reaching DNA depends on the balance between uptake through nucleoside transporters, activation by deoxycytidine kinase and destruction by cytidine deaminase, and in mouse tumors shifting that balance changed sensitivity; this is the proposed basis for combining gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel, which lowers cytidine deaminase. The same balance has not been measured in patients' tumors, so transporter or enzyme levels are not used clinically to choose treatment [[TX-008]][[TX-001]].

topics.clinical_status: Approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 as a single agent for the treatment of pancreatic cancer (NDA 020509, 15 May 1996) and, through the Abraxane label, in combination with nab-paclitaxel for first-line metastatic disease (6 Sep 2013). Adjuvant use after resection and use with radiation are guideline-recommended practice rather than labeled indications.

glossary.definition: A drug shaped like a DNA or RNA building block that cells mistakenly use, disrupting copying.
The enzyme that adds the first phosphate to gemcitabine, the step that activates it.
The enzyme that makes the deoxynucleotide building blocks of DNA, which gemcitabine inhibits.
The enzyme that inactivates gemcitabine; lower levels mean more active drug inside a cell.
A trial measure combining pain, performance status and weight that must improve and hold for at least four weeks.
Inflammation of the lung tissue between the air sacs, a rare serious side effect of gemcitabine.
Treatment given after an operation to attack microscopic cancer that may remain.

related.statement: Gemcitabine is one half of gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel, where nab-paclitaxel raises the active form of gemcitabine inside tumor cells.
Gemcitabine was the comparator that FOLFIRINOX beat in metastatic disease and that modified FOLFIRINOX beat after surgery.
Gemcitabine replaced weekly bolus fluorouracil as the reference drug in 1997, and capecitabine was later added to gemcitabine after surgery.
Gemcitabine is the chemotherapy given alongside radiation in the PREOPANC chemoradiation schedule.
Gemcitabine's adjuvant trial against observation established the place of chemotherapy after surgery in treatment sequencing.
Gemcitabine-based first-line treatment precedes the second-line setting in which liposomal irinotecan with fluorouracil and leucovorin was tested and approved.
Gemcitabine's effect is tracked by CA 19-9 in blood, where a 90% fall in the nab-paclitaxel trial marked longer survival.
Gemcitabine lowers neutrophils, so fever during treatment needs the urgent response described in the fever and infection topic.

faq.q: Is gemcitabine alone still used?
faq.a: Yes, for people whose fitness or organ function rules out combinations. Its survival effect is modest, 5.65 versus 4.41 months against weekly fluorouracil in its pivotal trial, but it improved pain, weight or function in about a quarter of people and is comparatively easy to tolerate [[TX-L03]][[TX-001]].

faq.q: Why is gemcitabine in so many trials as the comparison?
faq.a: Because its 1996 approval made it the standard, every later regimen had to beat it to be adopted: nab-paclitaxel added 1.8 months, FOLFIRINOX added 4.3 months, and after surgery modified FOLFIRINOX added 18 months to its medians in their respective trials [[TX-001]][[TX-L02]][[TX-003]].

faq.q: How soon will I know if it is working?
faq.a: The drug acts on dividing cells within hours, but the effect is judged on CA 19-9 blood levels over the first cycles and on restaging scans after several cycles; in the MPACT trial of nab-paclitaxel a 90% fall in CA 19-9 identified people who did better [[TX-001]].

topics.title: The Whipple operation (pancreatoduodenectomy)
topics.orientation: The Whipple operation removes the head of the pancreas together with the duodenum, the lower bile duct and the gallbladder, then rebuilds three connections so that pancreatic juice, bile and food reach the intestine. It is the standard operation for cancers of the pancreatic head that can be separated from the major vessels.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: The head of the pancreas sits in the curve of the duodenum and shares its blood supply with it, and the bile duct passes through the head, so a tumor there cannot be removed on its own. The surgeon takes the head, the duodenum, the lower bile duct, the gallbladder and lymph nodes as one block, sometimes with the lower stomach, then joins the remaining pancreas, the bile duct and the stomach to a loop of small intestine.
section1.full: The operation is defined by the vessels. The superior mesenteric vein and portal vein run behind the neck of the pancreas, and the superior mesenteric artery lies behind the head; the pancreas is divided at the neck over the vein, and the uncinate process, the hook-shaped lower part of the head, is peeled off the artery, which is where the margin closest to a tumor is usually found. Keeping the pylorus, the stomach's outlet valve, or removing the lower stomach with the specimen gives equivalent survival and complication rates in a Cochrane review pooling randomized trials, with only small differences in how quickly the stomach empties afterwards [[SEC-SURG-09]]. The three new joins are its vulnerability. The join to a soft remaining pancreas can leak enzyme-rich juice, a pancreatic fistula; in a Dutch nationwide series of the highest-risk glands (soft texture, duct 3 mm or less) a clinically relevant fistula occurred in 30.0% and raised major morbidity from 28.3% to 88.0% and in-hospital mortality from 3.5% to 6.3% [[SURG-016]]. Jaundice from the blocked bile duct is often present at diagnosis; draining it first with a metal stent proved as safe as operating promptly in a randomized trial (serious events within 120 days 29.0% versus 26.5%), though the risk shifts into the waiting period [[SUPP-008]]. A laparoscopic Whipple trial was halted for higher 90-day mortality, so most Whipples remain open operations [[SEC-SURG-08]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Four outcomes are worth keeping apart. Operative mortality, usually counted as death in hospital or within 90 days, was 4.1% in hospital in the highest-risk Dutch glands [[SURG-016]], and the adjusted odds of death are three to six times higher at very-low-volume than very-high-volume US hospitals [[SURG-003]]. Major complications within the first weeks affected 45.9% of those high-risk patients [[SURG-016]]. Recovery of strength takes months. Long-term function involves digestion, blood sugar and weight, which the operation changes permanently.
section2.full: Among US Medicare patients, the odds of dying after pancreatectomy at the lowest-volume hospitals compared with the highest fell from 5.83 in 2000 to 2001 to 3.08 in 2008 to 2009, a weakening seen for no other operation, yet the gap remained wide [[SURG-003]]. Without the duodenum and the head's enzyme-producing tissue, high-dose enzyme capsules raised fat absorption by 25.6 percentage points over placebo, but only 7 of 26 (27%) people with Whipple-type reconstructions reached near-normal absorption [[SUPP-002]]. New diabetes appeared in 30.2% within six months in one series, predicted by body-mass index rather than by how much pancreas remained [[SUPP-033]]. More than five years out, 248 survivors reported global quality of life in the normal range, with persistent pancreatic-type pain and altered bowel habit in many [[SUPP-031]]. The operation's purpose is to remove all visible cancer with a clear margin, but a clear margin is not a cure: in 1,426 up-front resections for anatomically resectable tumors, 18.9% ended in death or recurrence within six months [[SURG-008]], and genomic and modeling studies indicate that microscopic spread is usually already present at diagnosis [[SURG-002]][[SURG-009]]. This is why chemotherapy before or after surgery is part of every plan; six months of modified FOLFIRINOX after resection raised five-year survival from 31.4% to 43.2% in fit patients [[TX-003]].

action_note.heading: In the weeks after a Whipple
action_note.text: Fever of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher, new or worsening abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, or drain fluid that turns cloudy, dark or bloody can signal a leak, infection or bleeding at one of the new joins and should be reported the same day [[SEC-SURG-01]][[SEC-SUPP-03]]. Bleeding after pancreatic surgery can appear days to weeks later, sometimes announced by a small amount of blood in a drain or in vomit, and is a recognized emergency [[SEC-SURG-03]]. Fever with jaundice, dark urine or shaking chills suggests infection in the rebuilt bile duct and needs urgent assessment [[SEC-SUPP-14]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The complication figures [[SURG-016]] describe only the highest-risk glands in a centralized Dutch audit, so they overstate typical fistula rates and understate what low-volume settings experience; the volume analysis [[SURG-003]] uses Medicare claims for people 65 and older with no detail on complications. The enzyme trial [[SUPP-002]] was one week double-blind in 58 patients with mixed benign and malignant indications, and the five-year survey [[SUPP-031]] had no pre-operative baseline and by design excludes those who died early. The futility estimate [[SURG-008]] comes from European high-volume centers and a model not yet validated prospectively. None of the sources cited here reports length of hospital stay or time to return to usual activity after a Whipple, so recovery time is described without numbers.
research_notes.how_studied: Operative outcomes are read from nationwide audits that grade each complication by consensus definitions, fistula by drain amylase and clinical consequence, hemorrhage by timing and severity, and from administrative claims that allow risk-adjusted comparison across thousands of hospitals [[SURG-016]][[SURG-003]][[SEC-SURG-01]]. Technique questions such as pylorus preservation and laparoscopy are settled by randomized trials pooled in meta-analyses, with mortality and fistula as endpoints [[SEC-SURG-09]][[SEC-SURG-08]]. Long-term function is measured with fat-absorption tests on a fixed diet, scheduled glucose and HbA1c (a measure of average blood sugar over about three months), and the EORTC quality-of-life questionnaires with pancreatic-specific items [[SUPP-002]][[SUPP-033]][[SUPP-031]].

mechanism_notes.text: A complete resection fails to cure most people because disseminated cells are usually already outside the pancreas: clonal timing shows the metastasis-competent subclone arising within the primary years before the cancer becomes lethal, early recurrence within 12 months affects about half of those who recur, and even complete disappearance of tumor from the specimen after chemotherapy is followed by relapse in many, which fits local clearance with residual systemic disease rather than a failed operation [[INF-SURG-03]][[SURG-002]][[SURG-007]].

Persistent maldigestion after a Whipple is better explained by mistiming than by enzyme quantity: coated enzyme microspheres and food leave the stomach out of step into the loop of small intestine (jejunal limb) that lacks the duodenum's bicarbonate, so lipase, the fat-digesting enzyme, is released at the wrong moment and partly inactivated, which is why only about a quarter of patients normalize fat absorption even at high doses [[INF-SUPP-01]][[SUPP-002]].

topics.clinical_status: Standard surgical procedure (US and internationally, as of 8 Oct 2026). Candidacy depends on anatomy, chiefly whether the tumor can be separated from the superior mesenteric vein, portal vein and superior mesenteric artery, and on fitness for a major operation; US guidelines recommend that it be performed at high-volume centers.

glossary.definition: The formal name for the Whipple operation: removal of the pancreatic head and duodenum together.
The muscular valve at the outlet of the stomach that can be kept or removed during a Whipple.
The hook-shaped lower part of the pancreatic head that wraps behind the mesenteric vessels.
A surgical join between two hollow structures, such as the pancreas and the small intestine.
A leak of enzyme-rich pancreatic juice from the join between the pancreas and the bowel after surgery.
Death following a complication that might have been survived with earlier recognition and treatment.
An operation in which no tumor is found at the inked edges of the removed tissue.

related.statement: The Whipple operation removes the head of the pancreas, where most pancreatic cancers arise.
The Whipple removes the duodenum because it shares its blood supply with the pancreatic head.
The Whipple removes the lower bile duct and ampulla, which pass through the pancreatic head.
The superior mesenteric and portal veins run behind the pancreatic neck and set the inner boundary of a Whipple.
The uncinate margin of a Whipple is dissected off the superior mesenteric artery, the usual site of a close margin.
Pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying and bleeding are the characteristic early complications of a Whipple.
The Whipple operation precedes the months of recovery and the permanent digestive changes described under life after a Whipple.
A Whipple may include resection and reconstruction of the portal or superior mesenteric vein when the tumor touches it.
The Whipple specimen is examined to report margins, lymph nodes and treatment response in the pathology report.
Whether a Whipple is offered up front or after chemotherapy depends on the resectability category assigned on imaging.
Jaundice before a Whipple may be relieved with a metal biliary stent when surgery is delayed for chemotherapy.
Digestion after a Whipple is supported by enzyme replacement capsules taken with every meal.
New diabetes after a Whipple depends more on body weight than on how much pancreas remains.
Distal pancreatectomy is the counterpart of the Whipple for tumors of the pancreatic body and tail.
A Whipple is extended to a total pancreatectomy when the tumor crosses the neck or the neck margin is positive.
Chemotherapy before or after a Whipple is part of every plan because a clear margin alone is not a cure.
The Whipple specimen includes the regional lymph nodes along the pancreatic head and hepatic artery.

faq.q: If the margins are clear, am I cured?
faq.a: A clear margin means the pathologist found no tumor at the cut edges, which is the goal of the operation, but it is not a cure: in 1,426 up-front resections with clear-looking anatomy, nearly one in five patients recurred or died within six months [[SURG-008]], because microscopic spread is usually already present at diagnosis [[SURG-002]][[SURG-009]]. That is why chemotherapy accompanies surgery.

faq.q: Does it matter where I have the operation?
faq.a: Yes. In US Medicare data the adjusted odds of dying after pancreatectomy were three to six times higher at the lowest-volume hospitals than at the highest, a gap that narrowed over the decade but did not close [[SURG-003]]. Experienced units mainly do better at rescuing patients from complications rather than avoiding them [[SURG-016]].

faq.q: Will I eat normally afterwards?
faq.a: Most people return to regular meals but with enzyme capsules for life, smaller portions and some permanent changes: even on high doses only about a quarter of Whipple-type patients normalized fat absorption in a trial [[SUPP-002]], and five-year survivors still reported bloating and altered bowel habit, though overall quality of life was in the normal range [[SUPP-031]].

topics.title: Distal pancreatectomy
topics.orientation: Distal pancreatectomy removes the body and tail of the pancreas, usually together with the spleen, for tumors lying to the left of the vessels that run behind the pancreatic neck. It needs no rebuilt connections, and it is the one pancreatic cancer operation for which randomized evidence supports a keyhole approach.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: The body and tail of the pancreas lie behind the stomach and run leftward to the spleen, with the splenic artery and vein traveling along their upper and back surfaces. A cancer in this region reaches those vessels early, so the surgeon removes the body and tail, the splenic vessels, the spleen and the lymph nodes along them as one piece, dividing the pancreas at the neck and closing the cut end without any new join.
section1.full: Because nothing needs reconnecting, the operation is shorter and simpler than a Whipple, and the stomach, bile duct and duodenum stay in place. The characteristic complication is a leak of pancreatic juice from the closed stump rather than from a join; it is defined and graded by the same international criteria used after a Whipple [[SEC-SURG-01]]. A more radical version, radical antegrade modular pancreatosplenectomy (RAMPS), dissects from right to left on a deeper plane, taking the tissue layer behind the pancreas and sometimes the left adrenal gland, to secure a clear posterior margin and the lymph nodes along the splenic and celiac arteries. The randomized DIPLOMA trial, which enrolled 258 people with resectable body-and-tail cancer at 35 centers and blinded both patients and pathologists, found no significant difference in overall or disease-free survival between minimally invasive (laparoscopic or robotic) and open resection after at least three years, with comparable margin-negative rates [[SURG-004]]; this contrasts with the laparoscopic Whipple trial halted for excess mortality [[SEC-SURG-08]]. Losing the spleen leaves a lifelong vulnerability to certain bacterial infections, because the spleen filters encapsulated bacteria, those with a protective outer coat, from the blood, so vaccination and prompt attention to any fever become part of the plan.

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Body-and-tail cancers are found later than head cancers because they do not block the bile duct and cause jaundice, so they tend to be larger and more often spread at diagnosis: in 1,004 staging laparoscopies, a body-or-tail location nearly tripled the odds of finding metastases invisible on scans (odds ratio 2.78) [[DIAG-002]]. Candidacy therefore depends as much on excluding hidden spread as on the local anatomy.
section2.full: When the operation goes ahead, the long-term consequences are mostly metabolic. In a Swedish national cohort of 1,034 people without diabetes before distal pancreatectomy, 28% developed diabetes, at a median of about a year, and obesity more than doubled the risk, consistent with a remaining pancreas whose insulin capacity suffices for some bodies and not others [[SUPP-004]]. Exocrine insufficiency, a shortage of digestive enzymes, is less common than after a Whipple because the duodenum and the head's drainage are intact, but it can occur and is treated the same way. Operative mortality for pancreatectomy as a class is strongly linked to hospital volume, with three- to six-fold higher adjusted odds of death at the lowest-volume US hospitals, and nothing in the sources cited here suggests distal resection is exempt [[SURG-003]]. Specific operative mortality and 90-day morbidity rates for distal pancreatectomy are not reported in the sources cited here; the nationwide complication figures available describe the Whipple [[SURG-016]]. Tumors that reach the celiac artery at the base of the body sometimes prompt a resection of that artery relying on the liver's alternative blood supply; that is a rare, specialist operation that none of the sources cited here studies. A clear margin here means the same as elsewhere: complete removal of what could be seen, with systemic treatment still needed because recurrence after resection is usually at a distance [[SURG-014]].

action_note.heading: After distal pancreatectomy
action_note.text: Fever of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher, worsening abdominal pain, or drain fluid that becomes cloudy or bloody can signal a leak from the pancreatic stump or bleeding and should be reported the same day [[SEC-SURG-01]][[SEC-SURG-03]][[SEC-SUPP-03]]. Once the spleen is gone, any fever is treated as urgent for life, because infection by certain bacteria can progress within hours; keep the vaccinations the care team recommends up to date. Excessive thirst, frequent urination or unexplained weight loss in the months after surgery can be the first signs of new diabetes and warrant a glucose check [[SUPP-004]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The DIPLOMA trial [[SURG-004]] was powered for pathology endpoints with survival as a secondary outcome, in experienced centers and selected resectable tumors, so it shows that a keyhole approach does not compromise cancer outcomes when done well, not that every center achieves this. The diabetes cohort [[SUPP-004]] mixed malignant and benign indications and dated diabetes from the first registry visit, so onset is probably earlier than recorded; the lower risk after minimally invasive surgery (sub-hazard ratio 0.54) likely reflects smaller tumors and less pancreas removed rather than the approach itself. The laparoscopy yield study [[DIAG-002]] comes from a single referral center. The sources cited here include no distal-specific fistula, mortality or 90-day morbidity rates and no RAMPS outcome study.
research_notes.how_studied: Surgical approach is tested in randomized trials that blind the patient and the pathologist so that neither recovery reports nor margin assessment can be colored by knowing the arm, with overall and disease-free survival followed for at least three years [[SURG-004]]. Diabetes after surgery is counted by linking a national surgical registry to a national diabetes register, with death treated as a competing event so that people who died early are not miscounted as diabetes-free [[SUPP-004]]. Occult spread is quantified by the yield of staging laparoscopy with peritoneal washings against a background of CT, MRI and PET [[DIAG-002]]. Hospital volume effects use risk-adjusted claims data across volume quintiles [[SURG-003]].

mechanism_notes.text: Diabetes after removing the body and tail appears when the remaining gland's insulin capacity falls below the body's demand: surgery removes a roughly fixed fraction of the islets, the insulin-producing cell clusters, so obesity and insulin resistance, which raise demand, and a fatty or fibrotic remnant, which lowers quality, decide who crosses the threshold, which is why obesity doubled the risk while the amount removed was similar across patients [[INF-SUPP-02]][[SUPP-004]].

topics.clinical_status: Standard surgical procedure (US and internationally, as of 8 Oct 2026); minimally invasive distal pancreatectomy is accepted practice in experienced centers on the basis of randomized long-term data. Candidacy depends on anatomy, particularly the relationship to the celiac and superior mesenteric arteries, on the absence of spread beyond the pancreas, and on fitness for major surgery.

glossary.definition: Removal of the body and tail of the pancreas, the part to the left of the mesenteric vessels.
Removal of the spleen, usually done with distal pancreatectomy for cancer because the splenic vessels run with the tumor.
Radical antegrade modular pancreatosplenectomy, a deeper right-to-left dissection designed to clear the back margin and lymph nodes.
The closed cut end of the pancreas left after the body and tail are removed.
Surgery through small incisions using a camera and instruments, laparoscopic or robotic.
Bacteria with a protective coat that the spleen normally clears; losing the spleen raises the risk from them.
A camera inspection of the abdomen under anesthetic to look for spread that scans cannot show.

related.statement: Distal pancreatectomy removes the body and tail of the pancreas along with the spleen.
The spleen is removed with the pancreatic tail because its vessels run along the tumor and carry the draining lymph nodes.
The splenic artery and vein are divided and removed in a distal pancreatectomy for cancer.
A leak from the pancreatic stump is the characteristic complication of distal pancreatectomy.
About 28% of people develop new diabetes after distal pancreatectomy, most within a year or two.
Distal pancreatectomy is the counterpart of the Whipple for tumors of the body and tail and needs no rebuilt joins.
Staging laparoscopy is especially useful before distal pancreatectomy because body-and-tail tumors more often harbor hidden spread.
Whether a distal pancreatectomy is possible depends on the tumor’s relationship to the celiac artery at the base of the body.
The distal pancreatectomy specimen is examined for the posterior margin, splenic-vessel involvement and lymph nodes in the pathology report.
After splenectomy, fever is treated as an emergency because of the lifelong risk of overwhelming infection.
Distal pancreatectomy for cancer removes the lymph nodes along the splenic artery and at the splenic hilum.

faq.q: Is a distal pancreatectomy less risky than a Whipple?
faq.a: It avoids the three joins of a Whipple, so there is no bile-duct or stomach connection to leak, but the closed pancreatic stump can still leak juice and that fistula is graded by the same international definition [[SEC-SURG-01]]. The sources cited here give no distal-specific mortality or complication rates, and the hospital-volume effect on pancreatectomy mortality applies to both operations [[SURG-003]].

faq.q: Is keyhole surgery as safe as open surgery for this?
faq.a: For body-and-tail cancer, yes in experienced hands: the randomized DIPLOMA trial found no significant difference in overall or disease-free survival between minimally invasive and open resection after at least three years, with comparable clear-margin rates [[SURG-004]]. The same is not true of the Whipple, where a laparoscopic trial was stopped for higher mortality [[SEC-SURG-08]].

faq.q: Will I get diabetes?
faq.a: In a Swedish national cohort, 28% of people without diabetes before distal pancreatectomy developed it, typically about a year later, and the risk was more than doubled in people with obesity [[SUPP-004]]. Glucose is checked at follow-up visits for that reason.

topics.title: Total pancreatectomy
topics.orientation: Total pancreatectomy removes the entire pancreas, usually with the duodenum, lower bile duct, gallbladder and spleen, and is reserved for cancers that span the gland or for a few specific situations. It trades the risk of a pancreatic leak for guaranteed, lifelong insulin-dependent diabetes and complete loss of digestive enzymes.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: The operation combines a Whipple and a distal pancreatectomy in one: the whole gland is taken with the duodenum, lower bile duct, gallbladder, spleen and surrounding lymph nodes, and the bile duct and stomach are joined to the small intestine. Because no pancreatic tissue remains, there is no pancreatic join to leak, but every function the pancreas performed, insulin, glucagon and digestive enzymes, must be replaced from outside for life.
section1.full: It is chosen when a tumor extends across the neck into both halves of the gland, when a cancer arises in a pancreas whose ducts are lined throughout with precancerous cysts, or when the margin at the neck proves positive during a planned Whipple and the resection is extended to clear it. Removing the gland to pre-empt a fistula in a very soft, small-duct pancreas has been proposed, but in the Dutch nationwide audit only 4 of 190 total pancreatectomies (2.1%) were done for that reason [[SURG-016]]. The loss is more than insulin. Glucagon, the hormone that raises blood sugar, is also gone, so the diabetes that follows, called type 3c, is prone to swings and to low blood sugar; in a prospective French cohort of 41 patients, every one was diabetic from the day of surgery, and at 12 months the median HbA1c, the three-month average blood sugar, was 8.0% on multiple daily injections or a pump, while continuous glucose monitoring showed only 0.2% of time below 70 mg/dL [[SUPP-036]]. Digestion requires full-dose enzyme capsules with every meal and snack; in the enzyme trial that included people after total pancreatectomy, high doses raised fat absorption by 25.6 percentage points over placebo, but absorption rarely normalized after operations that also altered gut anatomy [[SUPP-002]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: The outcome that matters most after this operation is nutrition rather than blood sugar. In the French cohort, malnutrition rose from 25.0% before surgery to 59.5% at three months and was still 59.0% at one year, and more than half had lost over 10% of their body weight by then [[SUPP-036]]. Weight, muscle and enzyme dosing therefore need the same attention as insulin.
section2.full: The picture separates by time. Operative mortality and early complications track those of a Whipple without the fistula component; the sources cited here include no total-pancreatectomy-specific mortality or 90-day morbidity rate, and the Whipple figures, 4.1% in-hospital mortality and 45.9% major morbidity in the highest-risk glands, are the nearest available reference [[SURG-016]]. Recovery takes months and is complicated from the first day by learning to use insulin. Long-term function is dominated by the dual deficiency: without pancreatic bicarbonate and enzymes arriving in step with food, and without the duodenum, fat and protein absorption stay subnormal even on treatment, and malnutrition compounds chemotherapy toxicity and loss of muscle. For the cancer itself, total pancreatectomy does not improve on a partial resection; it is done when a smaller operation cannot clear the tumor, and the same rule applies that a clear margin removes visible disease but not the systemic disease that drives most recurrences [[SURG-002]][[SURG-008]]. Insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitors are standard FDA-approved tools; a bihormonal artificial pancreas that also delivers glucagon is being tested in a crossover trial but remains investigational [[SUPP-036]].

action_note.heading: After total pancreatectomy
action_note.text: Shakiness, sweating, confusion or unusual drowsiness can mean low blood sugar, which is more dangerous after this operation because the body can no longer release glucagon to correct it; treat it as the diabetes team has taught and report episodes. Fever of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher, vomiting that prevents insulin and food, or drain fluid that becomes cloudy or bloody needs same-day contact [[SEC-SUPP-03]][[SEC-SURG-03]]. Fever with jaundice or dark urine suggests infection in the rebuilt bile duct and needs urgent assessment [[SEC-SUPP-14]]. Steady weight loss after discharge should prompt a review of enzyme dosing and nutrition rather than being accepted as inevitable [[SUPP-036]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The only total-pancreatectomy outcome study among the sources cited here [[SUPP-036]] is a single-center prospective cohort of 41 people with mixed benign and malignant indications, so its malnutrition rate blends the effects of cancer and chemotherapy with those of the operation, and insulin doses were not reported. The audit figure for prophylactic total pancreatectomy [[SURG-016]] describes Dutch practice. No study here compares total with partial resection for survival, reports operative mortality for total pancreatectomy, or measures long-term quality of life after it; the enzyme trial [[SUPP-002]] included only a small number of total-pancreatectomy patients.
research_notes.how_studied: Glycemic outcome is measured by HbA1c and by continuous glucose monitoring, which reports the fraction of time spent below 70 mg/dL and so captures hypoglycemia that a single blood test would miss [[SUPP-036]]. Malnutrition is defined by combined criteria of weight loss, body-mass index and CT-measured muscle mass or muscle function, assessed before surgery and at fixed intervals after it [[SUPP-036]]. Fat absorption is measured by 72-hour stool fat collection on a standard diet, which quantifies digestion directly rather than inferring it from symptoms [[SUPP-002]]. Indications and frequency come from mandatory nationwide surgical audits [[SURG-016]].

mechanism_notes.text: Total removal is the boundary case of the diabetes-after-surgery relationship: when islet capacity goes to zero, tissue quantity becomes decisive and every patient is insulin-dependent at once, whereas after partial resections the body's insulin demand and the quality of the remnant decide who develops diabetes and when [[INF-SUPP-02]][[SUPP-036]][[SUPP-004]]. The persistent malnutrition despite enzymes likely reflects the same mistiming of enzyme and food delivery seen after a Whipple, compounded by the complete absence of pancreatic bicarbonate [[INF-SUPP-01]][[SUPP-002]].

topics.clinical_status: Standard surgical procedure (US and internationally, as of 8 Oct 2026) for the minority of cases in which a partial resection cannot clear the tumor; candidacy depends on anatomy, on the absence of spread, and on fitness and the capacity to manage lifelong insulin and enzyme replacement.

glossary.definition: Removal of the entire pancreas, usually with the duodenum, bile duct, gallbladder and spleen.
Diabetes caused by loss or disease of the pancreas itself, affecting glucagon as well as insulin.
The pancreatic hormone that raises blood sugar; its loss makes low blood sugar harder to correct.
A skin sensor that reads glucose every few minutes and shows how much time is spent too low or too high.
A blood test reflecting average blood sugar over about three months.
A state of insufficient weight, muscle or nutrient intake defined by set clinical criteria.
Too few digestive enzymes reaching the gut, causing fat malabsorption and weight loss.

related.statement: Total pancreatectomy removes every part of the pancreas described in the overview, so all of its functions must be replaced.
Total pancreatectomy removes all islets, so insulin and glucagon production stop at once.
Total pancreatectomy removes all acinar cells, the enzyme-making cells, so no digestive enzymes are made and full replacement is required.
The universal insulin-dependent diabetes after total pancreatectomy is managed with insulin injections or a pump and glucose monitoring.
Digestion after total pancreatectomy depends entirely on enzyme replacement capsules with every meal and snack.
A planned Whipple is extended to a total pancreatectomy when the neck margin is positive or the tumor crosses the neck.
Total pancreatectomy combines the Whipple and the distal pancreatectomy in a single operation.
Total pancreatectomy removes the possibility of a pancreatic fistula but keeps the bleeding and bile-duct risks of a Whipple.
The type 3c diabetes after total pancreatectomy lacks glucagon as well as insulin, so low blood sugar is harder to correct.
Malnutrition affects about six in ten people a year after total pancreatectomy and needs dietitian follow-up.
A pancreas with precancerous cysts throughout its ducts is one reason a total pancreatectomy may be chosen.
The spleen is usually removed with the pancreatic tail during total pancreatectomy.

faq.q: Can you live without a pancreas?
faq.a: Yes, with insulin and enzyme replacement for life. In a prospective cohort every patient was insulin-dependent from the day of surgery, with an average HbA1c of 8.0% at one year and very little time spent with low glucose on monitoring; the harder problem was nutrition, with 59% malnourished at one year [[SUPP-036]].

faq.q: Why not remove the whole pancreas and avoid the risk of a leak?
faq.a: Because a leak is usually survivable and treatable, whereas total removal guarantees lifelong insulin-dependent diabetes and full enzyme dependence. In the Dutch national audit only 2.1% of total pancreatectomies were done to avoid a fistula, even in the highest-risk glands [[SURG-016]].

topics.title: Vein and artery resection during surgery
topics.orientation: When a pancreatic cancer touches or wraps around the large vessels behind the pancreas, the surgeon may remove a segment of vein and rebuild it to take the tumor out whole. Vein resection is routine in experienced centers; artery resection is rare and far riskier, and the two should never be treated as one thing.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: The superior mesenteric vein and portal vein carry blood from the intestine to the liver and run directly behind the pancreatic neck; the superior mesenteric artery, celiac artery and hepatic artery supply the bowel, liver and stomach and lie close by. A tumor in contact with the vein is removed together with the involved vein segment, and the vein is repaired by direct suture, an end-to-end join or a graft, which works because veins tolerate brief clamping and reconstruction well.
section1.full: How much of the vessel's circumference the tumor touches on CT predicts what the surgeon will find. In 254 Whipple operations for head cancers, vein resection was needed in 12.9% with no contact, 36.4% with contact up to half the circumference, and about 90% beyond that, and microscopic invasion of the vein wall rose from 3.3% to 71 to 80% across the same categories [[DIAG-001]]. The margin-negative rate did not differ by category (91.6 to 100%), because when the vein is resected the margin is planned rather than left to chance [[DIAG-001]]. The term borderline resectable describes exactly this anatomy, a tumor touching the vein or abutting an artery over a limited arc; it says nothing about how aggressive the cancer is [[SEC-SURG-11]]. Arteries are different. The superior mesenteric artery carries the nerves whose removal causes intractable diarrhea, and its loss starves the bowel; the hepatic and celiac arteries feed the liver. Arterial resection is therefore a rare, specialist operation with higher mortality, offered selectively after chemotherapy, and none of the sources cited here studies it directly. Resected cohorts after total neoadjuvant therapy (all planned chemotherapy given before surgery), in which 65% had a vascular resection, had 90-day major morbidity of 36% and 90-day mortality of 6.7%, with vascular resection itself not associated with survival [[TX-L25]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Needing a vein resection is a marker of where the tumor sits, not an independent harm. In 117 people resected after chemotherapy for borderline or locally advanced tumors, those who had the vein removed had the same perioperative complications and no different survival from those whose vein was spared (median 16.0 versus 22.0 months, not significant); what mattered was whether the tumor had invaded the vein wall under the microscope [[SURG-017]].
section2.full: With invasion, median survival was 8.3 months against 24.0 without, and invasion together with a positive margin independently predicted death [[SURG-017]]. A separate series of 372 Whipples found the same pattern: how close the tumor came to the vein-related margin did not predict outcome once invasion of the vein wall was accounted for, and vein-wall invasion roughly doubled the hazard of death and of recurrence [[SURG-006]]. The practical implication is that a tumor abutting the vein is removable, and whether that removal helps depends on biology that the pathologist reads afterwards. Chemotherapy before surgery complicates the scans: after FOLFIRINOX, 28 of 40 resected tumors (70%) still looked locally advanced or borderline on imaging, yet 92% were removed with clear margins, because treated scar wrapped around a vessel looks identical to tumor [[DIAG-004]]. Surgeons therefore explore rather than trust the scan when the tumor marker and the patient's condition are favorable. A clear margin after vein resection, like any clear margin, removes what could be seen; in up-front resections 18.9% recurred or died within six months regardless [[SURG-008]]. The reconstructed vein can clot in the early days after surgery, a specific risk the team watches for with imaging if pain, fluid in the abdomen or liver tests change.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The contact-angle data [[DIAG-001]] come from head tumors only at one center where three quarters had chemoradiation first, and surgeons who saw the scans were more likely to resect the vein when contact was extensive, which inflates the apparent accuracy; arterial contact was not analyzed. The post-neoadjuvant resection series [[SURG-017]] and the vein-wall invasion series [[SURG-006]] are single-center and observational, and invasion may simply mark larger, more aggressive tumors. The total neoadjuvant therapy cohort [[TX-L25]] is available only as an abstract and describes only those who reached surgery. The sources cited here include no full study of arterial resection, so statements about it rest on anatomy and on the guideline framework that treats arterial involvement as locally advanced [[SEC-SURG-11]].
research_notes.how_studied: Radiologists grade the tumor-vessel interface on pancreatic-protocol CT as none, 180 degrees or less, more than 180 degrees, or occlusion, and these categories are compared against what the surgeon found and against microscopic examination of the resected vein, which is available only when the vein was removed [[DIAG-001]]. Survival analyses split patients by whether the vein was resected and, within resections, by histologic vein-wall invasion, using multivariable Cox models to separate the procedure from the biology [[SURG-017]][[SURG-006]]. Response to chemotherapy before surgery is judged by blinded re-review of before-and-after scans alongside CA 19-9 and final pathology [[DIAG-004]].

mechanism_notes.text: Chemotherapy before surgery appears to help most where a tumor touches a vessel because the value of converting a likely positive margin into a clear one scales with the baseline risk of leaving tumor behind, which is high at a vein interface and low for a tumor well away from vessels; that would explain why neoadjuvant therapy improved survival in borderline resectable disease but not in clearly resectable tumors, even though it improved margins and node status in both [[INF-TX-01]][[TX-004]][[TX-L10]].

topics.clinical_status: Venous (portal or superior mesenteric vein) resection and reconstruction is standard practice in experienced centers (US and internationally, as of 8 Oct 2026) when it allows complete removal; candidacy depends on the extent of contact on CT, the response to chemotherapy and fitness. Arterial resection is performed selectively in specializt centers after chemotherapy and is not standard.

glossary.definition: The vein that drains the intestine and runs behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein.
The vein carrying intestinal blood to the liver, formed behind the pancreas.
A tumor whose contact with major vessels makes complete removal uncertain; it describes anatomy, not how aggressive the cancer is.
Tumor cells found growing into the wall of a resected vein under the microscope.
A segment of vein or synthetic tube used to bridge the gap when a long vein segment is removed.
The fraction of a vessel’s circumference that the tumor touches on a CT scan.
A tumor that wraps around major arteries or long vein segments so that removal is not possible at diagnosis.

related.statement: Vein resection removes and rebuilds a segment of the superior mesenteric or portal vein that the tumor touches.
Resection of the superior mesenteric artery is rarely attempted because its loss starves the bowel and causes intractable diarrhea.
Resection of the celiac or hepatic artery is a rare specialist operation because these arteries feed the liver.
The need for vein resection is predicted by the degree of tumor-vessel contact measured on CT.
Borderline resectable tumors are those whose vessel contact makes a vein resection likely; the term describes anatomy, not malignancy.
Vein resection is performed as part of a Whipple when a head tumor touches the superior mesenteric or portal vein.
Whether the tumor invaded the resected vein wall is reported by the pathologist and predicts outcome better than margin distance.
Chemotherapy before surgery is standard for tumors touching vessels, where converting a likely positive margin matters most.
After chemotherapy, scans often still show vessel contact that proves to be scar, so restaging does not by itself rule out vein resection.
Vein resection adds the risk of early clotting of the reconstructed vein to the usual complications of pancreatic surgery.
Body tumors reaching the celiac artery occasionally prompt arterial resection during distal pancreatectomy, a rare operation that none of the sources cited here studies.

faq.q: Does "borderline resectable" mean my cancer is borderline malignant?
faq.a: No. Borderline resectable is a statement about anatomy, that the tumor touches a major vein or abuts an artery so that complete removal is uncertain without vessel resection; it says nothing about how aggressive the cancer is [[SEC-SURG-11]]. Such tumors are usually treated with chemotherapy first and then explored.

faq.q: If the vein has to be removed, is my outlook worse?
faq.a: Not because of the vein resection itself: in a series resected after chemotherapy, people who had the vein removed had the same complications and no different survival from those who did not [[SURG-017]]. What predicted outcome was whether the tumor had invaded the vein wall, which the pathologist reports afterwards [[SURG-006]].

faq.q: My scan still shows the tumor touching the vein after chemotherapy. Does that rule out surgery?
faq.a: Usually not. After FOLFIRINOX, 70% of tumors that were successfully removed still looked locally advanced or borderline on imaging, yet 92% had clear margins, because scar tissue around a vessel looks the same as tumor [[DIAG-004]]. Surgeons weigh CA 19-9 and general condition and often explore.

topics.title: Surgical complications: fistula, delayed emptying, bleeding
topics.orientation: Three complications account for most of the trouble after pancreatic surgery: a leak of pancreatic juice (fistula), a stomach that will not empty, and bleeding, and the first often sets off the other two. Each has an international definition with grades A to C, which is what makes complication rates comparable between hospitals.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: A postoperative pancreatic fistula is a leak of enzyme-rich juice from the cut surface or join of the pancreas. The 2016 international definition grades it: a biochemical leak (amylase, a pancreatic enzyme, in drain fluid above three times normal from day three with no clinical effect), grade B (a leak that changes management, needing prolonged drains, antibiotics or a radiologically placed drain), and grade C (one causing reoperation, organ failure or death) [[SEC-SURG-01]]. Only grades B and C count as clinically relevant.
section1.full: Risk is set by the gland itself: a soft pancreas with a duct of 3 mm or less, the group labeled ISGPS-D in the international surgical risk classification, is the hardest to join. In 1,402 Dutch Whipple operations in this group, a clinically relevant fistula occurred in 30.0%, and patients with a fistula had major complications in 88.0% versus 28.3% without and in-hospital mortality of 6.3% versus 3.5% [[SURG-016]]. The leaked enzymes digest surrounding tissue, which is how a fistula leads to the two other complications. Delayed gastric emptying is defined by the inability to return to a normal diet by the end of the first week, with a nasogastric tube needed beyond day three or reinserted, and graded A to C by how long the tube or liquid diet lasts [[SEC-SURG-02]]; it is miserable and prolongs the stay but is rarely dangerous on its own, and whether the pylorus is preserved changes it only slightly [[SEC-SURG-09]]. Bleeding after pancreatectomy is classified by timing, early within 24 hours and usually technical, or late, often from an artery eroded by leaked enzymes or infection; by site, into the gut or the abdomen; and by severity, with grades A to C [[SEC-SURG-03]]. Late bleeding is the most feared, because a small sentinel bleed can precede a massive one, treated by embolization (blocking the artery from inside through a catheter) or reoperation.

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: The complication rate and the death rate are different things, and the gap between them is called failure to rescue. In the Dutch highest-risk series, major complications affected 45.9% but in-hospital mortality was 4.1%, and 8.9% of those with a serious complication died [[SURG-016]]. Hospital volume works mostly here: adjusted odds of death after pancreatectomy were three to six times higher at very-low-volume US hospitals [[SURG-003]].
section2.full: Experienced units do not so much avoid fistulas as recognize and manage them before they become grade C, with drains placed by radiology, nutritional support, antibiotics and, for bleeding, round-the-clock access to interventional radiology. Complications also cast a shadow forward: a prolonged recovery delays or prevents chemotherapy after surgery, and in the adjuvant FOLFIRINOX trial patients had to be fit enough to start within 3 to 12 weeks, with completion of all cycles itself predicting survival [[TX-003]]. The shadow is shorter than people fear in the long run. Among 248 people surviving more than five years after a Whipple, those who had suffered a complication reported global quality of life no different from those who had not, and even lower fatigue and diarrhea scores, although survivors are by definition those who recovered [[SUPP-031]]. Infection in the rebuilt bile duct, cholangitis, is a separate late risk recognized by fever with chills and jaundice [[SEC-SUPP-14]]. The sources cited here give Whipple-specific rates for fistula but no pancreatic-cancer-specific rates for delayed gastric emptying or hemorrhage, and no rates for distal or total pancreatectomy; those operations use the same definitions. Avoiding a fistula by removing the whole pancreas is possible but rarely chosen (2.1% of total pancreatectomies in the Dutch audit) because it exchanges a usually survivable complication for lifelong diabetes [[SURG-016]].

action_note.heading: When to call the care team now
action_note.text: After discharge, a temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher, new or worsening abdominal pain, repeated vomiting or inability to keep fluids down, or drain fluid that turns cloudy, dark or foul-smelling should be reported the same day, because these are the signs of a fistula or abscess [[SEC-SURG-01]][[SEC-SUPP-03]]. Any blood in vomit, black or bloody stool, blood in a drain, or sudden dizziness is an emergency even if small, because late bleeding after pancreatic surgery can begin with a warning bleed [[SEC-SURG-03]]. Fever with shaking chills, jaundice or dark urine suggests cholangitis and needs urgent assessment [[SEC-SUPP-14]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The nationwide figures [[SURG-016]] apply to the highest-risk glands in a centralized system, so fistula rates for firmer, large-duct glands are lower and failure-to-rescue rates in low-volume settings are likely higher; the volume analysis [[SURG-003]] is limited to Medicare patients over 65 and cannot say whether volume itself or the systems that accompany it do the work. The long-term quality-of-life survey [[SUPP-031]] excludes those who died and mixes benign and malignant diagnoses. The pylorus comparison [[SEC-SURG-09]] and the consensus definitions themselves [[SEC-SURG-01]][[SEC-SURG-02]][[SEC-SURG-03]] are available only in summary form rather than full text.
research_notes.how_studied: Complication reporting depends on the International Study Group of Pancreatic Surgery definitions: fistula by drain amylase measured from day three and by clinical consequence, delayed gastric emptying by tube duration and diet tolerance, hemorrhage by timing, site and severity, each graded A to C [[SEC-SURG-01]][[SEC-SURG-02]][[SEC-SURG-03]]. Nationwide mandatory audits then capture every operation with these grades, allowing failure to rescue, the share of patients with a serious complication who die, to be calculated [[SURG-016]]. Hospital volume effects are estimated from risk-adjusted administrative data across volume quintiles and compared over time [[SURG-003]]. Long-term effects are surveyed with the EORTC quality-of-life questionnaires in survivors [[SUPP-031]].

mechanism_notes.text: The lower mortality at high-volume hospitals is probably mediated less by fewer complications than by faster rescue: recognizing a fistula early, draining collections and embolizing a bleeding artery before organ failure sets in, which is consistent with the failure-to-rescue rate of 8.9% reported in a centralized system and with the volume study authors' own note that failure to rescue, rather than volume as such, may explain the effect [[SURG-003]][[SURG-016]].

topics.clinical_status: Complications are defined and graded by international consensus definitions (ISGPS: fistula 2016, delayed gastric emptying 2007, hemorrhage 2007) that US practice adopts as of 8 Oct 2026; management follows standard surgical practice, and US guidelines recommend pancreatic surgery at high-volume centers.

glossary.definition: A leak of enzyme-rich pancreatic juice from the cut surface or join of the pancreas after surgery.
Raised amylase in drain fluid after surgery without any effect on the patient; not counted as a true fistula.
A stomach that will not empty normally after surgery, needing a tube or liquid diet beyond the first week.
Bleeding after pancreatic surgery, classed as early or late, into the gut or abdomen, mild or severe.
A small, self-limiting bleed that can warn of a major arterial bleed to come.
Death following a complication that might have been survived with earlier recognition and treatment.
Image-guided procedures such as placing a drain or blocking a bleeding artery without open surgery.
A scale of complication severity based on the treatment needed, from medication to reoperation or death.

related.statement: The Whipple operation is where pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying and bleeding are most frequent, because it creates three new joins.
After distal pancreatectomy the fistula arises from the closed stump rather than from a join, graded by the same definitions.
Total pancreatectomy removes the possibility of a pancreatic fistula at the cost of lifelong diabetes.
Early complications shape the first weeks after a Whipple but did not reduce quality of life in five-year survivors.
Fever after pancreatic surgery is treated as a possible fistula, abscess or cholangitis until proven otherwise.
A pancreatic duct of 3 mm or less, together with a soft gland, defines the highest fistula risk after a Whipple.
Delayed gastric emptying after surgery causes nausea and vomiting until the stomach recovers its rhythm.
Fistula and delayed gastric emptying are managed partly with nutritional support while the gut heals.
The enzymes that leak in a pancreatic fistula are made by acinar cells, and they digest surrounding tissue.
A slow recovery from complications can delay or prevent chemotherapy after surgery, which affects the whole treatment plan.

faq.q: What does a "grade B" fistula mean?
faq.a: It means the leak of pancreatic juice is changing how you are managed, for example drains left in longer, antibiotics, or a drain placed by radiology, but without organ failure or a return to the operating room; grade C is the leak that causes reoperation, organ failure or death, and a biochemical leak is a raised drain amylase that affects nothing [[SEC-SURG-01]].

faq.q: How common are these complications?
faq.a: In a Dutch nationwide series of Whipples in the highest-risk glands, a clinically relevant fistula occurred in 30%, major complications of any kind in 46%, and in-hospital death in 4.1% [[SURG-016]].
