Firmer glands with wider ducts leak less often, and the sources cited here lack pancreatic-cancer-specific rates for delayed gastric emptying and bleeding.

faq.q: Why is late bleeding treated as an emergency?
faq.a: Because late bleeding usually comes from an artery eroded by leaked enzymes or infection, and a small warning bleed can be followed by a massive one; the international definition classes bleeding by timing, site and severity so that even a minor late bleed triggers investigation and, if needed, radiological blocking of the artery [[SEC-SURG-03]].

topics.title: Radiation: chemoradiation and SBRT
topics.orientation: Radiation is a local treatment: it damages the DNA of cells inside the volume it is aimed at and nothing beyond. In pancreatic cancer it is used to answer particular questions in particular situations, not as a routine step, because the randomized trials that added it to chemotherapy improved local control without lengthening survival.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: High-energy X-rays break the DNA of cells inside the targeted volume, and cells that cannot repair those breaks die when they next try to divide. Conventional chemoradiation delivers about 50 to 54 Gy (gray, the unit of radiation dose) in 25 to 28 weekday sessions over five to six weeks together with a sensitizing drug such as capecitabine, whereas stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) gives a few much larger doses, typically five, using image guidance to keep the beam off the duodenum and stomach.
section1.full: Because the pancreas sits against the duodenum, stomach and small bowel, which tolerate radiation poorly, the dose that can safely be delivered is set by those organs rather than by the tumor. This is why a duodenal ulcer, bleeding or a fistula between tumor and bowel are the characteristic late harms, and why in a multicenter phase 2 trial of SBRT (33 Gy in five fractions with gemcitabine) late bowel toxicity of grade 2 (moderate) or worse occurred in 11 percent, with one death from gastrointestinal bleeding [[TX-026]]. Radiation oncologists compare schedules using the biologically effective dose (BED), which puts dose and fraction size on one scale: standard 50.4 Gy in 28 fractions is a BED of about 59 Gy, while an ablative course (one intended to destroy the tumor outright) of 75 Gy in 25 fractions, delivered with breath-hold or respiratory gating and daily soft-tissue imaging, reaches about 98 Gy [[TX-024]][[TX-025]]. Dose escalation of that kind was offered only to the 24 percent of patients whose tumor lay more than 1 cm from a hollow organ in one center's series [[TX-024]], and in another, 10 of 119 patients had upper gastrointestinal bleeds, 8 of them while on anticoagulants [[TX-025]]. The effect of radiation unfolds over weeks to months, and the scar tissue it leaves can be hard to distinguish from residual tumor on later scans, which complicates how a local response is judged.

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Radiation answers specific questions: can a tumor be held in place where it is, and can a margin that would be positive be converted to a clear one. The randomized trials that tested it after chemotherapy, LAP07 and CONKO-007 in locally advanced disease and A021501 in borderline resectable disease, delivered those local gains but no survival benefit, so radiation is a tool for selected situations rather than a step everyone passes through.
section2.full: In the LAP07 trial, 269 people with locally advanced disease controlled after four months of gemcitabine were randomized to chemoradiation (54 Gy with capecitabine) or two more months of chemotherapy; local progression fell from 46 to 32 percent, but median survival was 15.2 versus 16.5 months, hazard ratio 1.03 [[TX-L15]]. The CONKO-007 trial randomized 336 people after induction chemotherapy (an initial course given before any local treatment) to chemoradiation (50.4 Gy) or continued chemotherapy: among those operated, margin-negative resection rose from 50 to 69 percent, across everyone randomized it was 25 versus 18 percent, not significant, and survival did not differ, hazard ratio 0.94 [[TX-L16]]. In borderline resectable disease, A021501 closed its radiation arm early because only 10 of the first 30 people given mFOLFIRINOX (modified FOLFIRINOX chemotherapy) plus SBRT reached a clear margin against 17 of 30 on chemotherapy alone, and 18-month survival was 47 against 67 percent [[TX-012]]. Series reporting 2-year survival of 38 percent after ablative doses come from single centers treating people who had already completed months of chemotherapy without progressing, with no comparison group [[TX-025]][[TX-024]]. Before surgery, the PREOPANC trial's gemcitabine-based chemoradiation raised clear-margin rates among resected patients from 40 to 72 percent and improved 5-year survival over immediate surgery, 20.5 against 6.5 percent, but it compared chemoradiation with no preoperative treatment at all, so the radiation's own share cannot be separated from the chemotherapy's [[TX-004]][[TX-L10]], and FOLFIRINOX alone later proved no worse than that chemoradiation, hazard ratio 0.88 [[TX-L13]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Three randomized trials in two settings agree that radiation after effective chemotherapy improves what it is aimed at, local progression and margin status, without changing how long people live, which is the pattern expected when distant spread rather than the primary tumor sets the time of death [[TX-L15]][[TX-L16]][[TX-012]]. The dose-response signal in retrospective series is real but fragile: in the largest, median survival was 17.8 versus 15.0 months before adjustment and identical, 14.4 versus 14.4, after propensity weighting (a statistical adjustment for differences in who received higher doses), although dose remained associated with survival in the adjusted model [[TX-024]]. No randomized trial has tested ablative-dose radiation against continued chemotherapy after modern induction, so SBRT and ablative radiotherapy remain options whose survival value is unproven even where guidelines list them [[TX-025]][[TX-026]].
research_notes.how_studied: Local control is measured as time to progression inside the irradiated field on serial CT, a reading made uncertain by post-radiation fibrosis; margin status is read on the resected specimen by a pathologist; and survival is counted from randomization in everyone assigned, not only in those who reach surgery, which is why CONKO-007's margin gain among the operated did not become a gain across the trial [[TX-L16]]. Single-center series start their clock at the start of radiation, after people have already survived induction, which inflates their medians relative to trials counting from diagnosis [[TX-025]]. Propensity weighting in the dose-escalation cohort adjusted for measured differences only; tumor position relative to the bowel decided who could be escalated [[TX-024]].

mechanism_notes.text: The value of converting a margin should scale with how likely that margin was to be positive, which is high in borderline resectable disease and low in clearly resectable disease; the same logic predicts that radiation's local effect would matter most where local failure is the main threat, yet in locally advanced disease distant spread dominated survival in both randomized trials [[INF-TX-01]][[TX-L15]][[TX-L16]]. The competing explanation is that conventional doses are simply too low to sterilize the tumor, which the ablative-dose series suggest but have not tested against a control [[TX-024]][[TX-025]].

topics.clinical_status: Chemoradiation and SBRT are guideline-listed options in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 for selected locally advanced and borderline resectable pancreatic cancer and are not governed by an FDA drug or device label; ablative-dose radiotherapy is investigational, and no randomized trial has shown that adding radiation to modern chemotherapy lengthens survival.

glossary.definition: Radiation given in a few large, precisely aimed doses, usually five, with imaging to keep the beam off nearby bowel.
Daily radiation over several weeks combined with a low dose of a chemotherapy drug that makes tumor cells more sensitive to it.
A single number that lets radiation schedules with different dose sizes and numbers of sessions be compared.
An operation in which no cancer cells are found at the cut edges of the removed tissue, which lowers but does not remove the risk of recurrence.
Keeping the tumor from growing in the place it was treated, as distinct from preventing spread elsewhere.
A tumor that touches nearby blood vessels enough to make a clear surgical margin uncertain; it describes the surgical problem, not how malignant the cancer is.
One session of a radiation course.

related.statement: When radiation is used, it usually follows months of induction chemotherapy rather than being the first treatment.
Chemoradiation is considered mainly in borderline resectable and locally advanced disease, where the question is local control or margin conversion.
Radiation improved local control without survival while Tumor Treating Fields improved survival without local control, in the same locally advanced setting.
Whether chemoradiation converted a margin is read by the pathologist on the resected specimen.
In the A021501 trial, SBRT added to mFOLFIRINOX did not improve margin-negative resection over mFOLFIRINOX alone.
The duodenum's tolerance limits the radiation dose that can be delivered to a tumor in the head of the pancreas.
SBRT improved pancreatic pain scores in the phase 2 trial that measured them.

faq.q: Will I need radiation?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Many people with pancreatic cancer never receive radiation, because the randomized trials that added it to chemotherapy improved local control and surgical margins but not survival [[TX-L15]][[TX-L16]]. It is considered when a specific local problem needs answering, such as a tumor that cannot be cleared surgically or local symptoms.

faq.q: If radiation controls the tumor where it is, why doesn't that help people live longer?
faq.a: In the randomized trials, distant spread rather than the primary tumor set the course of the disease, so controlling the pancreas alone did not change survival [[TX-L15]][[TX-012]]. Whether much higher ablative doses change that is an open question that no randomized trial has yet tested [[TX-024]][[TX-025]].

faq.q: What is the difference between SBRT and conventional radiation?
faq.a: Conventional chemoradiation spreads the dose over five to six weeks with a sensitizing drug, while SBRT delivers a larger dose in about five sessions using image guidance to spare the bowel [[TX-026]]. Both are guideline-listed options, and neither has shown a survival advantage over chemotherapy alone in a randomized trial.

topics.title: Tumor Treating Fields
topics.orientation: Tumor Treating Fields (TTFields) are low-intensity alternating electric fields delivered through adhesive arrays worn on the skin of the abdomen for most of the day, added to gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel in locally advanced pancreatic cancer. The FDA approved the device in February 2026 on the strength of a two-month median survival gain in one randomized trial.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: The device generates electric fields at 150 kHz between pairs of arrays placed on the abdomen and connected to a portable generator that the person carries. It is meant to be worn continuously; in the pivotal trial people used it for a median of 62 percent of each day for a median of 27.6 weeks, alongside standard chemotherapy. The arrays themselves are the main source of side effects, through irritation of the skin beneath them.
section1.full: The laboratory rationale, developed for brain tumors before pancreatic cancer, is that fields at this frequency disturb the charged proteins a cell uses to pull its chromosomes apart during division, so that dividing cells are damaged while resting cells are not. Whether that is what happens inside a pancreatic tumor in a person has not been shown, and the pattern of trial results argues against a simple local effect. In the PANOVA-3 trial, 571 people with newly diagnosed, unresectable, locally advanced disease were randomized to gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel with or without the device [[TX-010]]. Device-related skin reactions occurred in 76.3 percent of users, 7.7 percent had a device-related adverse event of grade 3 (severe) or worse, and there was no increase in the chemotherapy's own systemic toxicity, so the harms are local, cumulative and tied to hours of wear [[TX-010]]. The practical burden is real: shaving, array changes, carrying the generator, and heat and itching under the arrays, for a treatment that must be worn for months to deliver its measured benefit. The device is not a substitute for chemotherapy; it was tested only as an addition to it, and only in disease confined to the pancreas and its surroundings, not in metastatic or resectable disease [[TX-010]][[SEC-TX-11]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Adding the device lengthened median survival from 14.2 to 16.2 months, hazard ratio 0.82, without lengthening the time before the cancer grew, without shrinking tumors more often and without making more tumors operable. Pain-free survival was longer, 15.2 against 9.1 months. A treatment that improves survival but not progression is unusual, and the reason is unexplained, which is why the result is read carefully rather than dismissed or oversold.
section2.full: Overall survival was the primary endpoint and it was met: 16.2 months (95 percent confidence interval 15.0 to 18.0) against 14.2 months (12.8 to 15.4), hazard ratio 0.82 (0.68 to 0.99), with 1-year survival 68.1 against 60.2 percent [[TX-010]]. Progression-free survival, however, was 10.6 against 9.3 months, hazard ratio 0.85, not significant; local progression-free survival and response rate did not differ; and 7.0 percent versus 10.1 percent went on to surgery, no different [[TX-010]]. Pain-free survival favored the device, 15.2 against 9.1 months, hazard ratio 0.74, and an analysis added after the trial (post hoc) found fewer distant progressions, which is the opposite of what a treatment confined to the abdomen was expected to do [[TX-010]]. The trial was open-label, so people and clinicians knew who wore the device; that matters most for pain, which is self-reported, and for the timing of progression calls, and there was no central review of scans or required staging laparoscopy, so some people with undetected metastases may have been included [[TX-010]]. On 12 February 2026 the FDA granted premarket approval to Optune Pax for adults with locally advanced pancreatic cancer in combination with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, citing the two-month survival gain; this is a device approval, a different regulatory pathway from a drug label [[SEC-TX-11]]. Among people who completed at least one cycle, median survival was 18.3 against 15.1 months, a selected group that excludes early dropouts [[TX-010]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The survival gain is statistically significant but modest and rests on one open-label trial; the hazard ratio's upper confidence bound of 0.99 sits close to no effect [[TX-010]]. The dissociation between survival and progression is the central puzzle: radiation improves local control without survival, while this device improved survival without local control, so either radiologic progression in treated locally advanced disease is too unreliable to register a real local effect, or the fields act on something other than the visible tumor, such as peritoneal or retroperitoneal micrometastatic spread, or the pain and supportive-care differences changed how much chemotherapy people could receive [[TX-010]][[INF-TX-03]]. None of these has been tested, and the open-label design leaves bias in how outcomes were judged, known as ascertainment effects, as a live alternative.
research_notes.how_studied: Survival was counted from randomization in everyone assigned, which is the right denominator; progression was judged by investigators on local imaging without central review, in a disease where fibrosis and tumor look alike on CT [[TX-010]]. Pain-free survival combines time to worsening pain or death, measured by patient questionnaire, and is therefore sensitive to knowing one's treatment arm. Usage is logged by the device, which is how the 62 percent median daily wear is known; a sham-device trial, which would blind participants, has not been done, and the analyses of distant progression were not prespecified [[TX-010]][[INF-TX-03]].

mechanism_notes.text: The device may act within the field on microscopic peritoneal and retroperitoneal spread rather than on the measurable tumor, which would fit the post hoc reduction in distant progression and the absence of local benefit [[INF-TX-03]][[TX-010]]. Alternatively, better pain control may have allowed more chemotherapy and supportive care, or unblinded assessment may have shifted progression calls; site-of-first-progression analyses and the blood marker CA 19-9 from the trial, or a sham-controlled study, would discriminate.

topics.clinical_status: FDA premarket approval (US) announced 12 February 2026 for Optune Pax in adults with locally advanced pancreatic cancer in combination with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel; a device approval rather than a drug indication, not covering metastatic or resectable disease. Checked 8 Oct 2026.

glossary.definition: Low-intensity alternating electric fields delivered through skin arrays, intended to disrupt dividing cells in the treated region.
The adhesive pad containing electrodes that is stuck to the skin to deliver the fields.
A tumor that has grown around nearby arteries enough to be unresectable but has not spread to distant organs.
The time from treatment start until the cancer is seen to grow on scans or the person dies.
The time until pain worsens by a set amount on a questionnaire or the person dies.
A trial in which participants and clinicians know which treatment was assigned.
The FDA pathway for high-risk medical devices, separate from the drug-approval process.

related.statement: Tumor Treating Fields were tested and approved only as an addition to gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel.
Tumor Treating Fields improved survival without local control, the mirror image of radiation's local control without survival.
The device is approved for locally advanced disease only, not for metastatic or resectable pancreatic cancer.
Tumor Treating Fields lengthened pain-free survival from 9.1 to 15.2 months in the pivotal trial.
The PANOVA-3 trial is an example of a trial that met its survival endpoint while missing its progression endpoint, which affects how its result should be read.

faq.q: Does the device replace chemotherapy?
faq.a: No. It was tested only on top of gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel, and the approval is for that combination in locally advanced disease [[TX-010]][[SEC-TX-11]].

faq.q: Why did it help people live longer if it did not stop the tumor growing?
faq.a: That is unexplained. Progression-free survival, local control and response rates were no different, while survival and pain-free survival were better; possible reasons range from an effect on microscopic spread to the unblinded design, and none has been tested [[TX-010]][[INF-TX-03]].

faq.q: What is it like to wear?
faq.a: Arrays are stuck to the shaved abdomen and connected to a carried generator, worn most of the day for months; in the trial median use was 62 percent of each day for about 28 weeks, and skin reactions occurred in three-quarters of users, with 7.7 percent having a severe device-related event [[TX-010]].

topics.title: Olaparib and PARP inhibitors
topics.orientation: Olaparib (Lynparza) is a tablet that blocks PARP, an enzyme cells use to repair minor DNA damage. In pancreatic cancer it is given as maintenance after platinum chemotherapy to the roughly 7 percent of people with metastatic disease who inherited a faulty BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene; it lengthens the time before the cancer grows again but has not been shown to lengthen life.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: PARP enzymes patch single-strand nicks in DNA as cells copy their genome. When olaparib blocks them, the nicks persist and become double-strand breaks at the next round of copying; a cell with working homologous recombination, the accurate repair system for double-strand breaks, repairs those, but a tumor cell that has lost BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 cannot and dies. Normal cells, which keep one working copy of the gene, are largely spared, which is what makes the drug selective.
section1.full: Olaparib does more than switch PARP off: it traps the enzyme on the DNA at the site of the nick, so that the stalled complex itself becomes an obstacle the copying machinery collides with, generating the double-strand breaks that only homologous recombination can resolve accurately. That dependence is the whole basis of the treatment, and it explains the selection rules: benefit tracks tumors that have lost repair function in both copies of a core gene, not merely a variant listed on a report [[GENE-016]]. In the POLO trial the dose was 300 mg twice daily, begun four to eight weeks after the last platinum dose and continued until the cancer progressed; the progression curves separated after about five months, so the effect is one of holding disease in check rather than rapid shrinkage, although 23 percent of people with measurable disease did respond, including two complete responses, against 12 percent on placebo [[TX-005]]. The main toxicity is on the blood: grade 3 (severe) or worse anemia occurred in 11 percent against 3 percent, and global quality of life did not change measurably [[TX-005]]; with the related drug rucaparib, anemia of any grade affected 74 percent and nausea and fatigue about half [[TX-017]]. No case of treatment-related leukemia or myelodysplasia (a bone-marrow disorder), a recognized rare risk of the class, appeared during the trial's follow-up [[TX-L24]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: In the POLO trial, maintenance olaparib doubled progression-free survival in inherited BRCA carriers whose metastatic cancer had not progressed on at least 16 weeks of platinum chemotherapy, 7.4 against 3.8 months, hazard ratio 0.53, and delayed the next chemotherapy. Overall survival did not differ, 19.0 against 19.2 months. The approval covers inherited BRCA1 or BRCA2 only, although the biology, and a smaller rucaparib study, suggest the dependence extends to PALB2 and to tumor-acquired BRCA loss.
section2.full: Of 3,315 people screened, 7.5 percent carried a germline (inherited) BRCA mutation, and 154 whose disease was stable after platinum were randomized three to two to olaparib or placebo [[TX-005]]. The primary endpoint, progression-free survival by blinded central review, was met [[TX-005]]. The final overall-survival analysis found 19.0 against 19.2 months, hazard ratio 0.83, not significant, with 3-year survival 33.9 against 17.8 percent; 27 percent of placebo patients who stopped went on to a PARP inhibitor, which the investigators believe diluted any survival effect [[TX-L24]]. The comparator was a treatment break, not continued chemotherapy [[TX-005]]. The FDA approved it on 27 December 2019 for germline BRCA-mutated metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma without progression on at least 16 weeks of first-line platinum, with the BRACAnalysis blood test as a required companion diagnostic [[SEC-TX-03]]. Rucaparib, a related drug not approved for this disease, was given as maintenance to 42 evaluable people with germline or tumor BRCA or PALB2 variants: 59.5 percent were progression-free at six months and 41.7 percent responded, including 3 of 6 with germline PALB2 and 1 of 2 with tumor-acquired BRCA2, without a control group [[TX-017]]. ATM and other non-core repair genes behave differently: in a trial of the related drug niraparib that enrolled by gene name, median progression-free survival was 2.0 months, and every durable responder had lost both copies of a repair gene [[GENE-025]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: A doubling of progression-free survival with no overall-survival difference admits two readings: crossover and platinum re-exposure in the placebo arm masked a true survival effect that shows only in the 3-year tail, or olaparib slows indolent, platinum-sensitive disease without changing the clone that eventually proves lethal [[TX-L24]][[INF-TX-02]]. The trial was small and underpowered for survival, so neither is settled [[TX-005]]. What the biology supports is that the operative variable is biallelic loss of repair function, meaning both copies of the gene are lost, since germline and tumor-acquired loss behaved alike and biallelic tumors carried more genomic scarring than monoallelic ones [[GENE-016]]; the label's restriction to germline BRCA reflects what was tested, not a biological boundary [[SEC-TX-03]].
research_notes.how_studied: Eligibility was established by a central germline test on blood, which detects inherited variants but not variants that arose only in the tumor; distinguishing one lost copy from two requires allele-specific copy-number analysis of tumor DNA, which POLO did not perform [[TX-005]][[GENE-016]]. Progression was judged by blinded central radiology, overall survival counted from randomization, and both arms were followed for subsequent therapies so that crossover could be described [[TX-L24]]. The rucaparib study was single-arm with a 6-month progression-free rate as its endpoint, which cannot separate the drug's effect from the lingering effect of the chemotherapy just stopped [[TX-017]].

mechanism_notes.text: The investigators' hypothesis is that subsequent PARP-inhibitor use and platinum re-sensitivity in the placebo arm, plus underpowering, hid a survival effect that appears only as the late 3-year separation among durable responders [[INF-TX-02]][[TX-L24]]. The competing reading is that olaparib delays radiologic progression without altering the kinetics of the lethal clone; a crossover-adjusted analysis, or a trial against continued chemotherapy, would discriminate [[TX-005]].

topics.clinical_status: Approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 (since 27 December 2019) as maintenance for germline BRCA1/2-mutated metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma that has not progressed after at least 16 weeks of first-line platinum chemotherapy, with an FDA-approved germline companion diagnostic; rucaparib and niraparib are not approved for pancreatic cancer, and tumor-acquired BRCA or PALB2 loss is not on the olaparib label.

glossary.definition: An enzyme that detects single-strand breaks in DNA and recruits the proteins that repair them.
A treatment continued after chemotherapy has controlled the cancer, intended to delay regrowth.
Inherited and present in every cell of the body, detectable in a blood or saliva test.
Arising in the tumor only, detectable by testing tumor tissue but not blood.
Drugs such as oxaliplatin or cisplatin that cross-link DNA strands, which cells lacking homologous recombination cannot repair.
A test the FDA requires to identify who may receive a particular drug.
The accurate repair of a double-strand DNA break using the matching sister copy of the chromosome as a template.

related.statement: Tumors that have lost BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 function are the ones olaparib and other PARP inhibitors can kill.
ATM and other non-core repair genes do not predict PARP-inhibitor benefit the way biallelic BRCA loss does.
At least 16 weeks of platinum-containing chemotherapy, usually FOLFIRINOX, precedes maintenance olaparib.
The same repair defect that makes a tumor sensitive to olaparib makes it sensitive to oxaliplatin and other platinum drugs.
Eligibility for olaparib is established by a germline BRCA blood test, which cannot detect loss that arose only in the tumor.
A germline BRCA result that qualifies someone for olaparib also has implications for relatives, who may carry the same variant.
PARP inhibition exploits the loss of one DNA-repair pathway by blocking another.

faq.q: My report lists an ATM mutation. Does that mean olaparib will work for me?
faq.a: Not on current evidence. The approval is for inherited BRCA1 or BRCA2 only, and in a trial that enrolled by gene name across BRCA, PALB2, ATM and CHEK2, median progression-free survival on a PARP inhibitor was 2.0 months; the few durable responses were in people whose tumors had lost both copies of a repair gene [[GENE-025]][[SEC-TX-03]].

faq.q: Why did olaparib not help people live longer?
faq.a: It doubled the time before progression, but median survival was 19.0 against 19.2 months. The investigators attribute this partly to placebo patients later receiving PARP inhibitors and more platinum, and the trial was too small to settle a survival question; 3-year survival did favor olaparib, 34 against 18 percent [[TX-L24]].

faq.q: My BRCA mutation was found only in the tumor, not in my blood. Does the drug still apply?
faq.a: The US label covers inherited (germline) BRCA only, because that is who POLO enrolled [[SEC-TX-03]]. Biologically, tumor-acquired and inherited loss behaved alike, and a rucaparib study saw responses in tumor-acquired BRCA2 carriers, but that use is outside the label [[GENE-016]][[TX-017]].

topics.title: Pembrolizumab for mismatch-repair-deficient tumors
topics.orientation: Pembrolizumab (Keytruda) is an antibody that releases a brake, PD-1, on T cells. It is approved for any solid tumor that has lost mismatch repair, pancreatic cancer included, but that defect is present in about 1 percent of pancreatic cancers, and in the other 99 percent checkpoint drugs have failed every randomized test.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: T cells that recognize a tumor carry a surface receptor, PD-1, that switches them off when it meets its partner PD-L1 on tumor or surrounding cells. Pembrolizumab binds PD-1 and blocks that signal, so the T cells stay active. It is given into a vein every three weeks for up to two years, and it only helps where T cells already recognize something on the tumor, which is why its benefit is tied to a specific molecular defect.
section1.full: A tumor whose mismatch-repair proteins (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2) have stopped working cannot correct the spelling errors made during DNA copying, so it accumulates thousands of mutations, many of which produce altered proteins that T cells can see as foreign; this state is called mismatch-repair deficiency (dMMR) and shows up on testing as microsatellite instability (MSI-high). In the trial that established the principle, 86 people with such tumors across 12 cancer types received pembrolizumab: 53 percent responded, 21 percent completely, and the T-cell clones that expanded in the blood were those reactive to mutation-derived antigens [[TX-007]]. Responses take time and then last: median time to response was 2.1 months in the larger follow-on study, and 86.9 percent of responses were still ongoing at 12 months [[TX-016]]. Eleven complete responders who stopped after two years had no recurrence at a median of 8.3 months off treatment [[TX-007]]. The price is that released T cells can attack normal tissue: immune-mediated adverse events or infusion reactions occurred in 23.2 percent and were severe (grade 3 or 4) in 6.0 percent, typically inflammation of the thyroid, bowel, lung, liver or skin that needs recognition and often steroid treatment [[TX-016]]. Primary resistance, where the tumor never responds despite the defect, occurred in 14 percent [[TX-007]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: The approval is tissue-agnostic, granted in 2017 and made permanent in 2023 because about half of mismatch-repair-deficient tumors respond regardless of organ. Pancreatic cancer tests the rule: only 4 of 22 such pancreatic cancers responded in the registration data, fewer than 1 in 100 pancreatic cancers has the defect, and the tests that find it can miss it. For the rest, checkpoint drugs have not lengthened survival.
section2.full: The FDA granted accelerated approval on 23 May 2017 and regular approval on 28 March 2023 for unresectable or metastatic MSI-high or dMMR solid tumors after prior treatment; the label lists 22 pancreatic cancers from the KEYNOTE-158 trial with a response rate of 18 percent (4 of 22) and responses lasting 8.1 to beyond 24.3 months [[SEC-TX-04]][[TX-016]]. The defect is rare: 7 of 833 consecutive patients at one center (0.8 percent), all with Lynch syndrome, an inherited mismatch-repair fault [[GENE-006]], about 1 to 2 percent pooled across 8,323 patients [[SEC-GENE-03]], and 4.7 percent of KRAS-wild-type (unmutated) tumors against 0.7 percent of KRAS-mutant ones [[GENE-005]]. Finding it is not routine: the three test types, protein staining (immunohistochemistry), PCR and sequencing, disagree, which is why older studies reported anything from 0 to 75 percent [[IMM-020]]; tissue staining missed a case that a blood test caught, and 7 of 9 people identified by blood testing responded [[IMM-021]]; and among 55 patients carrying a mismatch-repair gene variant only about half had MSI-high tumors, and a fifth were recognized as MSI-high only after a second method was applied [[IMM-027]]. Outside this group the class has not delivered: the checkpoint pair durvalumab plus tremelimumab added to gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel gave median survival of 9.8 against 8.8 months, hazard ratio 0.94, in 180 unselected patients, one of whom was MSI-high [[IMM-007]]; nivolumab plus ipilimumab combined with vaccines produced response rates of 0 and 7 percent [[IMM-012]]; and a vaccine regimen tested against chemotherapy did worse, hazard ratio 1.17 [[IMM-005]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The tissue-agnostic approval rests on a mechanism, mutation load creating visible antigens, that holds across organs, but the pancreatic cohort responded less often than the 34 percent average, 18 percent, for reasons that may include misclassified MSI status, clinical decline faster than an immune response can build, or a less permissive tumor environment [[TX-016]][[IMM-020]]. Small series of people confirmed MSI-high by careful testing report far higher response and disease-control rates, 7 of 9 and 80 percent, which suggests that who gets counted as eligible matters as much as the drug [[IMM-021]][[IMM-027]]. For unselected pancreatic cancer the randomized failures are consistent, and tumor mutational burden essentially never reaches the threshold of 10 mutations per megabase (million DNA letters) that carries a separate approval [[IMM-007]][[SEC-TX-04]].
research_notes.how_studied: Mismatch-repair status is read three ways: immunohistochemistry (staining) for the four repair proteins, PCR (a DNA-amplification test) for instability at defined microsatellite sites, and sequencing-derived instability scores; in pancreatic specimens, which often contain little tumor among dense stroma, each can fail, and a composite of all three with germline testing is the most reliable [[IMM-020]][[IMM-027]]. Plasma circulating-tumor-DNA assays offer a second route when tissue is scant [[IMM-021]]. Response in the basket trials (trials enrolling many cancer types by a shared molecular feature) was measured by independent central radiology against RECIST (the standard criteria for tumor shrinkage on scans), with pancreatic cases pooled with other organs, so the 4 of 22 figure comes from the label's per-tumor table rather than a pancreatic-specific trial [[TX-016]][[SEC-TX-04]]. The negative randomized trials used overall survival as the primary endpoint in biomarker-unselected populations [[IMM-007]].

mechanism_notes.text: In pancreatic cancers without mismatch-repair deficiency, releasing PD-1 may fail because too few tumor-reactive T cells exist and those that arrive are switched off inside the tumor by signals that PD-1 blockade does not touch, which would explain why T cells can be found inside tumors on combination immunotherapy with no shrinkage [[INF-IMMUNE-01]][[IMM-012]]. Mismatch-repair deficiency supplies the missing ingredient, abundant antigen, which is why the same drug works there [[TX-007]].

topics.clinical_status: Approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 (accelerated 23 May 2017, regular 28 March 2023) for unresectable or metastatic MSI-high or mismatch-repair-deficient solid tumors that have progressed after prior treatment, as determined by an FDA-authorized test, and separately for tumor-mutational-burden-high tumors (since 16 June 2020); no checkpoint inhibitor is approved for pancreatic cancer unselected by these markers.

glossary.definition: A receptor on T cells that switches them off when engaged, which tumors exploit to escape attack.
An antibody that blocks a switch-off signal such as PD-1 so that T cells remain active.
The proofreading system that corrects spelling errors made when DNA is copied.
The pattern of errors in repetitive DNA that reveals a tumor has lost mismatch repair.
An inherited fault in a mismatch-repair gene that raises the risk of several cancers.
A drug approval defined by a molecular feature rather than by the organ the cancer started in.
Inflammation of a normal organ caused by T cells released from their brakes.
The number of mutations per million DNA letters in a tumor, a rough measure of how foreign it may look to T cells.

related.statement: Mismatch-repair-deficient pancreatic cancers are the only ones for which pembrolizumab is approved.
Eligibility for pembrolizumab depends on mismatch-repair or MSI testing, which can miss the defect in low-cellularity pancreatic specimens.
Checkpoint drugs combined with chemotherapy or vaccines have not improved survival in unselected pancreatic cancer.
Pembrolizumab works only where the tumor already displays antigens that T cells recognize, which mismatch-repair deficiency supplies.
Pembrolizumab releases the PD-1 brake on T cells so that those already recognizing the tumor stay active.
Mismatch-repair deficiency is several times more common in KRAS-wild-type pancreatic cancers than in KRAS-mutant ones.
Most mismatch-repair-deficient pancreatic cancers arise in people with Lynch syndrome, an inherited condition.

faq.q: Can I get immunotherapy for pancreatic cancer?
faq.a: Only if the tumor has lost mismatch repair, which is found in about 1 in 100 pancreatic cancers, and even then 4 of 22 responded in the registration data [[GENE-006]][[SEC-TX-04]]. For everyone else, checkpoint drugs have not improved survival in randomized trials [[IMM-007]].

faq.q: My tumor was reported as microsatellite stable. Is that final?
faq.a: Usually, but tissue tests can miss the defect in specimens with little tumor: a blood test found a case that staining had missed, and about a fifth of variant carriers in one series were recognized as MSI-high only after a second method was used [[IMM-021]][[IMM-027]]. A germline test for Lynch syndrome is a separate question worth asking.

faq.q: What are the side effects?
faq.a: Released T cells can inflame normal organs; immune-mediated events occurred in 23 percent and were severe in 6 percent in the basket trial, most often thyroid, bowel, lung, liver or skin, and they need early recognition because steroids usually settle them [[TX-016]].

topics.title: Drugs for gene fusions and rare targets
topics.orientation: A gene fusion joins two genes so that the growth signal from one is switched on permanently by the other. In pancreatic cancer fusions sit almost entirely in the roughly 10 percent of tumors without a KRAS mutation, and several drugs that block specific fused or mutated proteins are approved in the US, most for any tumor type and one, zenocutuzumab, specifically for pancreatic cancer.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: Each of these drugs blocks one abnormal protein. Larotrectinib and entrectinib block the TRK kinases, growth-signaling enzymes, made by NTRK fusions, selpercatinib blocks the RET kinase, and dabrafenib with trametinib blocks the BRAF V600E mutant protein and the MEK protein beneath it. Zenocutuzumab is different: an antibody that binds HER2 and HER3 at once, so that the growth factor produced by an NRG1 fusion cannot activate them. Because each target is specific, responses are often rapid and side effects are drug-specific rather than chemotherapy-like.
section1.full: A kinase fusion typically welds the signaling part of a growth enzyme to a partner that forces it to pair up and fire without any external signal, so the tumor depends on that one output and a small-molecule inhibitor that fits the kinase pocket can shut it off. An NRG1 fusion works differently: it makes the cell display a tethered growth factor that continually stimulates HER3, which recruits HER2, and zenocutuzumab, given as 750 mg into a vein every two weeks, docks on both receptors and blocks the growth factor's binding site [[TX-020]]. Responses come quickly, within about two months, and in fusion-driven tumors they can last: median duration of response was 24.5 months with selpercatinib across tumor types and was not reached for larotrectinib at a year, when 71 percent of responses were ongoing [[TX-019]][[TX-018]]. Adverse effects differ by drug. Selpercatinib caused severe (grade 3 or worse) hypertension in 22 percent and liver-enzyme rises in 13 to 16 percent, with serious events in 40 percent [[TX-019]]; larotrectinib's events were mostly grade 1 (mild), with dose reductions in 15 percent [[TX-018]]; zenocutuzumab's were mainly low-grade, with grade 3 or 4 anemia in 5 percent [[TX-020]]; and dabrafenib plus trametinib caused fever in 40.8 percent and chills and fatigue in about a quarter each, with fatal serious events in 4.4 percent across a trial spanning many rare cancers [[TX-021]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: In 2,483 pancreatic cancers, 10.7 percent had no KRAS mutation, and 21 percent of those carried a fusion: BRAF 6.6 percent, FGFR2 5.2, ALK 2.6, RET 1.3, NRG1 1.3 and RAF1 1.3, against essentially none of the KRAS-mutant tumors. A KRAS-normal result is therefore the single strongest reason to order fusion testing by RNA sequencing. For each target, the approved indication, the pancreatic-specific evidence and the route to the drug differ.
section2.full: Zenocutuzumab is the one drug here with a pancreatic-specific indication: 15 of 36 previously treated people with NRG1-fusion pancreatic adenocarcinoma responded (42 percent), with a median duration of 7.4 months, all of them KRAS-wild-type (without a KRAS mutation), and the FDA gave accelerated approval on 4 December 2024 for NRG1-fusion pancreatic adenocarcinoma after prior systemic therapy [[TX-020]][[SEC-TX-08]]. The label states that no FDA-approved test for NRG1 fusions exists, so eligibility rests on laboratory sequencing [[SEC-DIAG-02]]. Selpercatinib's approval is tissue-agnostic (accelerated, 21 September 2022), but its registration cohort included 11 evaluable pancreatic cancers, of whom 6 responded [[TX-019]][[SEC-TX-06]]. Larotrectinib (26 November 2018) and entrectinib (15 August 2019) are approved for any NTRK-fusion solid tumor on a 75 percent response rate across 17 cancer types in which pancreatic cases were not enumerated [[TX-018]][[SEC-TX-05]]. Dabrafenib plus trametinib (accelerated, 22 June 2022) covers BRAF V600E solid tumors after prior treatment, yet the pivotal multi-cancer (basket) trial had no pancreatic cohort; the pancreatic support is that V600E occurs in about 3 percent of tumors, never alongside KRAS, and that a cell line grown from a patient's V600E tumor was as sensitive to a BRAF inhibitor as melanoma cells [[TX-021]][[SEC-TX-07]][[GENE-002]]. Most BRAF alterations in KRAS-normal pancreatic cancer are not V600E, and FGFR2 and ALK fusions, the next most common, have no pancreatic approval, so their drugs are reached through trials or off-label use [[GENE-005]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Three approval categories need separating. Zenocutuzumab has a pancreatic indication backed by pancreatic data, but it is accelerated, meaning confirmation of clinical benefit is still owed, and its pancreatic durability is shorter than its overall figure [[TX-020]][[SEC-TX-08]]. The tissue-agnostic approvals carry pancreatic evidence ranging from 6 of 11 for selpercatinib to none at all for dabrafenib plus trametinib, so a label that includes pancreatic cancer is not the same as evidence in pancreatic cancer [[TX-019]][[TX-021]]. All these responses occur in KRAS-wild-type tumors, which had better survival in both arms of a randomized trial regardless of treatment, so single-arm response rates overstate what the drug alone adds [[TX-020]][[IMM-007]]. The often-quoted survival advantage of matched therapy, 2.58 against 1.51 years, comes from an unplanned comparison among the 2 percent of referred patients who received one, and is confounded by who reaches treatment [[GENE-029]].
research_notes.how_studied: Fusions are detected most reliably by RNA sequencing of the tumor, because the joining point lies in DNA regions that DNA panels often do not cover; the 2,483-patient series required at least 10 percent tumor content, and a KRAS-wild-type call can itself be a false negative from scant tumor in a specimen [[GENE-005]]. Efficacy comes from single-arm basket trials with objective response by independent review as the primary endpoint and duration of response as the key secondary one; pancreatic numbers are subgroups within those baskets, 36 for zenocutuzumab and 11 for selpercatinib, with wide confidence intervals [[TX-020]][[TX-019]]. Accelerated approvals are granted on response and duration, not survival, and remain conditional until a confirmatory study reports [[SEC-TX-08]][[SEC-TX-07]].

mechanism_notes.text: Fusions and KRAS mutations are almost never found together because each is sufficient to drive the same growth pathway, so a tumor acquires one or the other; this is why fusion testing pays off almost only in KRAS-wild-type disease [[GENE-005]][[GENE-002]]. Part of the favorable survival of KRAS-wild-type tumors appears to be prognostic rather than drug-related, since it was present in both arms of a randomized trial, which should temper how single-arm response rates in this group are read [[IMM-007]][[TX-020]].

topics.clinical_status: Approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026: zenocutuzumab-zbco (accelerated, 4 December 2024) for NRG1-fusion pancreatic adenocarcinoma after prior systemic therapy; larotrectinib (26 November 2018) and entrectinib (15 August 2019) for NTRK-fusion solid tumors; selpercatinib (accelerated, 21 September 2022) for RET-fusion solid tumors; dabrafenib plus trametinib (accelerated, 22 June 2022) for BRAF V600E solid tumors after prior treatment. No approved drug exists for FGFR2, ALK or RAF1 fusions in pancreatic cancer, and no FDA-approved NRG1 fusion test exists.

glossary.definition: An abnormal joining of two genes that leaves a growth signal permanently switched on.
An enzyme that passes growth signals inside the cell by adding phosphate to other proteins.
The gene for neuregulin, a growth factor that activates HER3; when fused, it keeps that receptor constantly stimulated.
A receptor on the cell surface that, when stimulated by neuregulin, pairs with HER2 to drive growth.
A drug approval defined by a molecular feature rather than by the organ the cancer started in.
A conditional FDA approval based on tumor response rather than proven survival benefit, pending a confirmatory study.
A tumor with no mutation in the KRAS gene, which in pancreatic cancer is where most fusions are found.
Reading the tumor's RNA messages, which detects fusions that DNA-only panels can miss.

related.statement: NRG1, RET and NTRK fusions and BRAF V600E are the rare targets for which fusion-directed drugs exist.
Fusions are found in 21 percent of KRAS-wild-type pancreatic cancers and essentially none of the KRAS-mutant ones.
Fusion-directed drugs can only be offered after RNA-based sequencing has found the fusion.
Drugs for FGFR2 and ALK fusions have no pancreatic approval and are reached through trials or off-label use.
A tumor driven by a fusion almost never also carries a KRAS mutation, because either alone drives the same pathway.

faq.q: Should I be tested for gene fusions?
faq.a: If the tumor has no KRAS mutation, yes: 21 percent of such tumors carried a fusion in a large series, against essentially none of the KRAS-mutant ones, and the test needs to include RNA sequencing to catch them [[GENE-005]].

faq.q: What does accelerated approval mean for me?
faq.a: The drug can be prescribed, but the approval rested on how often and how long tumors shrank rather than on proven longer survival, and it remains conditional until a confirmatory study reports; zenocutuzumab's pancreatic indication is in this category [[SEC-TX-08]][[TX-020]].

faq.q: My tumor has a BRAF mutation. Is there a drug?
faq.a: Dabrafenib plus trametinib is approved for the V600E form of BRAF in any solid tumor after prior treatment, but the pivotal trial had no pancreatic patients, and most BRAF alterations in KRAS-normal pancreatic cancer are other forms that this combination does not target [[TX-021]][[GENE-005]].

topics.title: Daraxonrasib: the first approved RAS inhibitor
topics.orientation: Daraxonrasib (RASONQUE, formerly RMC-6236) is the first drug acting on RAS itself to be approved for pancreatic cancer, in the US on 26 August 2026, for metastatic disease after at least one prior treatment. In its pivotal trial it roughly doubled median survival compared with chemotherapy, and most tumors still eventually escape it.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: KRAS is a switch protein that, when mutated, stays in its ON state and drives the cancer's growth; it was long considered undruggable because its surface has no pocket for a drug to sit in. Daraxonrasib solves this by first binding an abundant cellular protein, cyclophilin A, and the drug-protein pair then clamps onto RAS in its ON state, physically blocking it from passing its signal to the next protein in the chain. It is a tablet taken once daily.
section1.full: The drug is multi-selective: it binds the active form of mutant and normal KRAS, NRAS and HRAS alike, rather than one mutant such as G12C, which is why it can treat the G12D, G12V and G12R mutations that account for most pancreatic cancers. In mice, the research compound of this class produced regression in 9 of 15 pancreatic, colorectal and lung models carrying KRAS mutations at position 12 (codon 12) and held them for up to 90 days, where blocking the pathway above RAS (SHP2) or below it (MEK) produced only modest slowing [[RAS-003]]; exposure-response modeling then predicted that 300 mg daily would produce measurable tumor shrinkage (objective responses) in people, which the first-in-human study bore out [[RAS-011]]. Among 168 previously treated pancreatic patients in that study, treatment-related adverse events of any grade occurred in 96 percent and severe (grade 3 or worse) in 30 percent: rash, diarrhea, nausea, mouth sores, vomiting and fatigue were each reported in at least 10 percent [[RAS-032]]. The rash is frequent enough that the US label recommends preventive and concurrent medication to reduce skin reactions [[SEC-RAS-02]]. In the 26 people with RAS G12 mutations treated second-line at 300 mg, 35 percent responded, responses lasted a median of 8.2 months and median time to progression was 8.5 months, so the effect is substantial but usually not permanent [[RAS-032]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: The RASolute 302 trial randomized 500 previously treated people with metastatic pancreatic cancer to daraxonrasib or the clinician's choice of chemotherapy: median survival 13.2 against 6.7 months, hazard ratio 0.40; median progression-free survival 7.2 against 3.6 months; response 30 against 11 percent; with fewer people stopping for side effects. The approval requires no RAS test, although the trial's primary endpoints were defined in the 92 percent with RAS G12 mutations.
section2.full: Overall survival was 13.2 against 6.6 months in the RAS G12 group and 13.2 against 6.7 months overall, hazard ratio 0.40 (95 percent confidence interval 0.30 to 0.53); progression-free hazard ratios were 0.45 and 0.49; severe (grade 3 or worse) adverse events occurred in 61.8 percent on daraxonrasib against 69.6 percent on chemotherapy, and treatment-related discontinuation in 1.2 against 11.2 percent [[RAS-033]][[SEC-RAS-01]]. Those figures come from the published abstract and the FDA approval notice; the full report is available only as an abstract and no results are posted on the trial registry, so crossover handling and subgroup results are not yet known [[RAS-033]]. The label indicates the drug for adults with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma after at least one systemic therapy, with no mutation requirement and no companion diagnostic, even though the trial was powered in the RAS G12 population; how much the 8 percent with RAS-normal tumors benefit is unknown [[SEC-RAS-02]][[RAS-033]]. Resistance follows a pattern: in 44 patients with paired blood samples, 25 percent had new alterations at progression, RAF-gene variants in 11 percent and receptor changes such as HER2 amplification or a MET fusion in 9 percent, usually with extra copies of mutant KRAS and never a mutation at the drug's binding site; in the other three-quarters no genetic cause was found [[RAS-012]][[RAS-010]]. The RASolute 303 trial (900 people, first-line) and RASolute 304 (500 people, after surgery) are recruiting, with no results expected before 2028 and 2029 [[SEC-RAS-06]][[SEC-RAS-07]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: A hazard ratio of 0.40 against active chemotherapy, with a control arm performing in line with historical second-line benchmarks, is the strongest drug effect recorded in this disease, and it was obtained in a randomized trial, so it is attributable to the drug rather than to selection [[RAS-033]]. Its limits are equally clear: median progression-free survival of about seven months and response duration of about eight months mean the drug delays rather than cures, and the mechanisms of escape, convergent reactivation of the same pathway by RAF, receptor or KRAS-copy changes, mirror what ended responses to the earlier G12C-selective drugs, with no binding-site mutations and most progressions unexplained genetically [[RAS-012]][[RAS-010]][[RAS-014]]. The mutation-agnostic label extends the indication beyond the population in which the endpoints were defined [[SEC-RAS-02]].
research_notes.how_studied: RASolute 302 was open-label with dual primary endpoints, overall and progression-free survival, defined in the RAS G12 subpopulation and tested hierarchically; survival is robust to unblinded assessment, progression less so, and quality of life was patient-reported [[RAS-033]][[SEC-RAS-05]]. Resistance was read from circulating tumor DNA sequenced across more than 800 genes before treatment and at progression in the same patients, then tested for sufficiency by engineering the candidate lesions into pancreatic cancer cells and organoids (miniature tumors grown in the laboratory); a blood panel cannot see structural or epigenetic escape, and pancreatic tumors shed DNA poorly, so a finding of no mechanism may partly be a detection limit [[RAS-012]]. Dose selection rested on exposure-response modeling from mouse xenografts [[RAS-011]].

mechanism_notes.text: A drug-tolerant residual population, maintained by growth-factor receptors assembling signaling complexes around normal RAS through the lipid enzyme PI3K and the scaffold protein GAB1, is probably established within days of starting treatment and sets the floor that imaging records as a partial rather than complete response; the genetic lesions found at progression, RAF variants and KRAS amplification, would then be late consolidating steps, which is why they are absent in most patients when growth first shows [[INF-RAS-01]][[RAS-012]][[RAS-027]]. The competing explanation is a host-side reversal of an early immune response; serial on-treatment biopsies at two to four weeks would discriminate.

topics.clinical_status: Approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 (since 26 August 2026) for adults with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma who have received at least one prior systemic therapy or who are not candidates for multi-agent systemic therapy, 300 mg orally once daily, with no RAS mutation requirement or companion diagnostic; not approved for first-line or adjuvant use, which RASolute 303 and 304 are testing.

glossary.definition: A family of switch proteins (KRAS, NRAS, HRAS) that relay growth signals; a mutated KRAS is stuck on in most pancreatic cancers.
A drug that binds RAS in its active, signal-sending state rather than its resting state.
Acting on mutant and normal forms of several RAS proteins, rather than on one specific mutation.
An abundant cell protein that daraxonrasib borrows as a partner to form the complex that blocks RAS.
The ratio of the rate of an event, such as death, in one group compared with another; 0.40 means the rate was 60 percent lower.
Fragments of tumor DNA in the blood that can be sequenced to detect new mutations.
Any mutation at position 12 of a RAS protein, the group in which the pivotal trial's endpoints were defined.

related.statement: Daraxonrasib blocks the active form of mutant KRAS, the driver of most pancreatic cancers.
Daraxonrasib is the first multi-selective RAS(ON) inhibitor to reach approval, and the RASolute trials are its development program.
Most tumors eventually escape daraxonrasib through RAF, receptor or KRAS-copy changes or by routes not yet identified.
Daraxonrasib was tested and approved after at least one prior systemic therapy, the setting previously held by second-line chemotherapy.
The daraxonrasib label requires no RAS test, although the trial's endpoints were defined in RAS G12-mutant tumors.
RASolute 303 and 304 are testing daraxonrasib first-line and after surgery, with no results yet.
Resistance to daraxonrasib was read from circulating tumor DNA sequenced before treatment and at progression.
Escape from daraxonrasib reactivates the same pathway as escape from the earlier G12C-selective inhibitors, without binding-site mutations.

faq.q: Do I need a KRAS test to get daraxonrasib?
faq.a: The US label does not require one: the indication is metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma after at least one prior systemic therapy, with no mutation requirement or companion diagnostic [[SEC-RAS-02]]. The trial's primary endpoints were defined in RAS G12-mutant tumors, which were 92 percent of participants, so how the 8 percent with RAS-normal tumors fared is not established [[RAS-033]].

faq.q: Can I take it as my first treatment?
faq.a: Not under the current label, which covers disease that has already been treated or people who cannot take multi-drug chemotherapy [[SEC-RAS-02]]. The RASolute 303 trial is testing first-line use, alone and with gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, with primary completion expected in 2028 [[SEC-RAS-06]].

faq.q: What are the main side effects?
faq.a: Rash, diarrhea, nausea, mouth sores, vomiting and fatigue, with treatment-related events of any grade in 96 percent and severe ones in 30 percent in the early-phase study; the label advises preventive medication for skin reactions, and in the randomized trial fewer people stopped for side effects than on chemotherapy, 1.2 against 11.2 percent [[RAS-032]][[SEC-RAS-02]][[RAS-033]].

topics.title: Growth-factor support and dose adjustments
topics.orientation: Chemotherapy doses are not fixed amounts on a fixed calendar. When a regimen such as FOLFIRINOX suppresses the bone marrow, the care team has three levers: delay the next cycle, lower the dose, or add a growth factor that speeds white-cell recovery. Which lever is pulled, and when, shapes both safety and how much of the planned treatment is actually delivered.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) is a natural signaling protein that tells the bone marrow to make neutrophils, the white cells that engulf bacteria. Given as an injection after a chemotherapy dose, as filgrastim or its long-acting form pegfilgrastim, it shortens the days when the neutrophil count is at its lowest. It does nothing for the other toxicities of chemotherapy, and it is one of three tools used to keep a regimen deliverable.
section1.full: Most chemotherapy drugs kill dividing cells, and the marrow precursors of neutrophils divide constantly, so the count falls to a trough about a week or two after each dose and climbs back before the next. Fever during that trough is treated as an emergency because infection can spread with few other signs [[SEC-SUPP-01]]. G-CSF shortens the trough by accelerating the maturation and release of neutrophils; its characteristic side effect is bone pain, and it does not raise platelets, prevent nerve damage or reduce diarrhea. A dose delay gives the marrow extra days to recover but stretches the calendar. A dose reduction lowers the peak toxicity of every later cycle but also lowers the amount of drug delivered. Growth-factor support tries to protect both dose and schedule at the price of an extra injection. The choice depends on which toxicity occurred: neutropenia (a low neutrophil count) alone can be met with G-CSF, whereas neuropathy, diarrhea or mouth sores are not helped by it and usually call for reducing or delaying the responsible drug. In the US, G-CSF products are approved to lower the risk of fever with infection in people receiving marrow-suppressing chemotherapy, and FOLFIRINOX is classed as a high-risk regimen, but preventive growth-factor use has not been tested in a randomized trial specifically in pancreatic cancer, so its use rests on that classification and on trials in other cancers [[SUPP-006]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: FOLFIRINOX carries a high risk of febrile neutropenia, fever with a dangerously low neutrophil count. Among 154 people receiving it as first-line treatment, it occurred in 31 (20.1 percent), mostly within the first four cycles, and the risk was about four times higher in people whose UGT1A1 gene clears irinotecan slowly [[SUPP-006]]. How the three levers are used decides how much of the planned chemotherapy a person actually receives.
section2.full: The trial that established modified FOLFIRINOX after surgery shows how much adjustment happens in practice. Irinotecan was lowered from 180 to 150 mg/m² after a safety review; only 33.6 percent of people received at least 80 percent of the planned dose intensity, against 79.0 percent on gemcitabine; 55.0 percent stopped oxaliplatin early; and 67.2 percent completed all twelve cycles [[TX-003]]. Even so, median survival rose from 35.5 to 53.5 months, and those who completed every cycle lived longer than those who did not, hazard ratio 0.64, a comparison that cannot separate the treatment's effect from the fitness of the people able to finish it [[TX-003]]. The genetic lever is pulled before the first dose. In 779 Dutch patients, about half with pancreatic cancer, people with two slow-clearing copies of the UGT1A1 gene started irinotecan at a 30 percent lower dose; their severe toxicity fell to the level of normal metabolizers and their survival did not differ, hazard ratio for death 1.10 [[GENE-018]]. The US irinotecan label asks clinicians to consider genotype testing and a lower starting dose in these poor metabolizers [[SEC-GENE-01]]. In the Korean cohort, women and people with a performance status of 1 rather than 0 (slightly restricted rather than fully active) also had two to three times the risk of febrile neutropenia, and the cumulative drug dose received by the fourth cycle was the same in those who did and did not develop it, which points to susceptibility rather than exposure [[SUPP-006]].

action_note.heading: When to call the care team now
action_note.text: A temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher at any point during chemotherapy, or shaking chills without a measured fever, needs an immediate call to the oncology team or a visit to the emergency department, because infection during neutropenia can become life-threatening within hours [[SEC-SUPP-03]]. When the neutrophil count is low, guidelines expect evaluation and a first dose of antibiotics within one hour of arrival [[SEC-SUPP-01]]. A growth-factor injection lowers this risk but does not remove it, so the same rule applies after one.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The 20.1 percent febrile-neutropenia rate comes from a single Korean center where UGT1A1*6, a gene variant rare in people of European ancestry, is common, so the genetic share of the risk may be larger there than in a US clinic; the overall rate sits inside the 5.4 to 22.2 percent range reported across FOLFIRINOX series, with 5.4 percent in the original metastatic trial [[SUPP-006]][[TX-L02]]. The adjuvant dose-intensity figures describe a selected, fit population aged up to 79, and the link between completing all cycles and survival is confounded by fitness [[TX-003]]. The Dutch cohort had no fully dosed poor-metabolizer arm, so it shows that reduced dosing equalized toxicity without showing what full dosing would have cost [[GENE-018]]. Whether preventive G-CSF from the first cycle changes any outcome in pancreatic cancer has not been tested in a randomized trial.
research_notes.how_studied: Febrile neutropenia is defined by a measured oral temperature of 38.3 °C once or 38.0 °C sustained for an hour with a neutrophil count below 500 per microliter, and in the Korean cohort it was identified from records after the fact, so milder fevers managed at home could have been missed [[SEC-SUPP-01]][[SUPP-006]]. Relative dose intensity divides the dose actually given per unit of time by the dose the protocol planned, so 0.80 means a person received four-fifths of the intended intensity; it is calculated across all cycles and does not say which drug was reduced [[TX-003]]. UGT1A1 phenotypes are predicted from genotype, grouping people as normal, intermediate or poor metabolizers, with the *28 and *6 alleles weighted differently in different populations [[GENE-018]][[SEC-GENE-01]].

mechanism_notes.text: Because febrile neutropenia clusters in the first four cycles and cumulative drug doses did not differ between people who did and did not develop it, fixed host factors such as UGT1A1 genotype and performance status appear to set the risk from the first dose rather than exposure accumulating over time [[SUPP-006]]. If that holds, an upfront genotype-guided dose or primary growth-factor support should matter most early, before the marrow has shown its tolerance; the competing explanation is that dose reductions made after a first toxicity simply remove the at-risk exposure from later cycles, which the Dutch cohort cannot distinguish [[GENE-018]].

Cachexia, the muscle-wasting syndrome of advanced cancer, is proposed to reduce chemotherapy tolerance through more dose reductions, delays and toxicity, so that the three levers get pulled more often in people losing muscle; muscle loss during chemotherapy predicts shorter survival independently of weight, and completing all adjuvant cycles predicted survival, which fits this chain without proving it [[INF-SUPP-03]][[SUPP-003]][[TX-003]]. The reverse direction, that a responding tumor both preserves muscle and lets treatment continue, explains the same observations.

topics.clinical_status: Filgrastim and pegfilgrastim are approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 to reduce the incidence of febrile neutropenia in people receiving marrow-suppressing chemotherapy; FOLFIRINOX is listed by US guidelines as a high febrile-neutropenia-risk regimen, but no randomized trial of growth-factor prophylaxis specific to pancreatic cancer has been located, and FOLFIRINOX itself is not an FDA-labeled combination. The US irinotecan label advises considering UGT1A1 genotype testing and a lower starting dose in poor metabolizers rather than requiring either.

glossary.definition: The most common white blood cell, which engulfs bacteria and is the first to fall after chemotherapy.
A fever occurring while the neutrophil count is dangerously low, treated as an emergency because infection can spread quickly.
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, a protein given by injection that speeds the bone marrow's production of neutrophils.
A long-acting form of G-CSF given once per chemotherapy cycle rather than daily.
The fraction of the planned chemotherapy dose per unit of time that a person actually received.
Postponing the next chemotherapy cycle to let blood counts or other side effects recover.
The gene for an enzyme that clears the active form of irinotecan; slow-working inherited versions raise toxicity.
The lowest point the blood count reaches after a chemotherapy dose, usually a week or two later.

related.statement: FOLFIRINOX is the pancreatic cancer regimen most often requiring growth-factor support, dose delays or dose reductions because of its high febrile-neutropenia risk.
Inherited slow-clearing UGT1A1 variants raise the febrile-neutropenia risk of irinotecan and are the reason for a lower starting dose in poor metabolizers.
Growth-factor support shortens the neutrophil trough during which fever and infection are most dangerous.
Irinotecan is the FOLFIRINOX component most often dose-reduced for neutropenia and the one whose clearance depends on UGT1A1.
Cachexia is hypothesized to force more dose reductions and delays, which is one rationale for the anti-cachexia drugs now in trials.

Oxaliplatin, whose dose-limiting toxicity is nerve damage rather than low blood counts, was stopped early by 55 percent of people on adjuvant modified FOLFIRINOX, an adjustment growth factors cannot prevent.

faq.q: Will I need growth-factor injections with FOLFIRINOX?
faq.a: Not everyone receives them. FOLFIRINOX is classed as a high-risk regimen for febrile neutropenia, which occurred in about one in five people in one cohort, and G-CSF is approved in the US to lower that risk, but no trial has tested it specifically in pancreatic cancer, so teams decide based on a person's own risk factors, such as performance status, sex and UGT1A1 status [[SUPP-006]][[SEC-GENE-01]].

faq.q: Does lowering the dose make the chemotherapy less effective?
faq.a: The adjuvant trial delivered modified FOLFIRINOX at reduced intensity in most people and still lengthened survival substantially, and UGT1A1 poor metabolizers given 30 percent less irinotecan had survival similar to fully dosed patients [[TX-003]][[GENE-018]]. Completing cycles was associated with longer survival, but fitter people complete more cycles, so that association is not proof that dose alone drives outcome.

faq.q: Why was my next cycle delayed a week?
faq.a: A delay is one of the three levers: it gives the marrow or the gut extra days to recover before the next dose without lowering the dose itself. Neutrophil counts reach their lowest point a week or two after each dose and usually recover before the next cycle, and a count that has not recovered is the commonest reason for a delay [[SEC-SUPP-01]].

topics.title: Biliary stents and drainage
topics.orientation: A tumor in the head of the pancreas often squeezes the bile duct that runs through it, so bile backs up into the blood and the skin and eyes turn yellow. A stent is a small tube placed inside the duct to hold it open. It relieves jaundice but brings problems of its own, and whether and when to place one before surgery has been settled by randomized trials whose answers changed with the type of stent.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: A biliary stent is a tube, plastic or expandable metal mesh, threaded through the narrowed length of bile duct during an endoscopic procedure called ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography), so that bile flows into the duodenum again. Bilirubin, the bile pigment that causes the yellowing, then falls over days to weeks and itching eases. When the endoscopic route fails, a radiologist can drain the duct through the skin and liver instead, a percutaneous transhepatic drain (PTC).
section1.full: The choice of stent trades caliber against permanence. Plastic stents are narrow, inexpensive and easy to remove, but they clog with bile sludge and bacteria within months. Self-expanding metal stents (SEMS) open to a much wider bore and stay open longer; a fully covered stent carries a membrane that stops tumor growing through the mesh but can slip out of position, whereas an uncovered stent anchors into the duct wall and lets tumor grow through it. In a randomized trial of 119 people stented before chemotherapy that preceded surgery, both metal types drained without any reintervention in about 72 percent of cases up to an operation at a median of 110 days; tumor ingrowth blocked 16.7 percent of uncovered stents and none of the covered ones, while 6.8 percent of covered stents migrated and none of the uncovered ones did [[SUPP-012]]. In a smaller Japanese series over a similar wait, recurrent obstruction occurred in 39 percent of plastic stents against 7.1 percent of covered metal stents, while pancreatitis and gallbladder inflammation were more frequent after metal stents, 43 against 15 percent [[SUPP-013]]. By the sixth day after a plastic stent was placed, the bile-duct wall was about thirteen times thicker with dense collagen, although operating time and complications did not differ [[SUPP-011]]. The harms belong beside the benefit: cholangitis (infection of the blocked duct) when a stent blocks, pancreatitis from the procedure, cholecystitis (gallbladder inflammation) when a covered stent occludes the gallbladder's outlet, and occasional bleeding or perforation.

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Whether to drain a jaundiced person before a Whipple operation was once answered no. A 2010 trial using mostly plastic stents found serious complications in 74 percent of drained people against 39 percent with surgery within a week [[SUPP-L07]]. A 2026 trial of 284 people using covered metal stents found 29.0 against 26.5 percent, which met its test for being no worse [[SUPP-008]]. The stent, not the act of draining, explains most of the difference.
section2.full: In the 2026 trial, drainage shifted when complications happened more than how many: serious events before surgery occurred in 15.2 percent of the drainage group against 5.1 percent of the early-surgery group, while among those who reached surgery operative and postoperative events were 19.3 against 23.1 percent, and 10 percent of people assigned to early surgery needed an urgent stent anyway for cholangitis, deep jaundice or a delayed operation [[SUPP-008]]. Deaths within 120 days of everyone randomized were similar, 7.6 and 7.9 percent, although more of the drainage-group deaths came before surgery and more of the early-surgery deaths after it [[SUPP-008]]. The practical reason most people are now drained is that surgery is rarely immediate: chemotherapy before surgery takes months, and a stent is what makes that wait possible with a bile duct the tumor is compressing. Over those months the stent is a maintenance item, with roughly one in four needing attention for blockage or migration [[SUPP-012]], and clinicians choose a metal stent because longer patency (time staying open) outweighs its higher rate of procedural complications [[SEC-SUPP-17]]. Guidelines do not recommend routine drainage when surgery can happen promptly, but accept it for cholangitis, severe jaundice, delayed surgery or chemotherapy before surgery [[SUPP-008]]. The older generalization that drainage is itself harmful no longer holds for metal stents.

action_note.heading: When to call the care team now
action_note.text: Fever or shaking chills together with new or returning jaundice, dark urine or pain under the right ribs in a person with a biliary stent are the signs of cholangitis, infection behind a blocked stent that can progress to sepsis within hours and needs same-day assessment, antibiotics and usually urgent re-drainage [[SEC-SUPP-14]]. A temperature of 100.4 °F (38 °C) or higher counts as a fever on cancer treatment [[SEC-SUPP-03]]. Yellowing, dark urine or pale stools returning without fever usually mean the stent has blocked and should be reported the same day, because blockage precedes infection [[SUPP-012]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The two drainage trials differ in more than stent type: the 2010 trial drained for four to six weeks with mostly plastic stents and recorded stent-related complications in 46 percent, whereas the 2026 trial used covered metal stents in 97 percent, ran at expert endoscopy centers, allowed a wide noninferiority margin of 15 percentage points and used a composite endpoint that mixes stent and surgical events [[SUPP-L07]][[SUPP-008]]. The covered-versus-uncovered comparison is known only from its abstract and registry entry, so its predictors of reintervention, a 4-cm stent and a gallbladder left in place, come without full methods [[SUPP-012]]. The plastic-versus-metal series was retrospective and underpowered, and its finding that large-caliber plastic stents performed comparably rests on 27 people [[SUPP-013]]. Survival beyond 120 days was not reported in the 2026 trial.
research_notes.how_studied: Drainage trials count serious adverse events within a fixed window, here 120 days, in everyone randomized, so a person who was drained and then found inoperable still counts, which is why complication rates run higher than in series restricted to those who reach surgery [[SUPP-008]]. Stent trials measure sustained drainage, meaning no reintervention from placement to surgery, and classify each failure at endoscopy as ingrowth, sludge or migration [[SUPP-012]]. Duct-wall fibrosis was quantified by staining resected bile-duct specimens for collagen and measuring wall thickness digitally, which shows a tissue change without showing that it alters the operation [[SUPP-011]].

mechanism_notes.text: The 2010 and 2026 trials give opposite answers because the harm of drainage lies in stent occlusion and the cholangitis that follows, not in the act of placing a stent: narrow plastic stents block within the weeks of waiting, whereas wide metal stents rarely do, and the 2026 trial's pre-surgery excess of complications is the residue of that risk [[SUPP-L07]][[SUPP-008]][[SUPP-013]]. The rapid duct-wall fibrosis seen within days of stenting did not lengthen operations or raise complications in the series that measured it, so it is a tissue change to note rather than a demonstrated harm [[SUPP-011]].

topics.clinical_status: Plastic and self-expanding metal biliary stents, covered and uncovered, are FDA-cleared devices in routine US use as of 8 Oct 2026. US practice does not drain routinely before prompt surgery but accepts drainage for cholangitis, severe jaundice, delayed surgery or chemotherapy before surgery, and prefers a metal stent when the drain must last months.

glossary.definition: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, a procedure in which a scope passed through the mouth reaches the bile-duct opening to place a stent.
A wire-mesh tube that springs open inside the bile duct to a wide bore and stays open longer than plastic.
A metal stent lined with a membrane that blocks tumor ingrowth but can migrate out of place.
