Bacterial infection of a blocked bile duct, causing fever, chills, jaundice and pain, that can progress to sepsis within hours.
Draining the bile duct through a needle passed through the skin and liver when the endoscopic route fails.
Blockage of a stent by sludge, tumor or displacement so that jaundice returns and a further procedure is needed.
Chemotherapy or radiation given before an operation rather than after it.
A trial designed to show that a new approach is not worse than the standard by more than a pre-set margin, rather than better.

related.statement: A biliary stent relieves the jaundice and itching caused by a tumor compressing the bile duct.
The stent sits in the lower bile duct where it passes through the head of the pancreas and opens at the ampulla.
A stent placed before a Whipple operation is removed with the bile duct segment the operation takes out.
Months of chemotherapy before surgery are only feasible for a jaundiced person if a stent keeps the bile duct open throughout.
A blocked biliary stent produces the same returning jaundice and cholangitis risk as the original obstruction.
A biliary stent is a route for bacteria into the bloodstream, so fever in a stented person raises the question of cholangitis.

faq.q: Why do I need a stent if I am having surgery anyway?
faq.a: If surgery is immediate, draining first offers no advantage and with plastic stents it added complications [[SUPP-L07]]. Most people, though, receive chemotherapy for months before an operation, and a metal stent is what keeps the bile duct open through that period; with metal stents, drainage before surgery was no worse overall than operating early [[SUPP-008]].

faq.q: How long does a stent last?
faq.a: In a trial of metal stents placed before chemotherapy, about 72 percent kept draining without any further procedure up to surgery at a median of 110 days, meaning roughly one in four needed attention for blockage or migration [[SUPP-012]]. Plastic stents block sooner, in 39 percent against 7 percent of covered metal stents in one series [[SUPP-013]].

faq.q: Will the stent be removed?
faq.a: If a Whipple operation follows, the lower bile duct containing the stent is removed with the specimen. If surgery does not happen, the stent stays in place as the route for bile, and a blocked one is cleared or a new stent placed through it at a further endoscopy rather than taken out [[SUPP-012]].

topics.title: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy
topics.orientation: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) gives back, in capsule form, the digestive enzymes that a blocked or partly removed pancreas can no longer deliver to the intestine. It is one of the simplest treatments in pancreatic cancer and, by the available evidence, one of the most often missed.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: Each capsule contains pancrelipase, a mixture of lipase, protease and amylase extracted from pig pancreas and packed into enteric-coated granules that survive stomach acid and release in the small intestine. Taken with every meal and snack, the enzymes meet the food where digestion of fat and protein would otherwise fail, so more of what is eaten is absorbed. US-approved products include Creon, Zenpep and several others.
section1.full: The pancreas normally delivers enzymes and bicarbonate into the duodenum in step with each meal; a tumor blocking the duct, or surgery removing enzyme-producing tissue, breaks that supply, and undigested fat passes through as pale, greasy stool while calories and fat-soluble vitamins are lost. In a double-blind trial of 58 people with proven fat malabsorption after pancreatic surgery, one week of high-dose pancrelipase raised the coefficient of fat absorption, the share of eaten fat that is absorbed, by 21.4 percentage points while placebo fell by 4.2, a difference of 25.6 points, and after a year of open-label treatment mean absorption had risen from 53.6 to 78.4 percent [[SUPP-002]]. In an 8-week placebo-controlled trial of 21 people with unresectable cancer of the pancreatic head, enzymes with dietary counseling produced a weight change of plus 1.2 percent against minus 3.7 percent on placebo, with higher energy intake [[SUPP-L01]]. In 29 people with metastatic disease followed by a palliative service, diarrhea scores fell within one week and pain and bloating within three [[SUPP-021]]. Side effects are mild; flatulence was the main excess over placebo in the surgical trial, 12.5 against 7.7 percent [[SUPP-002]]. Because lipase is destroyed by acid, an acid-suppressing drug is added when the response is incomplete, a step written into European guidance [[SEC-SUPP-09]][[SEC-SUPP-18]]. The US label sets ceilings, 2,500 lipase units per kilogram per meal and 10,000 per kilogram per day, beyond which further investigation rather than more enzyme is advised [[SEC-SUPP-10]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Most people with pancreatic cancer who would benefit never receive enzymes. In a US insurance database of 32,461 people with the diagnosis, 21.9 percent ever filled an enzyme prescription, 5.5 percent received at least 120,000 lipase units a day, and 1.9 percent were tested for enzyme insufficiency at all [[SUPP-001]]. The treatment is approved in the US, acts within weeks and is simple to try, so whether it applies is one of the most useful questions to bring to a care team.
section2.full: The gap matters because untreated malabsorption adds to the weight and muscle loss the cancer causes by other routes. A Spanish comparison of 160 people with unresectable disease found that those cared for in a unit that assessed and replaced enzymes lived a median 189 days against 95, and enzyme therapy stayed associated with longer survival after adjustment (the authors report a hazard ratio of 1.81 in favor of survival), but that group also received chemotherapy far more often, 71.6 against 46.5 percent, so the survival figure describes care in that unit rather than the capsules alone [[SUPP-020]]. The second reason the topic needs explaining is that enzymes do not fully restore digestion after a Whipple operation. In the surgical trial, only 7 of 26 people whose operation had altered the route or timing of food through the upper gut, a Whipple, a total pancreatectomy or a duodenum-preserving head resection, reached normal fat absorption above 85 percent on treatment, against a higher proportion after operations that leave that route intact [[SUPP-002]]. The rebuilt anatomy delivers food and enzyme granules into the jejunum, the next segment of small intestine, out of step and without the duodenum's bicarbonate, so lipase arrives at the wrong moment or is partly inactivated, which is why clinicians adjust the timing of capsules through the meal and add acid suppression rather than only raising the dose [[INF-SUPP-01]][[SEC-SUPP-18]]. Guidelines recommend enzymes for anyone with duct obstruction from a pancreatic tumor or after resection, diagnosed from symptoms and a fecal elastase test, a stool measure of the pancreas's own enzyme output, which loses accuracy after a Whipple [[SEC-SUPP-09]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The randomized evidence is strong for the surrogate it measured, fat absorption over one week, and weaker for weight and survival: the surgical trial mixed cancer with chronic pancreatitis and ran its blinded phase for a week, the 1998 cancer trial had 21 participants and is available only as an abstract, and the survival comparison was not randomized and is confounded by chemotherapy use [[SUPP-002]][[SUPP-L01]][[SUPP-020]]. The palliative pilot had no placebo group and lost 15 of 44 people before the three-week assessment, with completers fitter than non-completers [[SUPP-021]]. The under-prescription data come from 2001 to 2013, before current guidelines, and from commercially insured people only [[SUPP-001]]. An 8-week trial in 200 people with pancreatic cancer cachexia (cancer-driven weight and muscle loss) found an omega-3-enriched and a standard supplement halted weight loss equally, a reminder that digestion is only one of the drivers of weight loss [[SUPP-L02]].
research_notes.how_studied: The coefficient of fat absorption is measured by collecting all stool over 72 hours on a diet of known fat content and calculating the fraction absorbed; it is the most direct test of whether enzymes work but says nothing by itself about weight or quality of life [[SUPP-002]]. Fecal elastase-1 measures the pancreas's own enzyme output and is the recommended screening test, with values below 200 micrograms per gram indicating insufficiency, but it reads falsely low after a Whipple because the duodenum is gone and stool is diluted [[SEC-SUPP-09]]. Claims databases record filled prescriptions and billed tests, not symptoms, so they measure how often treatment was given rather than how often it was needed [[SUPP-001]].

mechanism_notes.text: After a Whipple-type reconstruction the enteric-coated granules and the meal leave the stomach at different rates and enter a jejunal limb that lacks the duodenum's bicarbonate, so enzyme release is mistimed and lipase is partly denatured by acid, which may explain why only about a quarter of such patients normalize fat absorption even at 225,000 to 375,000 lipase units a day [[INF-SUPP-01]][[SUPP-002]]. The competing explanation is that the remaining pancreas is simply too small and intake too low, in which case raising the dose would help as much as changing timing; no trial has yet compared coated granules, the same with acid suppression, and opened capsules mixed into food head to head.

topics.clinical_status: Pancrelipase products (Creon, Zenpep and others) are approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency from any cause, including after pancreatic surgery; pancreatic cancer is not named in the indication but is covered by it. The Creon label gives adults after pancreatectomy a starting range of 500 to 1,000 lipase units per kilogram per meal and ceilings of 2,500 units per kilogram per meal and 10,000 per kilogram per day, to be taken with meals and snacks.

glossary.definition: The pharmaceutical mixture of lipase, protease and amylase from pig pancreas used in enzyme capsules.
A shortage of pancreatic digestive enzymes in the intestine, so that fat and protein pass through undigested.
A coating on enzyme granules that resists stomach acid and dissolves in the small intestine where digestion happens.
The percentage of eaten fat that is absorbed rather than lost in stool, measured over 72 hours.
A stool test of the pancreas's own enzyme output used to screen for insufficiency; it reads low after a Whipple.
The enzyme that breaks dietary fat into absorbable pieces and the component by which enzyme doses are counted.
An acid-suppressing drug added when enzymes alone give an incomplete response, because acid destroys lipase.
Pale, greasy, foul-smelling stool that floats, the visible sign of undigested fat.

related.statement: Enzyme replacement therapy is the treatment for the exocrine insufficiency that a pancreatic tumor or resection causes.
Enzyme capsules replace the lipase, protease and amylase that acinar cells can no longer deliver to the intestine.
After a Whipple operation, enzyme replacement raises fat absorption but normalizes it in only about a quarter of people because the rebuilt anatomy mistimes enzyme release.
Loss of the duodenum removes the bicarbonate-rich chamber where enzymes and food normally mix, which limits how well enzyme capsules work.
Enzyme replacement corrects the digestive share of weight loss but not the cachexia driven by inflammatory signals (cytokines) that acts independently of digestion.
Enzyme capsules are the precondition for dietary advice to work, since food that is not digested cannot be absorbed.
Enzyme capsules with every meal and snack are a routine part of eating after a Whipple or pancreatectomy.

faq.q: If I am taking enzymes, why am I still losing weight?
faq.a: Enzymes fix only the digestive part of the problem. After a Whipple only about a quarter of people regain normal fat absorption even on high doses, because food and enzymes leave the stomach out of step and acid inactivates lipase, which is why teams adjust timing and add acid suppression [[SUPP-002]][[INF-SUPP-01]]. Separately, tumor-derived signals cause muscle and weight loss that no enzyme dose can reach.

faq.q: Do I need a test before starting enzymes?
faq.a: Guidelines recommend enzymes for anyone with a tumor obstructing the pancreatic duct or after resection, with diagnosis from symptoms and a fecal elastase stool test, although that test is unreliable after a Whipple [[SEC-SUPP-09]]. In practice fewer than 2 percent of people with pancreatic cancer in a US database were ever tested, so a trial of treatment guided by symptoms is common [[SUPP-001]].

faq.q: When should the capsules be taken?
faq.a: With food, with every meal and snack, so that enzymes and food reach the intestine together; the US label and European guidance both specify with-meal dosing and titration to response [[SEC-SUPP-10]][[SEC-SUPP-09]]. The exact number of capsules is set by the care team against the label's ceilings.

topics.title: Managing blood sugar after pancreatic surgery
topics.orientation: Removing part or all of the pancreas removes some or all of the islets that make insulin and glucagon. Whether diabetes follows depends on how much islet tissue remains, on the health of that remnant, and on how much insulin the body was already demanding before surgery, which is why two people with the same operation can have different outcomes.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: Blood-sugar care after pancreatic surgery means watching for diabetes that may appear months or years after a partial resection, and replacing insulin from the first day after a total pancreatectomy. The tools are those of any diabetes clinic, glucose meters or continuous glucose monitors (CGM), tablets or insulin, and an endocrinologist, but the diabetes itself is a distinct kind, called type 3c, because glucagon and digestive enzymes are lost alongside insulin.
section1.full: The islets of Langerhans are scattered through the whole gland, so a Whipple operation removes roughly the head's share and a distal pancreatectomy the body and tail's. After partial resection the remaining islets usually cope at first; diabetes appears when their capacity falls below what the body demands, and demand is set largely by body weight and insulin resistance. In a Swedish national cohort of 1,034 people without diabetes before distal pancreatectomy, 28 percent developed it, at a median of 354 days, and obesity more than doubled the risk, 44 against 25 percent [[SUPP-004]]. After a Whipple, 30.2 percent of 159 Turkish patients had new diabetes by six months, with body-mass index the only independent predictor and the volume of remaining pancreas not predictive [[SUPP-033]], whereas in a 66-person Korean cohort with serial scans, shrinkage of the remnant by 64 percent or more at six months predicted diabetes with an area under the curve of 0.809 (a measure of predictive accuracy on which 1.0 is perfect and 0.5 is chance) [[SUPP-034]]. A fatty remnant on CT together with a pre-operative HbA1c (average blood sugar measure) above 5.7 percent carried about five times the risk within two years [[SUPP-035]]. Total pancreatectomy is different in kind: every patient needs insulin from the day of surgery, and the loss of glucagon removes the body's main defense against low blood sugar, which is why continuous monitoring is used [[SUPP-036]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Two kinds of diabetes meet at pancreatic surgery. The cancer itself often causes a paraneoplastic diabetes that can improve when the tumor is removed: in 30 people whose diabetes began within the two years before a Whipple, it resolved in 17 (57 percent), while in 11 with long-standing diabetes it resolved in none [[ANAT-015]]. Surgical diabetes comes from lost islets and appears later. Knowing which kind a person has shapes what to expect.
section2.full: The paraneoplastic form is a reason not to assume that diabetes diagnosed shortly before surgery is permanent: fasting glucose fell from 174 to 110 mg/dL at a median of 48 days after head resection, and 16 of 30 people were still non-diabetic at a median of 237 days, even though the operation removed more gland [[ANAT-015]]. The surgical form arrives on a longer clock, a median of about a year after distal pancreatectomy and a cumulative 7.2 percent at one year, 21.3 percent at three and 28.0 percent at five after mixed resections, so glucose checks belong in follow-up for years rather than weeks [[SUPP-004]][[SUPP-035]]. After total pancreatectomy, a French cohort of 41 people reached a median HbA1c of 8.0 percent at one year on multiple daily injections or a pump, with time below 70 mg/dL of only 0.2 percent on continuous monitoring, which shows the diabetes is manageable; the harder problem in that cohort was malnutrition, present in 59 percent at a year [[SUPP-036]]. Chemotherapy adds a third, temporary strain: the steroid dexamethasone given with each infusion to prevent nausea raises blood sugar transiently, and in a lymphoma cohort on a different steroid schedule, those who became hyperglycemic did so in the first cycle, 12.2 percent with early and sustained high glucose; no pancreatic-specific study exists, so this is a pattern to expect rather than a measured risk [[SUPP-028]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The cohorts disagree about whether the amount of pancreas left behind predicts diabetes: a 159-person Whipple series found no association with remnant volume or atrophy at six months, while a 66-person series with protocolized scans found six-month volume loss the only predictor and did not model body-mass index [[SUPP-033]][[SUPP-034]]. The reading offered here is that quantity is decisive only at the extreme, total removal, where diabetes is universal, and that within partial resections the metabolic state of the host and the quality of the remnant dominate [[SUPP-036]][[SUPP-035]]. All of these cohorts mix cancer with benign indications, and registry-based diagnosis dates lag the true onset [[SUPP-004]]. The resolution of cancer-associated diabetes after resection was observed in 30 people at one referral center, and post-operative weight loss could contribute to the improvement [[ANAT-015]].
research_notes.how_studied: New-onset diabetes is defined by fasting glucose, HbA1c or the start of diabetes treatment, and in registry studies the date is the first diabetes-clinic visit, so onset is recorded late [[SUPP-004]]. Remnant volume is measured by tracing the pancreas on CT, and remnant fat by comparing its X-ray attenuation with the spleen's, a ratio below 0.66 indicating steatosis (fatty change); both are indirect measures of how many working islets remain [[SUPP-033]][[SUPP-035]]. Competing-risk models are used because death from cancer removes people before diabetes can develop, which would otherwise understate the risk [[SUPP-004]]. Continuous glucose monitors report time in range and time below range, which capture hypoglycemia that a single HbA1c would miss [[SUPP-036]].

mechanism_notes.text: Diabetes appears when functional beta-cell capacity, the remnant's volume multiplied by its islet density and reduced by fat, fibrosis and post-operative atrophy, falls below the insulin demand set by adiposity and insulin resistance; because surgery removes a roughly fixed fraction of capacity, differences in demand and remnant quality between people dominate, and only very large losses make quantity decisive [[INF-SUPP-02]][[SUPP-036]][[SUPP-035]][[SUPP-004]]. The competing explanation is that remnant atrophy is the true cause and the six-month null result was simply too early to see it [[SUPP-033]].

The diabetes that resolves after resection is proposed to be a functional suppression of insulin secretion or action by tumor-secreted mediators acting on a numerically preserved islet mass, so removing the tumor withdraws the mediator and function recovers within weeks, whereas surgery removes islet mass irreversibly [[INF-ANAT-01]][[ANAT-015]]. The competing explanation is that some improvement reflects post-operative weight loss and altered nutrition rather than withdrawal of a tumor signal.

topics.clinical_status: Insulin, including multiple daily injections and pumps, and continuous glucose monitors are approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 and are standard care after total pancreatectomy; after partial resection, follow-up glucose testing and ordinary diabetes care apply, and no drug is approved specifically for diabetes after pancreatectomy. A bihormonal artificial pancreas delivering insulin and glucagon is investigational.

glossary.definition: Clusters of hormone-producing cells scattered through the pancreas that release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
Diabetes caused by disease or removal of the pancreas, in which glucagon and digestive enzymes are lost along with insulin.
A blood test reflecting average blood sugar over the previous two to three months.
A small sensor worn on the skin that measures glucose every few minutes and warns of highs and lows.
The islet hormone that raises blood sugar and protects against hypoglycemia; it is lost after total pancreatectomy.
Diabetes caused by signals from a tumor rather than by loss of islets, which can improve when the tumor is removed.
Fat within the pancreas, seen on CT as lower density than the spleen, which reduces the working capacity of the remnant.
The portion of pancreas left in place after a partial resection.

related.statement: Blood sugar after surgery depends on whether a person's pre-existing diabetes was paraneoplastic, which can resolve, or long-standing, which persists.
Diabetes after surgery follows from loss of islets, and its timing depends on how much islet capacity the remnant retains.
Total pancreatectomy causes immediate, lifelong insulin-dependent diabetes in every patient because no islets remain.
After distal pancreatectomy, 28 percent of people developed new diabetes at a median of about a year in a national cohort.
After a Whipple, new diabetes developed in 24 to 30 percent of people in cohorts followed for six months to three years.
Glucose monitoring belongs in long-term follow-up after a Whipple because surgical diabetes can appear years later.
The dexamethasone given with chemotherapy to prevent nausea raises blood sugar transiently after each infusion.

faq.q: Will I become diabetic after a Whipple?
faq.a: Not most people, at least not soon. In cohorts followed after a Whipple, new diabetes developed in about 24 to 30 percent, more often in people with a higher body-mass index, a fatty pancreatic remnant or a borderline HbA1c before surgery [[SUPP-033]][[SUPP-035]]. The risk continues to rise for years, so periodic glucose checks are part of follow-up.

faq.q: My diabetes went away after surgery. How is that possible?
faq.a: Pancreatic cancer often causes a diabetes driven by tumor signals rather than by islet loss, and in 30 people whose diabetes had begun within two years before a Whipple it resolved in 17 after the tumor was removed, even though the operation took away more pancreas [[ANAT-015]]. Long-standing diabetes did not resolve in that study.

faq.q: Why is my blood sugar high the day after chemotherapy?
faq.a: The dexamethasone given with each infusion to prevent nausea raises blood sugar transiently. In a lymphoma cohort on a steroid-containing regimen, people who became hyperglycemic did so from the first cycle, which is why the first cycle is the time to check [[SUPP-028]]. That study is outside pancreatic cancer, so the size of the effect here is unmeasured.

topics.title: Preventing and treating blood clots
topics.orientation: Pancreatic cancer is among the cancers most likely to cause venous thromboembolism, clots in the deep veins, the lungs or the veins of the abdomen. Anticoagulant drugs can prevent some of these clots and are the treatment once one has formed, and every decision about them weighs clotting against bleeding.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: Anticoagulants slow the chain of reactions that turns liquid blood into a clot. Low-molecular-weight heparin, such as enoxaparin, is injected under the skin and amplifies the body's own clotting inhibitor; the direct oral anticoagulants apixaban and rivaroxaban are tablets that block a single clotting enzyme, factor Xa. At a low dose they lower the chance of a first clot; at full dose they stop an existing clot from growing while the body dissolves it over months.
section1.full: The tumor drives clotting through tissue factor, a clot-triggering protein, and through inflammation, and chemotherapy, central lines and reduced mobility add to it. In 762 people starting chemotherapy in a French cohort, the cumulative incidence of venous thromboembolism was 16.4 percent within six months and 25.6 percent over a median of 40 months; a third of events were in the portal, splenic or mesenteric veins, and more than half were found incidentally on routine scans [[SUPP-024]]. Two randomized trials have tested prevention in pancreatic cancer. In the CONKO-004 trial, 312 people starting first-line chemotherapy were assigned to enoxaparin or observation; symptomatic clots in the first three months fell from 15 of 152 to 2 of 160, cumulative symptomatic events from 15.1 to 6.4 percent, with 7 against 5 major bleeds and no change in survival [[SUPP-L09]]. In the pancreatic subgroup of the CASSINI trial, 273 people took rivaroxaban 10 mg or placebo for up to 180 days: while actually taking the drug, events fell from 10.1 to 3.7 percent, hazard ratio 0.35, but in the intention-to-treat analysis (counting everyone as assigned) the difference was 13.0 against 9.6 percent and not significant, because 43 percent of each arm stopped early; major bleeding was 1.5 against 2.3 percent [[SUPP-007]]. The harm of any anticoagulant is bleeding, from bruising to gastrointestinal or intracranial hemorrhage, and it is weighed more carefully when a tumor involves the lining of the gut [[SEC-SUPP-04]], when platelets are low, or around procedures and surgery.

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: US guidance from 2023 says that people with a Khorana score of 2 or more who are starting chemotherapy may be offered apixaban, rivaroxaban or low-molecular-weight heparin after a discussion of bleeding risk, and a pancreatic primary alone scores 2 [[SEC-SUPP-04]]. Neither oral drug carries an FDA indication for this prevention, so the use is guideline-supported but off-label [[SEC-SUPP-13]]. Prevention lowers the risk; it does not remove it.
section2.full: The risk scores built for all cancers do not help within pancreatic cancer: in the French cohort the Khorana, PROTECHT and ONKOTEV scores had concordance indices of 0.50 to 0.53, no better than chance, and 99 percent of people were classed high-risk by Khorana, because the tumor type dominates the score and leaves nothing to discriminate [[SUPP-024]]. Metastatic disease and a tumor in the neck of the pancreas each roughly doubled the risk, and a clot itself roughly doubled the hazard of death in the parent cohort [[SUPP-L11]]. Once a clot has formed, treatment is months of full-dose anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant or low-molecular-weight heparin; in 433 people with gastrointestinal cancers treated at one center with apixaban or rivaroxaban for at least six months, major bleeding occurred in 3.7 percent, clinically relevant minor bleeding in 5.3 percent and recurrent clots in 7.4 percent, with no difference between the two drugs [[SUPP-025]]. Apixaban and rivaroxaban are approved in the US for treating deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism and for reducing recurrence [[SEC-SUPP-13]]. Guidelines advise caution with oral anticoagulants when a tumor sits in the lining of the gut or urinary tract, and low-molecular-weight heparin remains the alternative there; the practical lesson from CASSINI is that a daily tablet works only while it is taken, and stopping it, for whatever reason, returns the risk to baseline [[SEC-SUPP-04]][[SUPP-007]].

action_note.heading: When to call the care team now
action_note.text: Sudden breathlessness, chest pain that is worse on breathing in, coughing blood, fainting, or new swelling, warmth or pain in one leg or arm need same-day emergency assessment, because a clot that has reached the lungs can be fatal without treatment [[SEC-SUPP-04]]. On any anticoagulant, black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, blood in the urine, a severe headache or bleeding that will not stop are signs of serious bleeding and also need immediate care; the drug should not be stopped or restarted without the care team's advice [[SEC-SUPP-13]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The CONKO-004 trial is available only as an abstract, was open-label and counted symptomatic clots only, while CASSINI's pancreatic analysis was a pre-specified subgroup of a larger trial, underpowered on its own and weakened by 43 percent discontinuation; its on-treatment benefit is not protected by randomization, because those who stopped differed from those who continued [[SUPP-L09]][[SUPP-007]]. CASSINI excluded people with clots on baseline screening, which removed 6.6 percent of pancreatic patients and lowers event rates [[SUPP-007]]. The French incidence figures include visceral-vein and incidental clots that trials often exclude, so they run higher than trial placebo arms [[SUPP-024]]. The bleeding data for oral anticoagulants come from people a referral center judged suitable for them, with no heparin comparison, and the pancreatic subgroup was not reported separately [[SUPP-025]].
research_notes.how_studied: Prevention trials count a composite of symptomatic deep-vein thrombosis, proximal clots found on scheduled ultrasound, any pulmonary embolism and clot-related death, adjudicated by a blinded committee, and report both intention-to-treat and on-treatment analyses; the first preserves randomization and the second shows what the drug does while taken [[SUPP-007]]. Major bleeding follows the International Society on Thrombosis and Hemostasis definition, a fall in hemoglobin of 2 g/dL or more, transfusion, or bleeding into a critical site, with clinically relevant non-major bleeding counted separately [[SUPP-025]]. Cohorts use competing-risk methods because death removes people before they can clot, and risk scores are judged by the concordance index, where 0.50 means no ability to rank [[SUPP-024]].

mechanism_notes.text: Within pancreatic cancer the tumor-driven component of clotting risk is so large that it saturates general-purpose scores, leaving adherence to preventive treatment and the type of clot as the main determinants of what is observed; this would explain why rivaroxaban's effect was clear on treatment and absent by intention to treat, and why a third of events were visceral-vein clots that trials rarely count [[SUPP-007]][[SUPP-024]]. A competing explanation is that a pancreatic-specific score using tumor location, stage and a biomarker such as D-dimer, which fell on rivaroxaban, could restore discrimination [[SUPP-L11]][[SUPP-007]].

topics.clinical_status: Apixaban (Eliquis) and rivaroxaban (Xarelto) are approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 for the treatment of deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism and for reducing recurrence; neither they nor enoxaparin (Lovenox) carries an indication for primary prevention in outpatients with cancer, which is guideline-supported, off-label use for people with a Khorana score of 2 or more who are starting chemotherapy.

glossary.definition: A clot in a vein, usually a deep-vein thrombosis in the leg or a pulmonary embolism in the lung.
A clot in a deep vein, most often in the leg, causing one-sided swelling and pain.
A clot that has traveled to the lungs, causing sudden breathlessness or chest pain and sometimes death.
A clot in the portal, splenic or mesenteric veins that drain the gut and liver, often found incidentally on scans.
An injectable anticoagulant such as enoxaparin that amplifies the body's own clotting inhibitor.
An anticoagulant tablet, such as apixaban or rivaroxaban, that blocks one clotting enzyme directly.
The clotting enzyme that apixaban and rivaroxaban block.
A point score for clot risk in cancer outpatients in which a pancreatic primary alone gives the 2 points that trigger a discussion of prophylaxis.
Analyzing everyone as assigned at randomization whether or not they took the treatment, which preserves the fairness of the comparison.
Bleeding that lowers hemoglobin by 2 g/dL or more, needs transfusion, or occurs in a critical site such as the brain.

related.statement: Anticoagulants are both the preventive option and the treatment for the clots that pancreatic cancer causes.
About a third of clots in pancreatic cancer form in the portal, splenic or mesenteric veins rather than the legs or lungs.
Clot risk is highest in the months after chemotherapy starts, which is when prevention trials enrolled people; in the French cohort most were on platinum- or gemcitabine-based regimens.
Endoscopic procedures such as stent exchange are a common reason anticoagulants are paused, during which clot risk returns.
Bleeding after surgery and clot prevention around surgery pull in opposite directions and are balanced by the surgical team.
Tumors in the neck (isthmus) of the pancreas carried about twice the clot risk of other locations in the French cohort.

faq.q: Should I be on a blood thinner during chemotherapy?
faq.a: US guidance says it may be offered to people with a pancreatic primary starting chemotherapy after a discussion of bleeding risk, because the six-month clot risk is about 16 percent [[SEC-SUPP-04]][[SUPP-024]]. Enoxaparin reduced symptomatic clots from 15.1 to 6.4 percent in one trial and rivaroxaban roughly halved them while taken in another, with no survival change in either [[SUPP-L09]][[SUPP-007]].

faq.q: My scan showed a clot I never felt. Does it still need treatment?
faq.a: More than half of clots in pancreatic cancer are found incidentally on routine scans, and a clot of any kind roughly doubled the hazard of death in the French cohort [[SUPP-024]][[SUPP-L11]]. Incidental clots are generally treated the same way as symptomatic ones, with full-dose anticoagulation for months, a decision the care team makes against bleeding risk.

faq.q: Injection or tablet?
faq.a: Both are guideline options for prevention and for treatment. Tablets are easier, but guidelines advise caution when a tumor involves the gut lining, where heparin injections are the alternative, and the CASSINI experience shows that a tablet protects only while it is being taken [[SEC-SUPP-04]][[SUPP-007]]. In one cohort of people treated for clots, apixaban and rivaroxaban had similar bleeding and recurrence rates [[SUPP-025]].

topics.title: Treatments for cachexia and appetite
topics.orientation: Cachexia is the loss of weight and muscle driven by signals from the tumor rather than by lack of food, which is why eating more fails as a remedy. Treatments aim at three targets, the appetite center in the brain, the muscle, and the signaling proteins themselves, and the most promising of them is still in trials.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: The treatments act at different points in the chain. Ponsegromab is an antibody that neutralizes growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15), a protein tumors release that acts on the hindbrain to suppress appetite and activity. Anamorelin mimics ghrelin, the stomach's hunger hormone, to raise appetite and growth-hormone release. Dietary counseling, protein supplements and short courses of appetite-stimulating drugs act on intake. None treats the cancer; all try to hold weight and function while chemotherapy does.
section1.full: In a phase 2 trial of 187 people with cancer cachexia and high GDF-15 levels, 32 percent of them with pancreatic cancer, ponsegromab given every four weeks for twelve weeks produced weight gain relative to placebo of 1.22, 1.92 and 2.81 kg at rising doses, improved appetite and cachexia symptom scores, and at the highest dose increased measured physical activity, while adverse events were no more frequent than with placebo, 70 against 80 percent [[SUPP-014]]. Anamorelin, in a single-arm Japanese study of 50 people with gastrointestinal cancers, five of them pancreatic, raised lean body mass by 1.89 kg and weight by 1.41 kg over twelve weeks, at the cost of raised blood sugar or new diabetes in about 6 percent each and a conduction change on the electrocardiogram in 6 percent [[SUPP-022]]; in routine use at one center, 38 percent stopped within three weeks and response was weaker over age 75 [[SUPP-023]]. On the intake side, a double-blind trial of 41 older people after pancreatic resection found that 18 g of extra protein a day for six weeks raised intake from 56.7 to 77.3 g and improved walking speed, nutritional status and quality of life [[SUPP-016]]. US guidance recommends dietary counseling for everyone with cancer-related weight loss, allows short courses of progestins (progesterone-like hormones) or corticosteroids and, since 2023, low-dose olanzapine (an antipsychotic that stimulates appetite), and advises against routine tube or intravenous feeding in advanced cancer [[SEC-SUPP-05]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Muscle loss predicts shorter survival in pancreatic cancer independently of weight: during first-line chemotherapy, muscle area fell in 61 percent of men and 41 percent of women while body-mass index fell in only 37 percent, and each kind of loss carried its own risk of death [[SUPP-003]]. A treatment that preserved muscle could in principle keep people fit enough for full-dose chemotherapy, which is the hypothesis the phase 3 ponsegromab trial is positioned to test.
section2.full: Two findings make the stakes clear and the evidence incomplete. First, six months of supervised resistance training in a randomized trial did not change CT-measured muscle, although it improved strength, which suggests that loading alone cannot overcome a body-wide catabolic (muscle-breaking) drive [[SUPP-015]]. Second, among people on anamorelin, those whose appetite and weight responded had disease control on chemotherapy of 75.0 percent against 37.5 percent in non-responders, which could mean that reversing cachexia improves tolerance of treatment or simply that responding tumors release fewer cachexia signals [[SUPP-023]]. What does not work is also known. An omega-3-enriched supplement halted weight loss no better than a standard supplement of the same calories in 200 people with pancreatic cancer cachexia [[SUPP-L02]]. Progestins such as megestrol and corticosteroids are allowed by US guidance only as short-term measures for appetite and weight, and anamorelin is not recommended there [[SEC-SUPP-05]]. Ponsegromab is not approved anywhere; its phase 3 trial, NCT06989437, began recruiting in late 2025 and plans about 982 people with pancreatic cancer cachexia [[SEC-SUPP-15]]. Anamorelin is approved in Japan but not in the US, where a pancreatic-specific trial closed after enrolling four people [[SEC-SUPP-16]]. Enzyme replacement and nutrition counseling remain the foundation on which any of these drugs would sit, because undigested food cannot feed muscle whatever the appetite.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The ponsegromab result is a phase 2 trial in people selected for high GDF-15, so it shows that blocking the pathway reverses weight loss in those whose cachexia runs through it, not that it works in everyone or that it changes survival, which was not an endpoint; whether the gained weight is muscle rather than fat or fluid, and how the pancreatic subgroup fared, are not reported in the available publication [[SUPP-014]]. The anamorelin studies were uncontrolled, Japanese, and included few people with pancreatic cancer; the association between response and disease control is open to reverse causation [[SUPP-022]][[SUPP-023]]. The protein-supplement trial was small, single-center and six weeks long, and the exact size of its functional gains is not given here [[SUPP-016]]. The null training result rests on 28 paired scans, so it is uninformative rather than negative [[SUPP-015]]. Muscle loss predicting death does not show that restoring muscle would prevent it [[SUPP-003]].
research_notes.how_studied: Cachexia trials measure body weight, lean mass by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry or by muscle area on routine CT at the third lumbar vertebra, appetite by questionnaire such as the FAACT anorexia-cachexia subscale, and activity by wrist-worn accelerometers, because weight alone cannot distinguish muscle from fat or fluid [[SUPP-014]][[SUPP-003]]. The phase 2 ponsegromab design used Bayesian analysis to estimate dose-response, reporting credible intervals rather than P values [[SUPP-014]]. Survival analyses of muscle loss adjust for stage and treatment but cannot exclude that an aggressive tumor causes both the muscle loss and the death [[SUPP-003]].

mechanism_notes.text: Cachexia reduces chemotherapy tolerance through dose reductions, delays and toxicity, so reversing the catabolic and anorexic drive could restore delivered dose intensity and physical reserve and thereby improve tumor control; the activity gains with ponsegromab and the higher disease control in anamorelin responders are consistent with this [[INF-SUPP-03]][[SUPP-014]][[SUPP-023]]. The competing explanation, raised by the anamorelin authors themselves, is reverse causation: responding tumors release less GDF-15 and less of the inflammatory signal interleukin-6, so appetite recovers and the drug merely marks the responders [[SUPP-023]]. The phase 3 ponsegromab trial can separate the two if delivered dose intensity differs between its arms [[SEC-SUPP-15]].

topics.clinical_status: Ponsegromab is investigational as of 8 Oct 2026, approved in no jurisdiction, with a phase 3 trial in pancreatic cancer cachexia (NCT06989437) recruiting. Anamorelin is approved in Japan since 2021 for cachexia in gastrointestinal and lung cancers and is not approved in the US, where guidelines do not recommend it. In the US, dietary counseling, oral nutrition supplements, short-course progestins or corticosteroids and off-label low-dose olanzapine are the guideline-supported options for appetite and weight.

glossary.definition: Loss of weight and muscle driven by tumor and inflammatory signals that cannot be fully reversed by eating more.
Growth differentiation factor 15, a protein released by tumors and stressed tissues that acts on the brain to suppress appetite and activity.
The stomach's hunger hormone, which anamorelin imitates to stimulate appetite and growth-hormone release.
Body weight minus fat, used in cachexia trials as a measure of muscle.
Abnormally low skeletal muscle mass, measured in cancer studies on CT scans at the level of the third lumbar vertebra.
A questionnaire scoring appetite and cachexia symptoms from the patient's point of view.
A synthetic progesterone-like hormone, such as megestrol, used short-term to stimulate appetite.
A large randomized trial designed to show whether a treatment works well enough to be approved.

related.statement: The drugs and nutritional measures described here are the treatments being used or tested for the cachexia that pancreatic cancer causes.
Dietary counseling and protein supplements are the foundation on which any cachexia drug would be added.
Ponsegromab's phase 3 trial is the main cachexia study now recruiting in pancreatic cancer.
Cachexia treatments address the signal-driven loss of muscle, whereas enzyme replacement addresses the digestive loss of calories; both are usually needed.
Resistance training improved strength but not CT-measured muscle in pancreatic cancer, which is why drugs targeting the catabolic signal are being tested.
If cachexia forces dose reductions and delays, reversing it could change how much chemotherapy is delivered, a hypothesis the phase 3 trial can test.
Anamorelin raised blood sugar or caused new diabetes in about 6 percent of people each, a concern in a disease already linked to diabetes.

faq.q: Can I get ponsegromab now?
faq.a: Only through a trial. It is not approved anywhere, and the phase 3 study in pancreatic cancer cachexia, NCT06989437, began recruiting in late 2025 [[SEC-SUPP-15]]. The phase 2 trial that preceded it showed weight gain of up to 2.8 kg over 12 weeks relative to placebo in people selected for high GDF-15 [[SUPP-014]].

faq.q: Would an appetite stimulant help?
faq.a: US guidance allows short courses of a progestin such as megestrol, a corticosteroid or low-dose olanzapine to improve appetite, framed as short-term measures rather than ways to rebuild muscle [[SEC-SUPP-05]]. Anamorelin, which raised lean mass in Japanese studies, is not approved in the US [[SUPP-022]][[SEC-SUPP-16]].

faq.q: Why is eating more not enough?
faq.a: Because the tumor's signals, GDF-15 among them, suppress appetite and drive muscle breakdown independently of intake, and during chemotherapy muscle was lost in 61 percent of men while weight fell in far fewer [[SUPP-003]]. Enzyme capsules and protein supplements still help with the digestive share of the problem, and an extra 18 g of protein a day improved walking speed after surgery in one trial [[SUPP-016]].

topics.title: KRAS G12C inhibitors
topics.orientation: KRAS G12C inhibitors were the first drugs to block a mutant KRAS protein directly, and two of them are approved in the US for lung and colorectal cancer. In pancreatic cancer they apply only to the 1 to 3 percent of tumors that carry the G12C change, and none holds a pancreatic indication.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: KRAS is a switch protein that passes growth signals while loaded with the energy molecule GTP and stops when that is spent to GDP. The G12C mutation replaces one glycine with a cysteine, and these drugs bond permanently to that cysteine while the switch sits in its OFF, GDP-bound state, trapping it there. Sotorasib and adagrasib are tablets taken daily; glecirasib is a newer agent built on the same principle.
section1.full: Because the drug fits only the OFF shape, it depends on the mutant protein passing through that state, and KRAS G12C keeps more of the normal protein's ability to switch itself off than most other mutants, which is why this variant became druggable first. The consequence shows up within hours in cell experiments. Once an inactive-state inhibitor shuts down most of the signal, about a fifth of cells keep dividing by making fresh KRAS G12C protein that the growth-factor receptor EGFR and the enzyme aurora kinase A hold in the ON state, out of the drug's reach [[RAS-008]]. The pancreatic cancer cell line MIA PaCa-2 behaves this way, and cells prevented from mounting that adaptation stayed durably inhibited [[RAS-008]]. A later design, elironrasib, instead binds the ON state of KRAS G12C through a complex with the cellular protein cyclophilin A and belongs to the RAS(ON) family described in its own entry [[RAS-042]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Three single-arm trials have given a G12C inhibitor to people with previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer. Sotorasib shrank tumors by the formal response standard in 21 percent of 38 patients, adagrasib in 33 percent of 21, and glecirasib in 47 percent of 32, with responses lasting about five to six months. Neither approved drug carries a US pancreatic indication, so use outside a trial is off-label.
section2.full: The sotorasib cohort of the CodeBreaK 100 trial enrolled patients after a median of two prior lines; some shrinkage occurred in 79 percent, median progression-free survival was 4.0 months and median overall survival 6.9 months, with severe (grade 3) treatment-related side effects in 16 percent and none forcing discontinuation [[RAS-001]]. Adagrasib's pancreatic result is a 21-patient slice of a multi-cancer (basket) cohort, with a median response duration of 5.3 months by central review and treatment-related side effects of any grade in 97 percent [[RAS-002]]. Glecirasib's pooled phase 1/2 analysis, investigator-assessed rather than centrally reviewed, reported median progression-free survival of 5.5 months and median survival of 10.8 months [[RAS-009]]. None had a comparison arm, so they show that a well-aimed drug can shrink a pancreatic tumor, not that it lengthens life. As of 8 Oct 2026 sotorasib and adagrasib are approved in the US only for KRAS G12C lung cancer and, with an EGFR antibody, colorectal cancer [[SEC-RAS-03]][[SEC-RAS-04]]; glecirasib is not FDA-approved [[RAS-009]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Three drugs at the same target, in the same disease and broadly the same treatment line, gave response rates of 21, 33 and 47 percent in cohorts of 21 to 38 patients, a spread wider than sampling noise alone comfortably explains but not wide enough to rule it out [[RAS-001]][[RAS-002]][[RAS-009]]. The later results argue that the first was not a ceiling set by pancreatic biology [[RAS-009]]. Across all three the median duration of benefit stayed near six months or less, and in a 22-patient resistance study no genetic cause of progression could be found in 54 percent [[RAS-010]].
research_notes.how_studied: Each study was a single-arm cohort selected by a tissue or blood test for the G12C allele, with objective response judged under RECIST, a rule that counts a response only when the summed diameters of tracked lesions fall by at least 30 percent and the fall holds on a repeat scan. Sotorasib and adagrasib used blinded independent central review; glecirasib used investigator assessment, which tends to read higher [[RAS-001]][[RAS-002]][[RAS-009]]. Resistance was studied by sequencing circulating tumor DNA before treatment and at progression, which finds pathway-reactivating gene changes but misses non-genetic escape [[RAS-010]].

mechanism_notes.text: The spread in response rates may reflect how completely and continuously each drug holds mutant KRAS below the level at which growth signaling collapses, rather than any difference in the target; agents designed for high trough occupancy (keeping the target bound even just before the next dose), and agents that bind the ON state, would hold it down for more of each dosing interval [[INF-RAS-03]][[RAS-009]][[RAS-015]]. The competing explanation is that investigator assessment, differing prior treatment and small denominators account for the whole gap. A pooled re-read of the existing cohorts under one blinded central review would separate the two [[INF-RAS-03]].

topics.clinical_status: No KRAS G12C inhibitor is approved in the US for pancreatic cancer as of 8 Oct 2026. Sotorasib (LUMAKRAS) and adagrasib (KRAZATI) are approved in the US for KRAS G12C non-small-cell lung cancer and, with an anti-EGFR antibody, colorectal cancer, each under accelerated approval; glecirasib is investigational in the US. Pancreatic use is off-label or through clinical trials, and the allele is present in about 1 to 3 percent of pancreatic cancers.

glossary.definition: A version of the KRAS protein in which the amino acid at position 12 has changed from glycine to cysteine, found in about 1 to 3 percent of pancreatic cancers.
A drug that binds KRAS only while it is in its switched-off, GDP-bound shape and keeps it there.
A tumor shrinkage large enough to meet a formal measurement rule, usually at least a 30 percent fall in summed lesion diameters confirmed on a repeat scan.
Scan assessment by radiologists who do not know which treatment a patient received and are not part of the treating team.
Use of an approved drug for a disease or setting that is not listed in its official prescribing information.

related.statement: KRAS G12C inhibitors lock one specific mutant form of the KRAS protein in its switched-off state.
KRAS G12C is one of the rarer alleles in pancreatic cancer, at about 1 to 3 percent of cases, compared with G12D at roughly four in ten.
Eligibility for a KRAS G12C inhibitor is established by sequencing tumor tissue or circulating tumor DNA for the G12C allele.
Tumors escape KRAS G12C inhibitors by reactivating the same pathway through new KRAS copies, receptor signaling or RAF changes.
Elironrasib applies the RAS(ON) design to KRAS G12C and is being tested after first-generation G12C inhibitors stop working.
Daraxonrasib, the approved RAS inhibitor, covers KRAS G12C together with the other RAS mutations rather than one allele.

faq.q: My tumor has KRAS G12C. Can I get sotorasib or adagrasib?
faq.a: Both are approved in the US for lung and colorectal cancer, not pancreatic, so any pancreatic use is off-label or inside a trial [[SEC-RAS-03]][[SEC-RAS-04]]. In the trials that exist, between one in five and one in two patients had a measurable response lasting about five to six months [[RAS-001]][[RAS-002]][[RAS-009]].

faq.q: Why did the first KRAS drugs not help most pancreatic cancer patients?
faq.a: They bond to a cysteine that only the G12C mutant carries, and only about 1 to 3 percent of pancreatic cancers have that mutation [[RAS-002]]. The common pancreatic mutations, G12D, G12V and G12R, needed different chemistry.

topics.title: KRAS G12D inhibitors
topics.orientation: KRAS G12D is the single most common mutation in pancreatic cancer, present in roughly four in ten tumors, and drugs that target it selectively are in human trials, but none is approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026. The strongest evidence so far comes from mice.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: The G12D mutation swaps a glycine for an aspartic acid at position 12 of KRAS, leaving the protein stuck in its signaling ON state. Unlike the cysteine in G12C, aspartic acid offers no reactive handle for a drug to bond to, so G12D inhibitors had to be built differently: MRTX1133 binds the switch pocket reversibly, and zoldonrasib borrows a cellular partner protein to force a covalent (permanent chemical) bond that would not otherwise form.
section1.full: G12D was the most common KRAS mutation, at 43 percent of KRAS-mutated tumors in a 2,483-patient pancreatic series [[GENE-005]]. MRTX1133 binds KRAS G12D in its GDP-loaded (switched-off) state with about 700-fold selectivity over the normal protein and caused regressions of at least 30 percent in 8 of 11 pancreatic xenograft models (human tumors grown in mice) [[RAS-035]]. In mice with intact immune systems, including a model whose tumors arise spontaneously in the pancreas, 12 of 13 tumors regressed after 14 days [[RAS-004]]. That regression was not purely a drug-on-cell effect: within 60 hours T cells carrying the killing enzyme granzyme B moved into the tumor, and when the investigators removed T cells with antibodies the tumors regrew [[RAS-004]]. Zoldonrasib first binds cyclophilin A, an abundant cellular protein, and the drug-protein pair creates a new surface against active RAS that catalyzes a covalent bond to the aspartic acid itself; its discovery paper reports antitumor activity across preclinical G12D models, but it is available only as an abstract, which gives no numbers [[RAS-034]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: MRTX1133 generated the strongest preclinical pancreatic data of any KRAS-selective drug, yet its first-in-human trial stopped after 63 patients for formulation problems, not for lack of effect, and the drug has to be given by injection. Zoldonrasib is the G12D drug now in people, with a phase 1 study recruiting and two phase 3 pancreatic trials opened in 2026, none of them with results.
section2.full: The registry record for the MRTX1133 phase 1 lists it as terminated, citing 'formulation challenges', so the drug that produced near-complete regressions in mice never completed a human efficacy evaluation [[SEC-RAS-09]]. Zoldonrasib's phase 1/1b trial includes pancreatic cancer and an arm combining it with daraxonrasib; it is recruiting toward an estimated 604 participants, with primary completion expected at the end of 2026 and no posted results [[SEC-RAS-10]]. Two phase 3 trials opened before any peer-reviewed efficacy publication appeared. The RASolute 305 trial randomizes an estimated 670 people with documented KRAS G12D tumors to zoldonrasib or placebo on top of first-line chemotherapy, double-blind, and RASolute 309 compares zoldonrasib plus daraxonrasib against gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel first line in an estimated 400 [[SEC-RAS-11]]. No publication yet states how many patients responded to zoldonrasib or for how long; the record consists of registry entries and a chemistry paper [[RAS-034]]. A trial is therefore the only route to a G12D-selective drug as of 8 Oct 2026.

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The mouse work established two things: blocking G12D directly can shrink pancreatic tumors that ignored every pathway drug tried before, and T cells are needed to keep them from regrowing [[RAS-004]][[RAS-035]]. It also showed the immune response does not last. The T-cell influx was gone by day 7, and in a separate mouse study long-term dosing actively reversed the early immune activation through the signaling enzyme CDK8 [[RAS-004]][[RAS-024]]. Human data cannot yet confirm or refute any of this, because the one G12D-selective drug with a completed trial stopped for formulation reasons and zoldonrasib's results are unpublished [[SEC-RAS-09]][[SEC-RAS-10]].
research_notes.how_studied: The key experiment used mice with working immune systems and a spontaneous-tumor model, which matters because most earlier xenograft work was done in immunodeficient animals and could not reveal an immune contribution [[RAS-004]]. Tumor size was followed by ultrasound, which has limited resolution, and T-cell dependence was tested by depletion with anti-CD4 and anti-CD8 antibodies, a loss-of-function design that shows T cells are necessary to sustain the response but not what draws them in [[RAS-004]]. Drug selectivity came from binding measurements and growth assays comparing G12D-mutant with normal (wild-type) cell lines [[RAS-035]].

mechanism_notes.text: KRAS inhibition may open a short immune window in which freshly released tumor antigen and relief from KRAS-driven suppression draw T cells in, and the window may close within days as CDK8-driven secretion of the signaling protein CXCL2 and a cell-state shift in the tumor switch immunity back off [[INF-RAS-02]][[RAS-004]][[RAS-024]]. If so, checkpoint immunotherapy would have a target only in the first weeks of G12D inhibition, which is when it has never been tried in people. The competing account is that the immune activation is a by-product of rapid cell death and durability depends only on how completely the pathway is shut down [[INF-RAS-02]].

topics.clinical_status: No KRAS G12D-selective inhibitor is approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026. The MRTX1133 phase 1 (NCT05737706) is terminated for formulation challenges after 63 enrolled. Zoldonrasib (RMC-9805) is investigational: phase 1/1b NCT06040541 is recruiting, and the phase 3 trials RASolute 305 (NCT07621718, with first-line chemotherapy, KRAS G12D required) and RASolute 309 (NCT07805954, with daraxonrasib, first line) are recruiting in metastatic pancreatic cancer with no results posted. Access is through clinical trials only.

glossary.definition: A version of the KRAS protein in which the amino acid at position 12 has changed from glycine to aspartic acid, the commonest KRAS mutation in pancreatic cancer.
A drug that forms a permanent chemical bond with its target protein rather than attaching and detaching.
An abundant protein inside cells that some RAS drugs bind first, so that the drug-protein pair can grip RAS together.
An animal model with a working immune system, in which the immune contribution to a drug's effect can be seen.
An experimental step that removes T cells with antibodies to test whether they are needed for an effect.

related.statement: KRAS G12D inhibitors act on the most common mutant form of the KRAS protein in pancreatic cancer.
KRAS G12D accounts for roughly four in ten pancreatic cancers, so a G12D-selective drug would reach far more patients than a G12C drug.
In mice, blocking KRAS G12D draws T cells into the tumor, and those T cells are needed to keep the tumor from regrowing.
Zoldonrasib is being tested together with daraxonrasib, which covers KRAS G12D along with the other RAS mutations.
Zoldonrasib belongs to the RAS(ON) tri-complex family that also produced daraxonrasib.
The short immune window after KRAS G12D inhibition in mice is the rationale for testing immunotherapy early in RAS-directed treatment.
RASolute 305 and RASolute 309 are the phase 3 trials of zoldonrasib in metastatic pancreatic cancer, both recruiting.

faq.q: My tumor has KRAS G12D. Is there a drug for it?
faq.a: Not an approved one in the US as of 8 Oct 2026. Zoldonrasib is in a recruiting phase 1 trial and two phase 3 trials; the RASolute 305 trial requires documented G12D status and adds the drug or placebo to first-line chemotherapy [[SEC-RAS-10]][[SEC-RAS-11]]. Daraxonrasib, which is approved, acts on G12D as one of the RAS mutations it covers.

faq.q: Why was the MRTX1133 trial stopped?
faq.a: The registry gives 'formulation challenges' as the reason, after 63 patients enrolled; the drug requires injection rather than a tablet [[SEC-RAS-09]]. The stated reason is pharmaceutical, not a finding that the drug did not work, and its mouse results remain the strongest preclinical G12D data [[RAS-004]].

topics.title: Multi-selective RAS(ON) inhibitors and the RASolute trials
topics.orientation: RAS(ON) inhibitors bind the active, signaling form of RAS by first attaching to a cellular protein, and the multi-selective versions act on mutant and normal KRAS, NRAS and HRAS together. This class produced daraxonrasib, the first RAS-targeted drug approved for pancreatic cancer, and the RASolute trials are testing where else it helps.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: Earlier KRAS drugs grabbed the protein in its OFF state and worked for one mutant only. RAS(ON) inhibitors instead bind cyclophilin A, an abundant protein inside every cell, and the drug-cyclophilin pair then wraps around RAS in its ON, GTP-loaded state, physically blocking its contact with the proteins it signals to. Because the pair does not depend on one specific mutant amino acid, a single molecule can cover G12D, G12V, G12R, G12C and normal RAS.
section1.full: The tool compound RMC-7977 set the pattern. Across 15 mouse models of pancreatic, colorectal and lung cancers carrying KRAS mutations at position 12 (codon 12), 9 regressed within 4 to 6 weeks, and over 90 days of dosing control tumors doubled in a median of 7 days while treated tumors never reached their doubling time [[RAS-003]]. Head to head, drugs blocking the pathway just above RAS (SHP2) or just below it (MEK), alone or together, gave only modest slowing where RMC-7977 gave deep regressions [[RAS-003]]. Daraxonrasib, the clinical analog, was dosed by modeling: mouse exposure-response curves predicted that 300 mg daily would produce measurable tumor shrinkage (objective responses), and the first two patients treated at that dose, one with pancreatic cancer, responded [[RAS-011]]. Hitting normal RAS is deliberate, because normal RAS carries bypass signaling once the mutant is blocked [[RAS-027]]. A G12C-selective relative, elironrasib, is in phase 1 trials; its discovery paper reports preliminary activity after first-generation G12C drugs fail, but only as an abstract without numbers [[RAS-042]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: Daraxonrasib is the first RAS-directed drug to lengthen survival in a randomized pancreatic cancer trial and the first approved in the US for this disease. RASolute 302 showed roughly a doubling of median survival over chemotherapy in previously treated metastatic disease. Two further phase 3 trials, RASolute 303 first-line and RASolute 304 after surgery, are recruiting with no results; the approved drug has its own entry.
section2.full: In the phase 1/2 program, 168 previously treated patients received up to 300 mg; treatment-related side effects occurred in 96 percent, severe (grade 3 or worse) in 30 percent, most often rash, diarrhea, nausea, mouth sores, vomiting and fatigue, and among 26 second-line patients with RAS G12 tumors 35 percent responded for a median of 8.2 months, per the abstract [[RAS-032]]. The RASolute 302 trial then randomized 500 such patients to daraxonrasib or chemotherapy: median overall survival 13.2 against 6.7 months, hazard ratio 0.40, and median progression-free survival 7.2 against 3.6 months, taken from the abstract and the FDA approval summary [[RAS-033]][[SEC-RAS-01]]. The US approval of 26 August 2026 covers metastatic disease after at least one prior therapy, or where multi-drug chemotherapy is not an option, with no RAS test required [[SEC-RAS-02]]. The RASolute 303 trial is enrolling an estimated 900 untreated patients across three arms, and RASolute 304 an estimated 500 after surgery against observation, with primary completion expected in 2028 and 2029 [[SEC-RAS-06]][[SEC-RAS-07]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: Three tiers of evidence should be kept apart. The preclinical comparison is the strongest mechanistic result in this field, because it isolated active-state RAS inhibition as the reason the approach worked where pathway drugs above and below RAS had failed [[RAS-003]]. The randomized trial establishes a drug-attributable survival benefit after prior treatment [[RAS-033]]. Everything else, including first-line use, use after surgery, elironrasib and combinations, rests on registry entries or abstracts without denominators [[SEC-RAS-06]][[SEC-RAS-07]][[RAS-042]]. Even responders eventually progress, and among 44 patients a genetic cause was found in only 25 percent [[RAS-012]].
research_notes.how_studied: The mouse 'clinical trial' format treats each of 15 tumor models as a patient, sampling genetic diversity better than one cell line, but its immunodeficient hosts hide the immune contribution seen with G12D inhibitors [[RAS-003]]. The human dose came from modeling mouse exposure against response and scaling to people, a prediction the phase 1 trial then tested [[RAS-011]]. RASolute 302 was open-label, so patients and doctors knew the assignment, which cannot bias survival but can bias progression and quality-of-life readings [[RAS-033]][[SEC-RAS-05]]. Its full text and registry results are not public, so numbers come from the abstract and the FDA page [[SEC-RAS-01]].

mechanism_notes.text: A drug-tolerant residual population may form within days of starting a RAS(ON) inhibitor, kept alive by growth-factor-receptor signaling that assembles normal RAS complexes through the lipid enzyme PI3K and the scaffold protein GAB1; progression would then be the outgrowth of that pool, with amplified KRAS or new RAF and receptor changes arriving late as consolidating steps [[INF-RAS-01]][[RAS-027]][[RAS-012]]. This would explain why no genetic cause is found in most progressions and why no drug-binding-site mutations appear. The competing account is a host-side reversal of the early immune response, which would call for timed immunotherapy rather than a receptor blocker [[INF-RAS-01]].

topics.clinical_status: Daraxonrasib (RASONQUE) is approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 (since 26 August 2026) for adults with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma after at least one prior systemic therapy or who are not candidates for multi-agent systemic therapy, with no RAS mutation requirement; no other RAS(ON) inhibitor is approved. RASolute 303 (first-line, NCT07491445) and RASolute 304 (after surgery, NCT07252232) are phase 3 trials recruiting with no results; elironrasib (NCT06128551) and zoldonrasib are investigational.

glossary.definition: A drug that binds RAS in its active, GTP-loaded state rather than its switched-off state.
The three-part assembly of drug, cyclophilin A and RAS that these inhibitors form to block signaling.
Acting on several forms of RAS at once, including mutant and normal KRAS, NRAS and HRAS, rather than one mutant.
A ratio of event rates between two groups over time, so that 0.40 means the event occurred at 40 percent of the comparison group's rate.
A trial design in which patients and doctors know which treatment was assigned.

related.statement: Daraxonrasib is the approved member of the multi-selective RAS(ON) inhibitor class, and its own entry carries the trial detail.
Multi-selective RAS(ON) inhibitors block the ON state of mutant and normal KRAS, NRAS and HRAS.
Elironrasib applies the RAS(ON) design to KRAS G12C alone and is being tested after first-generation G12C inhibitors fail.
Zoldonrasib applies the RAS(ON) tri-complex design to KRAS G12D and is being tested alone and with daraxonrasib.
RAS(ON) inhibition regressed mouse tumors where SHP2 and MEK inhibitors, the pathway drugs that failed in earlier trials, did not.
Tumors escape RAS(ON) inhibitors mostly without a detectable genetic cause, and never through drug-binding-site mutations in pancreatic cohorts.
RASolute 304 tests whether daraxonrasib after surgery and chemotherapy delays recurrence from microscopic disease that scans cannot see.
The RASolute 302 trial was open-label and its full publication is available only as an abstract, so its numbers come from the abstract and the FDA approval page.

faq.q: Is daraxonrasib the same thing as a RAS(ON) inhibitor?
faq.a: Daraxonrasib is the first multi-selective RAS(ON) inhibitor to reach approval; elironrasib and zoldonrasib are RAS(ON) inhibitors aimed at single mutants and remain investigational [[SEC-RAS-01]][[RAS-042]].

faq.q: Can I get daraxonrasib before chemotherapy, or after surgery?
faq.a: Not on label in the US as of 8 Oct 2026: the approval covers metastatic disease after at least one prior therapy or for people who cannot take multi-drug chemotherapy [[SEC-RAS-02]]. The RASolute 303 trial is testing first-line use and RASolute 304 use after surgery, with primary completion expected in 2028 and 2029 and no results yet [[SEC-RAS-06]][[SEC-RAS-07]].

topics.title: Resistance to RAS inhibitors
topics.orientation: Drugs that block mutated RAS shrink pancreatic tumors, and in most people the tumor eventually starts growing again. Resistance research asks what the cancer does to survive a drug that is, in most cases, still holding on to its target.

section1.label: What it does
section1.preview: Resistance comes in two broad shapes. On-target resistance alters the drug's landing site on the RAS protein so the drug no longer binds. Bypass resistance leaves the drug's grip intact and restores the same growth signal by another route: a second mutation in a related gene, extra copies of the mutant gene, or a growth-factor receptor turned up. The two shapes call for different answers.
section1.full: On-target escape is documented in lung and colorectal cancer: four of 38 patients progressing on an inactive-state KRAS G12C drug carried a secondary mutation in the drug's landing site, the switch-II pocket, which blocks binding while leaving the pathway otherwise normal [[RAS-006]][[RAS-015]]. Pancreatic cohorts look different. In 22 patients with KRAS G12C pancreatic cancer no switch-II mutation appeared at all, and a genetic cause of any kind was found in 9 of 22 (41%) [[RAS-010]]. Under daraxonrasib, 11 of 44 patients had an acquired change in blood DNA: RAF-gene variants in 11%, and receptor events such as HER2 amplification or a MET fusion in 9%, usually alongside extra copies of mutant KRAS [[RAS-012]]. Single-cell sequencing shows why these count as bypass: the new mutation sits inside the same cell as the original and restores signaling without displacing the drug [[RAS-014]].

section2.label: Why it matters here
section2.preview: In pancreatic cancer most progressions have no genetic explanation at all, which points to resistance that is a change in how cells behave rather than a change in their sequence. Laboratory work has found several such changes: a shift into a mesenchymal, basal-like cell state (a looser, more mobile and more aggressive cell type), rewired mitochondria (the cell's energy producers), and an immune response that the drug first switches on and then switches off. Each one suggests a partner drug.
section2.full: Sustained blockade drives pancreatic cells into an interferon-driven program ending in an epithelial-to-mesenchymal shift, and that state puts TROP2 on the cell surface, a protein an existing antibody-drug conjugate already attacks; the pairing suppressed tumor growth in mouse xenografts [[RAS-025]]. Blocking the pathway above and below RAS leaves mitochondria dependent on lipid-peroxide defense, exposing the cells to ferroptotic death (death by uncontrolled oxidation of membrane fats) [[RAS-029]]. On the host side, blocking mutant KRAS first draws T cells into mouse tumors within days, then with continued dosing shuts that response down through the kinase CDK8, which raises the signaling protein CXCL2 and suppresses the death receptor FAS; blocking CDK8, with or without the checkpoint antibody anti-CTLA-4, restored control [[RAS-024]][[RAS-004]]. Human results lag far behind. A SOS1 inhibitor (blocking the protein that loads RAS) with the MEK inhibitor trametinib produced no responses in 19 patients and three fatal first-cycle lung injuries [[RAS-018]], and a SHP2-plus-ERK combination, available only as an abstract, none in 24 [[RAS-039]].

research_notes.what_findings_mean: The large fraction with no genetic cause has a dull alternative explanation: pancreatic tumors shed little DNA into the blood, so a negative blood panel may mean undetected rather than absent, and the original authors state both possibilities [[RAS-010]][[RAS-012]][[RAS-022]]. The cell-state account also runs in both directions. In mouse and patient-derived tumors the mesenchymal and basal-like states were more sensitive to KRAS blockade than the classical state, the opposite of what cell cultures suggest, and flat culture is itself biased toward a basal-like state [[RAS-010]][[RAS-025]][[RAS-029]].
research_notes.how_studied: Resistance is mapped by sequencing the same patient twice, before treatment and at progression, usually from circulating tumor DNA rather than tissue; that shows what emerged but not whether it was sufficient to cause the escape [[RAS-012]][[RAS-010]]. Sufficiency is tested by engineering the candidate change into a drug-sensitive model and asking whether the drug stops working, and single-cell sequencing establishes whether the new mutation occupies the same cell as the old one [[RAS-014]]. Mouse tumors dosed until relapse supply the time course that patient samples cannot [[RAS-024]].

mechanism_notes.text: Genetic escape lesions may be late markers of an escape that was already functionally complete. Within hours of pathway blockade a minority of cells enter a drug-tolerant state kept alive by growth-factor-receptor signaling that recruits normal, non-mutant RAS into service, which would set the floor of residual tumor that imaging reports as a partial rather than a complete response [[INF-RAS-01]][[RAS-008]][[RAS-027]]. On this account amplification of mutant KRAS or of receptor genes is a consolidating step, which is why no such lesion is found in most patients at the moment scans first show growth [[RAS-012]][[RAS-010]]. The competing view is that the undetected lesions are simply below the sensitivity of a blood test.

Pathway blockade may open a short immunological window that then closes by its own action. In mice, T cells flood the tumor about 60 hours after KRAS G12D blockade and the increase is gone by day seven, and T cells are required to keep the tumor from regrowing [[INF-RAS-02]][[RAS-004]]. Prolonged dosing then installs counter-programs, CDK8-driven in the microenvironment and interferon-driven in the tumor cells, which would mean checkpoint drugs have a target only in the first weeks of RAS-directed therapy, the period in which they have not been tested [[RAS-024]][[RAS-025]]. The competing view is that the immune influx is a by-product of rapid cell death rather than a contributor.

topics.clinical_status: Daraxonrasib is approved in the US as of 8 Oct 2026 as a single drug for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma after at least one prior systemic therapy, or for people who cannot take multi-drug therapy. None of the combinations discussed here is approved anywhere for pancreatic cancer, and the TROP2, CDK8, ferroptosis and checkpoint-timing strategies exist only in laboratory models. The combination trials that follow from this work are listed as recruiting with no posted results.

glossary.definition: Resistance caused by a change in the drug's own binding site, so the drug can no longer attach to its target.
Resistance in which the drug still binds its target but the cell restores the same growth signal through a different route.
The groove on the RAS protein where several KRAS drugs attach; mutations there can block the drug from binding.
Fragments of DNA shed by cancer cells into the bloodstream, which can be sequenced from a blood sample.
An antibody that recognizes a protein on the cancer cell surface and carries a chemotherapy drug directly to it.
A shift in which an organized, sheet-forming cell takes on the looser, more mobile character of a connective-tissue cell.
A form of cell death caused by uncontrolled oxidation of the fats in a cell's membranes.

related.statement: Resistance to RAS inhibitors is what eventually ends the benefit most people get from daraxonrasib.
Multi-selective RAS(ON) inhibitors are the class in which the daraxonrasib resistance patterns described here were measured.
KRAS G12C inhibitors supplied the first human resistance data, including the drug-binding-site mutations that pancreatic cohorts do not show.
A shift between classical and basal-like cell states is one of the non-genetic routes by which pancreatic cancer survives RAS blockade.
Resistance to RAS inhibitors is mostly measured by sequencing circulating tumor DNA before treatment and again at progression.
The combination strategies aimed at resistance are tested against the record of earlier attempts on the KRAS pathway, which failed in people.

faq.q: If the drug stops working, does that mean the cancer mutated again?
faq.a: Often not. In pancreatic cancer, a genetic cause of progression is found in a minority of patients: 41% on KRAS G12C drugs and about a quarter on daraxonrasib [[RAS-010]][[RAS-012]]. The rest may reflect cells changing their behavior rather than their sequence, or a blood test that cannot see the change in a tumor that sheds little DNA [[RAS-022]].

faq.q: Could a second drug be added to stop resistance?
faq.a: That is the aim of the current combination trials, and several partner drugs prevent resistance in mice, including TROP2-directed and CDK8-directed approaches [[RAS-025]][[RAS-024]]. In people the record is still negative: pairing a RAS-pathway drug with a partner above or below it has so far hit its targets without producing tumor shrinkage, and in one case fatal lung injury [[RAS-018]][[RAS-039]].

topics.title: Earlier attempts on the KRAS pathway and why they failed
